items.text: Apple Foundation Models framework Backend abstraction: `LanguageModel` (declares `capabilities` and an `executorConfiguration`) plus `LanguageModelExecutor` (init from Configuration, `prewarm`, streaming `respond`). The session keeps an executor store keyed by the Hashable Configuration, not by model instance, so two model values... Backend abstraction: `LanguageModel` (declares `capabilities` and an `executorConfiguration`) plus `LanguageModelExecutor` (init from Configuration, `prewarm`, streaming `respond`). The session keeps an executor store keyed by the Hashable Configuration, not by model instance, so two model values with equal configuration share one executor and its KV cache. Releasing the session releases every executor. The executor receives the full transcript on every `respond` call. It diffs against the transcript it saw last time, keeps state when entries were only appended, and invalidates back to the divergence point when entries were removed or edited. This is prefix caching expressed as a protocol contract. One-shot `respond` is implemented as a collected stream. Streaming order contract: metadata update, then usage update (prompt tokens), then text deltas. Request carries `ContextOptions` (reasoning level, response schema) and `GenerationOptions` (sampling, temperature, maximumResponseTokens). If an executor cannot honor an option it should approximate or throw a built-in `LanguageModelError` (context overflow, rate limit, refusal, guardrail, unsupported capability, timeout). MLX bridge: `MLXLanguageModel` lives in the `MLXFoundationModels` library of `ml-explore/mlx-swift-lm`. It is built with the `#huggingFaceLanguageModel(configuration:capabilities:)` macro or the full initializer (`configuration`, `capabilities`, `weightsLocation:`, `load:`). Capabilities are declared, never inferred (default `[.guidedGeneration]`; others `.toolCalling`, `.reasoning`, `.vision`); a request beyond the declared set fails with a typed error. `availability` reports `.available`, `.downloading`, `.unavailable(...)`. The adapter compiles to an empty module unless the SwiftPM trait `FoundationModelsIntegration` (default on) and the 27.0 SDK are both present. fm CLI subcommands seen on the shipping build: `respond`, `chat`, `schema object`, `count-tokens`, `available`, `license`, `serve`. `respond` flags: `-i` instructions, `--text`, `--schema file`, `-g` greedy sampling, `--no-stream`, `--save-transcript`, `--resume`, `--image`, `--tool` (barcode, ocr), u

Availability is not guaranteed: SystemLanguageModel.default.availability returns .available or .unavailable with reasons deviceNotEligible, appleIntelligenceNotEnabled or modelNotReady, and Apple tells developers to check it before creating a LanguageModelSession and show a fallback. A Mac App Store diagnosis feature must therefore degrade to non-AI output on ineligible Macs or when the user has Apple Intelligence off. Platform floor in Package.swift: macOS, iOS, visionOS, watchOS 27.0; swift-tools-version 6.2; Swift 6 language mode. The README says "select Linux distributions like Ubuntu"; the source guards CoreImage and FoundationNetworking with `canImport`. Use needs the Xcode 27 SDK. Initializer: `ChatCompletionsLanguageModel(name:url:additionalHeaders:supportsGuidedGeneration:urlSessionConfiguration:)`. `additionalHeaders` (for `Authorization`) and `urlSessionConfiguration` (timeouts, proxy) are absent from the README examples. When `urlSessionConfiguration` is nil the executor makes a fresh ephemeral URLSession per request. Endpoint rule: if any URL path component matches `v<digits>`, it appends `/chat/completions`; else `/v1/chat/completions`. So `http://localhost:8000` and `http://localhost:8000/v1` both work; the README's `http://localhost/v1:8000` does not. Capabilities declared: `.vision`, `.toolCalling`, `.reasoning` always; `.guidedGeneration` only if `supportsGuidedGeneration` (default true). A server with no `response_format` support must set it false. Request body: always `stream: true` and `stream_options.include_usage: true`; `messages` from the transcript (instructions to system, prompt to user, response to assistant, tool calls to assistant `tool_calls`, tool output to `tool` with `tool_call_id`); `tools` as function definitions; `tool_choice` auto/required/none from `toolCallingMode`; `response_format` json_schema when a schema is set; `temperature`; `max_completion_tokens`; `top_p`. Sampling mapping: greedy sends `top_p` 0; `.randomProbabilityThreshold` sends its value as `top_p`; top-K sampling and any seed throw `RequestError.invalidRequest`. There is no top_k, min_p, repetition penalty or seed path, so local-model sampler tuning is not reachable. Response parsing: `delta.content` to response, `delta.reasoning_content` to reasoning, `delta.tool_calls[i]` to tool calls (id/name latched per index), `usage` to cumulative `updateUsage` including `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` and `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. items.text: Apple libthunderboltrdma tbt_post_recv SIGSEGV #4192 reproduces the SIGSEGV by unplugging a Thunderbolt cable mid-collective: both ranks die, 4/4 pulls, on 2x Mac mini M4 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, mlx at 596dc79f4 #4192 reproduces the SIGSEGV by unplugging a Thunderbolt cable mid-collective: both ranks die, 4/4 pulls, on 2x Mac mini M4 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, mlx at 596dc79f4 The #4192 repro is a bare C++ loop of jaccl all_sum over 256 floats, with no model and no Python #4192 trace goes through `jaccl::MeshImpl::all_reduce<float>` while #4319 goes through `RingImpl::all_reduce<2,unsigned char>` The last iteration before the #4192 crash takes about 200 ms versus about 3 us steady state Affected builds reported: macOS 26.5.1 (#4192), macOS 26.6.1 25G76 with mlx 0.32.0 and 0.32.2 (#4319 and production) On a 5x M3 Ultra TB5 mesh, links dropped on their own on 2026-09-18 and 09-20 and each time the rank at one end died with the tbt_post_recv trace via MeshImpl::all_gather That 5-node group had run 39 h with 1.25 M tokens and zero JACCL events before the first drop, so it is a link-loss path, not steady-state instability After the crash the node keeps about 140 GB wired and the port stays PORT_DOWN until reboot Status: #4192 and #4319 are open with labels bug and distributed, no assignee, no linked PR; #4319 has no linked fix Apple FB24371487 was filed for the no-unplug #4319 incident A 1 MiB unique all_gather keepalive does not certify the 256 MiB all_reduce path PR #4530 (open, from Sofille65) does not fix the crash; it adds side-channel peer-liveness so survivors raise `[jaccl] peer is gone` within about 0.25 s instead of spinning, plus JACCL_PROGRESS_TIMEOUT_S (default 600 s) Apple's TB RDMA UC queue pairs give no error completion for a dead peer and RC queue pairs fail with errno 102 Per-device limits measured: 10 queue pairs (errno 16 on the 11th), at least 512 MRs, no QP or MR leak across clean exit, _exit or SIGKILL Workaround: no known prevention; mitigate with the #4530 liveness patch on survivors, an orchestrator that purges and re-forms the group, checking the exit code of each rank (mlx.launch prints 0), and rebooting the crashed node The macOS 27 dylib rework claim is second-hand from dyld-cache diffs and unverified on hardware

Existing benchmarks that skip F_NOCACHE can serve reads from the unified buffer cache, so results vary with installed RAM (author's claim; a forum reply disputes it on the basis that SATA and HDD speeds looked like device speeds). DiskTruth author: BlackMagic and AmorphousDiskMark do not use F_NOCACHE and are inflated by RAM caching on large-memory Macs. A MacRumors reply (bzgnyc2/!!!) says those tools gave device-consistent speeds on SATA SSD (<500 MB/s) and HDD (~200 MB/s), so caching is not evident. Shown side by side, not resolved. DiskTruth (beta announced 2026-04-16) sets fcntl(fd, F_NOCACHE, 1) on every file descriptor before any I/O. DiskTruth measures random 4K IOPS and latency at QD1 with 10,000 operations per pass and reports average and p99. DiskTruth measures queue-depth scaling at QD1, QD4, QD16 and QD32 with 3,000 ops per level. Its author states Apple Silicon internal NVMe has "extraordinary QD1 latency" and less dramatic scaling at higher depths than desktop NVMe, with no numbers given in the post. DiskTruth uses a 16 GB test file, 3 iterations and the median for sequential tests. The ds4 QD16 stall estimate remains incomplete: no measured latency number exists in the sources read.

items.text: apple-silicon-llm-bench fairness rules and interleaved-arm protocol Run order is a hardware-state variable. A large model heats the GPU within seconds and decode tok/s on a Mac swings about 30% with thermal state, so block ordering measures the order. Disclosing thermal state (rule 9) does not neutralise it. Run order is a hardware-state variable. A large model heats the GPU within seconds and decode tok/s on a Mac swings about 30% with thermal state, so block ordering measures the order. Disclosing thermal state (rule 9) does not neutralise it. The per-trial spread check catches only an arm whose own trials drift. An arm that is uniformly depressed by the previous arm's heat passes the spread check, so spread cannot replace interleaving. Comparisons are made only inside one session window, and the session is part of every table cell. Across-session numbers are compared through an anchor cell re-measured in each sitting. Rule citations in code moved from numbers to slugs after the two numbering schemes collided and scripts cited "rule 3" ambiguously (the file's section 3 is quantization, CLAUDE.md's rule 3 is budget and mode mixing). 2026-07-13: the first-ever, cold and warm regimes were split after conflating them produced a 2.6x prefill "discrepancy" on the E2B card reconciliation. 2026-07-17: audit of the Gemma-4-E2B table found the "winner" trophy measured checkpoint quality (PTQ vs QAT) rather than runtime speed; rule 1 and rule 2 were added. 2026-07-28: audit addendum re-labelled the n>=7 floor as the bench's own convention and superseded an agreed-protocol section claiming LiteRT cannot report prompt tokens. 2026-08-15: rule 11 (interleave) added from a failed block-ordered capture of Muse-Glimmer-30B on M4 Max. items.summary: Percentage Used is a vendor-specific estimate of NVM life used, from actual usage and the manufacturer's life prediction. Apple publishes no prediction, so the percentage cannot be converted to terabytes written except by fitting observed pairs.
items.text: Apple Silicon SSD SMART telemetry and Percentage Used interpretation Percentage Used is a vendor-specific estimate of NVM life used, from actual usage and the manufacturer's life prediction. Apple publishes no prediction, so the percentage cannot be converted to terabytes written except by fitting observed pairs. Percentage Used is a vendor-specific estimate of NVM life used, from actual usage and the manufacturer's life prediction. Apple publishes no prediction, so the percentage cannot be converted to terabytes written except by fitting observed pairs. The controller updates Percentage Used once per power-on hour, so it lags writes by up to an hour of powered time. Data Units Written moves with every write. Data Units counters are in thousands of 512-byte units, rounded up. One count is 512,000 bytes, so a before/after delta of Data Units Written resolves a session to about half a megabyte. smartctl reads the Apple drive through the IOKit class IONVMeSMARTInterface (kIONVMeSMARTUserClientTypeID), which smartmontools added for Darwin in release 6.6 (2017) as "initial NVMe support based on undocumented API". On Apple silicon the SSD controller function is split between the NAND modules and cores inside the SoC, so wear leveling and the wear estimate come from SoC firmware, not from a standalone drive controller. macOS swap files live on a hidden VM volume in the boot volume group and cannot be moved to another disk on a current APFS boot volume group. smartmontools 6.6 (2017-11-05): Darwin initial NVMe support. 7.2 (2020-12-30): Darwin NVMe log support. 7.4 (2023-08-01): CI and release builds for x86_64 and arm64 macOS. 7.5 (2025-04-30): JSON value endurance_used and smartd checks of Percentage Used. Percentage Used may exceed 100 and a value of 100 does not mean the drive has failed. Values above 254 are reported as 255. A Data Units value of 0 means the drive does not report that counter, not that zero data moved. Critical Warning is a bit field: spare below threshold, temperature out of range, reliability degraded, media read-only. The smartctl overall-health PASSED result reflects only that field. Counters survive across sessions but include factory and setup writes (see existing dossier). The existing dossier cites HN and MacRumors posters who doubt Apple-silicon smartctl totals (DriveDX 6.1 TB versus smartmontools 6.7 TB for one block count). items.text: Apple silicon unified memory and LLM sizing Apple's own figures (Metal Compute on MacBook Pro tech talk): M1 Pro/Max 32 GB -> GPU can access 21 GB; M1 Max 64 GB -> 48 GB. Apple publishes no per-size rule beyond that. Apple's own figures (Metal Compute on MacBook Pro tech talk): M1 Pro/Max 32 GB -> GPU can access 21 GB; M1 Max 64 GB -> 48 GB. Apple publishes no per-size rule beyond that. The rule is not universal: an M4 Max 128 GB log shows 115,448.73 MB (107.5 GiB, 84%), so "3/4" is a floor on some newer parts. llama.cpp prints the value at init as `ggml_metal_init: recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize = <n> MB`. Builds before b2000 divided bytes by 1024^2 (b1400 labelled it "MB", b1600 "MiB"); from b2000 it divides by 10^6. Compare logs only within the same build era. llama.cpp's `ggml_metal_device_get_memory` reports total = recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize and free = total - currentAllocatedSize. Its source comment says it is possible to allocate more than the limit; going over only logs `warning: current allocated size is greater than the recommended max working set size`. The limit is a recommendation apps follow, not a wall (modelvram.com summary of ggml-metal-device.m). MLX uses the same number as the "system wired limit": `mx.device_info()["max_recommended_working_set_size"]` is the system wired limit and `["memory_size"]` is total RAM. `mx.set_wired_limit(bytes)` (MLX 0.32.3 docs): only useful on macOS 15.0+; the value must stay strictly below total memory; default 0; it is the total size of memory kept resident; a value above the system wired limit is an error; the doc names `sudo sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb=<MB>` as the way to raise the system limit; returns the previous limit. mlx-lm: for a model large relative to RAM it wires model+cache memory (macOS 15+ only) and prints `[WARNING] Generating with a model that requires ...` when slow; fix is `iogpu.wired_limit_mb=N` with N above the model size in MB and below machine memory. llama.cpp uses Metal residency sets only on macOS >= 15.0 (`GGML_METAL_HAS_RESIDENCY_SETS`; disable with env `GGML_METAL_NO_RESIDENCY`). A background thread re-requests residency; default keep-alive 3 minutes (`GGML_METAL_RESIDENCY_KEEP_ALIVE_S`). A dummy GPU op is issued to work around residency memory not being released when no GPU work occurs (Apple forum thread 839089, llama.cpp issue 25937). Ars Technica (June 2022) reports that the M2 13-inch MacBook Pro 256 GB uses one 256 GB NAND chip where the M1 model uses a pair of 128 GB chips. Its stated mechanism is interleaving: with more physical chips the controller reads and writes several at once, so fewer chips limit peak performance. Max Tech's Blackmagic sustained read fell from about 2,900 MB/s (M1) to 1,446 MB/s (M2); write fell from 2,215 to 1,463 MB/s. The same article says the 512 GB and 1 TB M2 versions looked similar to M1 speed. Ars (Jan 2023): the M1 Pro 512 GB used four 128 GB NAND chips (per iFixit), while the 9to5Mac M2 Pro 512 GB appeared to use two 256 GB chips. Measured on those two 512 GB machines: read 4,900 MB/s (M1 Pro) versus 2,973 MB/s (M2 Pro), a 40 percent drop; write 3,951 versus 3,154.5 MB/s, a 20 percent drop. The 2023 article says the 512 GB M2 Pro still has two chips, so it is much faster than the one-chip 256 GB M2 MacBook Pro and Air. items.text: Application-level no-progress watchdog and group re-formation for JACCL clusters An application-level watchdog is code outside the MLX/JACCL library that decides a collective is stuck (no completion within a deadline, or a dead process) and tears the group down. Group re-formation is the later step that builds a new group (new processes, new queue pairs, new ConnectToGroup) f... An application-level watchdog is code outside the MLX/JACCL library that decides a collective is stuck (no completion within a deadline, or a dead process) and tears the group down. Group re-formation is the later step that builds a new group (new processes, new queue pairs, new ConnectToGroup) from the survivors or from restarted ranks. exo's worker plan is an ordered chain: cancel tasks, kill runner, create runner, download model, init distributed backend (ConnectToGroup), load model, warm up, pending tasks. The first step that returns a task wins each tick. exo's `_kill_runner` returns a Shutdown for a runner when its instance is gone, when its own status is RunnerFailed, or when any peer runner of the same instance is RunnerFailed, so one failure tears down every rank of the instance. exo's `_create_runner` waits while any remote runner of the instance is failed, unless this node failed before, and also waits for the per-instance backoff. exo's worker logs "exceeded {EXO_MAX_INSTANCE_RETRIES} retries, requesting deletion" and sends DeleteInstance for an instance that passes `EXO_MAX_INSTANCE_RETRIES = 5`. exo processes a Shutdown task with `fail_after(3)` on the runner's start_task and then always calls `runner.shutdown()`; a timeout marks the task TimedOut. exo's RunnerSupervisor detects a dead runner by polling `runner_process.is_alive()` every 5 s. A runner that is alive but wedged in a collective passes this check. On a dead runner exo sets RunnerFailed with parsed stderr diagnostics (Metal GPU timeout, ring socket errno, ring transport abort) and sends an error chunk to every in-progress generation request. exo's supervisor file defines `PREFILL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60` and `DECODE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5` and a default `initialize_timeout` of 400 s. No code in the supervisor, generator or batch_generate files fetched here references the first two. exo had an in-process evaluation watchdog in April 2026. Key vectors in transformer self-attention contain sensitive channel-specific magnitude spikes that cause severe perplexity degradation if quantized uniformly with standard symmetric rounding. (high confidence) Asymmetric KV cache quantization preserves key vector outlier dimensions in FP8 or FP16 while quantizing value vectors to 4-bit affine blocks, reducing KV memory by up to 70% with less than 0.1 perplexity delta. (high confidence)

items.concept: Atlas Admin API GCP Auth
items.summary: MongoDB Atlas Admin API authentication on GCP uses OAuth 2.0 Service Accounts for API/administrative access, while cluster data access instead uses Workload Identity Federation (OIDC) for passwordless auth from GCP workloads.
items.text: Atlas Admin API GCP Auth MongoDB Atlas Admin API authentication on GCP uses OAuth 2.0 Service Accounts for API/administrative access, while cluster data access instead uses Workload Identity Federation (OIDC) for passwordless auth from GCP workloads. Atlas Admin API uses OAuth 2.0 Service Accounts with the Client Credentials flow; tokens are obtained from POST https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/oauth/token and are valid for 1 hour (3600 seconds), reusable within that window. Admin API authentication (managing projects, users, and networks) is a distinct concern from cluster data access (reading and writing documents) — the two use different auth mechanisms. GCP does not provide a native Admin API integration; the recommended pattern is to store Atlas API credentials in GCP Secret Manager and retrieve them from the workload (Compute Engine, Cloud Run, GKE). For cluster data access (not Admin API), Workload Identity Federation gives OIDC-based passwordless auth from a GCP Service Account to Atlas clusters on MongoDB 7.0.11+ running on M10+ tiers. The MONGODB-OIDC connection string uses authMechanismProperties=ENVIRONMENT:gcp,TOKEN_RESOURCE:<audience>; supported by PyMongo 4.7+, Node.js driver 6.7+, Go driver 1.17+, and Java driver 5.1+, among other current drivers. Assign minimal Atlas roles to service accounts — e.g. Project Data Access Admin — rather than Organization Owner. IP-allowlist token usage to known CIDR blocks (CI/CD runners, GCP NAT ranges) and rotate secrets on a fixed cadence, roughly every 90 days. Cache the 1-hour OAuth token and refresh it a few minutes before expiry rather than requesting a new token on every call. Store credentials in GCP Secret Manager rather than plain environment variables. No GCP-published SDK exists for the Atlas Admin API; implementations rely on generic OAuth 2.0 client libraries such as google-auth-library-python. Throughput characteristics for high-volume Admin API calls, and token-refresh/caching patterns at scale, are not documented publicly.

items.concept: Atlas AI Services Pricing (Agent Engine and Voyage AI)
items.summary: Atlas AI spend has two metered parts: Voyage AI embedding and reranking (per token, or per pixel for multimodal models, with 200 million free tokens for most current models) billed to the Atlas organization that owns the API key, and Automated Embedding in Atlas Vector Search, which uses the same per-token rates and meters initial sync, inserts, updates and queries. Atlas Agent Engine (Agent Runtime and Agent Memory), announced 2026-09-29 in public preview, is consumption-priced and draws down existing Atlas commitments, but no unit rates are published. The pack draws on 6 sources (the Atlas Embedding and Reranking API and Automated Embedding billing pages, the Automated Embedding models page, the Voyage pricing page, a MongoDB press release and IT Brief coverage) and flags 2 disagreements about which reranker and which legacy embedding models receive free tokens.

Atlas Embedding and Reranking API is pay-as-you-go: text models bill per token, multimodal models per pixel. Billing is set at organization level, and charges go to the Atlas account linked to the model API key. Atlas Agent Engine was announced 2026-09-29 and is in public preview. Atlas Agent Runtime and Atlas Agent Memory are consumption-priced, and usage counts against existing Atlas commitments, so no new contract is needed. MongoDB has launched Atlas Agent Engine, a new layer for running AI agents in production. The product is its latest effort to make the Atlas platform more central to enterprise AI deployments. Automated Embedding uses Voyage AI's embedding models, which Atlas hosts and manages in the Data Plane in a multi-tenant environment. Memory and retrieval are another part of the offering. Atlas Agent Engine uses Voyage AI embeddings and MongoDB's retrieval technology so agents can maintain context across tasks and interactions. Memory and retrieval built in. Without built-in memory, agents start every conversation from zero, and teams end up rebuilding memory infrastructure for every new agent. Atlas Agent Engine builds memory into the platform itself, using Voyage AI embeddings and MongoDB's native retrieval, so agents get more accurate while spending fewer tokens. Built on Atlas, Atlas Agent Engine combines execution, memory and governance in a single layer. Customers can use the memory and governance components on their own or with MongoDB's runtime, while continuing to use existing AI models and frameworks. Automated Embeddi

Usage Details is the line-item layer: dates used and billed, quantity (server hours), project, hosting cloud provider, SKU rate, and amount. Usage not tied to a cloud provider appears under 'Other Atlas Usage'. It can be downloaded as CSV. Atlas charges for services at the organization level and posts charges the day after they are incurred. Viewing billing needs Organization Billing Viewer or higher; changing payment method or billing profile needs Organization Owner or Billing Admin. Understand MongoDB Atlas billing components, set up cost alerts, query invoices via the API, and apply cost-saving strategies for your clusters. Payment Details columns: payment method (prepaid/promotional credits, monthly commitment, marketplace, credit card, PayPal), Date, Payment status, Usage, Billed Usage, Total Cost, Amount Due, Actions (PDF, VIEW DETAILS, PAY NOW for YayPay customers, RETRY for failed payments). Total Cost = unit price x billed usage + taxes. The current (pending) invoice page has: header card (amount due, total usage cost, billing info, downloads as PDF usage summary, CSV usage summary, or CSV FOCUS report), Payment Details, Total Usage chart, By Deployment chart, Summary By Project table (excludes subscription charges), Summary by Service table, and Usage Details. The Admin API exposes invoices at /api/atlas/v2/orgs/{ORG_ID}/invoices (list), /invoices/{INVOICE_ID} (single, JSON or CSV), and /invoices/pending. The list returns id, startDate, endDate, amountBilledCents; detail returns lineItems with sku, totalPriceCents (unit price x quantity x 100), groupId (project). Low-CPU is the cheaper option for memory-heavy, CPU-light workloads: similar RAM and storage at a lower price. Vantage (Jan 2024) says the same. (medium confidence) The RAM saving is below the vector-value ratio because the HNSW graph structure is not compressed. Sizing must therefore budget graph memory separately from vector memory. (medium confidence) Enabling Atlas Search on a cluster adds no fee when mongot is co-located with mongod, but co-located search consumes cluster CPU/RAM, and the docs warn of resource contention between mongod and mongot. The docs position co-located deployment for testing and prototyping. (medium confidence) An analytics node tier can be set larger or smaller than the base tier. A tier on the Analytics Tier tab is priced like the same tier on the Base Tier tab, with the price adjusted prorated per node when it differs. Atlas shows the price in the UI at create or edit time. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) Setting the analytics tier significantly below the base tier can cause replication lag; the analytics node might fall off the oplog. On Atlas Core, analytics storage size must match the base tab, so a small analytics tier does not shrink storage cost; mixing General and Low-CPU across the tabs disables disk auto-scaling. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) An arbiter holds no data and votes in elections, giving two data-bearing members an odd vote count at lower cost. The manual recommends at most one arbiter, warns that PSA sets can suffer performance problems with w:majority when a secondary lags, and warns that PSA shards can lose availability. The manual page covers self-managed sets and does not mention Atlas. (medium confidence) When sharding is enabled with dedicated config servers, Atlas adds three config servers billed at a separate rate. Cluster tier and data storage selections do not change that config server cost. The rate itself is not published on the billing page. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) Backup billing for a sharded cluster covers each shard replica set plus the config server replica set. Atlas may retain more than one full snapshot when topology changes (for example when a shard is added), which raises backup storage for a period. (high confidence) Atlas has native billing alerts in USD: the last daily amount billed (excluding credits applied) per org or project, and monthly totals per organization or per project that reset when the pending invoice closes. items.summary: Atlas Cost Explorer is a visual interface in the Billing section of the Atlas UI for viewing and analyzing monthly Atlas usage, visible to the Organization Owner, Billing Admin and Organization Billing Viewer roles. Available credits are drawn down in the order shown in the Available Credits table; when a Monthly Commitment organization runs out of credits it transitions to Elastic Billing and usage beyond the credits is billed, and when a subscription expires Atlas charges remaining usage to the payment method on file and reverts paid support plans to Basic. items.concept: Atlas Federated Authentication
items.summary: Atlas Federated Authentication implements Federated Identity Management (FIM) at the Atlas organization layer. Your identity provider (IdP) manages all credentials; Atlas acts as the SAML 2.0 Service
items.text: Atlas Federated Authentication Atlas Federated Authentication implements Federated Identity Management (FIM) at the Atlas organization layer. Your identity provider (IdP) manages all credentials; Atlas acts as the SAML 2.0 Service Atlas Federated Authentication implements Federated Identity Management (FIM) at the Atlas organization layer. Your identity provider (IdP) manages all credentials; Atlas acts as the SAML 2.0 Service Provider (SP). When a user logs in, their browser exchanges SAML assertions with the IdP instead of submitting MongoDB credentials directly. Scope of federation: One federation application can span multiple Atlas organizations under a single IdP, unified via the Federation Management Console (FMC). Federation covers Atlas UI access only - it does not control database-level user authentication. For OIDC workforce federation, X.509, SCRAM, or LDAP database auth, see [[mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]]. > SAML vs OIDC disambiguation: This skill covers SAML 2.0 federation for Atlas UI login (org-level SSO). If the question is about authenticating application workloads to the Atlas database via an IdP, that is Workload/Workforce Identity Federation (OIDC) - a different feature documented in [[mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]]. > Guardrail: Use only the API endpoint paths, attribute names, and URLs explicitly stated in this skill. Do not extrapolate or invent Atlas Admin API paths - verify any path not listed here against the Atlas Admin API reference before use. The SP-initiated SAML flow: User visits cloud.mongodb.com → enters email → Atlas matches domain to IdP → sends AuthnRequest → IdP authenticates → issues signed SAML Response → Atlas validates assertion (signature, audience, timestamps) → extracts NameID/firstName/lastName/memberOf → creates/updates account (JIT) → applies role mappings → user lands in org. SP-initiated (most common) vs IdP-initiated (tile click in My Apps; requires RelayState = Atlas Login URL). Both flows supported. Federation disables direct Atlas credential login and Atlas-managed 2FA for users on mapped domains - configure MFA at IdP level. Full tutorials: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), Google Workspace, PingOne. Any SAML 2.0 IdP works (JumpCloud, OneLogin, Auth0, custom). Create SAML 2.0 app in Okta with placeholder SSO URL/Audience URI Download Okta signing cert → convert to PEM (openssl x509) Create IdP in Atlas FMC with placeholder values + PEM cert; Request Binding: HTTP POST, Algorithm: SHA-256 Download Atlas metada

items.concept: Atlas Flex Pricing and Flex-vs-Dedicated Break-Even
items.summary: Atlas Flex is a usage-banded Atlas cluster tier billed hourly on operations per second: an $8 base for 100 ops/sec and 5 GB of storage, rising in $7, $6, $5 and $4 steps to 500 ops/sec and capped at $30 per month, which replaced the retired M2/M5 shared tiers and Serverless instances. At list price Flex is cheaper than the cheapest Dedicated tier (M10, $0.08/hr, "starts at $56.94/month" on the pricing page and "$60" in the Flex costs doc) at every load it can serve, so the move to Dedicated is driven by limits (5 GB storage, a 500 ops/sec hard limit with per-connection cooldown) and unsupported features rather than cost. The pack draws on 6 sources (MongoDB docs, pricing page, a MongoDB blog post, a MongoDB support FAQ and one third-party blog) and covers definitions, parameters, mechanism, how-to, examples, measures, problems, comparisons and history, with 3 flagged disagreements.

At list price Flex is cheaper than the cheapest Dedicated tier (M10, $0.08/hr, "starts at $56.94/month" on the pricing page and "$60" in the Flex costs doc) at every load it can serve, so the move to Dedicated is driven by limits (5 GB storage, a 500 ops/sec hard limit with per-connection cooldown) and unsupported features rather than cost. The pack draws on 6 sources (MongoDB docs, pricing page, a MongoDB blog post, a MongoDB support FAQ and one third-party blog) and covers definitions, parameters, mechanism, how-to, examples, measures, problems, comparisons and history, with 3 flagged disagreements. Flex pricing is a banded ops/sec model: $8 base (0-100 ops/sec, $0.0110/hr), then marginal $7 (to $15, $0.0205/hr), $6 (to $21, $0.0288/hr), $5 (to $26, $0.0356/hr), $4 (to $30, $0.0411/hr) for 400-500 ops/sec. Billed hourly, prorated. Flex clusters are low-cost cluster types suitable for teams that are learning MongoDB or developing small proof-of-concept applications. You can begin your project with an Atlas Flex cluster and upgrade to a production-ready Dedicated cluster tier at a future time. The monthly fee for each level of usage is prorated and billed on an hourly basis. All clusters on MongoDB Atlas, including Atlas Flex tier clusters, are pay-as-you-go. Clusters are only charged for as long as they remain active. For example, a workload that requires 100 ops/sec for 20 days, 250 ops/sec for 5 days, and 500 ops/sec for 5 days would cost approximately $13.67. If the cluster was deleted after the first 20 days of usage, the cost would be approximately $5.28. Flex clusters scale with your usage. If you use additional operations/sec, MongoDB charges you based on the following pricing tiers. 1. **Storage** - charged per GB-hour for the data and index storage consumed 2. **Read/Write Processing Units (RPUs/WPUs)** - charged per million operations executed Predictable pricing: Customers will be billed an $8 base fee and additional fees based on usage. items.text: Atlas Kubernetes Operator AKO lets you manage MongoDB Atlas cloud resources (clusters, users, networking, backup, search) as Kubernetes Custom Resources. For multi-tenant clusters: Subobject CRDs: Embedded in AtlasProject (e.g., spec.alertConfigurations) - managed as part of the project Independent CRDs: Deployed as separate Kubernetes objects - can be owned and managed by different teams (e.g., application teams own their AtlasDatabaseUser) AKO integrates natively with ArgoCD and Flux. Required Memory describes vector index memory, not total node capacity. MongoDB says Vector Search needs memory for both the index and the JVM; on co-located deployments, mongod also consumes node memory, leaving only the remainder for Vector Search and mongot. Add those process and workload needs when translating an index estimate into a node size. (high confidence) MongoDB reports that automatic scalar and binary quantization reduce vector RAM use by about 3.75x and 24x, respectively, while full-fidelity vectors remain on disk for exact search or rescoring; its deployment guidance suggests storage-to-RAM ratios near 4:1 for scalar and 24:1 for binary quantization, so Required Memory alone does not size disk. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) OneUptime's 2026-03-31 monitoring guide lists SEARCH_REQUIRED_MEMORY_SIZE and suggests alerting above 80% of available memory; the MongoDB sizing pages reviewed here give no such threshold, so treat this as a third-party heuristic pending workload validation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-04-13) Inference: per-vector payload math is a starting estimate rather than total RAM. MongoDB says vector space scales linearly with vector count and dimensionality and gives representation-specific examples; its index also contains metadata and an HNSW graph, while the original HNSW paper describes a multi-layer graph over nested subsets of stored elements. Do not treat raw embedding bytes as the complete Required Memory value. (medium confidence) Datadog's Atlas integration lists separate gauges for required memory bytes for Vector Search indexes, total index size on disk, and Search process resident memory. items.concept: Atlas Search and Dedicated Search Nodes Cost
items.summary: Atlas Search adds no fee when mongot is co-located with mongod, but co-located search shares cluster CPU and RAM and is documented for testing and prototyping, while dedicated Search Nodes need an M10+ cluster, a minimum of two nodes (up to 32 per region per shard) and bill per node-hour by tier and node class (high-CPU, low-CPU, storage-optimized). List prices differ by cloud (high-CPU S20 is $0.12/hr on AWS us-east-1, $0.14 on Google Cloud, $0.15 on Azure), search-to-database transfer appears under cluster network charges, and per-region node counts and the S10 tier are the newest cost levers. Drawn from 6 source pages, all MongoDB-authored, across measures, parameters, comparisons and problems; the pages disagree on the minimum production search tier (S20 versus the S10 announcement).
items.text: Atlas Search and Dedicated Search Nodes Cost Atlas Search adds no fee when mongot is co-located with mongod, but co-located search shares cluster CPU and RAM and is documented for testing and prototyping, while dedicated Search Nodes need an M10+ cluster, a minimum of two nodes (up to 32 per region per shard) and bill per node-hour by tier and node class (high-CPU, low-CPU, storage-optimized). List prices differ by cloud (high-CPU S20 is $0.12/hr on AWS us-east-1, $0.14 on Google Cloud, $0.15 on Azure), search-to-database transfer appears under cluster network charges, and per-region node counts and the S10 tier are the newest cost levers. Drawn from 6 source pages, all MongoDB-authored, across measures, parameters, comparisons and problems; the pages disagree on the minimum production search tier (S20 versus the S10 announcement). What it is: MongoDB is introducing the S10 Dedicated Search Node, a new, lower-cost entry tier for Atlas Search and Vector Search that sits below the current S20 floor. S10 gives smaller and growing workloads their own dedicated, isolated compute for search, provisioned from the same Atlas search-node experience you already use. It's available today on all three cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure) that Atlas uses . MongoDB supports separate Search Nodes on dedicated (M10 or higher) clusters. Search Nodes are deployed on compute-intensive instances with high-performance local storage. You must deploy a minimum of two nodes. You will be billed daily for hourly resource usage per node. To learn more, see Search Node Costs. Atlas provides different search tiers. Each search tier has a default RAM capacity, storage capacity, and CPU. Each search node's per-hour usage charge (as shown in the Atlas UI during cluster creation) is calculated based on these default values. In the following diagram of this deployment model, the MongoDB Search mongot process runs on dedicated Search Nodes, which are separate from the cluster nodes on which the mongod process runs. What it is: This functionality allows independent configuration of Dedicated Search Node counts across individual regions within a multi-region MongoDB Atlas cluster. Instead of maintaining identical node counts everywhere, a different number of nodes can be deployed in each region depending on regional requirements. items.text: Atlas Search for substring matching Source-anchored research for Atlas Search for substring matching. Run status: COMPLETED. MongoDB Search autocomplete fields expose edgeGram, rightEdgeGram, and nGram tokenization. MongoDB describes edgeGrams as left-to-right autocomplete and positions nGrams for character autocomplete in languages without whitespace. For arbitrary interior substrings, MongoDB's developer guide shows a custom nGram analyzer with the text operator; Elastic's analyzer documentation explains why nGram emits interior fragments while edge n-grams emit only token beginnings. Do not assume an autocomplete mapping with default settings provides general contains semantics. (high confidence) Atlas Search regex uses Lucene's limited regular-expression syntax, not full PCRE; anchors such as ^ and $ are unsupported, and a regex must match the whole indexed term. Use .*fragment.* for a contains-style regex, and escape reserved characters according to the Lucene regex rules. (high confidence) Use a MongoDB Search autocomplete mapping with tokenization set to nGram and the autocomplete operator for in-word partial matches; use edgeGram when only prefixes should match. The operator requires an autocomplete-mapped field. nGram emits character grams from within tokens, while edgeGram emits grams from the token's left edge. (high confidence) Leading-wildcard patterns such as *needle* are flexible but can be expensive: MongoDB classifies wildcard and regex queries as resource-intensive, Lucene warns that leading * wildcards can be extremely slow, and Elastic recommends n-grams as an alternative while noting their index-size cost. For frequent arbitrary-substring queries, compare the approaches using realistic data and query lengths. (high confidence) A Reddit report says a *248* Atlas Search wildcard query took up to 20 seconds on a collection of 800,000 documents; the author also reported that an initial autocomplete+nGram attempt was similarly slow or slower. Replies pointed to using autocomplete on an autocomplete-mapped field with explicit gram bounds. Treat this as a workload-specific anecdote, not a general performance result, and benchmark the actual index and query pairing. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) MongoDB Search wildcard and regex are term-level operators, so their query patterns are not analyzed. items.text: Atlas Search index sync lag and search-node sizing Source-anchored research for Atlas Search index sync lag and search-node sizing. Run status: COMPLETED. Diagnose lag by comparing Atlas Search replication-lag metrics with write volume, index size, Search Node CPU and memory or heap, and query load. Atlas recommends batching or throttling write bursts and increasing the oplog size on Atlas Core when the oplog window is the constraint; it recommends more Search Node CPU and memory when `mongot` is resource constrained. Independent monitoring guidance and a forum response also point operators to Atlas Search metrics and index status. (high confidence) Diagnose lag by comparing Search Max Replication Lag with source write volume, the oplog window, and Search-node metrics such as Process CPU, Page Fault, Process Throttling, and Index Size. Atlas says write bursts can exhaust the oplog and recommends batching or throttling bulk writes; on Atlas Core, increasing oplog size gives `mongot` more time to catch up. More Search-node CPU and memory can help when `mongot` is the bottleneck, but Atlas also identifies source-cluster load, complex indexing work, and many indexes as causes, so increasing Search-node size alone might not clear lag. (high confidence) Collection size is not a reliable proxy for Search-index size: mappings and features such as autocomplete can make an index much larger than its source data. MongoDB recommends estimating the index-to-collection ratio with representative sample data, then sizing memory against the measured index footprint and available Search-node RAM. If the index working set does not fit in memory, disk paging raises page faults and I/O wait. Current Atlas guidance also requires 20% local-SSD storage overhead for Search-node index operations. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) MongoDB's August 2025 sizing post gives about 10 queries per second per vCPU as a rough starting estimate and sub-100 ms as a general latency aim. The post says actual throughput depends on query complexity and index mappings, so treat these as starting points for representative load tests, not capacity guarantees. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-12) Atlas Search replication on dedicated Search Nodes pauses when disk utilization reaches 90% and resumes automatically below 85%. items.text: Atlas Search regex and wildcard operator cost Source-anchored research for Atlas Search regex and wildcard operator cost. Run status: COMPLETED. Patterns with a leading wildcard, such as `*suffix` or `.*suffix.*`, are a higher-cost risk than a fixed-prefix pattern with a trailing wildcard. Lucene warns that leading `*` or `?` wildcard queries can be extremely slow, and Elasticsearch independently warns that leading wildcards increase term iterations. MongoDB's pattern-matching guide says a fixed-prefix query such as `UI-*` is likely fast enough for many workloads, but still recommends testing at scale. The cross-product documentation corroborates the pattern-shape risk; it does not establish Atlas-specific timing. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Measure the $search stage separately from the rest of an aggregation. A community report involving a wildcard query also included a later $match, and the discussion attributed the extra latency to processing $search results after that stage. MongoDB's performance guidance recommends placing search logic inside $search and minimizing later blocking stages, so total pipeline time cannot be assigned to the wildcard operator alone. (medium confidence) Analyzer and field design change the query/index trade-off. On Atlas, rs.stepDown() and member-priority changes are unsupported, so the compact reference says to run compact on every node and use force: true on the primary. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) WiredTiger does not overwrite in place, so expect about 20% more disk than the compressed data occupies. Atlas delays an auto-scaling event until the oplog window covers the estimated scaling time. For storage auto-scaling to complete, Atlas requires oplogMinRetentionHours to be up to 60 seconds multiplied by the GB of configured disk space. When the oplog is too small Atlas raises 'Auto-scaling: Disk auto-scaling didn't initiate due to insufficient oplog size'. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) When the primary runs critically low on free disk, Atlas blocks writes on the replica set and keeps serving reads. On sharded clusters only writes routed to the affected shard are blocked. Writes resume automatically once free space passes the unblock threshold. Fix: raise storage or enable storage auto-scaling. Write blocking is active on M10+ clusters running MongoDB 8.0 or later. Neither the docs nor the plans page publishes prices; the only public formula is a January 2024 MongoDB staff forum reply (Developer the greater of $49 or 20% of total monthly charges, Pro the greater of $799 or 20%), and plan changes take effect on the first day of the next month while reactivation bills retroactively for up to 90 days. This pack draws on 5 source pages across 3 host labels and covers definitions, mechanism, parameters, how-to, measures, problems and comparisons, with 2 recorded disagreements.

items.text: Atlas Vector Search automatic quantization and rescoring Source-anchored research for Atlas Vector Search automatic quantization and rescoring. Run status: COMPLETED. Only `binary` quantization rescores. After the binary pass, Atlas re-evaluates the candidates with the original float vectors. Scalar quantization has no rescoring step. The full-fidelity vectors live in a separate on-disk structure and are read only for binary rescoring or for exact (ENN) search. (high confidence) Atlas binary quantization compares each dimension with a fixed midpoint of 0 (above 0 becomes 1), which the docs say suits embeddings normalized to length 1. Other engines treat centering as a precondition. Qdrant says binary quantization 'requires a centered distribution' of components. Azure AI Search says it works best when embeddings are centered around zero. Lucene's BBQ normalizes vectors around a per-segment centroid. (medium confidence) A 2026 single-author arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed) argues that binary-quantization ranking fidelity depends on the full covariance structure of the embedding space (off-diagonal terms supply 30-50% of the signal) and on per-coordinate variance heterogeneity. It tests 18 datasets across 9 embedding families. This is a theoretical reason binary quantization works on some models and fails on others. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-29) Atlas keeps the full-fidelity vectors on disk in a separate data structure. It reads them only for binary rescoring and for exact (ENN, `exact: true`) search. When automatic quantization is enabled, ENN queries use only the full-fidelity vectors. (high confidence) Low-dimension embeddings fit aggressive quantization poorly. MongoDB recommends at least 1024 dimensions with quantization over fewer dimensions without it, and its 1024-d and larger vectors reached the recall target at lower `numCandidates`. Elastic warns that BBQ datasets under 384 dimensions may see less accuracy. Qdrant says binary quantization works best on high-dimensional embeddings with centered components. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) On Atlas, automatic quantization is opt-in per vector field. The `fields.quantization` setting in the index definition takes `none` (the default), `scalar` (1-byte integers) or `binary` (1 bit). The choice applies to all indexed vectors and to query vectors at query time, so queries need no change. Changing it triggers an index rebuild. (high confidence) Exact (ENN) queries on a qua

items.summary: Reference for writing that will be heard, not read. The eye can re-scan a sentence; the ear gets one pass.
items.text: Audio Script Writing Reference for writing that will be heard, not read. The eye can re-scan a sentence; the ear gets one pass. Reference for writing that will be heard, not read. The eye can re-scan a sentence; the ear gets one pass. Listeners process roughly 150–160 words per minute for narration, 130–145 wpm for voice-UI prompts, and 110–125 wpm for IVR. They lose comprehension on: Subordinate clauses stacked more than one deep Parentheticals (the ear has no parens) Lists longer than three items without explicit numbering Numbers and proper nouns delivered without a beat of silence after Eye version (fine on the page): > The migration, which we'd been planning since February, finally launched on Tuesday after a final round of testing that revealed two minor bugs we patched overnight. Ear version: > We'd been planning the migration since February. It finally launched on Tuesday. The last round of testing turned up two small bugs. We patched them overnight. Signpost vocabulary: First / second / third / finally - explicit numbering Here's the thing - flag a key insight Two reasons - set up a numbered list Coming up - preview before an ad break Back to the story - return marker after a digression Before: "The team (which had only formed in January) shipped on time." After: "The team shipped on time. They'd only formed in January." Three patterns that work: Pattern A - Drop into a scene: > It's 2 a.m. The paging system goes off. Marcus rolls over, reads the alert, and the alert is wrong. Pattern B - A question with stakes: > What would you do if your entire backup tier disappeared in the middle of a restore? Pattern C - A single startling fact: > Last year, 47% of incident retrospectives never produced a single action item. Anti-pattern - The throat-clear: > Hi everyone, welcome to the podcast. Today we're going to be talking about... Three constraints beyond "writing for the ear": The prompt must end with an explicit prompt-for-input. Confirm without echoing. "Adding milk to your list" is good; "I heard you say milk; I will now add milk to your list" is voice-UI throat-clearing. Three-option ceiling. Lists of more than three options exceed working memory. Most-likely path first. Order by call-volume share, not alphabetical. Always offer a human escape. "Press 0 at any time to reach an agent." Confirm critical inputs. Read back at the cadence a person can write down. Re-prompt twice, then escalate. Caller silence twice in a row = route to agent. Required sec

items.text: Augmented Analytics and LLM-Assisted Analysis How AI augments or automates the analytical loop — preparing data, finding insights, answering natural-language questions, and explaining results — instead of a human writing every query and reading e How AI augments or automates the analytical loop - preparing data, finding insights, answering natural-language questions, and explaining results - instead of a human writing every query and reading every chart. The audience is an analyst, data/BI engineer, or product owner deciding whether and how to put an LLM between users and data, and how to keep the answers correct. Scope boundary. This skill is about the AI/LLM layer over analytics. It deliberately does not re-teach: The semantic/metrics layer itself → da-18-semantic-layer-headless-bi. Here we only cover how an LLM is grounded in that layer. Unstructured-text NLP (topic modeling, sentiment, NER, text embeddings) → da-36-text-analytics-nlp. Generic ML / LLM training, fine-tuning, eval theory → da-7-machine-learning. Generic RAG pipeline architecture with no numeric/analytical angle → rag-architecture. Gartner (Rita Sallam, 2017) defined augmented analytics as using ML/AI to assist data preparation, insight generation, and insight explanation to augment how people explore and analyze data. Gartner's evaluation criteria span six capabilities: ML-assisted insight discovery, NLP/NLQ querying, automated explanations (NLG), data-prep assistance, GenAI integration, and augmented data science. The 2025 evolution is agentic analytics (Gartner Market Guide for Agentic Analytics, Feb 2025): AI agents that don't just assist but autonomously plan, investigate, and act. Gartner predicts ~75% of analytics content will use GenAI for contextual intelligence by 2027, evolving toward "autonomous analytics" managing a slice of business processes. The four classic analytics tiers map onto this: descriptive (what happened) → diagnostic (why) → predictive (what will) → prescriptive (what to do) - augmented/agentic analytics automates the first two and increasingly drives toward the latter two. Natural-Language Query (NLQ) turns a plain-English question into a query against governed data, returns a result, a chart, and (via NLG) a written explanation. The non-negotiable lesson of 2024-2026: accuracy depends on grounding the LLM in a governed semantic model, not the raw schema. items.summary: > 兼容性说明 (v1.8.0): autonomous-loops 保留一个发布周期。
items.text: Autonomous Loop Patterns > 兼容性说明 (v1.8.0): autonomous-loops 保留一个发布周期。 > 兼容性说明 (v1.8.0): autonomous-loops 保留一个发布周期。 > 规范的技能名称现在是 continuous-agent-loop。新的循环指南应在此处编写，而此技能继续可用以避免破坏现有工作流。 在循环中自主运行 Claude Code 的模式、架构和参考实现。涵盖从简单的 claude -p 管道到完整的 RFC 驱动的多智能体 DAG 编排的一切。 为你的问题选择正确的循环架构（简单与复杂） 最简单的循环。 将日常开发分解为一系列非交互式 claude -p 调用。每次调用都是一个具有清晰提示的专注步骤。 > 如果你无法想出这样的循环，那意味着你甚至无法在交互模式下驱动 LLM 来修复你的代码。 claude -p 标志以非交互方式运行 Claude Code 并附带提示，完成后退出。链式调用来构建管道： 每个步骤都是隔离的 - 每次 claude -p 调用都是一个新的上下文窗口，意味着步骤之间没有上下文泄露。 顺序很重要 - 步骤按顺序执行。每个步骤都建立在前一个步骤留下的文件系统状态之上。 否定指令是危险的 - 不要说“不要测试类型系统。”相反，添加一个单独的清理步骤（参见去草率化模式）。 退出代码会传播 - set -e 在失败时停止管道。 使用 --allowedTools 限制： ECC 内置的持久循环。 一个具有会话感知的 REPL，它使用完整的对话历史同步调用 claude -p。 从 ~/.claude/claw/{session}.md 加载对话历史 每个用户消息都连同完整历史记录作为上下文发送给 claude -p 响应被追加到会话文件中（Markdown 作为数据库） 有关完整详情，请参阅 /claw 命令文档。 一个双提示系统，用于编排并行子智能体以进行规范驱动的生成。由 disler 开发（致谢：@disler）。 规范分析 - 编排器读取一个定义要生成内容的规范文件（Markdown） 目录侦察 - 扫描现有输出以找到最高的迭代编号 并行部署 - 启动 N 个子智能体，每个都有： 波次管理 - 对于无限模式，部署 3-5 个智能体的波次，直到上下文耗尽 创建 .claude/commands/infinite.md： 不要依赖智能体自我区分。编排器分配给每个智能体一个特定的创意方向和迭代编号。这可以防止并行智能体之间的概念重复。 一个生产级的 shell 脚本，在持续循环中运行 Claude Code，创建 PR，等待 CI，并自动合并。由 AnandChowdhary 创建（致谢：@AnandChowdhary）。 关键创新：一个 SHARED_TASK_NOTES.md 文件在迭代间持久存在： Claude 在迭代开始时读取此文件，并在迭代结束时更新它。这弥合了独立 claude -p 调用之间的上下文差距。 当 PR 检查失败时，持续 Claude 会自动： 通过 gh run list 获取失败的运行 ID 生成一个新的带有 CI 修复上下文的 claude -p Claude 通过 gh run view 检查日志，修复代码，提交，推送 重新等待检查（最多 --ci-retry-max 次尝试） Claude 可以通过输出一个魔法短语来发出“我完成了”的信号： 连续三次迭代发出完成信号会停止循环，防止在已完成的工作上浪费运行。 任何循环的附加模式。 在每个实现者步骤之后添加一个专门的清理/重构步骤。 当你要求 LLM 使用 TDD 实现时，它对“编写测试”的理解过于字面： 测试验证 TypeScript 的类型系统是否有效（测试 typeof x === 'string'） 对类型系统已经保证的东西进行过度防御的运行时检查 在实现者提示中添加“不要测试类型系统”或“不要添加不必要的检查”会产生下游影响： 与其限制实现者，不如让它彻底。然后添加一个专注的清理智能体： > 与其添加具有下游质量影响的否定指令，不如添加一个单独的去草率化步骤。两个专注的智能体胜过一个有约束的智能体。 最复杂的模式。 一个 RFC 驱动的多智能体管道，将规范分解为依赖关系 DAG，通过分层质量管道运行每个单元，并通过智能体驱动的合并队列落地。由 enitrat 创建（致谢：@enitrat）。 保持测试与实现在一起（永远不要分开“实现 X” + “测试 X”） 仅在实际存在代码依赖关系的地方设置依赖关系 这可以防止对简单更改进行昂贵的操作，同时确保架构更改得到彻底审查。 每个阶段在其自己的智能体进程中运行，拥有自己的上下文窗口： 关键设计： 审阅者从未编写过它要审阅的代码。这消除了作者偏见——这是自我审阅中遗漏问题的最常见原因。 驱逐恢复： 被驱逐时，会捕获完整上下文（冲突文件、差异、测试输出）并反馈给下一个 Ralph 轮次的实现者： 每个单元在隔离的工作树中运行（使用 jj/Jujutsu，而不是 git）： 同一单元的管道阶段共享一个工作树，在 research → plan → implement → test → review 之间保留状态（上下文文件、计划文件、代码更改）。 确定性执行 - 预先分解锁定并行性和顺序 在杠杆点进行人工审阅 - 工作计划是单一最高杠杆干预点 关注点分离 - 每个阶段在独立的上下文窗口中，由独立的智能体负责 带上下文的冲突恢复 - 完整的驱逐上下文支持智能重试，而非盲目重试 层级驱动的深度 - 琐碎更改跳过研究/审阅；大型更改获得最大审查 可恢复的工作流 - 完整状态持久化到 SQLite；可从任何点恢复 顺序流水线 + 去草率化 - 最常见的组合。每个实现步骤都进行一次清理。 连续 Claude + 去草率化 - 为每次迭代添加带有去草率化指令的 --review-prompt。

items.text: Autoscaling tier bounds as cost ceiling Source-anchored research for Autoscaling tier bounds as cost ceiling. Run status: COMPLETED. A maximum tier is not a whole-invoice cap: cloud provider and region affect cluster cost, and custom storage or IOPS, backups and restores, data transfer, add-on features, and support can add costs independently of the selected tier. (high confidence) A maximum tier is not a hard invoice cap. Atlas bills cluster and storage costs for each data-bearing node and may charge separately for non-default storage capacity or IOPS, backups, and data transfer. Percona and Amnic's Atlas cost breakdowns also identify storage, backup, and transfer as cost drivers outside the cluster tier rate. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Atlas prices a cluster tier by the hour, so the maximum bounds the tier-price component of ordinary auto-scale moves; MyDBOps and Cloud Cost Room recommend explicit maximum bounds to keep a traffic spike from leaving a cluster at a higher recurring tier. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) A maximum tier limits scaling magnitude, not time spent at that tier: Atlas only scales down when the configured minimum permits and cooldown and utilization checks pass, so a spike can leave the cluster at a higher tier for an extended period. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-19) On Atlas Core, the maximum is not absolute when storage autoscaling needs disk capacity that the configured maximum tier cannot support. Atlas raises the maximum to the next lowest tier that supports the required storage, scales to it, and disables automatic downscaling until it is re-enabled. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) Atlas Stream Processing has a separate analogous control: minTier and maxTier bound vertical autoscaling, and MongoDB describes maxTier as a cap on resource consumption and cost; if a processor reaches maxTier and exhausts memory, it fails with an out-of-memory error. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Set the maximum against the workload's expected peak capacity and tolerated compute spend, and set the minimum high enough for the baseline workload. MongoDB's scalability guidance says to use the range to control costs while preserving minimum performance; MyDBOps and Cloud Cost Room likewise recommend explicit bounds and review of tier changes to limit cost ratchets after traffic spikes. The curve does not decline, so the concept is not saturated. The next pass needs a live Atlas test, not more reading: 1. ES384 against the current Atlas version. 2. A token with an `aud` array. 3. A nested `principalName`. 4. Behaviour under key rotation and disable/re-enable. - **No MongoDB endorsement of this path.** The Atlas WIF page names AWS only for EKS and has no STS outbound recipe. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/workload-oidc/ A dated third-party walkthrough reports it working end to end (2026-03-23). https://jimmydqv.com/m2m-outbound-federation-mongodb/ This report treats the path as working but undocumented by MongoDB. - **ES384 on Atlas.** Source code says 7.0 and 8.0 are RSA-only (claims 28–29). The release that first ships EC support, and whether Atlas builds match the public branches, were not verified. - **Multi-audience tokens.** STS can put up IN: AWS IAM outbound identity federation (`sts:GetWebIdentityToken`) used as the token source for Atlas Workload Identity Federation (MONGODB-OIDC). This covers the AWS-side mechanism, the Atlas and MongoDB server constraints that the AWS token must satisfy, the timeline, and the primary sources. OUT: Atlas WIF in general, Azure and GCP built-in flows, EKS/IRSA, Workforce federation, and Resource Policies. Parent facts are not repeated here. - MongoDB server 4.4 added the older `MONGODB-AWS` mechanism. It signs an AWS Signature Version 4 request that MongoDB checks against AWS STS. items.concept: Backend Patterns
items.summary: Backend architecture patterns and best practices for scalable server-side applications.
items.text: Backend Patterns Backend architecture patterns and best practices for scalable server-side applications. Backend architecture patterns and best practices for scalable server-side applications. Designing REST or GraphQL API endpoints Implementing repository, service, or controller layers Optimizing database queries (N+1, indexing, connection pooling) Adding caching (Redis, in-memory, HTTP cache headers) Setting up background jobs or async processing Structuring error handling and validation for APIs Building middleware (auth, logging, rate limiting) Remember: Backend patterns enable scalable, maintainable server-side applications. Choose patterns that fit your complexity level. Designing a new REST or GraphQL API's endpoint and layering conventions before the first controller, service, or repository file is written. Diagnosing a database-bound slow endpoint by spotting N+1 query patterns, missing indexes, or an exhausted connection pool. Deciding where caching belongs in a request path — Redis, in-memory, or HTTP cache headers — to cut load on a hot read endpoint. Structuring background or async processing so long-running work such as emails, exports, or webhooks doesn't block the request-response cycle. Build a small service with clean repository/service/controller separation and compare it against a version with logic mixed directly into route handlers to feel the maintainability difference. Add a request-scoped middleware chain for auth checking, structured request logging, and rate limiting to an existing API and measure the added latency per middleware. Introduce a Redis cache layer in front of a read-heavy endpoint with explicit invalidation on writes, and load-test before and after. Move a slow synchronous operation, such as sending an email on signup, into a background job queue and confirm the API response time drops. Fetching a collection and then looping over it to fetch each related record individually, the N+1 query problem, instead of a single joined or batched query. Skipping connection pooling and opening a new database connection per request, which caps throughput under load far below what the database can actually handle. Putting business logic directly in route or controller handlers instead of a service layer, making the same logic impossible to reuse or unit-test in isolation. Adding caching without an invalidation strategy, so stale data silently persists past the point where the underlying record changed. Repository/service/controller

items.concept: Bayesian Data Analysis and Probabilistic Programming
items.summary: Applied Bayesian modeling: specify a generative model, fit the posterior with a probabilistic programming language (PPL), interrogate it with predictive checks and diagnostics, and compare alternative
items.text: Bayesian Data Analysis and Probabilistic Programming Applied Bayesian modeling: specify a generative model, fit the posterior with a probabilistic programming language (PPL), interrogate it with predictive checks and diagnostics, and compare alternative Applied Bayesian modeling: specify a generative model, fit the posterior with a probabilistic programming language (PPL), interrogate it with predictive checks and diagnostics, and compare alternatives. This skill is the workflow and tooling layer - it assumes Bayes' theorem and the frequentist/Bayesian contrast are already understood (see da-1-3-5, da-1-4-3). A Bayesian model combines a prior p(θ) and a likelihood p(y|θ) into a posterior p(θ|y) ∝ p(y|θ) p(θ). For all but trivial models the posterior is intractable analytically, so we approximate it by sampling (MCMC) or optimization (variational inference). The discipline is an iterative loop - model, fit, check, expand - formalized as the Bayesian workflow (Gelman, Vehtari, Simpson et al. 2020, arXiv:2011.01808). Use Bayesian methods when you want: full uncertainty quantification (posteriors, not just point estimates), principled regularization via priors, partial pooling across groups (hierarchical models), the ability to incorporate domain knowledge, and propagation of uncertainty into predictions/decisions. The Bayesian workflow (iterative). Build → simulate from priors → fit → diagnose computation → check against data → compare models → expand/simplify → repeat. Treats computational failure (divergences, bad R-hat) and model misfit (failed PPCs) as distinct problems (Gelman et al. 2020; Betancourt "Principled Bayesian Workflow" 2020; Gabry et al. JRSS-A 2019). Priors & prior predictive checks. Favor weakly-informative priors (Normal(0,1) on standardized predictors, HalfNormal/Exponential on scales, LKJ on correlations) over flat/diffuse priors. Validate via prior predictive check: draw θ from prior, simulate y, confirm plausibility (Stan Prior Choice wiki 2024; PyMC v5 docs 2024). MCMC: HMC & NUTS. HMC uses gradients for distant, high-acceptance moves; NUTS auto-tunes trajectory length + step size and is the default in every modern PPL. Continuous params only - marginalize discrete ones (Hoffman & Gelman JMLR 2014; Betancourt arXiv:1701.02434 2017; Stan Reference Manual 2024). Variational inference (VI/ADVI). Approximates the posterior by maximizing the ELBO - fast, scalable, but underestimates variance and can miss multimodality. ADVI automates it; n

Decision/social psychology went through a replication crisis. Several once-famous effects did not survive (power posing, social priming, and ego depletion are contested/failed). Block-ordered arms: a hot GPU from arm A depresses arm B uniformly, so the per-trial spread check cannot catch it. Interleave arms. First run after another arm pulled a multi-GB model through the page cache reads far below true (16.2 vs 27.4 tok/s). GPU contention (another app, a second server) roughly halves decode with the only tell being trial spread (72.7/117.9/72.4 contended vs 171.3/171.6/171.0 idle). Random-token prompts with EOS disabled (mlx_lm.benchmark) measure raw throughput but not realistic text, MTP/speculative acceptance, or MoE routing on natural text; treat as a ceiling for speculative setups. exo_bench defaults to --repeat 1 and --warmup 0: a default run is one cold sample. Budget semantics differ: max_tokens is generation budget in one runtime and total context in another; undersizing corrupts rather than truncates. Thinking mode defaults differ by chat template (HF renders ON, swift-transformers OFF); output token counts then differ. Quant label is not a spec (wNa8o8 schema, 4-bit affine vs Q4_K_M vs MXFP4), and a QAT vs PTQ checkpoint swing was worth ~9 GSM8K points on MLX. Cold vs warm as headline: apple-silicon-llm-bench says warm (median of runs 2-4) is the cross-vendor headline and cold is a first-use latency metric; app-launch and agent-restart use cases need cold. Report both. BFCL's `bfcl generate` can start vllm or sglang itself (`--backend`, default vllm) or reuse a running server with `--skip-server-setup`; the endpoint defaults to localhost:1053 and is set by LOCAL_SERVER_ENDPOINT and LOCAL_SERVER_PORT in `.env`. For a remote or existing OpenAI-compatible server, `REMOTE_OPENAI_BASE_URL`, `REMOTE_OPENAI_API_KEY` and an optional local tokenizer path are read from `.env`; `bfcl evaluate` then scores saved responses. The harness's own backends are CUDA-oriented (sglang needs SM 80+ GPUs); a Mac run must go through `--skip-server-setup` against llama-server, mlx-lm or Ollama. 2026: quantization claims moved from perplexity to task benchmarks; the bartowski study (already recorded) used BFCL, and a Neo-agent case study ran BFCL on Qwen3.6-27B at BF16, Q8_0 and Q4_K_M. Sample size: the Neo study used 400 BFCL samples and 200 samples for HumanEval and HellaSwag; its own text attributes Q8_0 beating Q4_K_M on HellaSwag-like orderings to possible variance. Wall time: BF16 averaged 37 s per BFCL sample, over four hours for 400, so long evals need checkpoint-and-resume (the study resumed at samples 139 and 152). Summary columns count unevaluated BFCL categories as zero, so a partial local run under-reports the aggregate unless categories are compared one by one. Does 4-bit hurt tool calls? Docker (qwen3:8B, F16 0.933 vs Q4_K_M 0.919; qwen3:14B Q6_K 0.943 vs Q4_K_M 0.971) saw "no significant difference". The Neo study saw BFCL 63.25 (BF16) vs 63.00 vs 63.00 but code generation fell 56.10 to 50.61 (HumanEval). bartowski's Q2_K result (already recorded) shows a 28-point BFCL loss at 2-bit without imatrix. These agree if loss only appears below roughly 4 bits or in generation tasks, but no source tests that boundary. Docker's Q4_K_M beating Q6_K at 14B contradicts monotone quality-with-bits; with 3,570 tests spread across 21 models, per-cell sample size is small and the gap is likely noise. BFCL multi-turn and agentic categories on a 4-bit local model: no source reports them. Whether the Neo BFCL score used the model's native tool parser or a prompt-mode handler. A three-way run of Qwen3.6-27B scored BFCL 63.25% at BF16, 63.00% at Q8_0 and 63.

items.summary: First Divergent Token (FDT): greedy-decode N tokens from the base model, feed that whole sequence to the compressed model once, and take the first index where the compressed model's logit argmax differs from the base model's token. One forward pass, same cost as a perplexity pass.
items.text: Branch-and-follow flip analysis harness for Mac GGUF and MLX quants First Divergent Token (FDT): greedy-decode N tokens from the base model, feed that whole sequence to the compressed model once, and take the first index where the compressed model's logit argmax differs from the base model's token. One forward pass, same cost as a perplexity pass. First Divergent Token (FDT): greedy-decode N tokens from the base model, feed that whole sequence to the compressed model once, and take the first index where the compressed model's logit argmax differs from the base model's token. One forward pass, same cost as a perplexity pass. Share of Divergent Tokens (SDT) counts all positions where the argmax differs on that same teacher-forced base rollout, instead of stopping at the first. FDT is symmetric in its two models, while perplexity is not. Greedy decoding is a discontinuous function of the logits, so two models can have equal perplexity and still produce different greedy output; the paper calls equal perplexity with divergent generation a false positive of PPL. FDT is not branch-and-follow: FDT stops at the first mismatch and never lets the compressed model continue from its own token. Branch-and-follow starts at that mismatch and generates onward to see recovery, meaning change or malformed output. Three things are called a "flip" and must not be pooled: (a) answer-level flips, where a benchmark answer changes between correct and incorrect; (b) teacher-forced token top-1 flips, where one position's argmax differs; (c) the first divergent token of a rollout. The answer-level flip metric excludes incorrect-to-incorrect changes, because exact free-text matches between models are rare and would inflate the count; an "AllFlips" variant includes them. llama-server `/completion` takes the prompt as a string or as an array of token ids, so a harness can feed exact token ids and skip chat-template and tokenizer drift. llama-server inserts BOS automatically only when the prompt is a string (or an array whose first element is a string) and the GGUF has `tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token` true; a pure integer array gets no BOS, so the harness must include BOS itself. llama-server `return_tokens: true` returns the raw generated token ids in the `tokens` field, which is the capture hook for branch futures. mlx_lm.server can return generated token ids together with log-probabilities and top-N token info per position when `logprobs` is requested. llama-server `cache_prompt` defaul

items.concept: Brand Voice Guide Writing
items.summary: Authoring craft for the brand voice guide as an artifact. The output is a document other writers will open, reference, and apply.
items.text: Brand Voice Guide Writing Authoring craft for the brand voice guide as an artifact. The output is a document other writers will open, reference, and apply. Authoring craft for the brand voice guide as an artifact. The output is a document other writers will open, reference, and apply. A brand voice guide answers four questions for every writer who opens it: Who do we sound like? (Voice - the constant.) How do we shift in different situations? (Tone - the variable.) Which words do we use, and which do we never use? (Vocabulary.) What does this look like in practice? (Examples - usually do/don't pairs.) If a guide doesn't make these four questions answerable in under 10 minutes of reading, it will be ignored. Voice - three to five attributes that describe the constant personality. State each as "We are X. We are not Y." (Bloomstein's BrandSort framing: include the not.) Tone - a matrix showing how voice flexes by situation. Vocabulary - preferred words, banned words, and grammar/style decisions specific to the brand. Examples - at least 5 do/don't pairs spanning the highest-traffic surfaces. The canonical format: > Confident, not arrogant. We make declarative claims when we know we're right. We don't oversell, hedge with weasel words, or talk down to readers who know less than us. > > Warm, not saccharine. We sound like a competent colleague who likes their job. We don't use exclamation marks to perform enthusiasm or call readers "friend." Three to five attributes is the sweet spot. The Nielsen Norman Group axes: formal↔casual, serious↔funny, respectful↔irreverent, enthusiastic↔matter-of-fact. Anti-pattern: Putting all markers in the middle. "Moderately formal, moderately serious, moderately enthusiastic" is no voice. > Do: "We paused your build. Resume it when ready." > Don't: "Oops! Looks like your build got paused. No worries - just click Resume whenever you'd like to keep going! 🚀" The don't side teaches more than the do side. Pick don'ts from real drafts your team has actually shipped. Preferred - words that carry the voice. ("ship" not "release"; "you" not "the user".) Banned - words that break the voice. ("leverage", "synergy", "seamless", "robust", "delightful", "passionate".) Decisions - product-name capitalization, oxford comma, contractions allowed, em dash vs en dash. Every voice guide should display: Version (semver or date) Last reviewed date Owner (a person, not a team) Next review date (no more than 12 months out) No "we are not." Lists three

items.text: BSON BinData vector ingestion Source-anchored research for BSON BinData vector ingestion. Run status: COMPLETED. BSON Binary subtype 9 is a typed vector envelope: it uses a dtype byte and a padding byte before the packed element data, stores values in little-endian form, and defines FLOAT32 (0x27), INT8 (0x03), and PACKED_BIT (0x10) dtypes. Drivers expose explicit vector encode and decode helpers, such as PyMongo's Binary.from_vector() and Binary.as_vector(). (high confidence) MongoDB documents about three times less cluster disk space for BinData vectors than standard float32 arrays. Pre-quantized int8 and int1 representations reduce mongot vector RAM by about 3.75x and 24x respectively; the HNSW graph itself does not shrink, so disk and index-memory savings must be estimated separately. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) A vector query must use the same embedding model as the indexed data and its length must match numDimensions. A full-fidelity query vector can match BinData(float32) data; using a mismatched subtype with int8 or int1 data can return no results without an error. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) MongoDB Vector Search accepts BSON BinData vector subtypes float32, int8, and int1 in vector index fields. The documented numDimensions range is 1–8192 for int8, a multiple of 8 for int1, and no more than 8192 overall. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) The client must convert pre-quantized embeddings to BSON BinData subtype 9 before inserting them, using a driver that supports vector encoding. The current MongoDB guide lists minimum supported driver versions, and PyMongo added Binary.from_vector() and Binary.as_vector() in version 4.10. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Quantization can trade retrieval precision for lower memory and faster comparisons. MongoDB's benchmark says binary quantization can materially reduce search precision and that rescoring candidates from full-fidelity vectors adds latency, so resource ratios do not guarantee equal quality or lower end-to-end latency for every embedding model and workload. (medium confidence) Embedding APIs can return quantized outputs, but those outputs are not automatically BSON vector values. Voyage AI and Cohere document int8 and binary-family output choices, while BSON subtype 9 requires its own dtype and padding metadata; convert the provider output using a compatible driver and verify the exact binary representation.
