items.summary: General educational information only — not financial advice. Methods, dollar
items.text: Budgeting and Saving General educational information only — not financial advice. Methods, dollar General educational information only - not financial advice. Methods, dollar figures, and program details below are stated as of 2026 and are general rules of thumb, not recommendations for your situation. Account rates, app availability, and program terms change. For decisions tied to your finances, consult a licensed professional or a nonprofit (NFCC-member) credit counselor. This is a spoke of the consumer-finance family; the consumer-finance hub is the anchor, and the sibling consumer-credit-and-debt hub owns credit-score and debt-collection/settlement work - see the SKIP list in the description for the siblings that own investing, banking mechanics, debt settlement, and credit-score work. Every method below is a way to run the same three-step loop. Get the loop right first; the method is just packaging. Know your income - total monthly take-home (net) pay, not gross. Use pay stubs. (See §6 if income is irregular.) Track your spending - log where money actually goes for at least a few weeks before trusting any budget. Most people underestimate discretionary spending until they see it. Start small (one week of receipts or one checking account) if it feels overwhelming. Plan and adjust - assign the income to categories, compare plan vs. actual at month-end, and adjust. Income minus expenses should be ≥ 0; if it's negative you're spending more than you make and need to cut, earn more, or both. A budget is simply a written plan for the money you expect each month. Its job is to make sure money covers obligations and leaves room to save. These are not exclusive. A common, durable combination: pay-yourself-first to automate savings off the top, run the rest as a zero-based plan, and use envelopes only on the one or two categories that tend to overspend. Pick a capture method you'll actually keep up with: a notebook/journal, a receipts-in-a-folder review at week's end, a spreadsheet, or an app that auto-imports transactions. Consistency beats sophistication. Categorize (housing, utilities, groceries, transportation, dining, entertainment, etc.) so you can see patterns, then compare to your plan. The CFPB publishes free, no-login Spending Tracker and Budget Worksheet tools (see References) that do this on paper or PDF. Review plan vs. actual monthly. The point of tracking isn't guilt - it's finding the one or two categories where small changes free up real money.

It is the highest-conversion content asset in B2B marketing because it does the one thing prospects A case study is a published narrative of one customer's outcome with a vendor's product or approach. It is the highest-conversion content asset in B2B marketing because it does the one thing prospects most need: prove that a buyer like them succeeded with this solution. The defining traits of a case study: Specific, named (or carefully anonymized) customer Concrete before/after with quantified outcomes At least one direct quote from a named customer stakeholder A clear narrative arc: Challenge → Solution → Result Customer approval in writing before publication A non-marketing tone - the customer is the protagonist, not the vendor Front-load the result. Place the hero metric in the title or subtitle, and again in the first paragraph. Name the customer when: Written marketing approval is signed; customer is referenceable; naming helps, not hurts. Anonymize when: Regulated industry; sensitive admission; customer in quiet period. Anonymization patterns: "A Fortune 500 financial-services firm headquartered in the U.S. Northeast" - High trust "A large healthcare provider" - Low trust Specific baseline: "down from 4.2 hours to 12 minutes" beats "much faster" Specific time window: "in the first 90 days" beats "over time" Specific scope: "across 1,200 trades per day" Verifiable source: the customer signed off on this number Attributed to a named individual with a title Sounds like a human said it (not vendor-speak) Specific, not generic ("we cut our deploy time in half" beats "Acme has been a great partner") Bad quote: "Acme is a true partner who has helped us leverage our data to drive transformational outcomes." Good quote: "We used to spend two full days every month reconciling reports. items.text: Causal Consistency MongoDB replication provides redundancy and high availability through replica sets -- groups of mongod processes that maintain the same data set. A replica set contains one primary member that receive MongoDB replication provides redundancy and high availability through replica sets -- groups of mongod processes that maintain the same data set. A replica set contains one primary member that receives all writes and one or more secondary members that replicate the primary's data asynchronously via the oplog (operations log). Replica sets are the foundation of MongoDB's data durability, fault tolerance, and read scaling strategy. Key guarantees of a properly configured replica set: Automatic failover: if the primary becomes unavailable, an election promotes a secondary to primary within ~12 seconds (median, with default settings). Data redundancy: every data-bearing member holds a complete copy of the data set. Read scaling: applications can distribute reads across secondaries using read preferences. Tunable consistency: write concern and read concern let applications choose their durability and consistency guarantees per operation. Primary: The only member that accepts write operations. Records all writes to its oplog. At most one primary per replica set at any time. Secondary: Maintains an identical copy of the primary's data set by asynchronously applying operations from the primary's oplog. Can serve read operations when read preference allows it. Can be elected primary during failover. Arbiter: Participates in elections but holds no data. Provides a tiebreaking vote in even-member-count topologies. Must not run on the same system as primary or secondary members. Has exactly 1 election vote and a default priority of 0. Hidden Members: Must have priority: 0, so they cannot become primary. Excluded from default client read routing. Use for dedicated tasks: reporting queries, backups, analytics workloads. Only reachable by direct connection. Delayed Members: Maintain a time-delayed copy of the data (configured via secondaryDelaySecs). Must be hidden and should be non-voting. Serve as a defense against accidental data destruction -- the delayed copy preserves the state from N seconds ago. Three-member replica set (P-S-S): One primary, two secondaries. Minimum recommended production topology. Tolerates one member failure while maintaining majority for elections and w: "majority" writes. Primary-Secondary-Arbiter (P-S-A): Costs less but carri

items.concept: Causal Discovery and Structure Learning
items.summary: Causal discovery (a.k.a. structure learning) learns the causal graph itself
items.text: Causal Discovery and Structure Learning Causal discovery (a.k.a. structure learning) learns the causal graph itself Causal discovery (a.k.a. structure learning) learns the causal graph itself from observational and/or interventional data - the edges and their directions - rather than assuming the graph and estimating an effect. This is the upstream problem to causal inference. This skill (discovery): "What is the causal structure? Which variables cause which?" → output is a graph (DAG, CPDAG, or PAG). da-12 (inference): "Given this DAG, what is the effect of X on Y?" → DiD, RDD, IV, propensity scores, synthetic control, backdoor/frontdoor adjustment. If the user already has/assumes a DAG and wants an effect estimate, defer to da-12-ab-testing-causal-inference. Use this skill only when the structure is the unknown. The hard truth of discovery: from purely observational data you usually cannot recover a single DAG - only an equivalence class of DAGs (a CPDAG or PAG). Pinning down direction requires extra assumptions (non-Gaussianity, nonlinearity), interventions, or time order. Always communicate which edges are oriented vs. undetermined. Two DAGs are Markov equivalent if they entail the same conditional independences - they have the same skeleton (undirected edges) and the same v-structures / colliders (A → C ← B with A, B not adjacent). Equivalent DAGs cannot be distinguished by observational independence tests alone (Verma & Pearl, 1990; Andersson, Madigan & Perlman, 1997). A CPDAG (Completed Partially Directed Acyclic Graph, a.k.a. essential graph) represents the whole Markov equivalence class: directed edges are oriented in every member, undirected edges flip across members. Constraint- and score-based methods return a CPDAG, not a DAG. Reporting a single oriented DAG from such output is a common, serious error. Causal Markov condition: each variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents. Faithfulness: every conditional independence in the distribution is implied by the graph structure (no exact cancellations). Near-violations cause unstable orientation in finite samples (Spirtes, Glymour & Scheines, 2000). Causal sufficiency: no unmeasured common causes (latent confounders). PC and GES assume this; FCI does not. Acyclicity: most methods assume a DAG (no feedback loops). Identifiability hinges on these. Be explicit which the chosen method needs. PC algorithm (Peter–Clark; Spirtes, Glymour & Scheines, 2000): start from a complete undire

items.summary: The MongoDB Connector for Apache Kafka is a Kafka Connect plugin that bridges MongoDB and Kafka in both directions:
items.text: CDC-patterns The MongoDB Connector for Apache Kafka is a Kafka Connect plugin that bridges MongoDB and Kafka in both directions: The MongoDB Connector for Apache Kafka is a Kafka Connect plugin that bridges MongoDB and Kafka in both directions: Source connector: MongoDB change streams → Kafka topics (CDC pipeline) Sink connector: Kafka topics → MongoDB collections (event consumer) Supports Confluent Platform, Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK, and self-managed Kafka. This publishes change events to topic mongo.mydb.orders (format: <prefix>.<db>.<collection>). The connector automatically persists the resume token in a Kafka Connect offsets topic. On restart, it resumes from the saved token. If the token expires (oplog window exceeded during connector downtime): Configure DLQ to route failed messages instead of stopping the connector: DLQ messages include headers with error context. Process DLQ messages with a separate consumer for alerting or manual replay. ChangeStreamHistoryLost (error code 286): The oplog has been truncated past the resume token. Resolution: Set startup.mode=timestamp to start from a recent time Or re-snapshot with startup.mode=copy_existing Increase oplog size to prevent future occurrences InvalidResumeToken: Resume token is corrupted or from an incompatible MongoDB version. Resolution: clear stored offset and restart connector. DuplicateKey (11000): Configure ReplaceOneDefaultStrategy instead of InsertOneDefaultStrategy to make sink idempotent. DocumentValidationFailure (121): Kafka messages don't match MongoDB $jsonSchema validator. Check message schema vs collection validator. Worker parallelism: Set tasks.max equal to the number of Kafka partitions for the topic. For near-real-time with low latency: Use poll.await.time.ms: 100 (shorter poll interval) Monitor consumer lag on the Kafka topic Keep poll.max.batch.size small (100-500) for lower latency at cost of throughput Single-partition topics with multiple sink tasks: Multiple sink tasks on a single partition = contention; match tasks.max to partition count Not configuring DLQ: Connector stops on first unprocessable message; always configure DLQ in production InsertOneDefaultStrategy for idempotent pipelines: Insert fails on duplicate; use ReplaceOneDefaultStrategy or BulkWriteStrategy for idempotent sinks Monitoring consumer lag but not resume token age: Consumer lag tells you about Kafka backlog; resume token age tells you about oplog risk (if token becomes invalid = full resync) Not in

A renderer that loops with `.All()` therefore emits keys in the order the client's JSON had them. The Qwen3.5 renderer writes the tool block first, inside the leading system turn, and serialises each tool with `marshalWithSpaces`. `marshalWithSpaces` runs `json.Marshal` and then inserts a space after every `:` and `,` that lies outside a string, to mimic Python `json.dumps` spacing. The Qwen3.5 renderer renders an assistant `<think>` block only for assistant turns after the last real user query, unless the Qwen3.8 variant flag `alwaysRenderAssistantThinkBlock` is set. The Qwen3-Coder renderer takes the first system message and drops later ones, and adds the default system text "You are Qwen, a helpful AI assistant that can interact with a computer to solve tasks." when tools exist but no system message does. The Qwen3-Coder renderer emits extra schema keys (anything except `type` and `description` on a property, and anything except `type` and `properties` on the parameters object) through `renderAdditionalKeys`. That helper marshals the object, unmarshals it into a `map[string]any`, and ranges over the map. Ollama moved newer models from Go `TEMPLATE` strings to registered renderer and parser pairs; the qwen3-coder renderer carries a TODO to match Python `json.dumps` spacing, and the later Qwen3.5 renderer added `marshalWithSpaces` to do so. llama.cpp issue 26974 (2026-08-12) showed template render time growing quadratically with tool count; PR 27034 merged 2026-08-14 with byte-identical prompts. items.summary: A chatbot is a conversation, not an interface. Every turn the bot takes should advance the user's goal or surface a clear next move. The work breaks into three layers:
items.text: Chatbot Conversation Writing A chatbot is a conversation, not an interface. Every turn the bot takes should advance the user's goal or surface a clear next move. The work breaks into three layers: A chatbot is a conversation, not an interface. Every turn the bot takes should advance the user's goal or surface a clear next move. The work breaks into three layers: Persona - who the bot is, what it sounds like, what it refuses to do. Turn design - the individual response, plus the choices it offers. Recovery design - what happens when the bot doesn't understand, when the user is angry, or when the conversation has to leave the bot. The four Gricean maxims: Quantity - say as much as is needed, not more Quality - only say true things Relation - stay on the user's topic Manner - be clear, brief, and orderly A minimum persona doc includes: Name (or explicit no-name policy) Role (what the bot is for - support? sales? in-product help?) Voice traits (3–5 adjectives - e.g., "warm, precise, never cute") Refuses to do (e.g., diagnose medical issues, take payment, promise pricing) Vocabulary (3–5 words it uses; 3–5 it doesn't) Disclosure boilerplate (the exact "I'm an AI assistant" line) Escalation trigger phrases As of 2026, plain-and-unambiguous AI disclosure is no longer optional: California SB 243 (effective Jan 1, 2026) requires disclosure, plus reminders every three hours for minor users EU AI Act requires upfront disclosure for any AI system interacting with natural persons FTC treats undisclosed AI as potentially deceptive Writing implications: Disclose in the first turn, not buried in a tooltip Use direct language: "I'm an AI assistant" - not "I'm an enhanced automation experience" If asked "are you a human?" answer plainly: "No, I'm an AI assistant." A conversational turn has three jobs: Acknowledge what the user just said Resolve the user's intent Hand the turn back with a clear next move Length convention: 1–3 short sentences per turn for support bots, 1–5 sentences for in-product help. When the bot doesn't understand, three things must happen: Admit it cleanly. "I'm not sure what you mean by 'reset'." Offer a small, finite menu. Two or three concrete interpretations. Provide a path out. Always include "talk to a human" no later than the second failed understanding. Three transfer rules: Drop the edge in failure modes. Humor in a working flow is fine. Humor when the user is locked out is not. Keep the rhythm, simplify the vocabulary. Reuse hero phrases spari

items.text: Claude Code effort levels forwarded to local Anthropic-compatible servers Claude Code resolves the session effort in this order: an explicit choice (`CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`, `--effort`, or `/effort`), then saved settings (`modelSettings` per model or the `effortLevel` key), then the model's default effort. Claude Code resolves the session effort in this order: an explicit choice (`CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`, `--effort`, or `/effort`), then saved settings (`modelSettings` per model or the `effortLevel` key), then the model's default effort. `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` accepts `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` or `auto`, takes precedence over `--effort`, `/effort`, `modelSettings` and `effortLevel`, and a `maxEffortLevel` cap still applies. The model-config page lists effort levels only for Claude models (Fable 5.x, Opus 5.x/4.8/4.7, Sonnet 5.x with five levels; Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 with low, medium, high, max) and says models not listed do not support effort. If the level set is unsupported by the active model, Claude Code runs the highest supported level at or below it, for example `xhigh` runs as `high` on Opus 4.6. Model default effort is `high` except Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 (`medium`) and Opus 4.7 (`xhigh`). `CLAUDE_CODE_ALWAYS_ENABLE_EFFORT=1` sends the effort parameter on every request even when Claude Code does not recognise the model ID as effort-capable, intended for gateways and providers serving custom identifiers; models that reject effort (Claude 3, Sonnet 4.0 and 4.5, Opus 4.0 and 4.1, Haiku 4.5) stay excluded. Claude Code enables effort and extended thinking by matching the model ID against known patterns, so Bedrock ARNs and custom deployment names leave them disabled; `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_{OPUS,SONNET,HAIKU,FABLE}_MODEL_SUPPORTED_CAPABILITIES` and `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION_SUPPORTED_CAPABILITIES` take a comma list such as `effort,thinking` to declare what a pinned or custom model supports. `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING=1` omits the `thinking` parameter from requests entirely as a compatibility option for proxies that reject it, and on models that think by default the model may still think. `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0` disables thinking on the Anthropic API but on third-party providers it only omits the `thinking` parameter. items.text: Claude Code reactive compaction error-wording recognition Claude Code documents three recognised too-long wordings: `Prompt is too long`, Bedrock's `Input is too long for requested model`, and the token `capability_rejected: prompt_too_long` from a Claude apps gateway. Claude Code documents three recognised too-long wordings: `Prompt is too long`, Bedrock's `Input is too long for requested model`, and the token `capability_rejected: prompt_too_long` from a Claude apps gateway. Claude Code did not recognise Bedrock's `Input is too long for requested model` before v2.1.217, so auto-compact never triggered on it and `/compact` failed with the same error. Claude Code did not recognise `capability_rejected: prompt_too_long` before v2.1.228. The gateway troubleshooting table names `ContextWindowExceededError` and `prompt token count of N exceeds the limit of M` as gateway-worded 400s that Claude Code does not recognise, so it does not compact and retry automatically. For a gateway-enforced limit the documented fix is `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` set to the gateway limit, which Claude Code clamps to at least 100,000 and at most the model's context window, so a gateway limit below 100,000 cannot be matched and `/compact` stays the recovery. The same table advises setting `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` below the gateway model's output limit. llama-server's slot-time overflow message is `request (%d tokens) exceeds the available context size (%d tokens), try increasing it`, raised when the request token count is at least the slot's `n_ctx`, with error type `ERROR_TYPE_EXCEED_CONTEXT_SIZE`. llama-server formats that error as JSON with `code` 400, the message, and `type` `exceed_context_size_error`. A user capture shows the same llama-server message in the form `request (4559 tokens) exceeds the available context size (2048 tokens), try increasing it`. Neither `exceed_context_size_error` nor the llama-server message text appears among the wordings the Claude Code errors page lists as recognised. An interactive session shows the too-long condition as `Context limit reached · /compact or /clear to continue`, while `-p` output and the transcript keep `Prompt is too long`; with `DISABLE_COMPACT` set the line names only `/clear`. When automatic compaction itself fails, the message is `Prompt is too long · automatic compaction failed: <underlying error>`, and `/compact` fails on the same error until the cause is fixed; before v2.1.229 the cause was omitted. Fact 61 mentions "Max has been called on to help in three (3) separate instances" which appears unrelated to client sessions and causal consistency, potentially indicating a data extraction error or irrelevant content. Sources: https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/DRIVERS-2860 [medium] Applications must ensure that only one thread at a time executes operations in a client session, as a session can only be used with the MongoClient object that created it and cannot be used concurrently. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/read-isolation-consistency-recency.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/Mongo.startSession.md [low] The following operations build in-memory structures and are not causally consistent, returning an error if associated with a causally consistent client session: $currentOp, getMore, ping, and serverStatus. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/read-isolation-consistency-recency.md [low] Drivers must raise an error if startSession is called when multiple users are authenticated, and once a ClientSession has ended, drivers must report an error if any operations are attempted with that session. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/sessions/driver-sessions.md [low] If sessions are not supported, drivers must raise an error for explicit sessions but must ignore the session for implicit sessions. items.concept: Cloudflare AI-crawler monetization & verification stack
items.summary: The stack Cloudflare built to answer three separated questions about AI crawler traffic — who is this crawler provably (Web Bot Auth, an RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures profile, feeding the BotBase behavior taxonomy of Verified Bots), may it have this content (AI Crawl Control's WAF-rule enforcement plus managed robots.txt and the Content Signals Policy, which are declarations, not enforcement), and at what price (Pay Per Crawl's HTTP 402 protocol, Stripe-settled with Cloudflare as Merchant of Record). Drawn from one 2026-09-02 research reference (10 sections, 81 footnotes) covering the default-block policy timeline, enforcement/evasion evidence (the Cloudflare vs Perplexity dispute), structural criticism (gatekeeper concentration, standards capture), and competing standards (RSL, TDMRep, ai.txt, AIPREF, x402).

Drawn from one 2026-09-02 research reference (10 sections, 81 footnotes) covering the default-block policy timeline, enforcement/evasion evidence (the Cloudflare vs Perplexity dispute), structural criticism (gatekeeper concentration, standards capture), and competing standards (RSL, TDMRep, ai.txt, AIPREF, x402). **Crawler-side onboarding is a five-step gauntlet**: set up a Cloudflare account → get the crawler **verified** (Web Bot Auth + verified-bot policy + Bot Submission Form, choosing bot type **Verified Bot** or **Signed Agent** and method **Request Signature**) → discover payable content → connect Stripe → crawl[^ppc-3][^ppc-9]. **Cloudflare is the Merchant of Record** — it both runs the payment relationship and provides the infrastructure[^ppc-1]. That is a stronger position than "payment processor": it is the counterparty of record on both sides. Absence from the list means the owner has not enabled charging for you. Cloudflare tells crawlers to cache and periodically refresh, and to still honor WAF rules and `robots.txt`[^ppc-10]. Note what this endpoint *is*: a Cloudflare-operated, Cloudflare-gated **registry of the sell side** — the marketplace's index, on a `cfdata.org` host, reachable only by crawlers Cloudflare has approved. ⚠️ **Crawl:refer ratios are the most-misquoted numbers in this space. items.summary: An Atlas cluster tier sets the RAM, vCPUs and storage of each data-bearing server and is billed per instance hour; the same M-size comes as a General tier, a Low-CPU tier that keeps RAM and storage but halves vCPUs at a lower hourly price, and an NVMe tier on locally attached ephemeral SSD with fixed storage (AWS and Azure only). Drawn from 7 source pages (MongoDB Atlas docs, the MongoDB on AWS pricing page, a Vantage blog) across definitions, parameters, measures, problems, comparisons and how-to; the only public hourly prices found are January 2022 AWS us-east-1 figures.

Drawn from 7 source pages (MongoDB Atlas docs, the MongoDB on AWS pricing page, a Vantage blog) across definitions, parameters, measures, problems, comparisons and how-to; the only public hourly prices found are January 2022 AWS us-east-1 figures. Atlas deploys all data-bearing servers in a cluster at the selected cluster tier, and the per-hour charge covers that tier's default RAM and storage. Each added data-bearing node is therefore a full node at the same hourly tier cost, except analytics nodes with a separate tier. On Atlas Core clusters, the cluster tier sets the RAM, vCPUs, and storage for each data-bearing server [1] in the cluster. On Atlas Infinite clusters, the cluster tier sets the RAM, vCPUs, and IOPS for each node in the cluster. We also offer low CPU instance types, with comparable amounts of RAM and storage, at slightly lower price points. For applications hosted on AWS or Azure that require low-latency and high-throughput I/O, Atlas offers storage options using locally attached ephemeral NVMe SSDs. NVMe clusters use a hidden secondary node that consists of a provisioned volume with high throughput and IOPS to facilitate backup. When creating a new cluster through the Atlas UI, Atlas automatically selects the Gen2 option under the Cluster Tier section for eligible clusters. For an Atlas Core cluster, you can select Gen1 instead to deploy a Gen1 cluster. When applied, the optimization efforts we went over in the previous section can provide a cost-benefit. If query performance is improved, it could reduce the need for higher RAM and CPU resources, making it feasible to consider a lower cluster tier. In addition, using sharded clusters distributes compute and storage resources across multiple nodes. This distribution can optimize resource utilization and potentially allow you to scale down to a less expensive cluster tier. See the MongoDB docs for instructions on how to deploy a sharded cluster. items.text: clusterTime Depth-first rabbithole dossier for clusterTime; source-anchored research pack. [medium] ClusterTime is incremented only when there is a write to a primary node's replication operation log (oplog), and every write or event that changes state is assigned a time when applied to the primary. Sources: https://mongodb.com/blog/post/casual-guarantees-anything-casual, http://muratbuffalo.blogspot.com/2024/04/implementation-of-cluster-wide-logical.html [medium] Cluster nodes (mongod, mongos, config server, clients) always track and include the greatest known ClusterTime when sending a message, a process called gossipping the cluster time. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/causal-consistency/causal-consistency.md, http://muratbuffalo.blogspot.com/2024/04/implementation-of-cluster-wide-logical.html [low] When a driver sends a non-SDAM command to a server, it MUST include the highest seen cluster time in a top-level field called $clusterTime, sending the greater of the clusterTime values from MongoClient and ClientSession. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/sessions/driver-sessions.md [low] A driver detects that it MUST participate in gossipping the cluster time when it sees a $clusterTime in a response received from a server, and if the new clusterTime is greater than the session's current clusterTime, the session's clusterTime MUST be advanced. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/sessions/driver-sessions.md [low] Cluster time is only used in replica sets and sharded clusters, and when connected to a deployment that does not support cluster times, messages sent to the server should not include $clusterTime. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/causal-consistency/causal-consistency.md [low] When connected to a deployment that does support cluster times, messages sent to the server should include $clusterTime, and the server reports its view of the current cluster time in the $clusterTime field in responses from the server. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/causal-consistency/causal-consistency.md [low] A driver MUST NOT use the clusterTime of a ClientSession anywhere else except when executing an operation with this session. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/sessions/driver-sessions.md [low]

items.text: CMAP Connection Pooling Depth-first rabbithole dossier for CMAP Connection Pooling; source-anchored research pack. Primary sources are the CMAP spec, its test README, and the DRIVERS-1943 ticket. The disconfirming sources are DRIVERS-1943 (against the fixed `maxConnecting` default) and HikariCP (against large default pools). - **One pool per server, per client.** Each `MongoClient` owns a separate pool for each server. If an application creates a client per request, the connection count multiplies. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/troubleshooting/connection-storms/ - **Connection storms.** Storms follow restarts, failovers, and traffic spikes when `minPoolSize` is far below `maxPoolSize`. The manual advises raising `minPoolSize` toward `maxPoolSize` to pre-warm the pool. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/troubleshooting/connection-storms/ CMAP's own brakes are `maxConnecting`, pausing on clear, and dropping the W - **Source count:** 9 sources on 5 hosts (specifications.readthedocs.io, mongodb.com, jira.mongodb.org, oneuptime.com, plus the mongodb.com community forum). The gate of 3 or more sources is met. - **Independence is weak.** Every source except oneuptime.com is written or hosted by MongoDB. The third-party source only confirms defaults and adds no independent analysis of the mechanism. I found no academic or independent analysis of CMAP. - **Disconfirming sources** were sought and found: the manual's "creates connections at startup" claim, the Ruby defaults and event ordering, and DRIVERS-1943 **Out of scope:** SDAM server monitoring beyond the rules that clear or ready a pool; server selection; CSOT; retryable reads and writes; the server-side pools on mongos and mongod; load balancer internals. Each one is a separate frontier item. This report cites SDAM only where it decides when CMAP clears a pool or marks it ready. **Out of scope:** SDAM (server discovery and monitoring), except where it triggers a pool clear. Also out of scope: the CSOT timeout spec, retryable reads and writes, server-side `mongos` task-executor pools, server ingress rate limiters, and general non-MongoDB pooling theory. items.text: Code comment narration and over-explanation Source-anchored research for Code comment narration and over-explanation. Run status: COMPLETED. The characteristic narration tell is a comment that restates the adjacent code, adding maintenance burden and burying the few comments that matter. (low confidence) Comment-based detection is a weak, proxy signal: the repository study calls its results proxy-based and warns detectors both under- and over-estimate LLM use, and other work reports commercial detectors are affected by comments and unreliable. (medium confidence) Agent guidance for avoiding the tell: do not add comments by default; add one only for non-obvious why (rationale, constraints, invariants, trade-offs, surprising external behavior); prefer better names, types and structure over narration. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-04) LLM comments are not uniformly poor: in a 415-comment Java evaluation, human experts judged 58.8% to match originals and 27.7% to surpass them; automated metrics such as BLEU correlated negatively with human judgment. (low confidence) A 2021-2025 study of eight GitHub repositories found comments flagged as likely LLM-generated concentrated in Meta and Explanation categories, and remained relatively stable over time. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-01)

items.summary: Translating a specification, requirement, or feature request into a structured sequence of implementable tasks.
items.text: Code Plan Writing Translating a specification, requirement, or feature request into a structured sequence of implementable tasks. Translating a specification, requirement, or feature request into a structured sequence of implementable tasks. Break-even point: any change touching 4+ files, any refactor with a coherent end state. Every plan document must contain these sections in order: Header - Feature name, one-sentence goal, architecture summary, tech stack File Map - Table: Action (Create/Modify/Delete) | File path | Responsibility Tasks - Numbered blocks with checkbox steps, exact code, commands, and expected outputs Validation - Per-task done criteria + overall acceptance criteria Not In Scope - Explicit list of excluded work Delivery: Save to docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-slug>.md unless the user specifies otherwise. Self-contained documents for autonomous multi-hour execution. Required sections: Purpose, Progress (timestamped checkboxes), Surprises & Discoveries, Decision Log, Context & Orientation, Concrete Steps (exact commands + expected outputs), Validation & Acceptance, Idempotence & Recovery. Planning Without a Spec - Plan solves the wrong problem Placeholder Steps - Defers decisions to the implementer Monolith Tasks - Tasks touching 10+ files are decomposition failures Plan-Then-Forget - Plan becomes fiction when reality diverges A feature request or spec needs to become a structured sequence of implementable tasks before any code gets written, rather than being coded ad hoc from the ticket description. The change touches four or more files, or is a refactor with a coherent end state, the pack's own stated break-even point for when a written plan is worth the overhead. Handing off implementation to an AI agent for autonomous multi-hour execution and needing an ExecPlan-style self-contained document with Purpose, Progress, Surprises and Discoveries, and a Decision Log. A File Map — a table of Create, Modify, or Delete actions per file path with each file's responsibility — is needed before starting, so the scope of a change is visible up front rather than discovered mid-implementation. Write a full plan document with the required sections in order, starting with a Header and a File Map, for a feature that touches at least four files, and use the break-even rule to confirm a plan was actually warranted. Build an ExecPlan template with the required sections, Purpose, timestamped Progress checkboxes, Surprises and Discoveries, and a Decisio

The Codex config reference lists `model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope` directly after `model_auto_compact_token_limit` with the values `total` and `body_after_prefix`. Codex exposes `compact_prompt` (an inline override of the history compaction prompt) and `experimental_compact_prompt_file` (the same override loaded from a file, marked experimental). Codex's hook events include `PreCompact` and `PostCompact`, configured as matcher groups under `hooks.<Event>`. Codex's `tool_output_token_limit` is the token budget for storing an individual tool or function output in history. `model_catalog_json` is an optional path to a JSON model catalog loaded at startup, and a profile file can override it per profile. Codex ships a built-in table of context windows, tool support and input modalities for OpenAI's own models; for any other slug it warns `Model metadata for <slug> not found. Defaulting to fallback metadata`, once per session. Unsloth's fix for that warning is `model_context_window = 131072` in `~/.codex/config.toml` for a 128K model, and a custom `ModelInfo` entry in the file named by `model_catalog_json` to control tool support and input modalities. A Codex remote-compaction call to an OpenAI model failed with `context_length_exceeded` ("Your input exceeds the context window of this model") in a long-running session, and the same session first showed a misleading "high demand" message on the older model. Inferred: `body_after_prefix` helps a local server only if the prefix it excludes is stable across compactions, so the local KV cache for that prefix stays warm; the docs do not say whether that is the intent. Inferred: for a local server with window W, setting `model_context_window` to W and `model_auto_compact_token_limit` below W minus the largest tool result is the same rule as for Claude Code, and the scope key changes only the quantity compared.

Per-thread `config` overrides are accepted but do not reapply this (no-ops)." The config schema describes `model_catalog_json` as "Optional path to a JSON model catalog (applied on startup only). Per-thread `config` overrides are accepted but do not reapply this (no-ops)." The catalog file is a JSON object with a `models` array; the Rust type `ModelsResponse` holds `models: Vec<ModelInfo>`. On main (read 2026-10-04) these `ModelInfo` fields have no serde default and no `Option` type, so a catalog entry must supply them: `slug`, `display_name`, `supported_reasoning_levels`, `shell_type`, `visibility`, `supported_in_api`, `priority`, `support_verbosity`, `truncation_policy` and `experimental_supported_tools`. An entry that has neither a top-level `base_instructions` nor `model_messages.instructions_template` fails to load with the error "model `<slug>` is missing both `base_instructions` and `model_messages.instructions_template`". The deserializer promotes a deprecated top-level `base_instructions` string into `model_messages.instructions_template` when no template is present. `shell_type` accepts `unified_exec` (aliases `default`, `local`, `shell_command`) or `disabled`; `visibility` accepts `list`, `hide` or `none`; `apply_patch_tool_type` accepts `freeform`; `web_search_tool_type` accepts `text` or `text_and_image`. `truncation_policy` is an object with `mode` (`bytes` or `tokens`) and an integer `limit`; `tool_mode` accepts `direct`, `code_mode` or `code_mode_only`. `input_modalities` takes `text`, `image` or `audio` and defaults to text plus image when omitted, so a text-only local model needs an explicit `["text"]`. `effective_context_window_percent` defaults to 95, and `usable_context_window` is `context_window * percent / 100`, where the window is `context_window` or else `max_context_window`. When `auto_compact_token_limit` is absent Codex derives it as 90 percent of the context window, and a configured limit is clamped to the smaller of the limit and 90 percent of the window. `supports_reasoning_summary_parameter` defaults to true and says whether the model accepts the Responses `reasoning.summary` parameter, so a local server that rejects it needs `false`. `supports_search_tool` and `use_responses_lite` default to false; `supports_reasoning_effort_updates` default

items.concept: Codex namespace and hosted tool types skipped by local servers
items.summary: In a `codex exec` run against llama-server with one MCP server, the outbound `tools[]` held 13 native Codex function tools, `{"type":"web_search"}` and one `namespace` entry with two nested `function` tools.
items.text: Codex namespace and hosted tool types skipped by local servers In a `codex exec` run against llama-server with one MCP server, the outbound `tools[]` held 13 native Codex function tools, `{"type":"web_search"}` and one `namespace` entry with two nested `function` tools. In a `codex exec` run against llama-server with one MCP server, the outbound `tools[]` held 13 native Codex function tools, `{"type":"web_search"}` and one `namespace` entry with two nested `function` tools. The same Codex session over the ChatGPT websocket transport sends an identical `namespace` shape, and the ChatGPT backend unwraps it server-side. The issue lists affected backends: llama.cpp skips `namespace` silently, LM Studio rejects it with `invalid_request_error`, DeepSeek via CLIProxyAPI returns plain text with no `function_call`, and Ollama's Responses API lost MCP tool invocation from Codex v0.117.0. The issue proposes that Codex flatten MCP namespaces into top-level function tools whenever the transport is not the ChatGPT websocket, keeping the namespaced name end to end. The Codex issue was labelled bug, CLI, mcp, custom-model and exec, and was still open with new comments on 2026-08-18. A user proxy (`codex-ollama-proxy`) flattens `namespace` tools, maps returned flat names back to `{namespace, name}`, lifts newer `additional_tools` input items into the top-level tool list, translates custom tools such as `apply_patch`, and translates ordinary `tool_search` function calls back into native `tool_search_call` items. A second gateway test with Ollama showed the model receiving only `function` tools and its call returning as `{"type":"function_call","name":"search","namespace":"mcp__open_websearch__",...}`, so same-named tools on two servers stay distinct. The llama.cpp PR 23041 author lists `file_search`, `web_search`, `mcp`, `image_generation` and `namespace` as Responses tool types beyond `function`, and says llama.cpp passes to the backend only the ones it can support. A reviewer on the PR called full parity infeasible because OpenAI keeps changing Codex, and the PR author said server-hosted tools (`web_search`, `code_interpreter`, `mcp`) belong in a separately maintained tools service, outside the PR. PR 23041 added a warning for each skipped Responses tool and kept a rejection for the Codex plus gpt-oss `apply_patch` freeform tool, but the author later dropped that legacy path after finding Codex 0.130.0 no longer advertised `apply_patch` for gpt-oss-20b. The PR was merged

Which commit removed `namespace_tools`, and whether a replacement gate exists in the app-server or in the Chat-Completions bridge. `ProviderCapabilities` has four fields: `image_generation`, `web_search`, `external_web_access` and `remote_compaction`. The struct's default sets `image_generation`, `web_search` and `external_web_access` to true and `remote_compaction` to `Unsupported`. `from_config` sets `remote_compaction` to `V2` for OpenAI and Azure Responses providers and applies config overrides only to `external_web_access` and `remote_compaction`. The doc comment calls these capabilities "a provider-owned upper bound" that model and turn settings can further restrict. `ModelProviderCapabilities` has two `Option` fields, `external_web_access` and `remote_compaction`, and denies unknown fields in its JSON schema. `RemoteCompactionSupport` has two values: `Unsupported` (local compaction) and `V2` (send `compaction_trigger` items over the Responses endpoint). `ModelProviderInfo` has `capabilities: Option<ModelProviderCapabilities>`, `wire_api`, `supports_websockets` and `supports_standalone_web_search` as separate fields. The `ModelProvider` trait's default `capabilities()` returns `ProviderCapabilities::default()` and the concrete provider returns `ProviderCapabilities::from_config(&self.info)`. `ToolSpec::Namespace` is serialized under the tag `namespace` with no provider condition. `create_tools_json_for_responses_lite` collects `Function`, `Freeform` and default-named namespace specs into one namespace named `DEFAULT_FUNCTION_NAMESPACE` and leaves other specs as they are. In `client.rs`, `use_responses_lite` selects `create_tools_json_for_responses_lite` and an `AdditionalTools` developer item; other requests use `create_tools_raw_json_for_responses_api`; `parallel_tool_calls` is `prompt.parallel_tool_calls && !model_info.use_responses_lite`. `spec_plan.rs` passes `model_info.supports_search_tool` to `append_mcp_tools` and merges same-named namespace specs in `merge_into_namespaces`. The string `namespace_tools` does not appear in `capabilities.rs`, `provider.rs`, `lib.rs` of `codex-model-provider-info`, or `spec_plan.rs` on main.

items.text: Codex Responses API compatibility on local servers Codex's `model_providers.<id>.wire_api` accepts only `responses`, which is also the default when omitted. Codex's `model_providers.<id>.wire_api` accepts only `responses`, which is also the default when omitted. Codex reserves the built-in provider IDs `openai`, `ollama` and `lmstudio`; `--oss` runs against LM Studio or Ollama and `oss_provider` sets the default. Codex provider keys include `stream_idle_timeout_ms` (default 300000), `supports_websockets`, `query_params` and `env_key`. In an April 2026 test with Codex CLI v0.123.0, `/v1/responses` worked for direct non-agent requests on llama.cpp but a real `codex exec` failed with HTTP 400 `'type' of tool must be 'function'`. The captured Codex `tools[]` held `function`, `web_search`, `image_generation` and `namespace` entries, and a small local proxy that dropped the non-function entries let Codex finish. On 2026-06-18, with codex-cli 0.141.0, the same capture still held function, several namespace, web_search and image_generation tools. An Unsloth maintainer stated Codex talks only to `/responses` and has dropped `/v1/chat/completions`, and that a GGUF served through Unsloth Studio exposes a tested `/responses` endpoint. llama.cpp commit 91e84fed (2026-05-15), "Support for Codex CLI by skipping unsupported Responses tools (#23041)", touches `tools/server/server-chat.cpp`. On master, the Responses converter skips any tool whose `type` is not `function` with the warning "unsupported Responses tool type '%s' skipped", and removes the `tools` key if none remain. The converter sets `strict` to true on a function tool that lacks it. The converter turns `instructions` into a leading system message and keeps `user`, `system` and `developer` input messages with their original role. The converter rejects `previous_response_id` with "llama.cpp does not support 'previous_response_id'." and rejects `input_file` parts. A `reasoning` input item is converted to `reasoning_content` from `content[0].text`, and the converter throws if `content` is missing, empty or its first part has no text. `max_output_tokens` becomes `max_tokens`, and of the `reasoning` object only `effort` is mapped. llama-server also serves `POST /v1/responses/input_tokens` for token counting and states `/v1/responses` works by converting the request into a Chat Completions request. llama.cpp PR 18486 (2025-12-30) emits Responses SSE and flags a caveat: all `response.output_item.done` events come at t

items.concept: Cohort and Retention Analytics
items.summary: Retention answers the single most important growth question: do users who join
items.text: Cohort and Retention Analytics Retention answers the single most important growth question: do users who join Retention answers the single most important growth question: do users who join keep coming back? Acquisition without retention is a leaky bucket - you pour users in the top and they fall out the bottom, so growth stalls no matter how much you spend. This skill covers the math and methods for measuring retention across cohorts (groups of users grouped by a shared start or behavior), reading retention curves, doing growth accounting (decomposing user and revenue change into its parts), and the SaaS revenue-retention metrics (NRR/GRR). It is the methods layer beneath product-led and SaaS growth. Scope boundary: this skill is the measurement of who stays and by how much. For funnels/activation/North-Star use da-21-product-analytics; for probabilistic CLV (BG/NBD, gamma-gamma) use da-23-customer-lifetime-value; for hazard-rate/survival modeling use da-24-survival-analysis; for experiment-driven lift use da-12-ab-testing-causal-inference. Acquisition (time) cohort - users grouped by when they first signed up or activated (same day/week/month). Answers when users churn and lets you compare cohort quality over time. It does not tell you why (Amplitude, Cohort Retention Analysis, 2024). Behavioral cohort - users grouped by what they did (completed onboarding, used a key feature, invited a teammate), independent of join date. Answers which behaviors correlate with retention - the input to finding your activation/aha moment (Amplitude, Guide to Behavioral Cohorting, 2024; Amplitude Docs, Behavioral Cohorts). Workflow: use acquisition cohorts to detect a retention problem, behavioral cohorts to diagnose and fix it (find the behavior that separates retained from churned users) (Chameleon, Cohort Analysis 101, 2024). A retention curve plots % of a cohort still active against periods-since-start. Canonical shapes (Amplitude, Retention Curve; Churnkey, Retention Curves, 2024; Product Growth, Retention Curves Guide): Declining - slopes to zero; no group finds lasting value → no PMF. Flattening - steep early drop, then levels off at a retention floor (the long-term stable %). A flattening curve is the classic signal of product/market fit: a stable set of users is hooked. Smile - drops, flattens, then rises as churned users resurrect (often via network effects or re-engagement). The aspirational shape (Slack, Airbnb). Dead-on-arrival - near-vertical drop to ~0 by per

items.concept: Commit message and PR description tells
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Commit message and PR description tells. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Commit message and PR description tells Source-anchored research for Commit message and PR description tells. Run status: COMPLETED. In one study of security-related AI-generated PRs, 70.4% of 2,823 commit messages were high quality (contain both Why and What) and 29.6% omitted one or both. (low confidence) A classifier on AIDev PRs identified which of five agents (Codex, Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code) authored a PR at 97.2% F1; commit-message features dominated, with multiline commit ratio the strongest single signal (44.7% importance). (low confidence) Per-agent signatures differ: Codex extensive multiline commits, Copilot longer PR descriptions, Cursor bullet points and hyperlinks, Devin multiline messages. Claude Code recall was only 57% in that study, so its tells are weaker. (low confidence) Claude Code by default appends a Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer to commit messages and a 'Generated with Claude Code' line to PR bodies; cloud sessions also add a claude.ai link. The attribution.commit, attribution.pr and attribution.sessionUrl settings change or hide them. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Trailer tells are easily removed (git commit --amend, force-push, commit-msg hook), so their absence does not show human authorship. (low confidence) Agent-authored PRs show message-code inconsistency: descriptions can claim functionality with no corresponding implementation, or describe changes incompletely. A description's confident summary therefore needs checking against the diff. (medium confidence)

items.concept: Commit Message Craft
items.summary: Subject line: hard limit 50 characters. Body: wrap at 72.
items.text: Commit Message Craft Subject line: hard limit 50 characters. Body: wrap at 72. Subject line: hard limit 50 characters. Body: wrap at 72. Mechanical rules: Subject line ≤ 50 chars. Hard ceiling is 72, but cross 50 only when truly unavoidable. Blank line between subject and body - required. No trailing period on the subject. Write the subject as a command the commit gives the codebase, not as a past-tense report. Test: prepend "If applied, this commit will ___". The result must be a grammatical English sentence. Add retry logic to S3 uploader - passes Added retry logic to S3 uploader - fails Types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert Method 1 - exclamation mark in the header: Method 2 - footer token: The diff already shows what changed. The body must explain why. Body content checklist: What problem did this commit solve? Why this approach and not an alternative? Any non-obvious side effect or trade-off? Links to tickets, design docs, or incident reports. Body anti-content: Don't restate the subject line. Don't narrate the diff line by line. Prep commits first - refactors, renames, type-only changes with no behavior change. The substantive commit - the one that does the actual feature/fix. Test commit(s) - if tests are separated. Cleanup commits last - docs, changelog, version bumps. git commit --fixup=<sha> writes a commit message starting with fixup! <original-subject>. --fixup discards the fixup's commit message; only the original is kept. Use for typo fixes. --squash keeps both messages joined. Use when the "fix" adds meaningful nuance. Never push fixup commits to a shared branch as-is. Use git commit -s (or --signoff) to add automatically. Co-authored-by: Name <email> - GitHub credits both authors Closes #123, Fixes #123, Resolves #123 - GitHub auto-closes the issue "Fixed bug" / "Updates" / "WIP" - useless. Past-tense subjects - Added, Fixed, Refactored. Restating the diff in the body. Stacking unrelated changes in one commit. Burying breaking changes without ! or BREAKING CHANGE:. Conventional Commits v1.0.0 specification Tim Pope - A Note About Git Commit Messages Chris Beams - How to Write a Git Commit Message Writing a commit subject line and needing a concrete, mechanical rule, a 50-character soft limit and a 72-character hard ceiling, instead of an arbitrary length guess. Deciding whether a fix belongs in the same commit as its context or as a separate prep commit for a PR reviewer to read in a deliberate order.

items.concept: Compound index vs index union for $or
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Compound index vs index union for $or. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Compound index vs index union for $or Source-anchored research for Compound index vs index union for $or. Run status: COMPLETED. MongoDB's manual recommends `$in` when `$or` contains equality checks on the same field. That is a different query shape from a cross-field `$or` and should not be conflated with choosing between a compound index and branch indexes. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) When all $or clauses are index-supported, MongoDB can plan an OR stage over branch scans, and each clause can use its own index. If a clause lacks index support, MongoDB's manual says the query uses a collection scan. In classic explain output, an indexed $or exposes an OR stage with inputStages that list the child scans. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) Under compound-index prefix rules, `{a: 1, b: 1}` supports a lookup on `a` but not a lookup on `b` alone. For `$or: [{a: ...}, {b: ...}]`, that single compound index therefore cannot provide an efficient access path for both branches; MongoDB recommends indexes for each branch field. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) MongoDB Jira SERVER-34012 recorded quadratic planning time for very large same-index `$or` lists while unionizing index-bound intervals, and lists 5.0.0-rc0 as the fix version. This is historical planner interval-union behavior; it does not establish that multi-index `$or` result merging is generally slow. (low confidence) (verified as of 2021-05-11) A University of Sydney study evaluating MongoDB 7.0.1 found cases where its optimizer chose an index scan even though a collection scan ran faster. The study used range-query templates rather than an $or comparison, so it supports measuring the actual workload but does not establish whether an index union or a compound index wins. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-24) An independent practitioner post, updated January 25, 2026, reports a query shaped like `category = ... AND (price < ... OR quantity > ...)` where the planner selected `{category: 1, quantity: 1}` over `{category: 1, price: 1, quantity: 1}`. Treat this as a case report, not a planner guarantee, and inspect `explain` on the deployed server version. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-01-25) There is no universal performance winner implied by index shape alone: MongoDB documents branch-specific `$or` scans and compound-index prefix behavior, while explain output varies with the query engine and plan. As an inference, compare equivalent predicates

items.concept: Conceptual metaphor source domains in technical prose
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Conceptual metaphor source domains in technical prose. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Conceptual metaphor source domains in technical prose Source-anchored research for Conceptual metaphor source domains in technical prose. Run status: COMPLETED. Lakoff defines a conceptual metaphor as a systematic mapping from a source domain (e.g. journeys) to a target domain (e.g. love); the mapping licenses source-domain language and inference patterns for the target. (high confidence) Source domains are typically more concrete than targets; ARGUMENT is understood via WAR, so 'attack' and 'win' apply to arguments. (high confidence) Software-development prose draws on a small set of source domains: construction (building a house), agriculture (garden), skilled craft, and finance (technical debt with interest). (medium confidence) Each source-domain lexical item may or may not use the mapping; conventional words in the source domain are not always conventional in the target, so extending a metaphor with new source vocabulary is a novel act, not automatic. (medium confidence) A corpus study on Common Crawl (Aono et al., 2024) found verb metaphors take direct objects with lower concreteness, imageability and familiarity, and appear more in emotional, subjective sentences; this supports abstract-target claims but suggests technical, unemotional prose may use fewer live metaphors. (medium confidence) Overextending a source domain beyond the initial need creates false equivalences and limits reflection. (low confidence) Critics say conceptual metaphors are often set up from intuitive, unsystematic evidence, and corpus-based validation is limited. (low confidence)

items.text: Confidence-conditioned top-1 flip rate for literal-copy tokens llama-perplexity does not compute this. Its `--kl-divergence` pass counts one number, `n_same_top`, over all scored positions, and its other per-position statistic, Δp, is the candidate probability minus the reference probability of the corpus's actual next token, not of the reference's top-1 token. llama-perplexity does not compute this. Its `--kl-divergence` pass counts one number, `n_same_top`, over all scored positions, and its other per-position statistic, Δp, is the candidate probability minus the reference probability of the corpus's actual next token, not of the reference's top-1 token. The saved base file does contain what is needed. It begins with the 8 bytes `_logits_`, then uint32 n_ctx, int32 n_vocab, int32 n_chunk, then n_ctx times n_chunk token ids, then one record per scored position. Each position record is nv = 2*((n_vocab+1)/2) + 4 values of uint16. The first four uint16 hold two float32 values, `scale` and `min_log_prob`, and each later value decodes as log-prob = scale * u16 + min_log_prob. The encoder sets min_log_prob = min_logit - max_logit - log_sum_exp and scale = (max_logit - min_logit) / 65535, and rounds to the nearest integer, so the resolution of every stored log-prob is one scale step. Only the second half of each chunk is scored: the record count per chunk is n_ctx - 1 - n_ctx/2. A small external reader can therefore decode each record, take argmax and its probability as the reference confidence, and join it with the candidate's argmax. The candidate's argmax is not saved by llama-perplexity, so the candidate pass needs its own dump (or a patched copy of the loop that records `imax == imax_base` per position and the base top-1 probability). KLD in the llama.cpp loop sums only over vocabulary entries whose reference log-prob is above -16, so reference probabilities below about 1.1e-7 are dropped from the KLD sum. Resolution check: with a logit range of about 30 nats, one step is about 4.6e-4 nats. A top-1 probability of 0.99996 has 1-p of 4e-5, so p must be taken as one minus the summed probability of all other entries, not from the top entry's stored value. A flip needs a minimum logit-gap swing. If the reference top-1 probability is p1, any rival has probability at most 1 - p1, so the log-odds gap is at least ln(p1 / (1 - p1)): about 7.0 nats at p1 = 0.9991 and about 2.4 nats at p1 = 0.9158. High-confidence flips therefore mean large errors, not near-tie noise.

items.concept: Conformal Prediction and Uncertainty Quantification
items.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) turns any point predictor into a set predictor with a
items.text: Conformal Prediction and Uncertainty Quantification Conformal prediction (CP) turns any point predictor into a set predictor with a Conformal prediction (CP) turns any point predictor into a set predictor with a finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee. Given a target miscoverage rate alpha, CP outputs a prediction set C(X) such that P(Y in C(X)) >= 1 - alpha - holding for any underlying model, any data distribution, and any sample size, requiring only that the calibration and test data are exchangeable. It is a wrapper, not a model. You keep your XGBoost, neural net, or random forest and bolt CP on top to get honest error bars. CP is the dominant frequentist answer to "how do I get valid uncertainty without trusting my model's probabilities." Compared to Bayesian credible intervals (which require a correct prior/likelihood) and the bootstrap (asymptotic, can under-cover), CP's guarantee is exact in finite samples and model-agnostic. The modern reference is Angelopoulos & Bates, "A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification" (arXiv 2107.07511, v-series 2021-2023). The theoretical foundation is Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer, "Algorithmic Learning in a Random World" (Springer, 2005; 2nd ed. 2022). Use this skill when someone needs calibrated intervals/sets on top of an existing model. For full Bayesian modeling use da-25; for point forecasting use da-15. Split-conformal gives the exact two-sided bound 1 - alpha <= P(Y_{n+1} in C(X_{n+1})) <= 1 - alpha + 1/(n+1), where n is the calibration set size. The guarantee is marginal (averaged over the random draw of calibration + test points), not conditional on a specific X or a fixed calibration set - coverage fluctuates around the target for any one fixed calibration set, and the spread shrinks as n grows. Distribution-free and finite-sample, no asymptotics. Source: Angelopoulos & Bates 2023 (arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511); Lei et al. "Distribution-Free Predictive Inference for Regression" JASA 2018; Vovk et al. 2005. CP requires only that (X_1,Y_1)...(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}) are exchangeable: their joint distribution is invariant to permutation. This is weaker than i.i.d. but is violated by distribution shift and temporal/serial dependence - the two main ways CP breaks in practice. Source: Vovk et al. 2005; Barber, Candès, Ramdas & Tibshirani "Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability" Annals of Statistics 2023 (stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/papers/nexcp.pdf). A fun

Hub for US personal/consumer finance - money management, coverage, and life planning. Educational only, not financial advice, as of 2026. Routes to 9 spokes. Owned topics: student loans (IDR/SAVE/PSLF programs, FAFSA, default and rehabilitation); personal banking (FDIC/NCUA insurance, HYSA rates, neobanks); individual income taxes (federal brackets, standard vs itemized deductions, W-4, self-employment taxes, NC state specifics); personal insurance (auto, home/renters, life, disability); health insurance (ACA marketplace, HSA, Medicare, Medicaid); medical bills and billing disputes (surprise billing, No Surprises Act); budgeting and saving; investing and retirement (401k, IRA, Roth, Social Security claiming strategies); estate planning and wills (POA, healthcare directives, NC probate). Route to consumer-credit-and-debt (sibling hub) for anything credit- or debt-law related; venture-nc-* for business/nonprofit/payroll topics. Getting oriented across a specific personal-finance decision — comparing income-driven repayment plans, choosing a health-insurance marketplace tier, or deciding between a traditional and Roth retirement account — before consulting a licensed professional. Understanding which US federal program or protection applies to a situation (FDIC/NCUA deposit insurance limits, PSLF eligibility, the No Surprises Act on a medical bill) so you know which rule actually governs it. Preparing questions for a fee-only financial advisor, tax preparer, or insurance broker by first understanding the landscape of options (HSA vs. FSA, term vs. whole life insurance, will vs. living trust). Triaging which sibling topic actually owns a question — credit and debt-collection issues route elsewhere, business and nonprofit finance route elsewhere — so you don't search the wrong domain for an answer. Map your own situation against the nine owned topics (loans, banking, taxes, insurance, health coverage, medical billing, budgeting, investing/retirement, estate planning) to see which apply and which don't yet. Before an open-enrollment period, review the ACA marketplace, HSA, Medicare, and Medicaid distinctions so you're choosing a health-insurance path based on eligibility and cost structure, not guesswork. Scoping: prompt wording effects on task performance are not simply predicted by word frequency or perplexity, and prompts transfer poorly across datasets and models; a single modal-verb change moved performance up to 17 points in the tested older models (2023, LLaMA/OPT). Do not extrapolate fixed contagion rules from vocabulary frequency. (low confidence) Repetition priming behaves differently in base LLMs, instruct LLMs and humans; instruction tuning appears to shift models toward more controlled processing, so contagion strength cannot be assumed identical across base and tuned models. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-31) LLMs reliably repeat contextual content faithfully rather than relying only on internal parameters; RepeatLeakage exploits this to extract system prompts from GPT-Store apps and ChatGPT contexts, and the copy-from-context ability cannot be disabled without hurting core capability. (medium confidence) Anthropic's official prompting guide states that the formatting style used in a prompt may influence Claude's response style, and advises matching prompt style to desired output style; removing markdown from the prompt can reduce markdown in the output. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) In controlled dative-completion experiments, structurally primed completions show greater lexico-semantic repetition of context, i.e. structural, lexical and semantic alignment reinforce each other during generation (EMNLP 2026 Findings, submitted 2026-09-03). items.concept: Context shift and cache-overflow policy for recurrent models
items.summary: llama.cpp classifies a context by `llama_memory_seq_rm`: partial removal works (no checkpoint needed), whole-sequence only (checkpoint needed), or bounded rollback for recurrent state (checkpoint needed past the bound).
items.text: Context shift and cache-overflow policy for recurrent models llama.cpp classifies a context by `llama_memory_seq_rm`: partial removal works (no checkpoint needed), whole-sequence only (checkpoint needed), or bounded rollback for recurrent state (checkpoint needed past the bound). llama.cpp classifies a context by `llama_memory_seq_rm`: partial removal works (no checkpoint needed), whole-sequence only (checkpoint needed), or bounded rollback for recurrent state (checkpoint needed past the bound). Recurrent layers keep one running state overwritten each step; a short ring of per-token snapshots allows rollback only within `n_rs_seq` tokens. Hence shifting or dropping the head of a prompt cannot be expressed for a hybrid model; `--context-shift` is off by default and `--cache-reuse` is disabled for such contexts. 2023-11 (issue 3969, attention models): a context-shift loop when `n_keep` left almost no room; reporters proposed capping discards. 2026: hybrid models make the overflow policy a client concern (compaction), not a server feature. A request larger than the slot context is rejected and the conversation can lose its slot, evicting its own warm state. When context fills and the cache limit forces eviction, a hybrid slot reprocesses the whole history. Speculative decoding with partial acceptance can need a rollback beyond `n_rs_seq`; PR 24797 makes that fall through to normal cell removal rather than fail. Operators disable shifting (`--no-context-shift`) for correctness with hybrid models; some Qwen3.6 reporters kept it on and never reached a diagnosis (23030, held elsewhere). items.text: Continuous batching on MLX Decode is bandwidth-bound at batch 1; each added sequence reuses the same weight reads, so aggregate throughput scales sub-linearly and saturates when compute or bandwidth is full. Decode is bandwidth-bound at batch 1; each added sequence reuses the same weight reads, so aggregate throughput scales sub-linearly and saturates when compute or bandwidth is full. vllm-mlx scheduler: pending queue, active batch with a max batch size M; new requests are admitted at token boundaries; completed requests exit immediately (Algorithm 1 of the paper). llama-server slot model: `--parallel N` is a slot count; each slot has its own KV region and decode state; decode steps from different slots merge into one forward pass; a single request gains nothing from more slots. `--batch-size` (logical) and `--ubatch-size` (physical, one Metal dispatch) govern prefill; ubatch is the one that most often moves Apple prefill throughput. Memory per slot in llama-server: weights + slots x ctx_per_slot x bytes_per_token + activations + DeltaNet state. For hybrid Qwen3.6-27B attention KV is about 64 KB per token (about 4 GB per 64K-context slot); Qwen3.5-9B about 32 KB per token. DeltaNet recurrent state is a small fixed per-slot allocation that does not grow with length. vllm-mlx memory knobs: `--max-num-seqs` (default 256, which the author says would blow up KV), `--max-cache-blocks` (64-token blocks; 16384 blocks = about 30 GB pool), `--cache-memory-mb`, `--kv-cache-quantization-bits 8`. vllm-mlx has two prefix caches by engine: text models use the paged cache (sized by `--max-cache-blocks`, ignores `--cache-memory-mb`); multimodal models use a memory-aware cache sized by `--cache-memory-mb`, 30 GB per resident multimodal engine. oMLX: BatchedEngine over mlx-lm BatchGenerator, FCFS scheduler, `--max-concurrent-requests` default 8, PagedCacheManager (GPU, block, copy-on-write, prefix sharing) plus PagedSSDCacheManager. oMLX started from vllm-mlx v0.1.0; Rapid-MLX is the renamed vllm-mlx lineage (renamed 2026-03-13 per its README) and is a separate project from waybarrios/vllm-mlx; the vllm-mlx maintainers' paper is arXiv 2601.19139. mlx-lm server batching existed by v0.31.0 (issue 965 reproduces on it, Mar 2026); a late-binding checkpoint bug (PR 976, closed 2026-03-10, shipped v0.31.2) caused cross-request contamination. mlx-examples issue 1198 (Jan 2025) asked mlx-lm for Ollama-v0.2-style concurrent requests; still open, cited in Mar 2026 by a user who put a

LLM path end to end: `uv run coreai.model.registry --list-models [--type llm] [--platform macOS]` -> `uv run coreai.llm.export <HF_ID> [--platform iOS]` -> resource folder (`.aimodel` + tokenizer + other resources) -> Swift `CoreAILanguageModel(resourcesAt:)` -> `LanguageModelSession(model:)`. Export is per platform because models are specialized to the device they run on. Export defaults: macOS = dynamic KV cache, full model context, `4bit` (INT4 weight-only, block size 32); optional `4bit_weights_8bit_kv_cache` (needs coreai-opt graph mode). iOS = static shapes with a mandatory `--max-context-length`, `4bit_weight_palettized_group32` default (embedding 8-bit). Mixed-precision recipes via `--compression-config` YAML. Debug info is stripped by default (`--include-debug-info` to keep). Apple's own doc says the engine (GPU, CPU or ANE) is selected "depending on how you export it"; there is no single fixed unit for CoreAILanguageModel. Reasoning models: Core AI routes chain-of-thought into `Transcript.Entry.reasoning`, not the response text; `model.capabilities.contains(.reasoning)` reports support. Loading is async (compile plus tokenizer); preload when a request is seconds away. Specialization control: `AIModelCache.default`, `cache.model(for:options:)` returns nil if not cached (does not specialize); `AIModel.specialize(contentsOf:options:cache:cachePolicy:)` pre-specializes without loading; `SpecializationOptions` `.default` (system picks units to minimize latency), `.cpuOnly`, `init(preferredComputeUnitKind:)`, `availableKinds`; `expectFrequentReshapes = true` skips per-shape optimization for dynamic LLM decode where the sequence grows each token. Cache lifetime: invalidated always on OS update, on source `.aimodel` change, and under storage pressure unless policy `.persistent`; delete via `deleteEntries(for:)`, `deleteEntry(for:options:)`, `deleteAll()`; share across apps via app group (`AIModelCache(appGroup:)`). Core ML side (stateless prefill, Yetter): the KV tensors leave the program as outputs. For a single-batch export the cache interface concatenates all layers into one tensor of shape (num_hidden_layers, num_key_value_heads, max_cache_len, head_dim), so a stateful Qwen3-0.6B has 2 states (key_cache, value_cache) instead of 56; non-first dims must be powers of two or the model fails at predict. Core ML buffers are static: capacity is fixed at conversion (max_cache_len, 512 in Yetter's runs) and valid rows are selected by a mask or position, so a hand-off must slice to the live length. MLX side: mlx-lm keeps one cache object per layer (KVCache, RotatingKVCache, ArraysCache for linear-attention layers), grown by concatenation; a hand-off therefore needs a split of the concatenated Core ML tensor into per-layer arrays. Memory model: MLX's unified-memory design means arrays on CPU or GPU need no transfer (SqueezeBits' description), and ANE I/O is IOSurface-backed shared memory that maderix showed GPU and ANE can share; neither source documents importing an IOSurface into an MLX array. Chunked decode: the model is split into 3-4 Core ML programs run serially; Gemma 4 E2B decode is `chunk1 + chunk2_3way (L8-24) + chunk3_3way (L25-34 + lm_head)` since v1.7.0, three ANE dispatches per step, bit-equivalent to the 4-chunk build, +8.2% tok/s on iPhone 17 Pro. Prefill stays 4-chunk with batched calls (one Core ML call per 512-token chunk; multifunction `prefill_b8` and T=32 variants for small models) so the vision-aware bidirectional mask is preserved. Op-level rewrites for ANE: RMSNorm as `cat([x,-x])` into LayerNorm then slice; `nn.Linear` as 1x1 Conv2d ("about 3x faster than matmul"); manual fp16 softmax; RoPE cos/sin precomputed as inputs to avoid int gather ops that fall to CPU; in-graph argmax; PLE in-graph (8 ms to 1.8 ms per token); shift-based sliding-window KV for 28 of 35 layers. KV handling is explicit input/output tensors copied back by the host for Gemma 4 (Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 use MLState); weights shared between decode and prefill graphs by hard links (-682 MB on disk). Quality gates: a compute-plan audit (non-ANE ops at most 5%), a Mac-only determinism oracle (fixed corpus, token IDs plus sha256 with drafters off), and parity against HF top-1. Process: the repo keeps a REJECTED_APPROACHES index with revisit rules (cite new upstream evidence, link a harness, update the file), and flags stale docs; commits are co-authored by Claude Opus 4.7. 2026-04-08 initial implementation (Qwen2.5-0.5B, MLState KV, int4 palettization, Swift API); 2026-04-13 MLState rejected for Gemma 4; 2026-04-15 pipelining spikes; 2026-04-17/18 CPU-bottleneck and drafter-dead investigations; 2026-04-24 SWA prefill-write bug found and fixed; 2026-04-26/28 Round 8 candidates and LFM2.5 conversion. v1.4.0 3-chunk opt-in (31.6 to 34.2 tok/s), v1.5/1.6 Qwen3-VL 2B stateful, v1.7.0 3-chunk default, v1.8.0 Qwen3.5, v1.9.0 Gemma 4 E4B multimodal 15.7 tok/s; last commit 2026-10-02 (471 commits, 112 branches, 28 tags, 25 forks). The project's own plan changed from "reach LiteRT-LM's 56 tok/s" to "power, TTFT and the ANE decode ceiling" on 2026-04-15 after the user rejected abandoning ANE placement. The pack draws on 6 sources (MongoDB docs, MongoDB blog, Atlas Architecture Center, Pulumi registry, Foojay, MongoDB feedback portal) and covers definitions, parameters, mechanism, how-to, examples, problems and facts. It flags 1 disagreement, about whether a monthly project billing alert exists. Atlas Resource Policies are org-level, Cedar-based, forbid-only rules (permit is not supported). With no policies, users can do anything their role allows. Resource Policies are organization-level rules in Atlas that are automatically enforced across all projects and clusters under that organization. Their goal is straightforward yet powerful: to restrict specific actions or configurations that could compromise security, increase costs, or violate compliance standards. MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies address this by defining and enforcing which cluster configurations are allowed across your organization, including approved cluster topologies (replica set, sharded, or global clusters) and minimum shard counts. These guardrails guide teams toward decisions that align with your architectural goals while creating the predictability needed for accurate capacity planning. Atlas Resource Policies are controls that enable Organization Owners to constrain the specific configuration options available to developers when they create or configure Atlas clusters. MongoDB uses the open-source Cedar policy language to define Atlas Resource Policies. Cedar's design balances expressiveness with simplicity, employing a concise syntax that streamlines both writing and understanding resource policies. mongodbatlas.ResourcePolicy provides a Resource Policy resource. The resource lets you create, edit and delete resource policies to prevent misconfigurations and reduce the need for corr
