items.summary: The evidence-based science of emotion: what it is, how it arises, how it
items.text: Emotion & Affect Psychology The evidence-based science of emotion: what it is, how it arises, how it The evidence-based science of emotion: what it is, how it arises, how it spreads, and how to regulate it - applied to two operator problems: The customer's emotion: de-escalating a furious stakeholder, reading the mood of a room, not getting infected by a tense call. Your own emotion: staying regulated in an escalation, not letting a bad mood color a judgment, not over-dreading a hard conversation. This skill owns emotion mechanics. Where emotion shades into a syndrome (chronic stress, burnout, resilience) it hands off to performance-and-resilience-psychology; where it shades into moving someone (persuasion, trust, adoption) it hands off to the relevant sibling. The handoff lines are in the SKIP block above - honor them so the family stays non-redundant. A note on honesty: emotion science is contested and partly unreplicated. There is no agreed-upon list of "the emotions". The most popular applied advice ("name it to tame it", "EQ predicts success", "always reappraise") is each either oversold or context-dependent. This skill flags every one of those. The foundational insight (Lazarus): an event does not cause an emotion directly. Your appraisal of the event does. The same outage makes one customer curious ("interesting, let's dig in") and another furious ("this will get me fired") - because they appraise it differently. This is the lever: you cannot always change the event, but you can almost always influence the appraisal. Lazarus split appraisal into two steps: Primary appraisal: Is this relevant to my goals, and is it good or bad? The event is classified as harm/loss (damage done), threat (harm coming), or challenge (a hard but winnable opportunity). Threat and challenge can attach to the same situation - the difference is largely in the appraiser. Secondary appraisal: Can I cope with it? What are my resources and options? High perceived coping → challenge emotions (engagement, determination). Low perceived coping → threat emotions (anxiety, dread, anger). Scherer's Component Process Model (CPM) formalizes appraisal into a sequence of Stimulus Evaluation Checks run very fast and roughly in order: Relevance: novelty, intrinsic pleasantness, goal relevance. Implication: causal attribution (who/what caused it), goal conduciveness, urgency, outcome probability. Coping potential: control, power, ability to adjust. Normative significance: does it fit my stand

Anthropic states Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6 are more responsive to the system prompt, so prompts written to reduce undertriggering may now overtrigger; the fix is to dial back aggressive language, e.g. replace 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...' with 'Use this tool when...'. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Anthropic also advises removing over-prompting such as 'If in doubt, use [tool]', which causes overtriggering, and says Claude 4.6 models may overtrigger on anti-laziness instructions that earlier models needed. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Independent evidence that emotional or emphatic framing improves accuracy is mixed: a 2026 arXiv study tests emotional framing across GPT, Llama, Qwen3 and DeepSeek on GSM8K, BBH, MedQA and others, and secondary reporting cites contradictory politeness studies (e.g. a 2025 GPT-4o result where impolite prompts scored 84.8% vs 80.8% for very polite). Effect sizes were not verified from the paper text. (low confidence) OpenAI's GPT-4.1 guide says all-caps or incentives like bribes or tips are generally unnecessary, recommends starting without them, and warns that existing prompts using them may make GPT-4.1 attend to them too strictly. It attributes this to GPT-4.1 following instructions more literally than predecessors. (medium confidence) Two vendors independently converge on the same hygiene rule: with current literal, steerable models, drop emphatic markers by default and add them back only if a specific prompt needs them. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Guidance is model-scoped: the Anthropic advice targets Opus 4.5/4.6 and later; the same emphatic wording may still be needed on weaker or older models, so a lint rule should be per-model, not universal. When mDNSResponder gets DoH/DoT designated-resolver info for the current network, it upgrades automatically and the traffic bypasses an active NEDNSProxyProvider; the proxy never sees those queries. Fleet cites Apple feedback FB11963304 as confirming this is intended. DoH on port 443 is indistinguishable from normal HTTPS, so a monitor may report zero DNS activity. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-15) Since iOS 16 / macOS Ventura, devices automatically upgrade to encrypted DNS via Discovery of Designated Resolvers (DDR): on joining a network the device issues an SVCB query for _dns.resolver.arpa and, if answered, uses TLS or HTTPS. DDR applies to one network at a time and does not work if the resolver has a private IP address. (high confidence) System-wide encrypted DNS can be configured manually with NEDNSSettingsManager in an app or a DNSSettings profile payload; individual apps can opt in with PrivacyContext on NWParameters. Client certificate auth via identityReference on NEDNSSettings is supported since iOS 16 / macOS Ventura. (high confidence) macOS 27 adds a DNS settings declarative (DDM) configuration for DoH (RFC 8484 URI template) or DoT (hostname), with optional supplemental match domains, failover to system DNS, client certificates and on-demand rules. It does not require supervision but requires MDM with Device Enrollment or Automated Device Enrollment (not User Enrollment). (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02) At WWDC26 Apple moved network configurations, including DNS Proxy and DNS Settings, to declarative device management for OS 27, with public release expected fall 2026. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-11) On macOS 26.6.1, a network advertising DoT/DoH via DHCP DNR/DDR (RFC 9463/9462) made mDNSResponder send all queries, including local and split-DNS names, to the network's DoH resolver, overriding Tailscale DNS; scutil --dns still showed the configured servers, so 'dig works, apps don't'. items.text: Energy per token measurement on Apple Silicon powermetrics prints per-sample CPU, GPU and ANE power in mW; energy is the sum of those samples times the interval, so the result depends on the sampler set, the interval and the window edges. powermetrics prints per-sample CPU, GPU and ANE power in mW; energy is the sum of those samples times the interval, so the result depends on the sampler set, the interval and the window edges. IOReport's "Energy Model" channel group gives cumulative per-subsystem energy counters read in-process with no sudo, which makes per-request windows possible; the values are believed to be model-based estimates (utilization, frequency, voltage), not sensor readings. Both routes measure SoC rails. DRAM is included only where the IOReport channel exists; powermetrics package figures exclude DRAM and peripherals; wall meters include everything. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so package power moves little with model size and J/token mostly tracks 1/(tok/s). Zeus (ml-energy) wrapped IOReport as zeus-apple-silicon: M5 support landed 2026-03-29 (release 1.1.0), multi-die Ultra support 2026-04-02. powermetrics on a macOS 27 beta lost its CPU power line; the bench moved its ranked Mac column to a GPU-only figure on 2026-07-28. GreenBench (arXiv 2608.28667, 2026-08-24) proposed energy per token as a standard benchmark metric alongside accuracy and throughput. On the macOS 27 beta the powermetrics CPU sampler read `CPU Power: 0 mW` on every sample of the raw log (288 of 288) and printed no cluster-level lines, while the GPU sampler read real values; any combined figure is then GPU+ANE only. The same sampler was flaky per cell: it fired in 2 of 8 cells (16.8 W and 23.5 W) and read 0 in the other six, so a recorded "combined" J/token mixed two bases within one arm (MLX read 0.116 in one round and 0.215 in the other). The bias is not symmetric across arms: llama.cpp does more host-side CPU work than the Metal-decode arms, so a GPU-only figure is a lower bound for it with a larger missing share. Rows from before the beta are not comparable with the beta rows, because it is not recorded whether their combined figure had a live CPU sampler. Battery-delta on iPhone quantises at 5% steps in practice, so a single cell carries about 10-20% error at a 5% drop and n=2 medians are not rankable; the earlier "misdiagnosis" that battery windows measured something else was corrected in the audit addendum (deltas are an outcome of power draw at gauge resolut

Practitioner glossaries describe the engineering-metaphor tic as models importing engineering language into ordinary life: leverage for use, unpack as the conversational cousin of delve, plus optimize, streamline, facilitate, harness, and promoting observations into pillars, layers, stages, dimensions. (low confidence) The cause of lexical overrepresentation is unresolved: Juzek and Ward found no evidence for architecture, algorithm or training-data causes; model testing is consistent with RLHF playing a role, but an exploratory human study gave mixed results. (medium confidence) Excess-word analysis of over 15 million PubMed abstracts (2010-2024) found an abrupt post-ChatGPT rise of style words (delve, underscore, crucial, pivotal, utilize, align), implying at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed, up to 40% in some subcorpora. (high confidence) A 2026 study of 160,000 responses from 8 frontier models (data collected 2026-03-01 to 2026-03-15) lists leverage, robust, streamline, holistic, landscape, foster among overused vocabulary; its Verbal Tic Index ranged from 0.295 (DeepSeek V3.2) to 0.590 (Gemini 3.1 Pro), and tic rates rose about 110% between conversation turn 1 and turn 20. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Word-list detection is contested: commentators attribute delve-style vocabulary to formal Nigerian business English of outsourced RLHF annotators, and vocabulary-based detectors risk false positives on formal or non-Western English. (low confidence) Quantitative studies mostly measure generic style words (delve, tapestry, intrinsic, crucial); no source found quantifies the engineering-metaphor subset (load-bearing, scaffolding, surface, anchor) separately, so claims that these are LLM-specific rest on anecdote. (low confidence)

items.concept: Engram and n-gram embedding tables read from disk per token
items.summary: Engram (arXiv 2601.07372) retrieves static embeddings for suffix n-grams by deterministic hashing, using tokenizer compression and K hash heads per n-gram order, then fuses them with the hidden state through context-aware gating.
items.text: Engram and n-gram embedding tables read from disk per token Engram (arXiv 2601.07372) retrieves static embeddings for suffix n-grams by deterministic hashing, using tokenizer compression and K hash heads per n-gram order, then fuses them with the hidden state through context-aware gating. Engram (arXiv 2601.07372) retrieves static embeddings for suffix n-grams by deterministic hashing, using tokenizer compression and K hash heads per n-gram order, then fuses them with the hidden state through context-aware gating. The published 27B configs use n-gram orders 2 and 3, 8 heads, d_mem 1280 and Engram layers 2 and 15. The hash is described as a lightweight multiplicative-XOR function into prime-sized per-head tables. Row indices are fixed once the token sequence is known and can be computed before the corresponding layer executes, so reads can be prefetched and overlapped with earlier blocks. The paper measured a 100B-parameter Engram table in host DRAM on one NVIDIA H800 with nano-vLLM: 4B dense baseline 9,031.62 tok/s versus 8,858.28 tok/s with offload, 8B dense 6,315.52 versus 6,140.02, a worst-case penalty of 2.8%. The paper's benchmark forced all retrievals over PCIe from host memory and used no locality cache, and the authors call it a conservative baseline. The paper describes a multi-level cache hierarchy (HBM or DRAM for hot rows, NVMe SSD for the long tail) as a design option motivated by Zipfian n-gram frequency, and reports no NVMe measurement. The paper states the effective communication volume per step scales with the number of activated slots rather than the total table size. The paper's ablation says modeling quality favors an early Engram layer while system latency hiding favors a later one, so placement must satisfy both. The official deepseek-ai/Engram repository contains the paper, figures and one standalone demo script (engram_demo_v1.py) and no inference or offload runtime. In XNU, F_NOCACHE sets VNOCACHE_DATA, which makes the cluster read path set IO_NOCACHE, which disables read-ahead and stops the read from taking a page reference. With IO_NOCACHE a user-space read becomes a candidate for the direct I/O path (cluster_io_type picks IO_DIRECT when the iovec is long enough), and in the buffered copy path the pages are aborted with UPL_ABORT_DUMP_PAGES instead of being committed to the cache. ds4's separate F_NOCACHE plus F_RDAHEAD 0 descriptor for Engram rows therefore matches what the kernel does: no read-ahead and no cache residency for s

items.concept: Engram row prefetch overlapped with preceding transformer blocks in Mac runtimes
items.summary: ds4 V4.1 prefill starts a reader pthread per Engram table that reads rows through `ds4_engram_read_batch` in 2,048-token chunks and publishes a completed-row counter with release semantics.
items.text: Engram row prefetch overlapped with preceding transformer blocks in Mac runtimes ds4 V4.1 prefill starts a reader pthread per Engram table that reads rows through `ds4_engram_read_batch` in 2,048-token chunks and publishes a completed-row counter with release semantics. ds4 V4.1 prefill starts a reader pthread per Engram table that reads rows through `ds4_engram_read_batch` in 2,048-token chunks and publishes a completed-row counter with release semantics. The prefill consumer waits on that counter, polling with a 1 ms nanosleep, so a chunk's Engram layer can start before later chunks have been read. ds4 enables the Engram overlap only when the prompt has at least 1,024 tokens, and offers environment switches to disable the prefetch, the pipelined wait, or the batched read. ds4 V4.1 Engram layers are indices 1 and 14; table 0's prefetch starts before the layer loop and table 1's starts at layer 2, with a code comment saying it fills the buffer for layer 14 while the intervening encoder layers run. Both prefetch starts write to the same `engram_prefetch` GPU-visible buffer. ds4's decode step (`ds41_graph_step`) reads both tables' rows synchronously with `ds4_engram_read_batch` before it begins the GPU command buffer on Apple platforms. ds4's Qwen n-gram path reads each 256-token chunk's rows synchronously, sorted by row id, with up to 16 readers via `dispatch_apply_f`, before the forward pass. ds4's Engram constants are 2 layers, n-gram size 4, 8 heads, 24 columns per token per layer, 256 dimensions and 264 bytes per row. `ds4_engram_hash` builds, for each of n-gram orders 2 to 4, 8 head ids per token per layer from a multiplicative hash modulo per-head primes, so 24 row ids per token per layer. The V4.1 GGUF metadata in ds4 names Engram row counts 384,006,168 and 384,016,682, the encoding `e4m3_e8m0_32_row264` and a compressed vocabulary of 99,092. One ds4 decode token issues 2 tables times 24 rows = 48 random 264-byte reads (12,672 bytes) before deduplication. The two V4.1 tables total about 769 million rows times 264 bytes, roughly 189 GiB, which matches the 189 GiB of Engram tables in ds4's model documentation. The paper's prefetch window is the compute of the blocks before the Engram layer, and the paper places the module at specific layers to use that buffer. llama.cpp PR 27794 has a reviewer remark that qwen4 gives n-grams to the second layer, not the first, which can hide the lazy read. A downstream fork's note on PR 27794 states upstream's own comm

items.concept: Equality-Sort-Range index ordering
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Equality-Sort-Range index ordering. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Equality-Sort-Range index ordering Source-anchored research for Equality-Sort-Range index ordering. Run status: COMPLETED. ESR is a workload guideline: put all equality predicates first, in any relative order. Put sort fields before range fields when avoiding an in-memory sort matters, or use ERS when a range predicate is very selective and reducing scan work matters more. (high confidence) A compound index orders keys by the declared field sequence. MongoDB can use index order for a requested sort when equality predicates constrain all prefix keys before the sort keys; a non-point range before the sort generally disrupts that order and requires a blocking SORT stage. (high confidence) The ESR classification treats operators such as $ne, $nin, and $regex as range predicates rather than exact-match equality predicates. (high confidence) Compare ESR and ERS on representative data with explain('executionStats') and index hints. A SORT stage identifies an in-memory ordering step; compare totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined with nReturned to decide whether avoiding the sort outweighs scanning more index keys. (high confidence) For one query with equality predicates on several fields, the equality keys need not be ordered by selectivity. Their order still controls which leading index prefixes can support other query patterns, so choose an order that preserves useful prefixes. (high confidence) With $in combined with sort, the current MongoDB guide treats lists with fewer than 201 values as equality probes that can be merged in sort order; lists of 201 or more act like a range and prevent later index keys from supplying the sort. The guide warns that this cutoff can change across versions. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) MongoDB stores compound-index keys in the declared field sequence. The leftmost prefixes determine which query shapes the index supports, and sort use depends on equality constraints on preceding keys. (high confidence) For a query with equality predicates, a sort, and a range, the baseline ESR order puts equality keys first, sort keys next, and range keys last. Equality keys can appear in any order relative to one another for that query, while their prefixes can affect support for other query shapes. (high confidence)

items.concept: Error Message Craft
items.summary: Error messages are the most-read text most software ever produces. They are also the worst-edited. The goal: tell the user what went wrong, why it went wrong, and what to do next.
items.text: Error Message Craft Error messages are the most-read text most software ever produces. They are also the worst-edited. The goal: tell the user what went wrong, why it went wrong, and what to do next. Error messages are the most-read text most software ever produces. They are also the worst-edited. The goal: tell the user what went wrong, why it went wrong, and what to do next. What went wrong - the observable failure, stated in user terms. Why it went wrong - only when the cause helps the user decide what to do. What to do next - a concrete action. The triple does not have to be three separate sentences. For a short field validation: > "Email must include an @ symbol." For an API 5xx: > "We couldn't save your changes (database unreachable). Wait 30 seconds and retry; if this persists, contact support with request ID req_abc123." Three substitutions do most of the no-blame work: "You [did wrong thing]" → "[Field] requires [thing]" "You failed to..." → "[Action] needs..." "Invalid input" → "[Field name] must be [format]" Test: replace "you" with "the system" in the draft. If the sentence now reads as the system admitting a defect, the original was probably user-friendly. If it reads as nonsense, the original was blame language. The user sees: > "Couldn't connect to the database. Try again in 30 seconds." The log sees: > ERROR svc=auth method=login userId=12345 cause=ECONNREFUSED host=db-primary:5432 UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for the identifier (INVALID_API_KEY, not invalid-api-key). Stable across versions - once published, never rename. Categorized by prefix - AUTH_, RATE_, VALIDATION_*. Documented - every code has a docs page explaining what triggers it. A complete next-action clause names one of: A retry hint with a time bound: "Try again in 30 seconds." Not "try again later." A specific input fix: "Add an @ symbol to your email." An escalation path with diagnostic info: "Contact support and include request ID req_abc123." The Google Developer Documentation Style Guide is explicit: avoid exclamation points in error messages. They read as shouting, performative panic, or sarcasm. ALL CAPS for emphasis: reads as shouting. Ellipses for trailing-off: reads as passive-aggressive. Avoid contractions where translation may be awkward ("can't" → "cannot"). Avoid idioms ("hit a snag", "ran into a wall"). They do not translate. Avoid concatenation in code ("Error: " + fieldName + " is invalid"). Breaks grammatical agreement in gendered languages. Plan for pluralization comple

items.text: ERS exception for selective range predicates Source-anchored research for ERS exception for selective range predicates. Run status: COMPLETED. The selective-range exception changes only the order of the Range and Sort keys: keep Equality fields first, then use ERS when the range narrows results enough to make sorting the smaller set worthwhile; otherwise favor ESR when avoiding an in-memory sort matters. (high confidence) When a range key precedes a distinct sort key, the compound index generally cannot provide the requested global sort order. ERS trades index-provided order for a blocking in-memory sort after range filtering; ESR avoids that sort but can scan more index keys. (high confidence) MongoDB's manual describes the condition qualitatively as a range predicate that is 'very selective' and sets no numeric cutoff on this page. An independent worked example says the winning order depends on the data, so assess the tradeoff on representative data instead of treating ERS as a fixed selectivity threshold. (medium confidence) In one synthetic 200,000-order example, for total >= 499, the ESR index scanned 2,338 keys to return one order while the ERS index scanned one key and sorted that one result; this illustrates a possible ERS win, not a portable performance ratio. (low confidence) (verified as of 2023-07-09)

The description's SKIP: clause is abbreviated for length; the full deferral set is here. items.concept: EU AI Act Article 53(1)(c) TDM Opt-Out
items.summary: EU AI Act Article 53(1)(c) is the GPAI-provider duty to maintain a copyright policy that identifies and honours text-and-data-mining (TDM) rights reservations made under DSM Directive Art. 4(3). Machine-readable means (Recital 18) is the operative standard for online content; robots.txt/RFC 9309 is the only protocol named in the GPAI Code of Practice's Copyright chapter (Measure 1.3), while W3C TDMRep, Cloudflare Content Signals and IETF aipref are credible but unrecognised candidates, and llms.txt/ai.txt are not opt-outs at all. Kneschke v LAION (OLG Hamburg) held a reservation must be machine-actionable, not just machine-readable; GEMA v OpenAI shows the TDM exception does not shelter memorisation/regurgitation. Sourced from 3 files (1 skill + 2 references) in the eu-ai-act-tdm-opt-out skill, covering the DSM/AI-Act legal framework, the Code of Practice, case law, and the protocol layer.

items.summary: Research date: 2026-05-31
items.text: Eval-Driven Development for LLM Apps Research date: 2026-05-31 Research date: 2026-05-31 Scope: The BUILD-TIME eval-driven-development discipline - the analyze->measure->improve loop, error analysis as the engine, eval levels (assertions / LLM-as-judge / human), golden datasets, judge calibration, CI/CD eval gating, and agent/trajectory evaluation. Scope boundary: Production runtime tracing/monitoring -> llm-observability. Academic benchmark harnesses (HELM/MMLU) -> da-7-machine-learning. This report flags those overlaps explicitly. The core thesis (Hamel Husain, "Your AI Product Needs Evals", hamel.dev): the single largest distinguishing factor between reliable AI systems and "YOLO cross-fingers" development is a robust eval system. In his consulting work, 60-80% of development time was spent on error analysis and evaluation, not prompt-writing. Evaluation is treated as part of the development inner loop, the way debugging is part of software development - not a separate line item. The loop: Analyze (look at data / error analysis) -> Measure (write evaluators for real failures) -> Improve (fix prompts/retrieval/architecture) -> repeat. Error analysis is the engine - you look at real traces, categorize the kinds of errors, and for each error write a test/evaluator. "Write evaluators for errors you discover, not errors you imagine." A mental model for where LLM-pipeline failures originate: Gulf of Specification - the gap between what you want and what you actually told the model (prompt under-specifies the task). Gulf of Generalization - the gap between what works on examples you saw and what works on the long tail of inputs. Gulf of Comprehension - the gap between what your system actually does and what you understand it to do (you can't see your data / failures). Error analysis primarily attacks the Gulf of Comprehension; better prompts/specs attack Specification; robust datasets + retrieval attack Generalization. [VERIFY exact gulf->fix mapping against primary source.] Borrowed from grounded-theory qualitative research: Open coding - read 30-50 traces, write freeform notes on each failure (no fixed taxonomy yet). Do this yourself first (the domain expert / "benevolent dictator"), don't outsource it. Axial coding - group the freeform notes into themes / failure-mode categories. The model's generated text is parsed by a PEG parser into a tool call with a JSON arguments string; the server returns it as `function.arguments` (a string) in the OAI-compatible message. On the next request, `func_args_not_string` runs when the template's original caps say `supports_object_arguments`: every string `arguments` value is `json::parse`d into an object before the template renders, and a parse failure throws `Failed to parse tool call arguments as JSON`. The template then re-renders the object (typically with `tojson` or per-key loops in the model's native syntax). The bytes it emits need not equal the bytes the model generated: whitespace, key order, number formatting and escape style are all decided by the template and JSON writer, not by the client's string. The slot stores the sampled tokens, so the prefix comparison is between the model's original tool-call tokens and the template's re-rendered tokens; the first difference sets `n_past`. Messages with `tool_calls` and no `content` get `content = ""` when the template supports tool calls (`requires_non_null_content`), which adds or changes tokens versus a message with no content field. Developer role is mapped to system unless the template source contains `<|channel|>`, and a template without a system role gets the system message merged into the next message with a single newline; both alter early bytes and so the whole prefix. On hybrid models a divergence inside an old assistant turn costs a restore from the nearest checkpoint before it, which may be many turns back (checkpoints sit at user-message starts and the prompt end). Tool-argument handling moved from client-supplied objects to server-side string parsing as templates diverged; the workaround functions are named `workaround::func_args_not_string` and `requires_non_null_content`. PR 22929 and 24176 added user-message-boundary checkpoints, which limit the cost of a mid-history divergence to the span since the last boundary. A client that re-serializes arguments (pretty-prints, reorders keys, converts floats) changes bytes before the server sees them; the server's own parse and re-render then sets the final bytes. items.concept: Excess-vocabulary frequency method
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Excess-vocabulary frequency method. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Excess-vocabulary frequency method Source-anchored research for Excess-vocabulary frequency method. Run status: COMPLETED. Headline estimate: lower bound of at least 13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts processed with LLMs, ranging roughly 5-40% across fields and countries. Earlier preprint versions reported 10%; the figure is a lower bound and moved between versions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-02) Frequency-based measurement is valid at population level only; it cannot label individual texts, and results from PubMed/arXiv abstracts may not generalise to other genres. (medium confidence) Excess words in 2024 are predominantly style words (about 66% verbs, 14% adjectives, e.g. 'meticulously', 'intricate', 'pivotal'), whereas COVID-era excess was mostly content nouns; this style-vs-content split is the diagnostic that separates LLM shift from topic shift. (low confidence) Model-side comparison of Llama Base vs Instruct on continuations of 9,853 PubMed abstracts finds large post-alignment increases (e.g. 'nuanced' +8,342%), and 400 raters preferred variants with more such words (52.4% vs 47.6%), linking part of the overuse to RLHF; scope is Llama only, English abstracts, with some false-positive words. (low confidence) The method projects each word's expected 2024 frequency by linear extrapolation from 2021-2022 (2023 excluded as possibly already LLM-influenced), then flags words whose observed frequency exceeds the projection; it needs no labelled LLM text. (high confidence) Two complementary metrics are used: frequency ratio r (observed/expected, surfaces rare words) and frequency gap delta (observed minus expected, surfaces common words); thresholds such as delta > 0.01 or a log-scaled ratio criterion were chosen so pre-pandemic years show minimal excess. (low confidence) Once a word list is publicised, frequencies change: 'delve' and 'intricate' dropped sharply on arXiv from March-April 2024, while less suspicious words like 'significant' and 'additionally' kept rising. Excess counts of famous tic words therefore understate later LLM use. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-02-13)

items.concept: $exists query bounds on indexes
items.summary: Source-anchored research for $exists query bounds on indexes. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: $exists query bounds on indexes Source-anchored research for $exists query bounds on indexes. Run status: COMPLETED. An all-ascending/descending compound sparse index includes a document when at least one indexed key has a value. Index membership therefore does not by itself prove that every individual component exists; the exact sparse-index claim above is limited to a single-field index. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) $exists:true matches documents where the field is present, including an explicit null value; $exists:false matches only documents where the field is absent. A null equality query is different because it also matches missing fields. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) A sparse index on f cannot answer {f: {$exists: false}} because it omits the matching missing-field documents, so MongoDB requires a COLLSCAN for that index. A non-sparse index can scan the null-key candidates and use FETCH to distinguish absent fields from explicitly-null fields; the optimizer may still prefer a collection scan. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) A partial index filtered by {f: {$exists: true}} only covers documents where f exists. MongoDB uses a partial index only when the query implies its filter, so that index cannot answer {f: {$exists: false}} without omitting matches. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) For a single-field sparse index on f, {f: {$exists: true}} can use the full [MinKey, MaxKey] range as an exact existence test: missing fields have no index entries, but explicit null values do. MongoDB does not need a FETCH just to recheck existence, though it may fetch documents to return fields that are not covered by the index. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) A non-sparse single-field index stores a null-like key for documents missing f. Therefore, {f: {$exists: true}} has no selective value bound from existence alone: an observed IXSCAN spans [MinKey, MaxKey] and FETCH applies the $exists filter, examining all index entries and documents. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18)

items.text: exo DeepSeek V4 expert sharding (ShardedMoEV4) as EP substitute `ShardedMoEV4` is a wrapper class in exo's `auto_parallel.py` that does for `DeepseekV4MoE` what `ShardedMoE` does for other MoE layers, with one signature difference: the V4 MoE call takes `(x, input_ids)`, since the V4 MoE call also receives `input_ids`. `ShardedMoEV4` is a wrapper class in exo's `auto_parallel.py` that does for `DeepseekV4MoE` what `ShardedMoE` does for other MoE layers, with one signature difference: the V4 MoE call takes `(x, input_ids)`, since the V4 MoE call also receives `input_ids`. The wrapper applies `sum_gradients(group)` to the input and `mx.distributed.all_sum(y, group)` to the output of the whole MoE block, then returns `y`. In inference `sum_gradients` is an identity in the forward pass (its all-sum is only in the backward rule), so each V4 MoE layer costs one all_sum. `DeepseekV4ShardingStrategy` slices `ffn.switch_mlp.gate_proj` and `up_proj` all-to-sharded and `down_proj` sharded-to-all in place, and does the same for `shared_experts` when present. In place means each rank holds a slice of the intermediate dimension of every expert, not a subset of whole experts. No `all_to_all` call and no expert-to-rank placement table exists in this file; its only gather calls are for pipeline output and the MiniMax q/k norm. V4 attention is head-parallel with interleaved-per-group sharding: V4 reshapes the flat head dimension into `(o_groups, heads_per_group, head_dim)`, so each rank takes `heads_per_group / N` heads from every group, kept in group-major order. A contiguous block split would put heads in the wrong `wo_a` group. The attention output uses `wo_a` sharded-to-all in place (a block split on the input dimension) and `wo_b` wrapped in `_AllSumLinear`, which all-sums the partial `wo_a` output on every rank and then runs the unsharded `wo_b` replicated. The `_AllSumLinear` docstring explains the choice: one collective per layer on the smaller of `n_groups * o_lora_rank` and hidden size; replicating `wo_b` costs about 30M FLOPs per layer at batch 1, less than "61 extra all_gathers/token". items.summary: An orphaned exo runner is a model-runner child whose parent worker was hard-killed; it keeps running and holds Metal memory and, for multi-node instances, RDMA queue pairs, so the next runner on that node cannot finish JACCL setup.

An orphaned exo runner is a model-runner child whose parent worker was hard-killed; it keeps running and holds Metal memory and, for multi-node instances, RDMA queue pairs, so the next runner on that node cannot finish JACCL setup. Besides the queue-pair crash loop, the orphan makes the node report low `ramAvailable`, so placements fail with a 503 "likely does not fit" for models that fit. The PR author checked that killing an orphan by hand returned the memory within seconds, and states that exiting is what releases the memory and the queue pairs. The PR's unit tests cover only the wiring (escape hatch, thread start, `entrypoint()` call). An end-to-end kill-and-reparent test was dropped because a launchd-managed runner reparents to pid 1 while a pytest-spawned child does not. A downstream fork that cherry-picked the PR wrote that an orphan holding queue pairs is "plausibly a root cause" of the stale queue-pair state its own RDMA watchdog was built to recover from. PR 2205 was opened by a user (aidiffuser) and cherry-picked by at least two downstream forks; its upstream branch was deleted when it was closed. A different launcher shows an orphan that `ppid==1` does not find. With `mlx.launch` over SSH, rank processes on peers have `sshd` as parent; when `mlx.launch` dies the rank and its sshd can both stick in uninterruptible sleep (`Us+`), keep their pid relationship and survive `kill -9`. A five-Mac-Studio cluster counted over 100 such ranks on one peer. In that cluster the failure after the pool filled was `RuntimeError: Couldn't allocate protection domain` at `mx.distributed.init()`, not RTR errno 16; the fix was a pre-start sweep that kills matching rank processes whatever their parent, and reboots were still the only cure for ranks already in `Us+`. The same write-up found `mlx.launch`'s remote teardown running `ssh ... kill $pid` with a pid-file path `tmp.None`, so remote ranks were never killed after a crash. Errno 16 is also the result of exceeding the device's queue-pair limit: apple-libthunderboltrdma-tbt-post-recv-sigsegv.md records 10 queue pairs per device with errno 16 on the 11th. items.text: exo ring-abort detection by stderr diagnostic (PR 2367) exo PR 2367, "fix(worker): stop a runner whose connection to its peers has failed" (commit b2fa0d2, opened 2026-09-30 by AlexCheema), makes a runner's supervisor stop the runner when the runner's stderr has shown MLX's ring abort. exo PR 2367, "fix(worker): stop a runner whose connection to its peers has failed" (commit b2fa0d2, opened 2026-09-30 by AlexCheema), makes a runner's supervisor stop the runner when the runner's stderr has shown MLX's ring abort. The trigger is a pair of ring lines: ten repeats of `[ring] Receiving from socket 51 failed with errno 54`, then `[ring] Too many send/recv errors. Aborting...`. The runner process does not exit after the abort. Its main thread stays blocked in the failed collective, so the instance produces no more tokens, and the runner still reports `RunnerRunning`. The detection already existed for crash diagnostics. The supervisor's stdio handler records stderr lines into `diagnostics`, and a `RunnerRingTransportError` entry is created from them. The PR adds a method `_lost_its_peers()` that returns true when any recorded diagnostic is a `RunnerRingTransportError`. `_watch_runner` gains a branch after the liveness check: if the process is alive and `_lost_its_peers()` is true, it calls `_check_runner(RuntimeError("Lost the connection to the instance's other runners"))`. The watch interval became a module constant, `RUNNER_WATCH_INTERVAL = 5.0`, so tests can shrink it. After `_check_runner`, the existing failure path runs: in-flight requests end with the error "Runner shutdown before completing command" plus the ring diagnostics, the runner is reported `RunnerFailed`, the worker shuts down the instance's other runners, and the worker recreates the runners with backoff. Merge order matters. The PR says "Merge after #2366". The error event that this PR creates carries the ring diagnostic across the network, and without PR 2366 the receiving node cannot parse it and exits. PR 2366 ("A runner failure on one node can crash another node, the master included") fixes that: the diagnostic field `evidence` is a `tuple[str, ...]`, JSON turns it into a list, and pydantic strict mode rejects it, giving `ValidationError: 79 validation errors for LocalForwarderEvent ... RunnerRingTransportError Extra inputs are not permitted`. The router then logs `Gossipsub receive loop terminated unexpectedly` and exo exits with `EXO terminated due to unhandled exception`. Errors are ignored. Step 2, remove the bridge from stored configuration: `PlistBuddy -c "Delete :VirtualNetworkInterfaces:Bridge:bridge0"` on `/Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/preferences.plist`, so it does not come back after reboot. Step 3, create and switch to a network location named `exo` (`networksetup -createlocation exo` if none exists, then `-switchtolocation exo`). The script therefore changes the active network location, not just one service. Step 4, loop over `networksetup -listallhardwareports`: names starting "Ethernet Adapter" and the "Thunderbolt Bridge" port are skipped; every other port named "Thunderbolt ..." gets a new service called `EXO <port name>` created with `-createnetworkservice` and set to DHCP with `-setdhcp`. Step 4 also recreates a service for every other hardware port (Wi-Fi and so on) under its own name if the new location lacks one, because a new location starts empty. Step 5, if a "Thunderbolt Bridge" service exists, it is disabled with `-setnetworkserviceenabled "Thunderbolt Bridge" off`. The script is idempotent on re-run: existing locations and `EXO ...` services are detected with `grep -q` before creation. The script needs root, since it edits the system preferences plist and network services, but contains no `sudo`; the caller must supply it. The script sets DHCP only. It never assigns a static address and never calls `route`, so its result is dynamic link-local per port, not the static schemes in static-link-local-ipv4-per-thunderbolt-port-for.md. New constants: `RUNNER_WATCH_INTERVAL = 5.0` and `RUNNER_STALL_TIMEOUT = 90.0`. The supervisor keeps `_last_heard`, set to `anyio.current_time()` at construction and refreshed on every event the supervisor forwards from the runner (inside `_forward_events`, before any other handling). Any event counts as a word, not only tokens. `_stuck()` is true only when all four hold: `bound_shard.device_rank == 0`, `status` is `RunnerRunning`, at least one `TextGeneration` task is in `in_progress`, and `now - _last_heard > RUNNER_STALL_TIMEOUT`. When `_stuck()` fires, `_watch_runner` calls `_check_runner(RuntimeError("Runner made no progress for 90s while generating"))`. This reuses the same failure path as PR 2367: in-flight requests get an `ErrorChunk`, the status becomes `RunnerFailed`, peers are shut down and runners are recreated with backoff. Only rank 0 is judged because only the first rank reports tokens and prefill progress; the other ranks are silent in normal operation. Stopping rank 0 brings the whole instance down and back. The PR argues 90 s is far outside normal behaviour: a generating runner reports a token every decode step and progress every prefill chunk, including remote prefill, "even for the largest models". Only generation tasks arm the watchdog. Loading, warm-up and idle runners are not judged, since the check needs a `TextGeneration` task in `in_progress`. Because the check runs every 5 s, the realistic stop time is between 90 and 95 s after the last event. The target causes in the PR text: a process that is alive but stuck (blocked on I/O, frozen by the OS, deadlocked), a transport that stops delivering without an error, and ranks that disagree about the batch so one waits for data the other never sends. Stack dumps of stuck runners in chaos runs "showed ranks waiting in different collectives of the same decode step". items.text: Expert-cache policy and on-disk layout for MoE streaming SpecMD (Apple, arXiv 2602.03921, ICML 2026) benchmarks routing, prefetch, miss-handling and eviction policies under emulated hardware and finds MoE expert access violates the temporal-locality assumption behind LRU and LFU: experts are accessed in a deterministic layer 0 to N sequence, so once a ... SpecMD (Apple, arXiv 2602.03921, ICML 2026) benchmarks routing, prefetch, miss-handling and eviction policies under emulated hardware and finds MoE expert access violates the temporal-locality assumption behind LRU and LFU: experts are accessed in a deterministic layer 0 to N sequence, so once a layer is passed its experts are not needed until the next forward pass, and LRU treats the most recently used (earlier-layer) experts as the safest to keep while evicting the next layer's experts. SpecMD proposes Least-Stale: the cache is split into a stale queue (experts last touched in an earlier forward pass) and a current queue (touched, or prefetch-selected, in this pass). Stale experts are evicted first, current ones only to avoid out-of-memory, and each queue is FIFO by layer position. This minimizes "collision misses" (an expert evicted and needed again in the same pass). On OLMoE-1B-7B with a 5% cache (0.6 GB) Least-Stale cut collision misses to 1.6-1.9% against 4.5-12.6% for LRU and 42.6-60.9% for a score-based (gate-score history) eviction, reached 88-92% hit rates, and cut time-to-first-token 10.7-34.7% as a drop-in eviction swap under other approaches' prefetch and routing. At 1% capacity it reduced collision misses up to 85x versus LRU. SpecMD's prefetch result: score-based prefetching (prefetch every expert above the 80th percentile of the next layer's softmax score) beats fixed top-k prefetch on hit rate and synchronous stall despite lower prediction accuracy, because it adapts the prefetch count per layer to the bandwidth available. Mixtral is the exception: with 336 MB experts bandwidth is the limit and simple top-k stays competitive. SpecMD's miss-handling result: dropping a missing expert is the fastest option but costs quality, -5% to -15% on the wide OLMoE (64 experts, top-8) and -25% to -30% on Qwen1.5-MoE at 4-bit (60 experts, top-4), so fewer active experts means each miss matters more. ds4 seeds its GPU expert cache from per-model compiled hotlists and a runtime profiler (see ds4-antirez-ssd-streaming-runtime.md); entries become priorities scaled 1..32 on Apple rather than pins, and a `re

A January 2024 llama.cpp discussion (#5114) shows `--override-kv llama.expert_used_count=int:3` on a Mixtral GGUF printing `n_expert = 8` and `n_expert_used = 3`; the key prefix is the model architecture name. Exllamav2 exposed the same knob as "Number of experts per token". In streaming runtimes the override changes I/O directly: SwiftLM reads fewer experts per layer at lower top-k and Flash-MoE hard-codes K=4. SSD bytes per token scale with K (Flash-MoE: 4 experts x about 6.75 MB x 60 layers at 4-bit). Published evidence on tolerance (Apple, MoE-PHDS, arXiv 2509.23012): pretrained OLMoE-1B-7B-0125 loses 1.2% relative multiple-choice accuracy and gains 6.4% wikitext perplexity when k drops from 8 to 6, and Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B loses 0.43% accuracy and gains 1.2% perplexity from k=4 to k=3. Reducing k by up to 25% keeps relative QA drop at or under 1-2%; "below k_pre/2 degradation becomes more pronounced". MoE-PHDS is a short supervised fine-tune that mixes training across sparsity levels with a curriculum anchored at a low k, turning one checkpoint into a "dial k" control surface; it matched or exceeded checkpoints trained at each k on OLMoE, Qwen1.5-MoE and internal models, and improved cross-sparsity agreement by up to 22%. Ada-K routing (ICLR 2025) replaces fixed top-k with learned per-token allocators trained with PPO; on four baseline models it cut FLOPs more than 25% and sped inference more than 20% while improving benchmark scores, and found harder tasks, middle layers and content words activate more experts. Roster of Experts (Apple, January 2026) goes the other direction: it is training-free, injects controlled stochasticity into routing and aggregates several expert samples per token to raise quality at inference, i.e. it spends extra expert compute rather than saving it. SpecMD's miss-handling experiment (a "drop priority" policy that skips missing experts) is effectively a per-miss top-k cut: -5% to -15% on 64-expert top-8 OLMoE but -25% to -30% on 4-bit Qwen1.5

items.text: Expert-deduplicating gather kernels for verify windows on Metal llama.cpp's Metal `GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_ID` (routed-expert matmul) has two branches. The matrix-matrix branch runs only if `has_simdgroup_mm && ne00 >= 64 && ne21 >= 32`, where `ne21` is the number of tokens in the ids tensor. Otherwise the matrix-vector branch `mul_mv_id` runs. llama.cpp's Metal `GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_ID` (routed-expert matmul) has two branches. The matrix-matrix branch runs only if `has_simdgroup_mm && ne00 >= 64 && ne21 >= 32`, where `ne21` is the number of tokens in the ids tensor. Otherwise the matrix-vector branch `mul_mv_id` runs. The matrix-matrix branch is expert-grouped by design. A `map0` kernel (one threadgroup, one thread per expert) builds a per-expert token count `tpe` and a per-expert token list `ids`. The `mul_mm_id` kernel is then dispatched on a grid of `(ne21 + 31) / 32` by `(ne01 + 63) / 64` by `ne02` (experts) threadgroups, so each expert's weight tile is processed once per block of up to 32 of that expert's tokens. The matrix-vector branch is per pair. The `mul_mv_id` grid has `ne20 * ne21` threadgroups in its third dimension (experts used per token times tokens), with one row of the src1 batch per threadgroup (`_ne1 = 1`), so a window of T tokens at top-k k launches T*k expert matvecs and nothing merges two tokens that picked the same expert. Dense `mul_mat` switches to its matrix-matrix kernel at `ne11 > 8` tokens, so the dense layers of a hybrid MoE target leave the matvec path 24 tokens before its routed experts do. A speculative verify window of 2 to 16 tokens (any DFlash block, MTP chain, or a tree budget below 32) therefore reads each selected expert once per pair on llama.cpp Metal, and only a window of 32 or more tokens reaches the grouped kernel. The 32-token threshold is a batch-size property of the whole `ubatch`, not a per-expert property, so a window whose tokens all pick the same experts still takes the per-pair branch below 32 tokens. The MLX analogue (`gather_qmm_rhs`) needs `B >= 16` pairs with `B / E >= 4`, which for 128 to 256 experts means about 64 to 128 tokens; both stacks therefore leave the verify window range on a per-pair kernel. Low k/N keeps the layer bandwidth-bound at larger batch sizes. Verification cost ratio T(K+1)/T(1) decides speedup because draft cost is small. The cost splits into routed-expert weight loading (fraction f, scaling with unique experts) and everything else (fixed at small batch). Routing statistics are compared against a uniform baseline (overlap k/N), an independence baseline (empirical popularity, no temporal correlation) and the empirical measurement; the gap between the last two isolates temporal correlation. Neighboring draft tokens share experts, so a drafter can predict which experts verification will need (SP-MoE prefetches them from the draft pass). 2025: SP-MoE (arXiv 2510.10302, 11 Oct 2025) uses draft-token expert overlap to prefetch experts on offloaded GPU setups. 2026: Cohere's write-up measures unique experts per verification window and the overlap decay with token distance (the data below). Weight-traffic savings from overlap exist only if the kernel reads each unique expert once. The MLX `gather_qmv` path in the existing MLX dossier reads per-token blocks, so the GPU measurements below bound what a deduplicating kernel could save, not what current MLX gains. At BS=1 a second effect, amortized fixed overhead, adds speedup that expert overlap does not explain. A long verify block approaches full expert activation, which removes the overlap benefit. llama.cpp DFlash on gpt-oss-20b ran slower than baseline (0.61x to 1.27x) because the verify block activates more experts than one decode step. The flash-moe paper measured 8 to 34% per layer at K=4 on a different model and 200 tokens. Both are held side by side; the models, k and sampling differ. items.text: explain multiKeyPaths interpretation Source-anchored research for explain multiKeyPaths interpretation. Run status: COMPLETED. An empty per-key list does not prove that the source document path contains no array. A positional key such as e.0 can read e[0] from an array without generating multiple index keys, so its multiKeyPaths entry can be empty while e is an array. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-21) multiKeyPaths is per indexed key, while isMultiKey describes the index as a whole. Thus isMultiKey: true can coexist with one key having an empty list while another key has a non-empty list; an empty list means no multikey path component is recorded for that key, not that the whole index is non-multikey. (high confidence) For an IXSCAN, multiKeyPaths maps each key in keyPattern to the indexed path prefix or prefixes that cause multikey expansion. For example, stock.quantity: ['stock'] identifies an array ancestor, while a compound index can have isMultiKey: true and Owner: [] because the array expansion applies to another indexed key. (high confidence) MongoDB issue SERVER-130777 reports a narrow resumable index-build failure where a concurrent array write can be lost from multikey state, leaving explain to report isMultiKey: false and causing a matching array document to be missed. The issue lists MongoDB 6.0.0, 7.0.0, and 8.0.0 as affected and was unresolved in code review as of 2026-10-12. items.concept: Explain verbosity modes
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Explain verbosity modes. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Explain verbosity modes Source-anchored research for Explain verbosity modes. Run status: COMPLETED. MongoDB provides three explain verbosity modes: `queryPlanner`, `executionStats`, and `allPlansExecution`. The selected mode determines whether output contains completed execution statistics and whether it includes plan-selection trial data. (high confidence) The database `explain` command defaults to `allPlansExecution`, while mongosh `cursor.explain()` and `db.collection.explain()` default to `queryPlanner`. Passing the verbosity explicitly avoids different output when moving between the command and helper methods. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Use `queryPlanner` to inspect the winning plan structure and considered alternatives. Use `executionStats` to assess the completed winning plan with counters such as `nReturned`, `totalKeysExamined`, and `totalDocsExamined`. Use `allPlansExecution` when candidate-plan trial results are needed; the rejected candidates' execution data is partial. (high confidence) `queryPlanner` returns planner information without the completed `executionStats` section. `executionStats` executes the winning plan to completion and adds full-run statistics. `allPlansExecution` includes that winning-plan data plus partial plan-selection statistics for candidate plans, including rejected plans. Those candidate figures are trial data, not completed-query totals. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) MongoDB Compass's Explain Plan modal presents a visual plan tree and a query-performance summary with winning-plan counters such as documents returned, documents examined, and index keys examined; Raw Output exposes the JSON explain details. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-19) Do not treat `executionStats.executionTimeMillis` as a direct measure of application latency. Explain ignores existing plan-cache entries and does not cache the winning plan; the reported time includes plan selection and query execution but excludes network transmission, so steady-state cached queries can complete faster. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) `queryPlanner` runs the query optimizer and returns planning information for the evaluated operation, including its winning plan and rejected plans. It does not return completed `executionStats` for the winning plan. (high confidence) `executionStats` runs the optimizer-selected winning plan to completion and adds execution counters such as `nReturned`, `totalKeysExamined`

items.concept: Extraction Evaluation Frameworks
items.summary: The transition from traditional Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to Large Language Model (LLM)-driven document extraction has fundamentally altered the landscape of automated data extraction. While
items.text: Extraction Evaluation Frameworks The transition from traditional Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to Large Language Model (LLM)-driven document extraction has fundamentally altered the landscape of automated data extraction. While The transition from traditional Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to Large Language Model (LLM)-driven document extraction has fundamentally altered the landscape of automated data extraction. While LLMs offer unprecedented capabilities in understanding context and unstructured data, they introduce novel failure modes such as hallucinations, subtle omissions, and structural collapse on long documents. To rigorously evaluate these systems, a new generation of evaluation frameworks has emerged. Two prominent examples are ExtractBench and ParseBench, which move beyond legacy surface-level string-matching metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE) to assess semantic correctness, structural integrity, layout awareness, and schema compliance. ExtractBench focuses on schema-guided extraction from long enterprise documents, penalizing systems that fail to trace extracted values to source texts or collapse when processing multi-page files. ParseBench focuses on the reliability of document parsing for AI agents, measuring the semantic correctness of elements like tables, charts, and reading orders to prevent downstream reasoning errors. Alongside other frameworks like SCORE, these benchmarks are standardizing "LLM-as-a-judge" methodologies and establishing rigorous performance baselines for modern text extraction systems. Historically, text extraction relied heavily on template-based parsing, regular expressions, and layout-specific rules. If a document's layout shifted, the extraction pipeline broke. The advent of vision-language models (VLMs) and LLMs introduced zero-shot and few-shot extraction capabilities, allowing systems to ingest raw text, PDFs, or images and output structured JSON based on natural language prompts. However, this generative approach introduced new complexities: Hallucinations: Models fabricating data that structurally fits the requested schema but does not exist in the source document. Omissions: Models silently dropping fields or skipping rows in complex tables. Structural Variability: Models producing valid JSON that violates the requested schema (e.g., nesting arrays incorrectly or altering key names). Context Loss: Degraded performance on long-context documents where the model forgets instructions or loses track of docum

items.text: $facet Depth-first rabbithole dossier for $facet; source-anchored research pack. 7. Independent coverage dated 2017-01-19 records the pre-`$facet` state of the art that motivated the stage: before 3.4 a developer had to "either re-structure your data specifically for faceted search or execute a separate aggregation for every single individual 'facet' you want to filter by." <https://thecodebarbarian.com/a-nodejs-perspective-on-mongodb-34-facet.html> 11. The server source describes the stage as blocking and single-output: "A $facet stage contains multiple sub-pipelines. Each input to the $facet stage will feed into each of the sub-pipelines. The $facet stage is blocking, and outputs only one document, containing an array of results for each sub-pipeline." <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.h> 4. `$facet` emits exactly one document and then EOF, regardless of input cardinality. The stage's own class comment: "A $facet stage contains multiple sub-pipelines. Each input to the $facet stage will feed into each of the sub-pipelines. The $facet stage is blocking, and outputs only one document, containing an array of results for each sub-pipeline." (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.h) 6. `$facet` is built from three cooperating parts: a single `TeeBuffer` that holds input, one `DocumentSourceTeeConsumer` prepended as the initial source of each sub-pipeline, and the `DocumentSourceFacet` stage that drains them. The constructor wires each sub-pipeline with `facet.pipeline->addInitialSource(DocumentSourceTeeConsumer::create(expCtx, facetId, kTeeConsumerStageName));`, indexing the consumer by `facetId`. (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp) 17. `LookupRequirement::kAllowed` and `UnionRequirement::kAllowed` mean the exclusion is one-directional: `$facet` may not contain another `$facet`, but `$facet` may itself appear inside a `$lookup` or `$unionWith` sub-pipeline. (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp) The strongest convergence: four independent searches all found disconfirming evidence against the stage's own stated rationale. "Input documents are passed only once" is a true mechanism description and *not* a performance guarantee — two community threads measure it slower for paginate-with-count, and Payload

items.text: fdesetup authrestart and FileVault pre-boot unlock for headless Macs authrestart was added in OS X 10.8.2 (2012). It asks for the password or recovery key of an account enabled for FileVault 2, puts an unlock key in system memory, and reboots; the reboot clears the key from memory, so the bypass is one use. The Mac then goes to the normal login window, not to the ... authrestart was added in OS X 10.8.2 (2012). It asks for the password or recovery key of an account enabled for FileVault 2, puts an unlock key in system memory, and reboots; the reboot clears the key from memory, so the bypass is one use. The Mac then goes to the normal login window, not to the desktop. Remote form: `sudo fdesetup authrestart -delayminutes -1` (a forum answer quotes -1, meaning restart is not scheduled by a timer but happens when the machine is next restarted by other means; this reading of the flag is the answerer's context, not verified against the man page). Apple documents SSH unlock directly: on Apple silicon with macOS 26 or later, FileVault can be unlocked over SSH after a restart if Remote Login is on and a network connection is available. Pre-boot SSH needs Remote Login (Sharing, "Remote Access") enabled in advance; the administrator logs in over SSH before user login and enters the account password to unlock, after which normal SSH and Screen Sharing work. 2012 OS X 10.8.2: authrestart added. 2025 macOS Tahoe 26: pre-boot SSH unlock. Jeff Geerling's 2025 post first reported it only worked over Ethernet; his update says that as of macOS 26.5 unlock over Wi-Fi also worked. authrestart cannot bypass OS updates; the Mac still stops at the FileVault screen after an update restart. It is not a persistent setting. If a user, power loss or panic restarts the Mac instead of an issued authrestart, the Mac stops at the FileVault lock screen. With FileVault on, Apple Remote Desktop and Screen Sharing cannot reach the Mac before unlock; the unlock screen has no network connectivity (the 2024 answers predate macOS 26 SSH unlock). On Apple silicon at least one account must hold a Secure Token to enable FileVault, and only Secure Token holders can unlock at the FileVault screen. A service account created without a token cannot unlock. Apple silicon institutional recovery keys do not give functional value (they cannot reach recoveryOS), so they are no substitute for authrestart or SSH unlock on a headless Mac. In one Scope, the business strategy may require extra focus on Workload Optimization or Rate Optimization, and in another Scope, the business may require extra priority on Allocation, or in another on Forecasting accuracy. FinOps Framework 2025 was approved in March 2025. It adds Scopes, defined as a segment of technology-related spending to which practitioners apply FinOps concepts. The initial Scopes are Public Cloud, SaaS and Data Center. Scopes are not mutually exclusive. A FinOps Scope is defined as a segment of technology-related spending to which FinOps Practitioners apply FinOps concepts. A FinOps Capability describes how to achieve a specific outcome (i.e., Domain), such as Understanding Costs, Optimizing Usage, or Quantifying Business Value. By comparison, a FinOps Scope represents a collection of Capabilities for a specific context – like public cloud, or AI, or licenses. A FinOps Scope for Licensing, for example, involves multiple Capabilities and may span across multiple types of infrastructure. The reported 2-bit RMSE (0.0017 gate, 0.0018 up, 0.0023 down on average, rising from 0.0012-0.0018 in layers 0-14 to 0.0021-0.0028 in layers 45-59) is measured against the dequantized 4-bit weights, not against the original model. Expert reads use parallel `pread()` through GCD dispatch groups; only the K=4 active experts per layer (about 6.75 MB each at 4-bit) are loaded per token. The FMA dequant kernel rearranges `(nibble * scale + bias) * x` into `fma(nibble, scale*x, bias*x)` so the GPU fused multiply-add does dequantize plus multiply in one instruction; this gave GPU compute -12% and +12% tok/s (3.90 to 4.36). Expert forward (CMD3) is submitted without waiting ("deferred"); the GPU runs it while the CPU prepares the next layer, and combine, residual and norm run on GPU feeding the next layer's attention projections. The GatedDeltaNet recurrence over the 64-head 128x128 state uses Accelerate (`cblas_sscal`, `cblas_sgemv`, `cblas_sger`), cutting CPU attention from 0.78 to 0.28 ms (64% faster). Measured per-layer pipeline at 4-bit (4.28 ms average): CMD1 attention projections plus delta-net 1.22 ms GPU, CPU flush 0.01 ms, CMD2 o_proj/norm/routing/shared 0.55 ms GPU, softmax plus top-K 0.003 ms, parallel `pread` of 4 experts 2.41 ms SSD, CMD3 encode 0.04 ms (deferred). The project claims SSD DMA and GPU compute share the memory controller and cannot be profitably overlapped: GPU dequant kernels are bandwidth-saturated near 418 GiB/s and even small background DMA causes GPU latency spikes, so a serial GPU, SSD, GPU pipeline is "hardware-optimal". The I/O write-up from the same authors reports the GPU last-level cache bandwidth at about 418 GB/s with a 93.4% L1 read hit rate for the input vector. Its README lists the failure strings it cures: "unsupported call", "MCP tools are visible but never invoked", "tool_search aborts", "namespace tools are rejected" and "apply_patch uses the wrong format". It exposes `mcp__storefront_builder.list_storefront_build_sessions` to the model as `mcp__storefront_builder__list_storefront_build_sessions` and translates the returned call back to the namespace and tool name Codex expects. When a provider cannot call Codex's managed `tool_search`, the proxy exposes a plain function shim and maps the result back into a native `tool_search_call`; tools discovered by `tool_search` are made callable on the following request. For `apply_patch`, which Codex may expose as a custom or freeform tool, the proxy keeps the format Codex requires while making the surrounding tool list acceptable to custom providers. It supports Ollama-compatible Responses servers, OpenRouter, native OpenAI Responses, any `POST /v1/responses` server and, through a built-in adaptor, Chat Completions servers; Anthropic is reached through its OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, not native Messages. Its stated limits: unofficial and experimental, Codex tool schemas may change between releases, and web search falls back from Ollama cloud search to local Ollama search to DuckDuckGo HTML. The proxy writes a model picker catalog, and its README says the Windows Codex Desktop app may fail to load it, with `codex-universal-proxy run <preset> --model-override "<model>"` as a workaround that writes a hardcoded top-level `model`. Debug logging is off by default (`verbose_tools = false`, `log_upstream_body = false`), and its README warns that body logging may capture prompts and tool arguments. Flex does not support private endpoints or VPC peering, so clients must use public endpoints. Atlas recommends Dedicated clusters when private connectivity is required, and a MongoDB Community response confirms that Flex clients connect through the public endpoint. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Atlas does not support scaling a Dedicated cluster back to Free or Flex, so treat the tier conversion as one-way when selecting the target. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Two public user reports describe Flex-to-Dedicated upgrades failing during migration or rollback: one Flex-to-M20 report in August 2025 and one Flex-to-M10 report in September 2026. The latter author says they created a new M10 and migrated manually. These reports establish that failures have been reported, but they do not establish cause or frequency. (medium confidence) Atlas Flex limits total data storage to 5 GB of uncompressed BSON plus indexes, caps read and write throughput at 500 operations per second, and allows at most 500 connections. Above 500 operations per second, Atlas applies a hard limit and cooldown or queuing; it does not offer a higher Flex price tier to buy more throughput. Treat either the storage or throughput threshold as a Dedicated migration trigger. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) Flex does not support Continuous Backup or point-in-time restore, sharded clusters, or dedicated workload-isolation nodes. Flex snapshots are daily and cannot use custom schedules or on-demand snapshots; Dedicated clusters can add configurable backups and point-in-time restore, and dedicated nodes require M10 or higher. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Flex clusters cannot be paused while idle. Dedicated clusters can be paused for up to 30 days, but storage remains billable and backups stop while paused. Scheduled idle windows can therefore change the TCO comparison. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-30) Atlas's native tier-change path is one-way: an M10+ Dedicated cluster cannot be scaled down to Flex or Free. Scaling Flex to M10+ requires an initial sync and downtime; Atlas says to stop writes for the duration, and notes that migration can affect performance while nodes resync. items.text: Founder Letter Writing A founder letter is the annual public document a CEO or co-founder writes directly to owners — shareholders, users, or the general "fellow travelers" audience — to account for the year, reaffirm opera A founder letter is the annual public document a CEO or co-founder writes directly to owners - shareholders, users, or the general "fellow travelers" audience - to account for the year, reaffirm operating principles, admit mistakes, and frame what comes next. It is the genre Warren Buffett perfected at Berkshire Hathaway (1977–present), Jeff Bezos institutionalized at Amazon (1997–2020), and Patrick and John Collison adopted at Stripe (2019–present). The form is distinct from: An internal executive memo (which talks down the org chart, not out to owners) A press release or marketing post (which is selling, not reporting) An op-ed (which argues a public-interest point, not company-specific accountability) A whitepaper (which makes a technical or policy case, not a stewardship report) What makes a founder letter work is candor, operating principles that repeat year over year, and a long-horizon frame ("Day 1," "10-year zoom-out") that lets the reader weigh the current year against the company's deeper trajectory. Write as if to an intelligent non-specialist who owns shares and deserves the truth in plain English. Pronoun is "we" or "your company," never "the corporation." Three beats: (1) Where we are - year's results in plain terms. (2) What we learned - what went wrong, what surprised us. (3) Where we're going - unchanging principles plus bets for next 5–10 years. Bezos re-attached the 1997 letter to every subsequent letter for 20 years. Buffett restates Berkshire's "owner-related business principles" nearly every letter. Repetition is a feature. Name a specific mistake. Explain why you made it. Say what you changed. Vague self-criticism ("we have work to do") does not count. Amazon's "It's still Day 1." Buffett's 10- and 20-year per-share book value comparison. Pick a frame, stick to it, refer to it in every letter. Bezos's 2007 frame: missionaries paradoxically make more money than mercenaries trying to flip stock. Treat capital allocation as the most important decision the CEO makes that year. Pick 3–5 metrics that genuinely run the business and report them every year. Amazon: free cash flow per share. Stripe: total volume processed. Berkshire: operating earnings and per-share book value. items.concept: FP16 attention partial-sum overflow in split attention kernels on M1 and M2
items.summary: Pass 1 (`sdpa_vector_2pass_1`) holds its query, output accumulator, max and sum in float (`typedef float U`) and writes the block's running max and sum to float device buffers `maxs` and `sums`.
items.text: FP16 attention partial-sum overflow in split attention kernels on M1 and M2 Pass 1 (`sdpa_vector_2pass_1`) holds its query, output accumulator, max and sum in float (`typedef float U`) and writes the block's running max and sum to float device buffers `maxs` and `sums`. Pass 1 (`sdpa_vector_2pass_1`) holds its query, output accumulator, max and sum in float (`typedef float U`) and writes the block's running max and sum to float device buffers `maxs` and `sums`. Its output accumulator is updated as `o[j] = o[j] * factor + exp_score * values[j]` and is never divided by the sum in pass 1, so the partial is an unnormalized weighted sum of values. The partial is written with `out[i] = static_cast<T>(o[i])`, so it is rounded to fp16 for an fp16 model. Pass 2 reads each partial as `T`, casts it to float, scales it by `exp(block_max - global_max)`, sums over blocks and divides by the total sum. The division happens in float after the fp16 rounding. The 1-pass kernel differs: it divides by the sum in float before `static_cast<T>`, so its stored output is already a convex combination of values. The steel (full, query length above 8) attention kernel keeps its score and output tiles in `AccumType = float`, so the prefill path has no fp16 partial. Which chips reach 2-pass: chip class 'd' or 's' at 1024 keys or more, or any class with GQA at 4096 keys or more. Blocks for classes other than 's' and 'd' are 64 when `n_simds` is 4 or more, else 32. 2026-07-20: PR 3875's author notes in passing that the pass-2 partials offset arithmetic is 32-bit and would overflow once B x H x qL x blocks x D reaches 2^31. The PR does not change it. 2026-08-05 to 2026-08-16: issue 4022 reports garbage decode from the first 2-pass step on an M3 Max; it was not reproduced elsewhere and was closed for inactivity. The report does not mention overflow. Every exponential in a block is at most 1, so one block's fp16 partial is bounded by (keys in block) x (largest absolute value entry). For 8192 keys over 64 blocks that is 128 keys per block, so a block can exceed fp16's 65,504 only if its weighted values sum past that, for example 128 flat-weight keys with an average value magnitude above about 512. Such value magnitudes are unusual but the Gemma 3 reports in existing dossiers show activations reaching about 800,000 in fp16, so the bound cannot be ruled out for those checkpoints. items.text: Frontend Design This skill guides creation of distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces that avoid generic "AI slop" aesthetics. Implement real working code with exceptional attention to aesthetic details and This skill guides creation of distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces that avoid generic "AI slop" aesthetics. Implement real working code with exceptional attention to aesthetic details and creative choices. The user provides frontend requirements: a component, page, application, or interface to build. They may include context about the purpose, audience, or technical constraints. Before coding, understand the context and commit to a BOLD aesthetic direction: Purpose: What problem does this interface solve? Who uses it? Tone: Pick an extreme: brutally minimal, maximalist chaos, retro-futuristic, organic/natural, luxury/refined, playful/toy-like, editorial/magazine, brutalist/raw, art deco/geometric, soft/pastel, industrial/utilitarian, etc. There are so many flavors to choose from. Use these for inspiration but design one that is true to the aesthetic direction. Constraints: Technical requirements (framework, performance, accessibility). Differentiation: What makes this UNFORGETTABLE? What's the one thing someone will remember? CRITICAL: Choose a clear conceptual direction and execute it with precision. Bold maximalism and refined minimalism both work - the key is intentionality, not intensity. Then implement working code (HTML/CSS/JS, React, Vue, etc.) that is: Production-grade and functional Visually striking and memorable Cohesive with a clear aesthetic point-of-view Meticulously refined in every detail Typography: Choose fonts that are beautiful, unique, and interesting. Avoid generic fonts like Arial and Inter; opt instead for distinctive choices that elevate the frontend's aesthetics; unexpected, characterful font choices. Pair a distinctive display font with a refined body font. Color & Theme: Commit to a cohesive aesthetic. Use CSS variables for consistency. Dominant colors with sharp accents outperform timid, evenly-distributed palettes. Motion: Use animations for effects and micro-interactions. Prioritize CSS-only solutions for HTML. Use Motion library for React when available. Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered micro-interactions. Use scroll-triggering and hover states that surprise. Spatial Composition: Unexpected layo
