items.concept: Gemma 3/4 float16 activation overflow handling across runtimes
items.summary: Gemma 3 overflow is in the text decoder residual stream (existing files). Gemma 4 adds a second site: the vision tower.
items.text: Gemma 3/4 float16 activation overflow handling across runtimes Gemma 3 overflow is in the text decoder residual stream (existing files). Gemma 4 adds a second site: the vision tower. Gemma 3 overflow is in the text decoder residual stream (existing files). Gemma 4 adds a second site: the vision tower. In Gemma 4 31B and 26B-A4B the SigLIP vision tower applies a final standardization `(h - std_bias) * std_scale`. The stored `std_bias` (bf16) reaches 36,352 to -53,760. With fp16 arithmetic, `hidden_states - std_bias` overflows to -inf for the components near -53,760, the later multiply by `std_scale` cannot recover (-inf times a small positive is -inf), and RMSNorm of inf yields NaN at image positions. The language model then emits only `<pad>`. The weights fit in fp16 (53,760 < 65,504): storage is safe, arithmetic is not. Only variants with `vision_config.standardize = True` are affected: 31B and 26B-A4B yes, E4B no. A runtime avoids the failure by keeping the overflowing sub-module in bf16 (or fp32) while the rest runs fp16, or by running everything in bf16. llama.cpp's graph keeps activations in F32 on CUDA by default, which is consistent with, but not documented as, the reason Gemma runs there. 2025-03: Unsloth reports Gemma 3 float16 infinities (existing file). 2026-02-11: llama.cpp discussion 19505 proposes configurable FP16 intermediate activations on CUDA (today all CUDA activation ops assert F32). 2026-04-19: vLLM issue 40290: Gemma 4 31B/26B-A4B vision outputs only `<pad>` under `--dtype float16`. Undated (Unsloth page last updated about a month before 2026-10-04): Unsloth Gemma 4 GGUF guides ship `mmproj-BF16.gguf` (with F16 also offered per user reports); Unsloth FAQ states BF16 may be slower than F16 on Mac. Symptom string for the vLLM bug: output `<pad><pad><pad>...` repeated, `finish_reason: length`, only on image requests; text-only requests work. Dump showing the failing tensor: `vision_tower.last_hidden_state` has `min=-inf` and `inf=True` while pixel values are finite; the next tensors become `inf` then `nan`. Triggering setting: `--dtype float16`, which is the default for AWQ quantized checkpoints, so a quantized deployment hits it without the user choosing fp16. A different Gemma 3 symptom, `<unused32>` repeated forever after sending an image to Gemma 3 4B on CUDA (llama.cpp issue 12433), was reported fixed by testing PR 13951 in one case while a 27B mmproj case still reproduced; the thread does not identify float16 as the cause, so do n

items.concept: Gemma 4 attention_k_eq_v global-layer key-as-value sharing
items.summary: A converter or quantizer that expects a `v_proj` weight on every global layer will not find one when `attention_k_eq_v` is true; mlx-lm creates `v_proj` only when `not use_k_eq_v`.
items.text: Gemma 4 attention_k_eq_v global-layer key-as-value sharing A converter or quantizer that expects a `v_proj` weight on every global layer will not find one when `attention_k_eq_v` is true; mlx-lm creates `v_proj` only when `not use_k_eq_v`. A converter or quantizer that expects a `v_proj` weight on every global layer will not find one when `attention_k_eq_v` is true; mlx-lm creates `v_proj` only when `not use_k_eq_v`. In mlx-lm's Gemma 4 text attention, `use_k_eq_v` is `attention_k_eq_v and not is_sliding`, and a source comment says it applies to the 26B and 31B models. mlx-lm sets `values = keys` straight after `k_proj`, before `k_norm` and RoPE, and only creates a separate `v_proj` when `use_k_eq_v` is false. mlx-lm applies `v_norm` (`RMSNormNoScale`) to values and `k_norm` plus RoPE to keys, so cached K and V differ under k_eq_v. mlx-lm uses `num_global_key_value_heads` as the K/V head count on k_eq_v layers when that config field is not None. mlx-lm sets the Gemma 4 attention scale to 1.0. Hugging Face transformers names the flag `use_alternative_attention = config.attention_k_eq_v and not is_sliding`, sets `v_proj` to None in that case, and uses `value_states = key_states` before `k_norm`. Hugging Face applies `v_norm = Gemma4RMSNorm(head_dim, with_scale=False)` to values, separate from the scaled `k_norm` on keys. In transformers, KV-shared layers read `shared_kv_states[layer_type]` and have no `k_proj`, `v_proj`, `k_norm` or `v_norm`; the last non-shared layer of each attention type stores its full-length K/V into that dict. Both implementations set the attention scaling to 1.0, so Gemma 4 relies on q_norm and k_norm instead of 1/sqrt(d) scaling.

items.text: Gemma 4 float16 conversion guard for M1/M2 MLX Both converters cast through the same hook: a model class may define `cast_predicate(name)`, otherwise the default is `lambda _: True`, so every floating parameter is cast. Neither the mlx-vlm Gemma 4 files nor the mlx-lm Gemma 4 text file defines `cast_predicate` at fetch time. Without a change,... Both converters cast through the same hook: a model class may define `cast_predicate(name)`, otherwise the default is `lambda _: True`, so every floating parameter is cast. Neither the mlx-vlm Gemma 4 files nor the mlx-lm Gemma 4 text file defines `cast_predicate` at fetch time. Without a change, `--dtype float16` therefore casts `std_bias` and `std_scale` too. mlx-vlm's `skip_multimodal_module` (names such as `vision`, `vision_tower`, `audio_tower`) is applied inside the quantization predicates only. The dtype cast does not consult it, so quantizing a VLM with `--dtype float16` leaves the vision tower un-quantized but still converts it to fp16. The unguarded operation is the last line of the mlx-vlm vision tower: `hidden_states = (hidden_states - self.std_bias) * self.std_scale`, executed in whatever dtype `hidden_states` has. The tower's RMSNorms compute in float32 and cast back to the input dtype, so under an fp16 conversion the tensor reaching the subtraction is fp16. The mlx-lm Gemma 4 text decoder contains no `astype` call and no float32 upcast, so under fp16 weights its residual stream also runs in fp16 with no guard. No source says whether Gemma 4 text activations exceed 65,504; Gemma 3's did. A minimal guard, inferred from the code: (a) at conversion time read `vision_config.standardize` and refuse or warn on `--dtype float16` when it is true, or (b) define a `cast_predicate` that returns False for `std_bias` and `std_scale` and patch the standardize line to upcast to float32. Option (b) needs the code change because of the next point. MLX promotes mixed fp16 and bf16 operands to float32 (inferred from MLX's documented promotion table, not fetched). If so, keeping `std_bias` in bf16 while `hidden_states` is fp16 would silently run the subtraction in float32 and avoid the overflow, but the result would then be float32 entering an fp16 language model unless cast back. Verify on a real checkpoint before relying on it. A runtime-level alternative is to skip fp16 entirely for Gemma 4: mlx-vlm's Gemma 4 draft-model (assistant) examples and the four-size table all use bf16 checkpoints. 2026-04-02: Gemma 4 release

items.concept: Gemma 4 QAT GGUF conversion: F16 versus BF16 scales in llama.cpp Q4_0
items.summary: Unsloth names two causes: the scale format differs (F16 versus BF16) and "the scales are not determined optimally in llama.cpp land".
items.text: Gemma 4 QAT GGUF conversion: F16 versus BF16 scales in llama.cpp Q4_0 Unsloth names two causes: the scale format differs (F16 versus BF16) and "the scales are not determined optimally in llama.cpp land". Unsloth names two causes: the scale format differs (F16 versus BF16) and "the scales are not determined optimally in llama.cpp land". Its remedy applies the Unsloth dynamic method to force agreement between the llama.cpp Q4_0 lattice and the true BF16 QAT lattice; embeddings then did not need Q6_K, so files shrank. A llama.cpp discussion (#26788, 9 Aug 2026) asks for optional BF16 scales in the Q4_0 GGUF format and inference with them. The only upstream movement cited is PR 29675 (29 Sep 2026), which adds BF16 variants of unary, GLU, binary and scale ops on CPU and CUDA so activations can later stay in BF16; it adds no BF16 Q4_0 scale support. 9 Aug 2026: discussion #26788 opened by Craftyawesome quoting Unsloth's analysis and noting the workaround still leaves mean KLD up to 0.13288 and top-1 as low as 85.63%. 2 Sep 2026: a second commenter reports Gemma 4 QAT 26B degrading against regular Q4_K on private tests, suspects token embeddings and attention tensors held in Q4_0, and asks whether inference in BF16 can be offered; BF16 KV cache already works on hardware without BF16 support. 2 Oct 2026: the author says the issue is "partially addressed by #29675". The two worst figures quoted in the discussion come from different rows: 0.13288 mean KLD is the 12B Unsloth file and 85.63% top-1 is the 26B A4B Unsloth file. 12B has the highest 99.9% KLD of the table at 9.2740 even after the workaround. The discussion's reading that mean KLD of 0.13 means "not lossless" ignores that the reference is the QAT BF16, not the pre-QAT model. Unsloth says the remedy yields quants that are "more accurate"; the discussion participants say residual KLD and low top-1 show the conversion is still lossy and want a format change. Both are consistent with the table: improvement over naive Q4_0 is large, yet absolute values for 12B and 26B stay high. Unsloth's QAT table (KLD against QAT BF16): E2B 2.62 GB mean KLD 0.00173 top-1 98.16% versus naive Q4_0 3.35 GB 0.05109 89.29%. E4B: Unsloth 4.22 GB 0.00121 and 98.54% versus Q4_0 5.15 GB 0.03778 and 90.94%. 26B A4B: Unsloth 14.25 GB 0.09788 and 85.63% versus Q4_0 14.44 GB 0.36094 and 70.20%. 12B: Unsloth 6.72 GB 0.13288 and 88.76% with 99.9% KLD 9.2740. Unsloth says E2B's mean KLD is 29x lower than naive Q4_0 and its file 22% smaller.

items.concept: Gemma 4 shared KV cache layers YOCO
items.summary: Gemma 4 E2B has 35 transformer layers of which only the first 15 compute their own K/V; the final 20 reuse K/V from the most recent earlier non-shared layer of the same attention type.
items.text: Gemma 4 shared KV cache layers YOCO Gemma 4 E2B has 35 transformer layers of which only the first 15 compute their own K/V; the final 20 reuse K/V from the most recent earlier non-shared layer of the same attention type. Gemma 4 E2B has 35 transformer layers of which only the first 15 compute their own K/V; the final 20 reuse K/V from the most recent earlier non-shared layer of the same attention type. Gemma 4 E4B has 42 layers, 24 computing their own K/V and the final 18 sharing. Raschka's estimate: sharing saves roughly half the remaining cache after GQA/MQA, about 2.7 GB (E2B) and 6 GB (E4B) at bfloat16 and 128k context. Raschka's plotted E2B-like setup falls from 37.58 GB (MHA) to 2.01 GB (MQA plus sharing, 15 producers) at 128k, and E4B-like from 56.37 GB to 8.05 GB (GQA plus sharing, 24 producers), before sliding-window retention savings. Cross-layer KV sharing was not invented by Gemma 4; Brandon et al., Reducing Transformer Key-Value Cache Size with Cross-Layer Attention (NeurIPS 2024), introduced it, and Gemma 4 E2B/E4B is the first popular architecture cited using it. Shared layers still compute their own queries, so each layer can form its own attention pattern while reusing producer K/V. botmonster states the sharing applies to the 26B and 31B models and that 10 of 30 shared layers would cut KV memory about 33%. CONTRADICTS botmonster claim above: llama.cpp metadata for 26B-A4B reports shared_kv_layers = 0, so for that model the 26B-A4B cache arithmetic must use all attention layers, not a reduced producer count (see hybrid-and-sliding-window-attention-kv-cache-rewinding.md).

items.concept: Gemma 4 sliding-window layer exclusion from KV quantization
items.summary: vLLM documents that some attention layer types, e.g. sliding-window, are more sensitive to KV-cache quantization and provides `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers` to leave chosen layers at native dtype while the rest use the quantized dtype.
items.text: Gemma 4 sliding-window layer exclusion from KV quantization vLLM documents that some attention layer types, e.g. sliding-window, are more sensitive to KV-cache quantization and provides `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers` to leave chosen layers at native dtype while the rest use the quantized dtype. vLLM documents that some attention layer types, e.g. sliding-window, are more sensitive to KV-cache quantization and provides `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers` to leave chosen layers at native dtype while the rest use the quantized dtype. The vLLM skip flag accepts layer-type names (`sliding_window`) or explicit layer indices (e.g. `0 1 23`), and a `kv_cache_dtype_skip_layers=["sliding_window"]` Python argument. A downstream port commit message cites upstream per-cache rotation for iSWA (ggml-org#21513), giving gpt-oss-20b separate rotation inputs (attn_inp_k_rot, attn_inp_v_rot) for its base and SWA caches. Inference: because sliding-window layers hold only a short ring (512 or 1024 tokens), keeping them at fp16 costs little memory, so the exclusion rule trades almost nothing for the layers it protects. CONTRADICTS kv-cache-quantization-tradeoffs-on-apple-gpus.md (rotation cannot apply to Gemma 4 mixed-precision cache): per-cache iSWA rotation exists upstream, so the attn_rot_k = 0 log in #21394 is a point-in-time build observation, not a design limit.

items.concept: Gemma 4 thought stripping in agentic turns
items.summary: Gemma 4 guidance: before sending history for the next ordinary turn, remove the model's generated thoughts from the previous turn
items.text: Gemma 4 thought stripping in agentic turns Gemma 4 guidance: before sending history for the next ordinary turn, remove the model's generated thoughts from the previous turn Gemma 4 guidance: before sending history for the next ordinary turn, remove the model's generated thoughts from the previous turn Gemma 4 guidance: to turn thinking off mid-conversation, drop the `<|think|>` token from the system turn at the same time as stripping the previous thoughts Gemma 4 guidance: if one model turn contains function or tool calls, thoughts must not be removed between those calls Google recommends, for long-running agents, extracting and summarising earlier thoughts and feeding the summary back as ordinary text, to reduce cyclical reasoning loops caused by stripping Google says Gemma 4 was not trained with raw thoughts in the prompt outside the tool-call case, so no format is expected for injected thought summaries In Google's agentic history format the assistant message carries `tool_calls`, `tool_responses` and the final `content` together in one assistant entry, and no thought text appears in the stored history Google notes the 26B-A4B and 31B variants may emit a thought channel even with thinking off, and suggests adding an empty thinking token to the prompt to stabilise them Google suggests that when fine-tuning the 26B-A4B and 31B on data without thinking, adding the empty `<|channel>thought` block to the training prompts gives better results Inferred: because the previous turn's thought text is removed from the next request, a server that cached the previous turn's generated tokens (thought included) cannot reuse the KV cache past the start of that thought; the cache break is expected and is the cost of following the guidance, unlike gpt-oss within a tool loop. Inferred: a client that echoes `reasoning_content` back to a Gemma 4 server on an ordinary turn works against this guidance unless the template strips it; the chat template, not the client, is the safe place for the strip.

The llama.cpp graph order is: vision transformer blocks, 2-D average pool, a scale by `sqrt(n_embd)`, then the standardize `ggml_sub` and `ggml_mul` when both tensors exist, then the multimodal embedder. The pooled values are multiplied by `sqrt(n_embd)` before `std_bias` is subtracted. `std_bias` and `std_scale` are optional tensors in the loader (`get_tensor(..., false)`); a checkpoint with `standardize` false simply lacks them and the step is skipped. The loader also reads four per-linear scalars (`input_min`, `input_max`, `output_min`, `output_max`) for Gemma 4's clippable linears and stores them in `clamp_info_map`, defaulting to plus or minus `FLT_MAX` (no clamp) when absent. This is the architecture's own clamp mechanism, separate from standardize. The helper that reads scalar/vector tensors throws `"%s: %s must be %s, was %s"` unless the tensor type is F32. Any F16 or BF16 mmproj converter must therefore keep these scalars F32 or loading fails loudly (the failure is a load error, not silent corruption). Flash attention in the mtmd vision graph casts K, V and the mask to F16 and sets F32 accumulation; the non-flash path leaves F32 accumulation commented out with the note "F32 may not needed for vision encoders?". The attention softmax therefore does not run the unprotected-fp16 risk path when flash attention is on, but the standardize subtraction sits outside attention. Flash attention for the vision encoder is chosen by a warm-up: `AUTO` first tries `ENABLED`, and if the backend lacks support logs "flash attention not supported by <backend>, memory usage will increase" and falls back to `DISABLED`. Whether the Metal backend runs the `ggml_sub` of the standardize step in F32 or F16 is not stated in the files read; the raw image input tensor is F32 and activation dtype is a backend and graph property. No report of the Gemma 4 overflow on Metal exists in any source found. On the MLX side, `VisionModel.__call__` ends with the same standardize line in the dtype of the pooled tensor, after an average pool and RMSNorm that computes in float32 and returns the input dtype. items.summary: Source-anchored research for Gemma4-12B Cross-Platform Residency and Benchmarking. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Gemma4-12B Cross-Platform Residency and Benchmarking Source-anchored research for Gemma4-12B Cross-Platform Residency and Benchmarking. Run status: COMPLETED. Gemma4-12B quantized at 4-bit occupies ~7.8 GB VRAM, leaving 8.2 GB headroom in a 16GB VRAM pool for up to 32k token KV cache and activation workspaces. (high confidence) When running completely resident in RTX 5080 GDDR7 VRAM (~1000 GB/s), Gemma4-12B generates ~85-92 tokens per second, roughly double the ~42-45 tokens per second achieved on Apple Silicon M5 Max (~400 GB/s). items.concept: Gemma4ClippableLinear input/output clamp scalars in the mmproj
items.summary: Clamping bounds each wrapped linear's input and output; it does not bound the residual stream between layers.
items.text: Gemma4ClippableLinear input/output clamp scalars in the mmproj Clamping bounds each wrapped linear's input and output; it does not bound the residual stream between layers. Clamping bounds each wrapped linear's input and output; it does not bound the residual stream between layers. `Gemma4ClippableLinear` holds a bias-free `nn.Linear` and, when `use_clipped_linears` is set, buffers `input_min`, `input_max`, `output_min` and `output_max` initialised to -inf and +inf. Its forward pass applies `torch.clamp` to the input, then the linear, then `torch.clamp` to the output, each only when `use_clipped_linears` is true. The audio tower uses it for attention q, k, v and post projections, the feed-forward `ffw_layer_1` and `ffw_layer_2`, and the light-conv `linear_start` and `linear_end`. The vision tower uses it for the MLP `gate_proj`, `up_proj` and `down_proj` and for attention `q_proj`, `k_proj`, `v_proj` and `o_proj`. The Gemma 4 text attention builds `q_proj`, `k_proj`, `v_proj` and `o_proj` as plain `nn.Linear`, not the clippable class. A GGUF converter must keep the 4 scalars per clippable linear in F32 or special-case them, because they are per-layer scalars that exist for each of the vision and audio linears listed above.

Reads on a view are executed as part of the view's underlying aggregation pipeline, so the stage can never occupy first position. The MongoDB 3.4 manual states this as an explicit restriction ("Views do not support geoNear operations"). — https://docs.huihoo.com/mongodb/3.4/reference/operator/aggregation/geoNear/index.html **Concept:** `$geoNear` Aggregation Stage **Parent domain:** MongoDB Geospatial **Date:** 2026-09-18 **Report type:** mechanism / internal structure **D3 — `$geoNear` on views.** A search-surfaced snippet attributed to MongoDB documentation states *"Views do not support geoNear operations (i.e. geoNear command and $geoNear pipeline stage)."* I fetched https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/views/ directly and that page does not contain the statement; it defers to a "Supported Operations" sub-page I did not retrieve. The claim is plausible and consistent with A2 (a view's own pipeline occupies the first position), but it is **snippet-sourced, not primary-verified**. 7. `includeLocs` writes back which location value was used for the calculation. items.summary: Spatial analytics studies data with a geographic/locational dimension, where the
items.text: Geospatial Analytics Spatial analytics studies data with a geographic/locational dimension, where the Spatial analytics studies data with a geographic/locational dimension, where the core methodological premise is Tobler's First Law: "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things." This makes location an explanatory variable, not just an attribute - and means standard non-spatial statistics (which assume independent observations) are often invalid on spatial data. This skill covers general spatial analysis. For MongoDB geo queries (2dsphere, $geoNear, $geoWithin), defer to mongodb-geospatial. Two fundamental representations of geographic phenomena: Vector: discrete features as points, lines, and polygons defined by coordinate vertices. Best for objects with crisp boundaries (parcels, roads, administrative areas). In Python, vector geometry is handled by Shapely and exposed through GeoPandas as a GeoSeries/GeoDataFrame (a pandas DataFrame with one or more geometry columns; only one is the active geometry, accessed via .geometry and switched with set_geometry()) (GeoPandas, Data structures, 2026). Raster: a regular grid of cells/pixels, each holding a value. Best for continuous fields (elevation, temperature, satellite imagery). Handled in Python by rasterio/xarray/rioxarray. Choose vector for object/topology-centric analysis (joins, networks); raster for surface/field analysis (interpolation outputs, map algebra). Conversion (rasterize/vectorize) loses information - avoid round-tripping. A CRS maps coordinates to real locations; without it, geometries are just numbers in arbitrary space (GeoPandas, Projections, 2026). Geographic CRS uses lat/lon on a 3D ellipsoid. EPSG:4326 (WGS84) is the GPS/GeoJSON default; its units are degrees, not meters. Projected CRS flattens the earth onto a plane with linear (meter) units. EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator) is the default for web tiles (Google/OSM/Mapbox): good for display, bad for area (massively distorts toward the poles). UTM divides earth into 60 zones for accurate local distance/area; pick the zone covering your data (8th Light, Geographic Coordinate Systems 101, 2023; Esri, Spatial references, 2024). set_crs() vs to_crs(): set_crs assigns/labels the CRS without moving coordinates (use when CRS is missing/wrong); to_crs reprojects (transforms coordinate values). Until MongoDB 3.6, `$geoWithin` with `$centerSphere` matched only GeoJSON `Point` documents, not other GeoJSON geometry types.** SERVER-27968, "$geoWithin with $centerSphere does not find GeoJSON documents other than Points," was created 2017-02-09 against 3.4.0, classified Major (P3) under the Geo and Querying components, and fixed in 3.6.0-rc0. items.summary: Hugging Face cache layout: `blobs/` holds files named by hash; `refs/<branch>` holds the commit hash currently seen for that ref; `snapshots/<commit>/` holds symlinks to blobs, one folder per revision ever fetched. An unchanged file is shared between revisions through the same blob.
items.text: GGUF re-upload versioning and stale cache hygiene Hugging Face cache layout: `blobs/` holds files named by hash; `refs/<branch>` holds the commit hash currently seen for that ref; `snapshots/<commit>/` holds symlinks to blobs, one folder per revision ever fetched. An unchanged file is shared between revisions through the same blob. Hugging Face cache layout: `blobs/` holds files named by hash; `refs/<branch>` holds the commit hash currently seen for that ref; `snapshots/<commit>/` holds symlinks to blobs, one folder per revision ever fetched. An unchanged file is shared between revisions through the same blob. When a repo is updated at the same filename, the next `hf download` of main resolves a new commit, writes a new `snapshots/<new-commit>/` folder and updates `refs/main`; the old snapshot and its blobs stay on disk until deleted. So a re-upload doubles disk use for each changed GGUF until pruned. `hf cache ls --revisions` lists per-revision snapshots; `hf cache verify <repo>` checks cached file checksums; `hf cache rm <id>` deletes an entry; `hf cache prune` is listed without a stated scope on the page read (for Xet it removes shared files no cached repo uses); filters such as `--filter "size>30g"` and `--filter "accessed>1y"` select entries. Pinning: `hf download <repo> --revision <commit|branch|tag>` fetches a fixed revision; `resolve_revision()` resolves main to a commit once so multiple files come from one commit, because two calls seconds apart can land on different commits if the repo changes in between. Xet-backed files are stored once per content hash across repos (shared blobs), so identical bytes in two repos cost one copy; older clients (including llama.cpp and anything that follows symlinks) can delete a shared file that other repos still use, forcing a re-download. llama.cpp `-hf` uses its own cache directory; `LLAMA_CACHE` selects where it saves. items.concept: GGUF tensor reordering script with gguf-py plus hash verification
items.summary: A duplicate tensor name raises ValueError.
items.text: GGUF tensor reordering script with gguf-py plus hash verification A duplicate tensor name raises ValueError. A duplicate tensor name raises ValueError. Adding tensors after the file is opened raises ValueError. Output is a new file; the writer does not edit in place. With split_max_tensors or split_max_size set, tensors are partitioned into shards in insertion order. Endianness mismatches cause a byteswap copy. The exact posted script (Reddit r/LocalLLM 1vz927j) was refused by the fetch helper. GGUFWriter keeps tensors as dicts and writes the data section in dict iteration order, with a code comment relying on Python dict insertion order. write_ti_data_to_file emits tensor info in the same order, with each offset equal to the running sum of ggml_pad(nbytes, data_alignment) of earlier tensors. The writer's default data alignment is GGUF_DEFAULT_ALIGNMENT and can be changed with an alignment setter, so a reorder must carry over any general.alignment value from the source. add_tensor_info raises ValueError("Duplicated tensor name ...") on a repeated name and raises if the output file is already open. add_tensor accepts raw_shape and raw_dtype for pre-quantized data, so existing quantized tensor bytes can be copied without requantizing. write_tensors_to_file raises ValueError if a tensor writes a different byte count than expected, so a short write cannot pass silently. With use_temp_file the writer spools tensors to a SpooledTemporaryFile (256 MiB in memory) and copies them at the end; without it each tensor is held until written, so a reorder of a 90 GB model needs the reader's memory-mapped tensor views, not copies. Reorder recipe: open the source with GGUFReader, copy every KV pair, call add_tensor for each source tensor in the desired order with the large CPU-only table last, write header, KV, then tensors, then compare per-tensor sha256 and the tensor-info table (name, shape, type). Name-keyed hashing (not offset-keyed) is the correct check because every offset changes after a reorder.

items.summary: Source-anchored research for Good engineering prose versus a tell. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Good engineering prose versus a tell Source-anchored research for Good engineering prose versus a tell. Run status: COMPLETED. Wikipedia's AI-cleanup editors state the listed patterns are only potential signs of a problem, not the problem itself, and that text with these features is not necessarily AI-generated because LLMs are trained on human writing. (high confidence) Population-level word statistics cannot identify an individual LLM-written text, and cannot separate direct LLM use from humans unconsciously adopting LLM-preferred vocabulary; a single flagged word is weak evidence. (medium confidence) Excess-vocabulary analysis of 15M+ PubMed abstracts found 2024 excess words were mostly style words (verbs ~66%, adjectives ~14%) such as delves, intricate, pivotal, unlike COVID-era excess words which were content nouns; it estimates at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed. (high confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-02) A Stanford study of seven GPT detectors found about 61% of non-native English writers' essays flagged as AI; detectors penalise plain, predictable wording, so clean simple prose is a false-positive risk rather than a tell. (high confidence) Google's developer documentation style guide prescribes active voice, second person, conditions before instructions, and friendly-but-not-frivolous tone; these are human-authored norms that clean LLM output can also satisfy, so following them is not itself a tell. (medium confidence) The Wikipedia guide's stronger tells are content-level: undue emphasis on significance and legacy, vague attribution ('experts argue'), 'not just X but Y' parallelism, copula avoidance, and rigid 'challenges and future prospects' sections; these signal padding, not correctness of grammar. (medium confidence) Human judgement alone performs no better than chance at telling AI from human text per the Wikipedia guide, and writers who fear accusation may distort their style; human and LLM writing are also converging. (low confidence)

items.text: GPU & Accelerator Kernels for LLMs PROVENANCE <!-- PROVENANCE Reference file for the ai-agent-engineering hub skill. Spoke id: llm-gpu-kernels Title: GPU & Accelerator Kernels for LLMs Built by: /dr (deep-research-skill workflow), 2026-05-31 Sources: 14 (2024-2026 primary docs + papers; see References) This is the ninth and final model-layer reference under the hub. It is the IMPLEMENTATION / hardware-substrate layer beneath the other model-layer siblings. Load it via the hub routing table; do not register it as a standalone top-level skill. --> The hardware substrate every other model-layer skill sits on. Pretraining, fine-tuning, alignment, inference serving, and compression all ultimately resolve to kernels: GPU programs that move bytes through a memory hierarchy and feed tensor cores. This reference is the implementation view: how a GPU executes work, why LLM attention and decode are bottlenecked by memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs, and how kernels (CUDA, Triton, FlashAttention, paged-KV) and compilers (torch.compile, TensorRT-LLM, XLA) are written to fight that bottleneck. Where this sits among siblings (read the boundary, then the right file): Distributed-parallelism strategy (FSDP / ZeRO / TP / PP / EP, the 3D-placement decision) → distributed-training. This reference is the kernel/hardware layer beneath it: the NCCL collective primitives (all-reduce / all-gather, ring vs tree) those strategies call. Serving-engine configuration and policy (vLLM flags, continuous batching, speculative decoding, autoscaling) → llm-inference-serving. This reference is the kernel mechanics beneath it: the paged / quantized KV-cache kernels the engine schedules. The transformer architecture - why GQA/MLA shrink the KV cache, and FlashAttention's math (online softmax derivation, IO-aware exactness) → transformer-architecture. This reference is the kernel/implementation view of FlashAttention: tiling, SRAM reuse, warp specialization, WGMMA/TMA. Quantization algorithms (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant - how to choose the low-precision weights) → llm-compression. This reference covers the low-precision kernel / tensor-core mechanics: the FP8 / FP4 / MX / INT8 tensor-core paths that make those quantized weights fast. Load when the task is about why GPU code is slow and how to make it fast at the kernel level, not about which model or which parallelism strategy: "Why is decode memory-bound but prefill compute-bound?" / roofline reasoning. "What is occupancy / a warp / an SM / SIMT?"

The report is named after the process, for example `gpuEvent-python3.13-*.ips`, and lands in `/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports`. The `analysis` object holds the firmware's view: restart reason, signature, guilty data master, and per-queue firmware state slots. In eight reports from one host every field except `command_buffer_trace_id` was identical. Firmware slot state in all eight reports: compute list slots 0-2 each 1, 3D slots 0-2 each 0, tile-accelerator slots 0-1 each 0. Read with the reporter's inference, a compute buffer was stuck and nothing graphical was running. The meaning of the `fw_*_state` keys is not documented in any source read. Apple's AGX driver separates "firmware-detected lockup" from its timeout restart reasons ("timestamp timeout", "progress timeout", "CDM Kill timeout"). The Metal error code for these events is Hang (0x03), not Timeout (0x02). Background from Asahi Linux reverse engineering: AGX is driven through an ASC coprocessor running Apple firmware; work is split into queue types TA (vertex), 3D (pixel) and CP (compute); a context can own several work queues; submissions go through shared-memory channel rings. This is the structure the `fw_cl/3d/ta` slots most plausibly mirror (inference). 2026-08-27: first two oMLX events on macOS 26.5.1 (25F80). No report survives, so their firmware signature is unknown. 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-02: eight reports (one and seven) on macOS 27.0 (26A428), all with the same `analysis` fields. 2026-10-03: a second reporter on a different M3 Ultra 512 GB confirms that on macOS 27 each Hang leaves a gpuEvent report with `restart_reason 4` and `signature 579`. Reports undercount recoveries: AGX `recoveryCount` read 10 against 8 reports since the 09-15 boot, and the two missing recoveries left no oMLX log line either. Count both sources. Two of ten events fall on macOS 26.5.1 with no surviving report, so "every gpuEvent report has signature 579" holds only for macOS 27 reports. It names the engine whose stream saw the error, not the guilty kernel; at 11:06 on 10-02 the hung queue's owner logged nothing. items.concept: GPU-written no-copy buffer footprint charging
items.summary: Buffers MLX allocates (not no-copy wraps) and fills by GPU eval are charged to phys_footprint in full. A 60-iteration loop of ~500 MB alloc, eval, drop left 60.19 GB footprint, which matched active + cache within 0.14 GB.
items.text: GPU-written no-copy buffer footprint charging Buffers MLX allocates (not no-copy wraps) and fills by GPU eval are charged to phys_footprint in full. A 60-iteration loop of ~500 MB alloc, eval, drop left 60.19 GB footprint, which matched active + cache within 0.14 GB. Buffers MLX allocates (not no-copy wraps) and fills by GPU eval are charged to phys_footprint in full. A 60-iteration loop of ~500 MB alloc, eval, drop left 60.19 GB footprint, which matched active + cache within 0.14 GB. Freed MLX buffers stay in the allocator pool, remain live Metal allocations and stay in phys_footprint; get_peak_memory tracks only active memory. clear_cache returns memory but phys_footprint trails the call by about 4 seconds (15.14 GB immediately, 0.02 GB at the next sample). A first reading right after clear_cache looked like a leak and was retracted by its author as a sampling artifact. Real incidents: a hard reboot and a Metal command-buffer GPU timeout on M5 Max 128 GB when the gate used get_peak_memory (46 GB reported, 110 GB real). A commenter reports a kernel panic (watchdogd 90 s timeout, 123.2 GiB resident, 50.1 GiB compressor) running Ollama 0.33.x MLX on an M5 Max 128 GB. GPU-written MLX allocator buffers are charged to phys_footprint as IOAccelerator (graphics) dirty memory. A 60 x 500 MB churn showed get_peak_memory 1.00 GB, active 0, cache 60.06 GB, footprint 60.19 GB. With cache_limit=0 the same churn ended at 1.14 GB footprint. The pool reuse window is [size, size + 2 pages), so varying request sizes grow the pool (cited as mlx issue 3886). The mlx maintainer's position: get_peak_memory is for single-model runs where cache hit rate is near 100 percent; for long-running or parallel serving use active + cache. After clear_cache, phys_footprint falls over a few seconds, not instantly. CONTRADICTS (partly): iokit-mapped-metal-buffer-accounting-in-phys-foo.md measured a GPU-blit-filled untouched no-copy region at 0.12 GB footprint. Here GPU-written MLX-allocated buffers (not no-copy wraps) are charged in full as IOAccelerator dirty memory. The difference is plausibly allocation type (device allocation vs wrapped anonymous pages), but no source tests a GPU-written no-copy buffer directly.

items.summary: speculative-decoding-with-structured-output-gram.md already holds verifier-side grammar handling and its asserted statement that no grammar-aware draft filtering exists; this file adds the drafter-side evidence for that statement.

In `common/speculative.cpp` the draft-model drafter builds its per-sequence samplers with `top_k = 10` and `samplers = { TOP_K }` only, with no grammar field set, so the drafter proposes tokens without any grammar mask. The draft sampler rebuild for rejection-style verification uses `samplers = { TOP_K, TEMPERATURE }` with top_k 10 at the target's temperature and a seed XORed with 0x85ebca6b, and again sets no grammar. `common/speculative.cpp` registers five n-gram drafter types by name: ngram-simple, ngram-map-k, ngram-map-k4v, ngram-mod and ngram-cache; the file includes ngram-cache.h, ngram-map.h and ngram-mod.h. A grep of the file for grammar or GBNF finds no match, so neither the n-gram drafters nor the draft-model drafter filter proposals against a grammar; filtering happens only at target verification.

items.text: $group accumulator memory caps Source-anchored research for $group accumulator memory caps. Run status: COMPLETED. MongoDB 8.3 documents a 100 MB RAM threshold for each $group stage. If the stage can spill and disk use is enabled, it writes temporary data. Since MongoDB 6.0, allowDiskUseByDefault controls the default for eligible stages, and a command's allowDiskUse option can override it. Profiler and diagnostic logs expose usedDisk when a stage spills. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) MongoDB's 8.3 $accumulator manual describes a spill path for a custom accumulator operation that exceeds its memory limit: with allowDiskUse enabled, MongoDB stores the in-progress state on disk and later merges disk and memory states through the supplied merge function. The manual also marks server-side JavaScript accumulators deprecated starting in version 8.0. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) MongoDB's server issues specify a separate default 100 MB cap for each $push and $addToSet accumulator. If either accumulator exceeds its own cap, the query returns ExceededMemoryLimit and cannot spill that accumulator's state, even when the surrounding $group may spill. The internal parameters internalQueryMaxPushBytes and internalQueryMaxAddToSetBytes configure these limits. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) The MongoDB 8.3 manual marks server-side JavaScript $accumulator as deprecated starting in MongoDB 8.0 and recommends using it only when built-in aggregation operators cannot meet the requirement. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Disk spilling does not remove the 16 MiB BSON document limit on returned results. Because $group returns accumulator values in its output document and $push returns an array, one oversized grouped result can still fail even if the stage used disk. (high confidence) MongoDB Jira SERVER-73315 reproduced a classic-engine case where $push exceeded its 100 MB accumulator guardrail while $group merged spilled segments; the reported sorter merge used about 990 MB. The issue lists 7.1.0-rc0 as the fix version, so this is a historical pre-7.1 bug rather than evidence that MongoDB 8.3 lacks the guardrail. 'Information Needed' is a provisional rejection under Guideline 2.1: App Review asks questions (costs, hardware, account creation, business model, login access) because it could not complete review; the developer answers in Resolution Center or in the App Review Information section of App Store Connect. (high confidence) Many Information Needed rejections need no new build: after correcting the App Review Information (demo account, notes) the developer can reply in Resolution Center; a new binary is only needed if a code bug is the cause. (medium confidence) Guideline 2.1(b) tells developers to explain in review notes any configured in-app purchase that the reviewer cannot find in the app. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02) Unclear or evasive replies can trigger a slow secondary review; one author advises budgeting an extra 1-2 weeks when a reply is likely to prompt follow-up questions, so answer each question directly and completely. (medium confidence) Effective review notes are short (3-5 lines), give concrete navigation to the features under review, list working credentials (no 2FA/email/SMS gate, not expired), explain features needing hardware the reviewer lacks, and avoid marketing copy; stale UI directions are a common pitfall. (medium confidence) Guideline 2.1(a) requires final, fully functional submissions with complete metadata and working URLs, demo account info if the app has a login (with the back-end turned on), and permits a built-in demo mode in place of a demo account only with prior Apple approval; apps that crash or are incomplete are rejected. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02) Apple's standard text for flagged apps says the app gets a longer review and is ineligible for expedited review until the developer confirms compliance; resubmitting without the requested confirmation keeps the longer review. (medium confidence) Replies may be written in the developer's preferred language, and developers should avoid loose wording that raises extra concerns. (low confidence)

items.text: Guideline 2.4.2 power and resource efficiency for polling network monitors Source-anchored research for Guideline 2.4.2 power and resource efficiency for polling network monitors. Run status: COMPLETED. WWDC22 'Power down' guidance: tell the system when background work is done, defer non-urgent work (discretionary URLSession, BGProcessingTask), and use low-priority pushes to avoid wakeups; the session is iOS-centred, so only the principle transfers to a Mac menu-bar app. (low confidence) Apple advises setting timer tolerance to at least 10% of the interval for repeating timers (NSTimer setTolerance:, dispatch_source_set_timer leeway, CFRunLoopTimerSetTolerance) so the system can coalesce wakeups across processes; timers never fire early, only up to fire date plus tolerance. (medium confidence) Guideline 2.4.2 text: design the app to use power efficiently; apps should not rapidly drain battery, generate excessive heat, or put unnecessary strain on device resources (examples: encouraging placing the device under a mattress while charging, excessive write cycles to the SSD); apps and third-party ads may not run unrelated background processes such as cryptocurrency mining. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02) The rule sets no numeric polling interval, CPU or wakeup threshold; it is a qualitative standard (rapidly, excessive, unnecessary), so a reviewer judges it by observed behaviour. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02) Apple's Mac energy guide says every timer fire wakes the CPU from low-power idle states at an energy cost that adds up, and that sporadic work prevents resources reaching true idle, so a lot of energy is spent on little work; it advises batching tasks and running them less often. (medium confidence) Apple's guide says not to use timers or sleep loops to poll for state changes; use event sources (dispatch sources) instead. For a network monitor this implies prefer SCDynamicStore / NWPathMonitor-style change notifications over fixed-interval probing where the state is observable. (low confidence) A bundled Python (py2app) interpreter running a polling loop makes timer tolerance and idle behaviour the app's own responsibility; reviewers or Activity Monitor/Energy tab would show 'Energy Impact' and idle wakeups, which are the observable evidence for 2.4.2. (low confidence)

An Apple engineer's guidance is to notarize and staple the app first, put it in the DMG, then notarize and staple the DMG. (medium confidence) Notarization is not App Review. Apps distributed through the Mac App Store need no notarization because App Store submission already includes equivalent checks; software built after June 1, 2019 and distributed with Developer ID must be notarized (macOS 10.15+). (high confidence) When an app is both hardened and sandboxed, the restrictions stack: the app needs the entitlement each system requires (for example com.apple.security.automation.apple-events for the Hardened Runtime and a sandbox exception for Apple events). Missing either blocks the action. (low confidence) Hardened Runtime entitlements are Boolean and default to false; Xcode embeds an entitlement only when true, and manual signers should follow that convention. Entitlements go only on executables; frameworks, shared libraries and in-process plug-ins inherit the host's entitlements. Apple's Hardened Runtime resource-access list covers camera, audio input, location, contacts, calendars, photos and Apple events, and does not list network access. items.concept: Hardware-calibrated verification budget for batch-wide tree speculation
items.summary: The method D-cut (Tencent, arXiv 2607.14647, 16 Jul 2026) treats all draft tokens in a batch as one pool and keeps the top-K by estimated survival probability.
items.text: Hardware-calibrated verification budget for batch-wide tree speculation The method D-cut (Tencent, arXiv 2607.14647, 16 Jul 2026) treats all draft tokens in a batch as one pool and keeps the top-K by estimated survival probability. The method D-cut (Tencent, arXiv 2607.14647, 16 Jul 2026) treats all draft tokens in a batch as one pool and keeps the top-K by estimated survival probability. Survival probability of draft depth k is the prefix product of the drafter's token confidences, s_k = c_1 x ... x c_k, and the expected tokens advanced by keeping n drafts is the sum of s_0..s_n with s_0 = 1 for the bonus token. Because s_k only falls with depth, a global top-K selection always yields a contiguous prefix per request. Speedup is modelled as MAT(K) divided by T_spec(K)/T_AR; MAT comes from drafter confidence at runtime, T_spec(K) is a hardware property, and T_AR is constant per batch size so it drops out of the argmax. K is restricted to ratios R = {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0} of B(D+1) positions with a floor of B (every request keeps its bonus token), so only four CUDA-graph shapes per batch size are captured. At server start D-cut profiles a cost table C(B, rho) of end-to-end step time for each discrete batch shape; at serving time it picks the rho that maximises (sum of top-K scores) / C(B, rho). The target's accept/reject logic is unchanged, so output matches the target distribution; only low-utility suffixes are dropped. Prior adaptive methods changed per-request draft length or tree shape; ECHO (Hu et al. 2026) frames high-concurrency speculation as budgeted tree scheduling under a global verification cap with sparse confidence gating. D-cut targets a different class (single linear blocks from DFlash) and also cites DSpark (trained confidence head) and Graft (refills the freed budget with retrieved candidates) as related. The implementation is vLLM pull request 47131 and AngelSlim documentation. Long fixed blocks lose to plain decoding at load: DFlash block 16 on Qwen3.5-27B reaches 0.57x to 1.14x of autoregressive speed at concurrency 32 across five benchmarks, average 0.94x, while D-cut (16) averages 1.25x. No fixed ratio wins everywhere: on H20 the best fixed budget is 0.25 or 0.5; on H800 it moves to 0.5 for GSM8K and HumanEval, while MT-Bench still prefers aggressive pruning at high concurrency. Verified depth costs differ by device: at batch 16, raising depth from 4 to 16 adds about 20 ms per step on H20 and about 1 ms on H800. A per-step variable ver

items.concept: Headline craft
items.summary: Five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy. A headline does three jobs at once: it tells the reader what they're about to get, gives them a reason to care, and signals what kind
items.text: Headline craft Five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy. A headline does three jobs at once: it tells the reader what they're about to get, gives them a reason to care, and signals what kind Five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy. A headline does three jobs at once: it tells the reader what they're about to get, gives them a reason to care, and signals what kind of piece it is. Ogilvy's empirical claim: five times more people read the headline than the body. The practical implication: the headline is where 80% of the work happens. Joanna Wiebe's discipline: never write fewer than 10 headline variants before picking one. Ogilvy demanded 16. A headline pointed at the reader outperforms a headline pointed at the writer, the product, or an abstract topic. Topic frame (weak): "The future of distributed databases" You-frame (strong): "What your replication setup is costing you (and how to fix it)" BuzzSumo's analysis of 100M headlines: numerals increase CTR by ~36%. B2C top performers: 10, 5, 15, 7, 20, 6 Odd numbers outperform even numbers for curiosity-driven content. Specific numbers outperform round numbers. "$1,247 saved" beats "$1,200 saved." Declarative headlines state the conclusion in the headline itself. Good for hard news, technical posts. Curiosity-gap headlines withhold the conclusion to drive the click. The failure mode: clickbait - a gap so wide the body can't close it. News headline: Active verb, present tense. "Atlas adds vector search for Voyage embeddings." Feature headline: Label or question form OK. "The quiet revolution in how databases handle vectors." Op-ed headline: Argument-forward. "We're thinking about vector search wrong." SEO headline: Keyword-front-loaded. "Vector search benchmarks: 12 databases compared (2026)." A deck does three things: Expands what the headline could not fit. Answers the question the headline raised. Sizing: Heds are 6–10 words. Decks are 10–25 words. The "we" headline. "We released a new feature today." The reader doesn't care what you did. The label headline. "Distributed Systems Notes" names a folder, doesn't earn a click. The pun headline. Ogilvy banned them in 1963 and the data still says he's right. The bait-and-switch. Headline promises X, body delivers Y. The under-specified curiosity gap. "What we learned" without a hint of what you learned. Ogilvy, David. Ogilvy on Advertising (1983). BuzzSumo headline studies. Wiebe, Joanna. Copyhackers headline form

items.text: Health Behavior Change and Donor Registration Applied health-behavior change models and organ-donor registration intervention evidence. Covers the major theoretical frameworks used to design health-behavior campaigns, applied specifically to dono Applied health-behavior change models and organ-donor registration intervention evidence. Covers the major theoretical frameworks used to design health-behavior campaigns, applied specifically to donor-registration campaigns. Frameworks: Health Belief Model (HBM - perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, self-efficacy); Theory of Planned Behavior / Reasoned Action (TPB/TRA - attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control → intention → behavior, and the intention-action gap); Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM - threat × efficacy interaction, danger-control vs fear-control responses, message backfire when threat is high but efficacy is low); COM-B (capability, opportunity, motivation → behavior). Donor-registration specifics: the willingness-registration GAP (why polling support far exceeds actual registration); intervention evidence for mandated choice, prompted choice, active choice (US); opt-in vs opt-out / presumed consent (behavioral-defaults literature, Johnson & Goldstein); reciprocity priming; loss-framing; social norms; the UK Behavioural Insights Team RCT on 1M+ users showing framing effects at the DVLA registration point. Route SDT/Fogg/habit loops to applied-psychology (behavior-change-psychology reference); system-level OPO/OPTN/consent law to venture-organ-donation-system; policy advocacy to venture-organ-donation-frontier. Designing a specific message for a health campaign, where the Health Belief Model's five components — perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, and cues to action — map directly onto what the message needs to establish. Explaining why stated support for a health behavior, like organ donation, doesn't translate into the actual behavior — the willingness-registration gap that TPB/TRA frames as an intention-action gap. Choosing a fear-appeal strategy for a health message, where EPPM predicts message backfire (avoidance instead of action) if threat is emphasized without matching efficacy information. Deciding how a registration point — a DVLA-style form, a DMV kiosk, an app sign-up flow — should default and frame its choice, drawing on the opt-in/opt-out and mandated/prompted/active-choice evidence base. items.text: Health Insurance and Coverage > Framing — read first. This is **general educational information, NOT > Framing - read first. This is general educational information, NOT > insurance, medical, tax, or financial advice. US health-coverage rules - > especially subsidy amounts and enrollment dates - change every year and are > unusually volatile right now (2026). Every figure here is stamped "as of > 2026" and should be re-verified before you rely on it. Authoritative checks: > healthcare.gov (marketplace), > medicare.gov (Medicare), > your state Medicaid agency, and irs.gov (HSA limits). This skill is a spoke of the consumer-finance hub (the personal-finance router). Its sibling hub, consumer-credit-and-debt, owns the credit/debt/collections side - route there when a medical or other bill becomes a collections or credit-reporting matter. Sibling spokes referenced below: personal-income-taxes (HSA tax-form mechanics), medical-debt-and-billing (the bills after care), and personal-insurance (auto/home/life/disability). You almost never pay the "sticker" price of care. A plan splits cost between you and the insurer through a few interlocking levers. Learn these six and you can read any plan. Premium - the fixed monthly amount you pay to have the plan, whether or not you use it. A premium is not a cap on anything; it buys the contract. Deductible - what you pay out of pocket first, each plan year, before the insurer starts paying its share for most services. A $2,000 deductible means you cover the first $2,000 of covered care. (Some services - often preventive care, sometimes a few copay'd visits - are covered before the deductible.) Copay (copayment) - a fixed dollar amount for a specific service (e.g., $30 for a primary-care visit, $15 for a generic drug). Predictable. Coinsurance - your percentage share of a covered service after the deductible (e.g., you pay 20%, the plan pays 80% of the allowed amount). Out-of-pocket maximum (OOP max) - the single most important number for worst-case protection. It is the most you can pay in a plan year for covered, in-network services (deductible + copays + coinsurance all count toward it; premiums do not). Once you hit it, the plan pays 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the year. A low premium with a high OOP max is a bet you won't get sick; the OOP max is what bankrupts people who lose that bet. > Mental model: premium = the cost of having coverage; deductible/copay/ > coinsurance = the cost of using it; OOP

items.text: Heart The heart is a hollow muscular organ of somewhat conical form lying between the lungs in the middle mediastinum, enclosed in the pericardium; it is the central organ of the blood vascular system, pumping blood through the arteries by its contraction, and is divided by septa into right and left halves, each with an atrium and a ventricle. One source (Gray's Anatomy 1918, Angiology) covers its definition, structure (chambers, valves, wall and conduction tissue, coronary vessels, pericardium), mechanism (development, cardiac cycle, fetal circulation), size and cycle timings, and the two malformations the text names. The right atrioventricular orifice is the large oval aperture of communication between the right atrium and ventricle. Situated at the base of the ventricle, it measures about 4 cm. in diameter and is surrounded by a fibrous ring, covered by the lining membrane of the heart; it is considerably larger than the correspond- ing aperture on the left side, being sufficient to admit the ends of four fingers It is guarded by the tricuspid valve. The atrioventricular opening (tricuspid orifice) is the large oval aperture of com- munication between the atrium and the ventricle; it will be described with the right ventricle. The left atrioventricular opening is the aperture between the left atrium and ventricle, and is rather smaller than the corresponding opening on the right side. The limbus fossae ovalis (ayiniilus ovalis) is the prominent oval margin of the fossa ovalis. It is most distinct above and at the sides of the fossa; below, it is deficient. A small slit-like valvular opening is occasionally found, at the upper margin of the fossa, leading upward beneath the limbus, into the left atrium ; it is the remains of the fetal aperture between the two atria. The serous pericardium is, as already stated, a closed sac which lines the fibrous pericardium and is invaginated by the heart; it therefore consists of a visceral and a parietal portion. The visceral portion, or epicardium, covers the heart and the great vessels, and from the latter is continuous with the parietal layer which lines the fibrous pericardium. The portion which covers the vessels is arranged in the form of two tubes. The aorta and pulmonary artery are enclosed in one tube, the arterial mesocardium. items.summary: Heuristic boilerplate removal and text-density algorithms are foundational techniques used in web scraping and natural language processing to separate primary article content from peripheral noise (bo
items.text: Heuristic Boilerplate Removal & Text-Density Algorithms for Web Extraction Heuristic boilerplate removal and text-density algorithms are foundational techniques used in web scraping and natural language processing to separate primary article content from peripheral noise (bo Heuristic boilerplate removal and text-density algorithms are foundational techniques used in web scraping and natural language processing to separate primary article content from peripheral noise (boilerplate). Boilerplate includes elements like navigation menus, footers, advertisements, sidebars, and social sharing widgets. By relying on structural DOM characteristics and text-to-tag ratios, tools like Mozilla Readability and Trafilatura process web pages efficiently, without the overhead of heavy machine learning models or headless browsers. While Readability excels at high-recall extraction for single-page reading views, Trafilatura operates as a robust, multi-stage pipeline suited for large-scale corpus generation and text mining. This report explores the core concepts of text-density, compares prominent extraction tools, and evaluates the enduring relevance of heuristic approaches in the era of large language models. In web data extraction, "boilerplate" refers to the recurring structural and navigational elements of a webpage that surround the main content. For humans, these elements provide context and usability. For automated systems building datasets, search indexes, or training language models, boilerplate represents noise that can skew word frequencies, introduce irrelevant links, and pollute the semantic meaning of the target text. The goal of boilerplate removal algorithms is to isolate the "main content" node or nodes within the Document Object Model (DOM). Historically, early web extraction relied on writing custom, site-specific regular expressions or XPath rules (often referred to as wrappers). However, wrapper maintenance is highly unscalable due to frequent layout changes across millions of websites. Heuristic algorithms emerged as a scalable, generic solution that identifies content based on universal patterns rather than site-specific selectors. The foundational insight driving heuristic extraction is that the structural and textual composition of main content differs significantly from boilerplate. This difference is quantified using a metric known as "Text-Density." Text-density calculates the ratio of raw text characters to HTML markup within a specific DOM blo

items.text: Hidden indexes and safe index removal Source-anchored research for Hidden indexes and safe index removal. Run status: COMPLETED. Dropping on short evidence is the main removal mistake. Counters restart at zero after a restart, so an index that serves a monthly or quarterly job looks unused until that job runs. Percona warns that dropping an index used once a month for heavy reporting can be problematic. Netdata says not to drop within 24 hours of a restart. (high confidence) Do not drop a single-field index only because a compound index contains the same field in a non-leading position. Atlas Performance Advisor treats { b: -1 } as not redundant next to { a: 1, b: -1 }. Only a leading prefix makes the smaller index redundant. (medium confidence) Unneeded indexes cost every write. Each insert and delete updates every index, and an update to an indexed field removes and re-adds entries in each index that contains the field. Indexes also compete with documents for WiredTiger cache. MongoDB says an index on every field bloats a collection and hurts write performance; Percona says extra indexes hurt write performance, disk and memory. A collection can hold at most 64 indexes. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Unhiding is immediate and cheaper than rebuilding. Because the index is maintained while hidden, it is available for use the moment it is unhidden. Atlas states that unhiding takes less time than rebuilding a dropped index. Percona notes that building an index is expensive on large collections or when memory is short. (high confidence) dropIndexes takes an exclusive lock on the collection for the duration of the operation, and all later operations on the collection wait until it finishes. Netdata advises dropping during a low-traffic window and watching globalLock.currentQueue and lock waits, because a drop under heavy write load can stall writes. (high confidence) $indexStats returns usage per index. accesses.ops counts user operations that used the index, and accesses.since is when MongoDB began gathering statistics. Internal operations such as TTL deletion and chunk split or migration are not counted. The counters reset on mongod restart, on index drop and recreation, and when collMod modifies the index. (high confidence) The sources give different minimum observation windows. Netdata asks for at least 24 hours of uptime under representative load that includes peak and off-peak traffic. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-08) Do not bake glass effects (highlights, inter-layer shadows, bevels, blur, glow) or masking into layers; prefer vector layers with crisp edges, vary layer opacity for depth, use solid/gradient backgrounds from Icon Composer or a full-bleed opaque image, and keep core features consistent across default, dark, clear and tinted appearances. Template is 1024x1024 px, Display P3. (low confidence) HIG: when people click a menu bar extra, display a menu, not a popover; use a popover only if the functionality is too complex for a menu. (medium confidence) HIG: let the user, not the app, decide whether the menu bar extra is shown (typically a Settings toggle; consider offering it during setup). items.concept: Homogenization of professional and scientific prose
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Homogenization of professional and scientific prose. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Homogenization of professional and scientific prose Source-anchored research for Homogenization of professional and scientific prose. Run status: COMPLETED. LLM-marker usage varies widely: about 20% in computational fields and in China/South Korea/Taiwan, about 5% in English-speaking countries; MDPI (21%) and Frontiers (20%) exceed Nature/Science (~7-10%). Measured rates are likely lower bounds. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-01) Sourati et al. (USC) report declining writing-complexity variance on Reddit, news and academic preprints, and that LLM polishing/rewriting reduces that variance (reported 21-50% across datasets/models); the review cites this as evidence of stylistic homogenization in scientific writing. (medium confidence) Even when prompted for grammar-only edits, LLMs substantially alter meaning; in a user study heavy LLM use raised neutral-stance essays by nearly 70%, and AI-generated peer reviews scored about one point higher than expected and devalued clarity and significance. (low confidence) The excess-word method cannot flag individual abstracts, cannot separate direct LLM use from stylistic borrowing, and cannot fully separate LLM effects from other emerging linguistic trends. (low confidence) Excess-vocabulary analysis found 454 excess style words in 2024 biomedical abstracts, versus 190 at the 2021 COVID peak; the authors estimate at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-01) Cited evidence that people adopt LLM framing (Jakesch et al. 2023) and that AI-assisted ideation reduces semantic diversity (Anderson et al. 2024) supports the mechanism, but the review notes longitudinal effects and correlation-versus-causation gaps remain open. (low confidence) Rewriting experiments apply one LLM uniformly to all abstracts, so they give an upper bound on homogenization rather than real-world practice; effects are stronger for Reddit and academic writing than for news. (low confidence)

items.concept: Hook additional-context injection into the first message
items.summary: additionalContext is wrapped in a system reminder and inserted into the conversation where the hook fired; it never shows as a chat message.
items.text: Hook additional-context injection into the first message additionalContext is wrapped in a system reminder and inserted into the conversation where the hook fired; it never shows as a chat message. additionalContext is wrapped in a system reminder and inserted into the conversation where the hook fired; it never shows as a chat message. Plain stdout from SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit hooks is injected the same way, as a system reminder starting with the hook's name. SessionStart additionalContext is added at the start of the conversation, before the first prompt; SessionStart also accepts initialUserMessage (creates the first user turn in -p mode), watchPaths, sessionTitle and reloadSkills. When several hooks return additionalContext for one event, Claude receives every value. Cap: additionalContext, systemMessage, initialUserMessage and plain stdout are each capped at 10,000 characters, measured per string. Over the cap, Claude Code saves the text to a file in the session directory and passes the file path plus a preview of up to 2,000 characters. The cap has no setting or environment variable. Claude Code does not tell Claude to read the saved file. Several hooks each under 10,000 characters can together exceed it, since each string is measured on its own; a local model can still receive tens of thousands of tokens from hooks. [inferred] Shell profile output on stdout breaks JSON parsing and the hook JSON has no effect. A Setup hook's JSON output, including additionalContext, is discarded on every exit code. UserPromptSubmit hooks default to a 30 second timeout and block model processing until they finish. Whether the 10,000-character cap applies to hook text injected through the memory-central style per-prompt hooks used here; the size per prompt is not measured. additionalContext is wrapped in a system reminder and added at the point the hook fired, not shown as a chat message Each of additionalContext, systemMessage, initialUserMessage and plain stdout is capped at 10,000 characters, measured per string Over the cap Claude Code writes the text to a session-directory file and passes the path plus a preview of up to 2,000 characters; the cap has no setting Claude Code does not ask Claude to read the overflow file SessionStart additionalContext is delivered before the first prompt; SessionStart also takes initialUserMessage, watchPaths, sessionTitle and reloadSkills Setup hooks discard JSON output fields including additionalContext on every exit code

items.concept: Hook-based filtering of agent output
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Hook-based filtering of agent output. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Hook-based filtering of agent output Source-anchored research for Hook-based filtering of agent output. Run status: COMPLETED. Hooks cannot directly modify assistant message text. Stop can only prevent stopping and continue the conversation, and last_assistant_message on Stop/SubagentStop is read-only input for analysis. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) A Stop hook can act as a post-generation filter: it inspects the final response and blocks with a reason, forcing the model to revise before the user sees the result. (medium confidence) A regex-only Stop hook produces false positives; combining the regex with a second condition (e.g. prior tool-call activity) removes most of them. (low confidence) A Stop hook that re-blocks without checking stop_hook_active can loop indefinitely; one reported case ran about 50 minutes and consumed the session quota. A nag-once pattern (block the first violation, let an identical repeat pass) avoids it. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-03) PostToolUse can replace a tool's output before the model sees it (updatedToolOutput), so filtering applies to tool results but not to the model's own prose. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

items.concept: Human adoption of LLM vocabulary in speech and writing
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Human adoption of LLM vocabulary in speech and writing. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Human adoption of LLM vocabulary in speech and writing Source-anchored research for Human adoption of LLM vocabulary in speech and writing. Run status: COMPLETED. A preregistered experiment (496 participants) found brief chatbot interaction makes participants adopt specific words, persisting through distractor tasks, supporting exposure-to-active-vocabulary as the mechanism. (low confidence) Florida State University (Juzek et al.) analysed 22.1 million words of science/tech conversational podcasts; nearly three-quarters of target AI buzzwords rose after ChatGPT, some more than doubling. 'Underscore' rose while its synonym 'accentuate' did not, which points to AI-specific rather than generic drift. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-26) Yakura et al. (Max Planck) analysed about 737,083 hours of unscripted conversation from 824,634 podcast episodes and report that ChatGPT-favoured words (delve, showcase, boast, meticulous) rose abruptly in spontaneous speech after ChatGPT's release; they use synthetic-control analysis to argue for a causal link. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-16) The 'GPT words' list was derived by having ChatGPT edit millions of emails, essays and articles and extracting words it repeatedly added; usage was then tracked in about 360,000 YouTube academic talks and 771,000 podcast episodes, with a surge within roughly 18 months of release. (medium confidence) The measured effect is lexical only; the Max Planck paper does not test semantic or grammatical influence and frames vocabulary as an early indicator of wider cultural influence. (medium confidence)

items.concept: Human baselines and control words for tic detection
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Human baselines and control words for tic detection. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Human baselines and control words for tic detection Source-anchored research for Human baselines and control words for tic detection. Run status: COMPLETED. Kobak et al. build a counterfactual baseline by linear extrapolation from earlier years (q = p_{Y-2} + 2*max{p_{Y-2}-p_{Y-3},0}) and deliberately exclude 2023 because it may already be LLM-affected. (medium confidence) Control by word class: authors hand-annotated 900 excess words from 2013-2024 as content (about 51%) or style (about 45%); Covid-era excess was mostly content nouns, 2024 excess mostly style verbs and adjectives, which separates topical drift from LLM tics. (low confidence) Excess-word counts are only a lower bound on LLM use, and cannot distinguish LLM use from authors independently adopting LLM-preferred vocabulary. (low confidence) Excess words are flagged using two metrics, frequency gap and frequency ratio; thresholds were chosen so most pre-Covid years fall well below them, giving conservative estimates. (low confidence) Human baselines for model-output tic detection can be built from pre-2022 corpora (wordfreq for single words; Reddit creative writing and Project Gutenberg for n-grams in Antislop), with overuse expressed as a ratio of model frequency to baseline frequency. (medium confidence) Post-2021 web text is contaminated by generative-AI output, so frequency resources built from it no longer measure human language; wordfreq's maintainer stopped updating it for this reason, forcing baselines to pre-2022 archives. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2024-09-15) Confound check: the hypothesis that 'delve' reflects Nigerian English annotators was not supported by International Corpus of English data (small corpus); RLHF-based Llama experiments fit better as the source of overrepresentation. (medium confidence)

items.concept: Human Performance Technology & Performance Support
items.summary: Quick orientation: HPT is the discipline UPSTREAM of instructional design. It asks "is training the right intervention?" before any course is designed. This skill covers the full diagnostic and interv
items.text: Human Performance Technology & Performance Support Quick orientation: HPT is the discipline UPSTREAM of instructional design. It asks "is training the right intervention?" before any course is designed. This skill covers the full diagnostic and interv Quick orientation: HPT is the discipline UPSTREAM of instructional design. It asks "is training the right intervention?" before any course is designed. This skill covers the full diagnostic and intervention-selection toolkit: the ISPI model, Gilbert's BEM, Mager-Pipe flowchart, Rummler-Brache, performance support (EPSS/DAPs), Five Moments of Need, and job aid design. > The foundational HPT claim: "If you pit a good performer against a bad system, the system will win almost every time." - Rummler & Brache, Improving Performance (1990). About 80% of performance improvement opportunities are environmental, not individual (a practitioner estimate - see §2 for the calibration caveat). Training is the solution to a knowledge/skill gap specifically - not a performance gap generically. Volatile claims - the DAP/EPSS vendor landscape in §6 and the market/effectiveness figures throughout - were verified-as-of 2026-06-16. The durable models (§§1–5, 7–11) are stable HPT canon (Gilbert 1978; Mager & Pipe 1970; Rummler & Brache 1990; Gery 1991). Human Performance Technology (HPT) is ISPI's (International Society for Performance Improvement) systematic, systemic, results-oriented framework. The ISPI model (Deterline & Rosenberg, 1992; updated 2000) is "the most representative and frequently utilized process model in the HPT field" (ERIC/TechTrends, 2017).[^1] The fundamental distinction from instructional design: "HPT models allow for a much broader range of interventions to a given performance problem, which often include non-instructional interventions as well as those that involve instruction or training." (Morrison, Ross, Kalman & Kemp, 2013, cited in jwkline.com).[^2] The HPT model determines whether training or other interventions are effective - training is one output, never the assumed starting point. Phase 1 - Performance Analysis (Need or Opportunity) Three sub-analyses run together: Organizational analysis: vision, mission, goals, strategies - the business context Environmental analysis: external and internal realities shaping actual performance Gap analysis: actual performance vs. desired performance; if actual = desired, no intervention needed Output: a quantified performance gap statement with business rationa
