items.text: Hybrid and recurrent model checkpoint handling in oMLX PR 3288 fixes a store-side drop: when the speculative-decode skew guard skips every decode-time boundary capture, `_cleanup_finished` raised `_BoundaryStoreUnavailable` in scheduler.py and discarded the recurrent state, so a growing agent context stored no reusable prefix and showed `served cache... PR 3288 fixes a store-side drop: when the speculative-decode skew guard skips every decode-time boundary capture, `_cleanup_finished` raised `_BoundaryStoreUnavailable` in scheduler.py and discarded the recurrent state, so a growing agent context stored no reusable prefix and showed `served cached_tokens=0`. PR 3288 adds `_verify_live_boundary_aligned(request_id, uid, boundary_tokens)`: when `len(cacheable_sequence) % block_size == 0` it stores the live cache only if the leaf cache offset equals the boundary token count, otherwise it keeps the old drop. PR 3288 trusts the live cache offset rather than the emitted token length because the MTP emit queue can make the emitted length misleading. The 0.7.0.dev1 release notes list PR 3288 among the changes behind 'restored hybrid GDN boundary storage', next to PRs 3327, 3369, 3355, 3428, 3367, 3447 and 3525. PR 3288 is listed in the notes as authored by contributor apcooley; PR 3314's reporter was cross-linked to it on 2026-08-30. 0.6.3rc3 hardened recurrent-state correctness: storage no longer attaches end-of-prompt recurrent state to an earlier full block when a partial tail was skipped, pre-call GDN state is restored before stock fallback, shared-prefix hashes are verified on acquisition, and blocks whose stored KV lengths disagree with the declared token count are rejected (PRs 3085, 3086, 3087, 3094). 0.6.3rc3 PR 3066 stops prefix caching from splitting a 4,096-token forward into two 2,048-token forwards on validated classic-Metal Qwen3.8 configurations; the split had caused agent sessions to repeat completed tool calls only when prefix caching was on. NAX-capable and smaller-memory systems keep the validated 2,048-token cache geometry after PR 3066. A 0.6.4 fix (PR 3227) makes ArraysCache hybrids such as GLM-5.3 materialize recurrent state periodically, release boundary snapshots and paged-cache blocks on failures, and skip unnecessary hot-cache payloads, to avoid Metal resource-count exhaustion in long decode. items.text: Hybrid and sliding-window attention KV cache rewinding mlx-lm gate: `can_trim_prompt_cache()` returns `all(c.is_trimmable() for c in cache)`, so one non-trimmable layer disables the "longer cache" trim path in `fetch_nearest_cache()`. `ArraysCache` (DeltaNet/Mamba state) inherits `is_trimmable() -> False`; `RotatingKVCache.is_trimmable()` is `offset ... mlx-lm gate: `can_trim_prompt_cache()` returns `all(c.is_trimmable() for c in cache)`, so one non-trimmable layer disables the "longer cache" trim path in `fetch_nearest_cache()`. `ArraysCache` (DeltaNet/Mamba state) inherits `is_trimmable() -> False`; `RotatingKVCache.is_trimmable()` is `offset < max_size`, so it turns False once the ring wraps. mlx-lm cache-class census from a repro: Qwen3.5-9B = 24 `ArraysCache` + 8 `KVCache` (32 layers); Nemotron-H 30B-A3B = 52 layers, 29 cache-bearing, 23 `ArraysCache` + 6 `KVCache`. Failure shape in mlx-lm: when a request shares only the system prompt with the stored entry (divergent suffix, typical agent tool call) the stored entry is "longer", needs trimming, cannot be trimmed, so the server prefills everything. Strictly appended conversations hit the "shorter cache" path and still reuse. The rewind fix for rings (mlx-lm PR #999, draft 2026-03-14): separate `_offset` (physical buffer size) from `offset` (logical RoPE position), linearise the ring with `_temporal_order()` on `trim(n)`, clip physical deletion to `min(_offset, n)`, and make `server.py` evict intermediates only when the trim distance fits `min(c.size())`. Without separating the two offsets, trimming breaks RoPE for later tokens. Why the same trick is unsafe for recurrent state: resetting only the Mamba layers while keeping attention layers would feed the new suffix into an empty state and silently hallucinate. The designed fix is a saved snapshot, not a trim. The checkpoint fix for recurrent state (mlx-lm PR #1006, 2026-03-15): in `_compute_prompt_checkpoint`, for non-trimmable models save the cache at the last-user-message boundary during prefill; later requests find it via the "shorter cache" path. The boundary is found by a sentinel trick: tokenise the conversation with the last user message replaced by "x" and take the token-wise common prefix, because `apply_chat_template(messages[:-1])` is not a token prefix of the full render under Qwen3.5's template. mlx-lm PR #923 (dexloom, 2026-02-22) took another route: `LRUPromptCache` boundary caching at message delimiters (`<|im_end|>`), `keep_original` co

items.concept: Hybrid GatedDeltaNet state rollback and checkpoint prefix caching
items.summary: llama.cpp's hybrid memory is two sub-caches: an attention KV cache and a recurrent cache with one cell per sequence.
items.text: Hybrid GatedDeltaNet state rollback and checkpoint prefix caching llama.cpp's hybrid memory is two sub-caches: an attention KV cache and a recurrent cache with one cell per sequence. llama.cpp's hybrid memory is two sub-caches: an attention KV cache and a recurrent cache with one cell per sequence. A checkpoint stores only the part that cannot be rebuilt by truncation (`LLAMA_STATE_SEQ_FLAGS_PARTIAL_ONLY`); the attention KV prefix stays in the slot. The recurrent cache also keeps a short ring of per-token snapshots (`n_rs_seq`), used when speculative decoding rejects part of a draft. Restore picks the latest checkpoint at or before the shared prefix and reprocesses from there. 2026-04-26: issue 22384 shows the restore test never succeeds for recurrent state. 2026-06: PRs 24176, 24411 and 25472 repair placement, erasure and eviction; PR 24797 (draft) targets the `seq_pos_min()` root cause. ik_llama.cpp keeps the same logic and the same failure (issue 1762, May 2026). Speculative decoding on hybrid models uses checkpoints: the server logs `speculative decoding will use checkpoints` at load. Partial acceptance beyond `n_rs_seq` used to fail `seq_rm` and leave the attention cache with stale entries. The recurrent snapshot is not precise after a fall-through rollback: the model reprocesses from the last valid checkpoint. The hybrid `seq_pos_min()` was written as `max()` of both sub-caches; the PR 24797 author argues it should return only the attention cache's minimum, as non-hybrid memory does. Whether other hybrid types (Mamba-based) should follow is untested. Merge state and effect of PR 24797 on the residual misses reported after 24411 and 24176. Whether Metal's behavior differs; every cited log is CUDA or ROCm. PR 24797 states hybrid memory consists of two independent cache subsystems with different positional semantics: for the attention cache `pos_min` is the earliest cached KV position, and for the recurrent cache `pos_min == pos_max ==` the current position. PR 24797 says the old `seq_pos_min()` returned the `std::max()` of both caches' minimums, which made a cached prefix look absent and forced full reprocessing on any prompt variation (stripped thinking, injected timestamp). PR 24797 keeps `seq_pos_max` with intersection semantics because it bounds valid attention entries by where the recurrent state has advanced. PR 24797 notes other hybrid types with recurrent memory would probably benefit from the same `seq_pos_min()` change but were not tested. On

items.text: Hybrid graphics on Linux: Intel iGPU plus NVIDIA eGPU for headless compute Running an Intel integrated GPU alongside an NVIDIA Thunderbolt eGPU used only for compute on Linux — xe versus i915 binding on Arrow Lake, how the desktop picks a primary GPU, keeping GNOME off the e Running an Intel integrated GPU alongside an NVIDIA Thunderbolt eGPU used only for compute on Linux - xe versus i915 binding on Arrow Lake, how the desktop picks a primary GPU, keeping GNOME off the eGPU, PRIME render offload versus pure CUDA, and sharing one 16 GB GPU between several compute servers. verified-as-of: 2026-09-25 Tags: [SOURCED url] = read/returned by a fetched page or search result during the research pass; [INFERRED] = reasoned from mechanism, verify on your box; [BOX] = observed on the reference machine (Intel NUC 15 Pro, Arrow Lake-P iGPU at 00:02.0, Ubuntu 26.04.1 GNOME Wayland, kernel 7.0.0-34, RTX 5080 over TB4, nvidia 610.57.04-open loaded late). Two independent GPU roles. A display/compositor GPU owns scanout and the desktop; a compute GPU only runs CUDA/Vulkan-compute. In a hybrid box the goal is usually: iGPU = display, eGPU = compute only. Arch's eGPU page states compute-only workloads (CUDA) that display nothing "should work without any extra configuration", and monitors on the iGPU work out of the box [SOURCED https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/External_GPU via search result]. Kernel driver vs userspace stack. xe/i915 (kernel DRM drivers for Intel) and nvidia/nvidia_drm (NVIDIA) are separate kernel stacks; CUDA talks to the nvidia module through /dev/nvidia*, not through DRM. DRM nodes (/dev/dri/cardN, renderDN) matter only to compositors, Vulkan/EGL/GL and PRIME. [INFERRED] Compositor multi-GPU model. Mutter picks one primary GPU, composites there, and copies buffers to displays on other GPUs [SOURCED https://github.com/GNOME/mutter/blob/main/doc/multi-gpu.md]. Any DRM device it can open may still get probed/initialised, which is the likely source of a few MiB of gnome-shell VRAM on a second GPU [INFERRED]. PRIME render offload = per-application choice of render GPU while display stays on the primary; pure compute = no graphics API at all. They are different mechanisms; CUDA does not need PRIME [INFERRED from NVIDIA PRIME README scope]. Selection is by identifiers, not by order. Dense 4B and MoE 30B-A3B decode at nearly the same rate on llama.cpp Metal (88 vs 86 tok/s), so MoE active-parameter savings do not appear there. Same model, two engines: llama.cpp Metal 86.2 tok/s versus MLX 159.7 tok/s (1.85x) on M4 Max for Nemotron-3 Nano 30B-A3B, but the two quants differ (about 6.2 bpw versus 4-bit), so bytes moved per token are not equal. Whether llama.cpp Metal has a fused SSM (Mamba-2) kernel or runs it as separate ops is not stated in the sources read; the 88 vs 86 result suggests a fixed per-token cost. No batched-decode measurement of a Mamba-2 hybrid on Mac was found. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super is a 120B hybrid Transformer-Mamba MoE with 12B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. llama.cpp discussion 20421 (ggerganov, 2026-03-11) summarizes llama.cpp performance for the Nemotron 3 family. On an M4 Max 128 GB (macOS 27.0), Nemotron-3 Nano 30B-A3B decodes at 86.2 +/- 0.5 tok/s on llama.cpp Metal (b8680, unsloth Q4_K_M 24.6 GB) and 159.7 tok/s on mlx-lm 0.31.3 (mlx-community 4-bit, 17.8 GB). On the same M4 Max, Nemotron-3 Nano 4B decodes at 88.4 tok/s on llama.cpp Metal (Q4_K_M 2.84 GB), 176.8 tok/s on MLX (4-bit 2.24 GB) and 85.2 tok/s on Apple Core AI (int8-head export, 4.6 GB). Apple Core AI ran the Nano 4B at 16.0 tok/s on an iPhone 17 Pro (AOT, cooled). llama.cpp Metal prompt processing on the M4 Max: pp512 1212.8 tok/s for Nano 30B-A3B and 1308.8 tok/s for Nano 4B, with max RSS 24.4 GB and 3.0 GB; llama-bench used `-p 512 -n 256 -ngl 99 -fa 1 -r 3` and `-fa 0` was within noise. The contributor flagged that on llama.cpp the dense 4B decodes almost as slowly as the 30B-A3B despite a 9x smaller file, while MLX shows 177 versus 160 tok/s; he did not investigate the cause. Column caveats stated by the contributor: the unsloth Q4_K_M is about 6.2 bits per weight, the Core AI artifact is not a 4-bit run, and peak memory is max RSS for llama.cpp but Metal peak allocation for MLX. A guide to running Nemotron on a Mac with MLX says the 30B Nano hybrid Mamba2-Transformer is still maturing in mlx-lm and recommends the 9B or 12B v2 variants if problems appear, and quotes about 80-100 tok/s for the 30B in 4-bit o

items.concept: Hybrid Score Fusion (Reciprocal Rank Fusion - RRF)
items.summary: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the industry standard zero-shot method for combining ranked lists in hybrid search pipelines (e.g., merging sparse BM25 and dense vector results). It computes a unified
items.text: Hybrid Score Fusion (Reciprocal Rank Fusion - RRF) Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the industry standard zero-shot method for combining ranked lists in hybrid search pipelines (e.g., merging sparse BM25 and dense vector results). It computes a unified Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the industry standard zero-shot method for combining ranked lists in hybrid search pipelines (e.g., merging sparse BM25 and dense vector results). It computes a unified score based solely on a document's rank position across multiple retrieval lists, avoiding the complexity of normalizing disparate score distributions. While highly stable and effective as a baseline, RRF struggles in advanced multi-stage pipelines because it discards confidence magnitude, lacks query-dependent weighting, and its recall gains are frequently neutralized by subsequent Cross-Encoder reranking stages. RRF is a position-based aggregation algorithm. It calculates a final score by summing the inverse of a document's rank across all candidate lists. The formula is: $\text{RRFscore}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + \text{rank}(r, d)}$ (Google Vertex AI). The constant $k$ (typically set to 60) acts as a smoothing factor. It prevents a single #1 ranking from dominating the final score, allowing documents that perform consistently well across multiple sources to rise to the top. By discarding raw scores, RRF effectively bypasses the difficult problem of normalizing unbounded lexical scores (BM25) against bounded semantic scores (cosine similarity) (OpenSearch). The primary alternative to RRF in zero-shot or lightly-tuned systems is Convex Combination (CC), which uses raw similarity scores. CC uses a weighted sum: $\alpha \cdot \text{Score}_{\text{lexical}} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \text{Score}_{\text{semantic}}$. While CC allows for fine-grained domain tuning and can outperform RRF when properly optimized, it is highly sensitive to score distribution outliers and requires rigorous score normalization (e.g., Min-Max, Sigmoid). RRF remains the default choice for its "set-it-and-forget-it" robustness, whereas CC is favored by mature pipelines with high-quality feedback loops. As search pipelines mature into multi-stage retrieval architectures, RRF's limitations become apparent. Insensitivity to Confidence: By stripping out raw scores, RRF treats a marginal rank match identically to a highly confident rank match. items.concept: ibv_devinfo hang as an RDMA health probe
items.summary: The probe idea: run `ibv_devinfo` and treat a hang as a sign that Thunderbolt RDMA is wedged, then show a dashboard warning. It comes from one sentence in exo issue 1712.
items.text: ibv_devinfo hang as an RDMA health probe The probe idea: run `ibv_devinfo` and treat a hang as a sign that Thunderbolt RDMA is wedged, then show a dashboard warning. It comes from one sentence in exo issue 1712. The probe idea: run `ibv_devinfo` and treat a hang as a sign that Thunderbolt RDMA is wedged, then show a dashboard warning. It comes from one sentence in exo issue 1712. The issue says jaccl errors such as exo issue 1711 recover only by unplugging and replugging the Thunderbolt 5 cable or rebooting, and that "usually when these errors happen, the `ibv_devinfo` command hangs". It asks for a dashboard warning with advice to reconnect cables, then reboot. The issue has one participant, no comments, no assignee, no linked branch or pull request, and the label `enhancement`. It gives no logs, no macOS version and no reproduction. ds4's docs use `ibv_devinfo -v` the other way round: as a static check that the port is active and has an IPv4-mapped GID, and as the place to read `--rdma-device` and `--rdma-gid-index` values. They do not mention hangs. Exo's reliability PRs 2367 and 2370 took other routes to the same goal. PR 2367 stops a runner when its supervisor sees MLX's ring diagnostic "Too many send/recv errors. Aborting..." on stderr. PR 2370 stops the first-rank runner after 90 seconds without a token or prefill progress report while a generation is in flight. Neither uses `ibv_devinfo`. Both PRs target a stuck runner process. A wedged driver that hangs `ibv_devinfo` is a different layer, and a runner blocked inside JACCL would already be caught only by the 90-second rule. A hung probe may not be killable: processes stuck in the Thunderbolt RDMA stack have been seen in uninterruptible sleep (`Us+`) where `kill -9` does nothing. A probe run without a timeout, or with one that only sends a signal, can leave stuck probe processes behind. `ibv_devinfo` reports `PORT_ACTIVE` only when all connected Macs have RDMA enabled (per distributed-inference-across-macs.md), so a clean exit with `PORT_DOWN` and a hang are different signals. Probe versus progress watchdog. Issue 1712 proposes a link-layer probe; the merged-or-open reliability PRs use runner-level signals (stderr diagnostic, token silence) and recreate the runner. The sources do not compare them. Whether `ibv_devinfo` hangs on macOS 26.5 and later, or on macOS 27's reworked library. No fetched source tests it after March 2026. [low] An explicit session is started by the application calling `startSession`, while an implicit session is started by the driver when an operation is called without an explicit session. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/sessions/driver-sessions.md [low] Session consistency is a practical version of causal consistency where a process accesses the storage system in the context of a session, and using sessions makes the stickiness of clients to the server explicit. Sources: https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html [low] If a session terminates due to a failure scenario, a new session must be created, and the consistency guarantees do not overlap the sessions. Sources: https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html Fact 29 mentions "Max has been called on to help in three (3) separate instances" which is unrelated to the technical definition of implicit vs explicit sessions and appears to be noise or a misclassified fact. Sources: https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/DRIVERS-2860 Fact 37 lists "Fix Version/s: 3.6.0-rc0" which is a specific version tag for a fix, not a general property of implicit vs explicit sessions. Sources: https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-30977 [medium] For explicit sessions, the default value of the `causalConsistency` property is `not supplied`, and if no value is supplied, it is inherited from the global default which is defined to be `true`. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/specifications/master/source/causal-consistency/causal-consistency.md, https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/DRIVERS-2369 [low] For implicit sessions, the `causalConsistency` property MUST be set to `false` to avoid potential conflicts with an operation's read concern level, a requirement established on 2022-11-11. items.concept: Independent shard scaling and per-shard tiering
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Independent shard scaling and per-shard tiering. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Independent shard scaling and per-shard tiering Source-anchored research for Independent shard scaling and per-shard tiering. Run status: COMPLETED. Zones are the supported way to steer data onto particular shards. A zone maps shard-key ranges to one or more shards. The balancer moves chunks that fall in a zone range only to shards in that zone. A document that matches a zone can be written only to a shard in it; a document that matches no zone can land on any shard. The MongoDB manual lists routing data by shard hardware or performance as a common zone use. (high confidence) Resizing a shard is a rolling change. Atlas documents zero downtime for tier changes up or down: it elects a secondary as the new primary, then replaces the old member. Reverting an asymmetric cluster to symmetric tiers starts a rolling resize of all shards. Expect a primary election on each shard that is resized. (medium confidence) Atlas NVMe clusters are not compatible with independent shard scaling. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18) Atlas deploys Search Nodes per shard: two Search Nodes on a three-shard cluster means six Search Nodes. The docs describe one node-count and node-size setting, from 2 to 32 nodes per region per shard, and document no per-shard Search Node tier. A Feb 2025 feedback idea asks to scale Search Nodes per shard (for example none on two shards and S40 on a third). It still showed status Submitted, 3 votes and no reply on 2026-10-20. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Per-shard auto-scaling is not active on every cluster. Terraform configs written before v1.23.0, clusters imported from the legacy schema, and configs moved straight from v1.x to v2.0.0 may lack shard-level auto-scaling until an update triggers it, for example by temporarily changing compute_min_instance_size. For UI-managed clusters that enabled compute auto-scaling before the default changed, the Atlas docs say to contact MongoDB support to get independent scaling. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) SERVER-2218, 'Make sharding balancer smarter when asymmetric hardware', asks for a shard-size-aware balancer. Its example: 2 TB shards extended with 3 TB shards leave the extra 1 TB unused. The ticket was created 2010-12-14 and last updated 2023-11-17. It is Unresolved in Backlog with no fix version and shows no engineer comments. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Adding or removing zones or zone ranges triggers chunk migrations that can hurt cluster

Index filters exist only for the server process and disappear after shutdown; MongoDB also says it is difficult to create them on every cluster node. Query settings apply to the query shape across the cluster and persist across restarts. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Neither mechanism guarantees an index scan: index filters only restrict the indexes evaluated and can still yield COLLSCAN, while query-setting indexHints restrict available indexes without forcing the planner to use one. A matching query setting with index hints also takes precedence over command-level index hints. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) To recreate an index restriction, define query settings for the corresponding query shape with setQuerySettings and place the namespace and allowed indexes in settings.indexHints. setQuerySettings accepts either a query definition or an existing query-shape hash; inspect saved settings with the $querySettings aggregation stage and verify behavior with explain(). (medium confidence) MongoDB documents deprecate index filters starting in 8.0 and recommend query settings instead; the same docs say query settings have more functionality, while filters are nonpersistent and difficult to configure on every cluster node. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) MongoDB's documented replacement can express index allowlists: setQuerySettings accepts a representative find, distinct, or aggregate command or a query-shape hash, and settings.indexHints.allowedIndexes can list index names or key patterns. Teams can inspect settings with $querySettings and verify them in explain output. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) The reviewed MongoDB manuals document planCacheSetFilter and setQuerySettings as separate commands and describe no one-step conversion. I infer that migration requires recreating each filter's intended restriction as a setting for the matching query shape, then validating it with explain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) MongoDB 8.0 distinguishes the legacy plan-cache query shape used by index filters from the new query shape used by query settings. The old queryHash field is renamed planCacheShapeHash, while the new shape uses queryShapeHash; verify the target queryShapeHash before applying settings by hash after a version or cluster migration. (high confide

Child pack of Indexing. GiST indexes are a versatile type of index that can handle complex data types, such as geometric shapes, full-text search, and network addresses. [They are implemented using a custom data structure optimized for searching large amounts of data1](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gist.html). Here are some key points: SP-GiST (Spatial Generalized Search Tree) indexes are a versatile index type offered by PostgreSQL. They are designed for complex, non-rectangular data types and work especially well with geometrical and network-based data. Here are some key points: An expression index stores the result of an expression rather than a raw column value. Use expression indexes when queries frequently filter or sort by a computed value. The `where` argument allows you to define [partial indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html) (also known as filtered indexes). A partial index only includes rows that match a specified condition, which reduces the index size and improves both write performance and query performance for the indexed subset of data. The SP-GiST index is a good choice for many different non-balanced data structures. If the query matches the partitioning rule, it can be very fast. Bounds intersection refers to the point where multiple bounds overlap. For example, given the bounds `[ [ 3, Infinity ] ]` and `[ [ -Infinity, 6 ] ]`, the intersection of the bounds results in `[ [ 3, 6 ] ]`. items.text: Individual Buyer Best Practices at Salvage Auctions Depth-first rabbithole dossier for Individual Buyer Best Practices at Salvage Auctions; source-anchored research pack. **U-1. Is a broker a protection or a liability for an individual buyer?** Sources framing broker use as best practice emphasize access and bidding expertise (<https://www.carproxy.com/how-it-works/preview-copart-vehicles>), while the retitling literature requires the salvage title, parts receipts, and bill of sale to be in one and the same name (<https://carregistrationfee.com/articles/salvage-rebuilt-title-registration.html>). Whether a broker-mediated purchase satisfies that name-matching test, and under which states' rules, is not resolved by any source found. **This is the single most cons This report covers what an *individual, non-dealer buyer* must do to buy safely and legally at a salvage auto auction in the United States: gaining access to the auction, checking title and brand history before bidding, inspecting the vehicle and its safety-critical repaired parts, and retitling the vehicle after purchase. It traces how individual access to salvage auctions came about, and identifies the primary and official sources that govern each step. - **How many states actually let an individual bid on a salvage vehicle.** Secondary sources give specific counts — one commercial blog claims roughly 28 states require a licensed broker for private buyers of salvage vehicles. No official or primary source was found that enumerates this nationally; the only verified state-level rule in this run is Wisconsin's, which forbids personal purchases on a BID card. The national count is therefore **unverified** and should not be treated as fact. NMVTIS and the Copart 10-K both confirm the underlying structure (state-by-state regulation), not the tally 48. The FTC Used Car Rule's Buyers Guide requirement, which is the main federal disclosure protection in retail used-car buying, does not apply here in either of the two ways that matter: "The Rule does not apply at auctions that are closed to consumers," and excepted from the Rule is "any vehicle sold for scrap or parts if the dealer submits title documents to the appropriate state authority and obtains a salvage certification" — https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/dealers-guide-used-car-rule. 49. Run status: COMPLETED. Key vectors in transformer self-attention contain sensitive channel-specific magnitude spikes that cause severe perplexity degradation if quantized uniformly with standard symmetric rounding. (high confidence) PCIe protocol tunneling encapsulates Transaction Layer Packets (TLPs) into transport frames, incurring packet assembly and disassembly overhead at host and device controllers. (high confidence) Super-block K-quants (Q4_K) group 256 weights into chunks with a shared FP16 super-block scale and eight 6-bit sub-block scales, reducing quantization noise in attention projection layers. (high confidence) Asymmetric KV cache quantization preserves key vector outlier dimensions in FP8 or FP16 while quantizing value vectors to 4-bit affine blocks, reducing KV memory by up to 70% with less than 0.1 perplexity delta. (high confidence) Synchronously blocking CPU execution on MTLCommandBuffer waitUntilCompleted() prevents overlapping CPU dispatch with GPU execution, causing up to 25% throughput degradation on small models. (high confidence) When speculative verification achieves an acceptance rate greater than 60%, end-to-end token generation throughput increases by 25% to 45% on memory-bandwidth-constrained devices. (high confidence) PAM3 signaling achieves a 50% data rate improvement over binary NRZ at identical Nyquist frequencies by encoding three voltage levels into two transmitted unit intervals. (high confidence) Speculative decoding amortizes parameter weight memory loading across K candidate tokens by evaluating candidate sequences as a small parallel GEMM batch instead of K sequential GEMV reads. (high confidence) Retimer jitter and transport layer flow control credits cause non-deterministic round-trip DMA completion times, necessitating large contiguous transfers rather than layer-by-layer handshakes. (high confidence) Prompt pre-fill evaluates GEMM operations where high arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte > 100) saturates GPU tensor cores and scales linearly with compute clock frequencies. (high confidence) Auto-regressive decoding executes GEMV operations with minimal arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte approx. 1), causing GPU compute ALUs to sit idle while awaiting memory bus DRAM/GDDR reads. items.summary: Source-anchored research for Inter-model homogeneity in open-ended generation. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Inter-model homogeneity in open-ended generation Source-anchored research for Inter-model homogeneity in open-ended generation. Run status: COMPLETED. Homogeneity is a distributional property, not a lack of individual quality: in the PNAS Nexus study LLMs matched or slightly beat humans on individual originality for two of three tasks, while population-level diversity was much lower. The Hivemind paper likewise finds comparable overall quality but poor calibration of LMs, reward models and LM judges on generations that draw differing idiosyncratic human preferences. (medium confidence) Scope limits on the homogeneity findings: the PNAS Nexus study covers only publicly hosted, aligned LLMs and three divergent-thinking tasks. The longitudinal study cannot separate distillation, shared training data or shared techniques, samples one response per model per prompt, and notes some Infinity-Chat prompts themselves request similar outputs. (medium confidence) In a PNAS Nexus study of 22 LLMs and 102 humans, LLM response variability was lower than human variability on all three divergent-thinking tasks: Alternative Uses 0.459 vs 0.699, Forward Flow 0.518 vs 0.642, Divergent Association 0.632 vs 0.791 (p<0.01). LLM responses mirror other LLM responses more than humans mirror other humans. (medium confidence) The Artificial Hivemind paper defines two effects: intra-model repetition (one model repeats similar outputs) and inter-model homogeneity (different models independently converge on similar ideas with minor phrasing variations). It uses Infinity-Chat, 26K real-world open-ended queries with 31,250 human annotations (25 annotators per example). (high confidence) A longitudinal study of 68 models from 12 providers (March 2023 to July 2026) reports cross-family semantic distance falling over time: on the Alternate Uses Task from about 0.50 to below 0.40, and on Infinity-Chat100 from about 0.34 to just above 0.32. All 1,000 resampling iterations gave negative slopes. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) The Hivemind paper measures similarity with cosine similarity of OpenAI text-embedding-3-small embeddings; secondary summaries note this is sensitive to surface phrasing and could overstate homogeneity, though verbatim-overlap examples suggest it is not a pure artifact. (low confidence)

items.text: Interface-bound sockets IP_BOUND_IF and required_interface and sandbox behaviour Source-anchored research for Interface-bound sockets IP_BOUND_IF and required_interface and sandbox behaviour. Run status: COMPLETED. Binding to the physical interface's IP with bind() makes traffic bypass a NetworkExtension-based VPN tunnel; Apple said in 2017 this is not a vulnerability because NetworkExtension makes no guarantee about traffic flow. Always-On VPN is not affected. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2017-12-19) Inside a NEPacketTunnelProvider, setsockopt IP_BOUND_IF to the tunnel does not work because NECP prevents VPN loops (the call can succeed but data takes the default interface). This is irrelevant to a plain sandboxed monitor app. (low confidence) (verified as of 2022-09-01) A VPN that sets includeAllNetworks can still send traffic over the VPN interface even when IP_BOUND_IF names another interface, so an interface-bound monitor probe cannot be assumed to leave via that interface on such hosts. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2024-01-01) IP_BOUND_IF (IPPROTO_IP) and IPV6_BOUND_IF (IPPROTO_IPV6) take an interface index from if_nametoindex() and limit transmission and reception to that interface; Apple's recommendation is to use them rather than bind() to an interface's IP address. (high confidence) An Apple DTS test on macOS 13.5 showed IP_BOUND_IF forcing a connection through a VPN utun interface versus the default en0 route; DTS said it has worked this way for decades. (medium confidence) Do not hard-code BSD interface names such as pdp_ip0 or assume IPv4 is present; resolve the interface at runtime and use IPV6_BOUND_IF where only IPv6 exists. For TCP/UDP, Apple DTS prefers Network.framework requiredInterfaceType. (medium confidence) NWParameters exposes requiredInterface, requiredInterfaceType, prohibitedInterfaces and prohibitedInterfaceTypes under 'Selecting Paths' for connections and listeners (and browsers for requiredInterface); this is the Network.framework counterpart of interface-bound sockets. Exact availability strings were not retrieved. (low confidence) Sandbox behaviour: sources show only that network operations are denied without the network entitlements (sandbox log 'deny(1) network-bind*:0' on iOS, where App Sandbox entitlements do not apply). No source states that the IP_BOUND_IF setsockopt itself is sandbox-restricted or exempt; assume it is governed by the network.client/server entitlement on connect/bind and verify empiricall

Verify against the primary sources in References before relying on anything, and for your own situation consult a licensed fee-only fiduciary advisor and/or a tax professional. Where this sits. Spoke of the consumer-finance family; the consumer-finance hub is the anchor. The sibling consumer-credit-and-debt hub owns credit/debt routing. This skill owns the investing + retirement-savings layer. It states the tax treatment of accounts but hands off tax-form depth to personal-income-taxes, deposit accounts/CDs to personal-banking, and life-insurance-as-"investment" to personal-insurance (see cross-references at the end). This skill is deliberately boring: the evidence favors low-cost, diversified, long-horizon investing over stock-picking and market-timing. It will not give hot tips. Risk and return are linked. Evidence the bug is in the driver and not in MLX or in memory exhaustion: (1) the kernel panics, a process-level OOM would not; (2) every memory-bounding arm of the controlled test (rotating KV cache, wired cap 5 GiB under recommended, `MLX_MAX_OPS_PER_BUFFER/MB=200`) ended in an ordinary userspace `kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorOutOfMemory` and never panicked; (3) the panic reproduced with 10 GB headroom, at ~20% cache use, and idle after the last request; (4) the panic string names IOGPU reference counts, and the author of the controlled test places the underflow on the synchronous command-buffer completion path, because disabling the IOGPU wired collector and Metal4 async mapping changed nothing (109.6 s vs 102-108 s). The controlled test's discriminating variable: the per-buffer MTLResidencySet wire/unwire plus commit traffic that `mx.set_wired_limit` switches on. Removing only that (R1) protects; removing only `clear_cache` destroy bursts (R2) does not. Concurrency matters because completion handling overlaps residency mutation; single-stream traffic with identical flags never panicked. The no-op shim: assign `mx.set_wired_limit` a function returning 0 at `mlx.core` module level before `mlx_lm.server` starts. mlx_lm shares that module object, so one assignment covers all 7 call sites in the package, including `server.py` which calls it unconditionally in 0.31.3. Toggle name `MLX_LM_DISABLE_WIRED_LIMIT=1` belongs to the shim, not to mlx-lm. The shim also offers a capped variant (`MLX_LM_WIRED_HEADROOM_GB`, cap = recommended working set minus N GiB; mutually exclusive with the no-op), `MLX_LM_NO_CLEAR_CACHE`, `MLX_LM_CACHE_LIMIT_GB`. items.concept: IOKit-mapped Metal buffer accounting in phys_footprint
items.summary: `alternate_accounting` is "the number of internal dirty pages which are part of IOKit mappings"; they are counted in both internal and iokit_mapped, so they are subtracted from the footprint sum.
items.text: IOKit-mapped Metal buffer accounting in phys_footprint `alternate_accounting` is "the number of internal dirty pages which are part of IOKit mappings"; they are counted in both internal and iokit_mapped, so they are subtracted from the footprint sum. `alternate_accounting` is "the number of internal dirty pages which are part of IOKit mappings"; they are counted in both internal and iokit_mapped, so they are subtracted from the footprint sum. A map entry gets the IOKit charge only when the entry is created with the iokit_acct flag AND its object is internal (anonymous). The code sets `iokit_acct = TRUE`, `use_pmap = FALSE` and calls `vm_map_iokit_mapped_region` with the entry size. Therefore a file-backed (external) object mapped through the same path takes the plain pmap branch and is not charged to `iokit_mapped`. Page queries treat non-purgeable internal IOKit memory as present and dirty across its whole virtual range ("phys_footprint includes the entire virtual mapping"). Objects flagged `vo_no_footprint` are excluded from the footprint entirely ("does not count in footprint"). Measured: a 2 GiB `MTLResourceStorageModeShared` buffer from `newBufferWithLength:` added 0 to `phys_footprint` and `internal` when created, and 2.15 GB to both only after the CPU wrote the pages with memset; `resident_size` tracked the same. [asserted] (measured locally 2026-10-04, Apple M5 Max, macOS 27.2, via TASK_VM_INFO) Measured: a 2 GiB anonymous mmap that was touched, then wrapped with `newBufferWithBytesNoCopy:`, added nothing at wrap time (4.30 GB before and after); footprint rose only by the touched pages. Releasing the Metal buffer left the anon pages. [asserted] (same host) Measured: a 2 GiB shared file mapping written and msynced, then wrapped with `newBufferWithBytesNoCopy:`, showed `phys_footprint` 0.01 GB, `external` 2.16 GB and `resident_size` 2.16 GB before and after wrapping. [asserted] (same host) Measured: wrapping an untouched anonymous 2 GiB region as a no-copy buffer then filling it with a GPU blit raised `phys_footprint` only to 0.12 GB and left `resident_size` at 0.01 GB, so GPU-written pages in that case were not charged to the task as dirty internal pages in the way CPU writes were. [asserted] (same host; one run, cause unexplained) Not documented in sources read. The vmlx 130 GB footprint at first prefill therefore needs another explanation (touched or GPU-written pages, wired memory, or a different allocation path). The test here cannot show which.

A Frida trace of `powermetrics --samplers cpu_power` on Mac14,7 (Apple M2) under macOS 26.5.2 found three successful IOReport subscriptions: "CPU Complex Performance States" (4 channels), "CPU Core Performance States" (8 channels) and "Energy Model" (13...
items.text: IOReport Energy Model channels versus powermetrics samplers powermetrics reads energy through IOReport. A Frida trace of `powermetrics --samplers cpu_power` on Mac14,7 (Apple M2) under macOS 26.5.2 found three successful IOReport subscriptions: "CPU Complex Performance States" (4 channels), "CPU Core Performance States" (8 channels) and "Energy Model" (13... powermetrics reads energy through IOReport. A Frida trace of `powermetrics --samplers cpu_power` on Mac14,7 (Apple M2) under macOS 26.5.2 found three successful IOReport subscriptions: "CPU Complex Performance States" (4 channels), "CPU Core Performance States" (8 channels) and "Energy Model" (136 channels). The Energy Model subscription is the whole group even when only the `cpu_power` sampler is requested: the 136 channels include CPU, GPU, ANE, DRAM, display, media, SRAM and other SoC energy channels. Which of them powermetrics prints is a separate, sampler-controlled step. Each reporting cycle samples every subscription once with `IOReportCreateSamples` and takes one `IOReportCreateSamplesDelta` against the previous cycle's sample. The requested interval does not subdivide into hidden samples; it only sets the wait between cycles. The real window is a little longer than requested and is written in the plist as `elapsed_ns`. Measured windows: a 1000 ms request gave a median 1009.3 ms (range 1003.5 to 1011.4), 250 ms gave 258.1 ms, 100 ms gave 107.9 ms. Energy divided by the requested interval overstates power by about 1%, 3% and 8% at those settings; use `elapsed_ns`. Consequence: a zeus (or macmon, TokenWatt) reading and a powermetrics reading of the same run draw on the same counters, so they cannot disagree about the hardware's report. Differences come from window alignment, from which channels each tool sums, and from sampler formatting. Apple's own man page says average power values are "estimated and may be inaccurate" and "should not be used for any comparison between devices", but may help optimize apps. The IOReport energy values that back them are believed to be model-based (utilization, frequency, voltage). Both statements apply to every IOReport-based tool. powermetrics needs sudo and reports only at fixed intervals; zeus-apple-silicon gives energy over arbitrary code windows without sudo, plus per-core and DRAM values. powermetrics only aggregates CPU, GPU and ANE per its samplers. On M1, zeus's DRAM, ANE and GPU SRAM fields may be None; on M2 and later all fields are typically present.

items.summary: Source-anchored research for IPv6-only DNS64 NAT64 review network and IPv4-literal probes and Guideline 2.5.5 and Internet Sharing NAT64 testing. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: IPv6-only DNS64 NAT64 review network and IPv4-literal probes and Guideline 2.5.5 and Internet Sharing NAT64 testing Source-anchored research for IPv6-only DNS64 NAT64 review network and IPv4-literal probes and Guideline 2.5.5 and Internet Sharing NAT64 testing. Run status: COMPLETED. RFC 8880 defines ipv4only.arpa (A: 192.0.0.170, 192.0.0.171) for NAT64 prefix discovery; a DNS64 resolver synthesizes AAAA records from the local prefix. Queries must go to the interface's own advertised resolver, not user-configured, VPN or local resolvers, because the NAT64 prefix is per-interface. (medium confidence) To reach an IPv4-literal-only target on a NAT64 network, pass the literal string to getaddrinfo with AF_UNSPEC (AI_DEFAULT); on OS X 10.11.2+/iOS 9.2+ it synthesizes an address such as 64:ff9b::192.0.2.1. Apple warns against synthesizing the Well-Known Prefix address manually. (high confidence) Apple's recommended app-side checks: dig AAAA for each server; an IPv4-mapped ::ffff:x.x.x.x in AAAA is invalid; a crash or failure on the review network is treated as an app bug, not a network problem. (low confidence) Apple lists these as common IPv4-literal failures on DNS64/NAT64: IP literals in protocols and config files, network preflighting with 0.0.0.0 or 169.254.0.0, and IPv4-only low-level APIs (gethostbyname, inet_aton, inet_addr, inet_ntoa) and storage (in_addr, sockaddr_in rather than sockaddr_storage). (high confidence) App Review Guideline 2.5.5 states apps must be fully functional on IPv6-only networks; Apple's IPv6 page says support has been required for all App Store submissions since June 1, 2016. (high confidence) Reachability guidance: do not use SCNetworkReachabilityCreateWithAddress with 0.0.0.0; use SCNetworkReachabilityCreateWithName with a hostname instead. (medium confidence) Local NAT64 test network: connect the Mac to the Internet by a non-Wi-Fi link, Option-click Sharing, choose Internet Sharing, tick Create NAT64 Network, configure Wi-Fi Options, then enable Internet Sharing. On the client, disable other interfaces (cellular/other Wi-Fi) so only the NAT64 network is used. (high confidence) Apple DTS says the App Review NAT64 network (ARNAT64) now behaves like the Mac Internet Sharing NAT64 (MacNAT64): it always synthesizes IPv6 addresses and lacks direct IPv6-to-IPv6 egress. So MacNAT64 is a close local proxy for review, though not identical. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2017-09-27)

Dispatch gate: ggml_metal_op_mul_mat picks the small-batch mat-vec kernels first when src1 is F32 and ne00 % 128 == 0, for batch (ne11) 2 to 8 on F32, F16, BF16, Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0, MXFP4 and IQ4_NL, but only for ne11 4 to 8 on Q2_K to Q6_K, using nsg 2. So at batch 2 or 3 (a two-token speculative verify) a Q6_K or Q4_K tensor misses the small-batch kernel and takes the general mat-mat path, while a Q8_0 tensor of the same shape stays on the mat-vec path. Unsloth's per-type table for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (hardware not stated) gives tg128 of 90.38 for q4_k, 90.50 for q6_k and 90.33 for q8_0, within 0.2%, though q8_0 moves 1.9 times the bytes of q4_k. That flatness shows decode in that setup is not scaling with weight bytes, so a byte-ratio prediction (1.46 for Q6_K over Q4_K) cannot be checked from it. An end-to-end tg number on a 3B-active MoE can sit on a launch or overhead floor, so equal tg for Q4_K, Q6_K and Q8_0 does not prove equal kernel cost. A valid microbenchmark must use shapes with ne00 % 256 == 0, F32 activations, and a batch of 1 (the mat-vec path) separately from 4 to 8. "Q6_K costs its byte ratio on a bandwidth-bound GPU" (covering file) versus a flat tg across q4_k, q6_k and q8_0 (Unsloth table): the two predict different outcomes and no source reconciles them. A per-type kernel timing (Metal capture or a test-backend-ops style op perf run) of MUL_MAT for Q4_K, Q6_K, Q8_0 at fixed shape on one M-series chip. The Metal small-batch mat-vec gate admits Q8_0 and the legacy types at batch 2 to 8 and K-quants only at batch 4 to 8, and requires F32 src1 and ne00 divisible by 128. Unsloth's Qwen3.5-35B-A3B tg128 column shows q4_k 90.38, q6_k 90.50, q8_0 90.33, mxfp4 90.67 and q2_k 90.77, while iq3_xxs, iq2_xxs and iq3_s sit near 84 to 86. No isolated Metal Q6_K versus Q4_K microbenchmark was found in any cached source.

The TCP star coordinator at `JACCL_COORDINATOR` stays the default, and a caller may instead pass `all_gather_factory` to `mx.distributed.init(backend="jaccl", ...)`. PR 3899 turns the JACCL bootstrap all-gather into a pluggable "side channel". The TCP star coordinator at `JACCL_COORDINATOR` stays the default, and a caller may instead pass `all_gather_factory` to `mx.distributed.init(backend="jaccl", ...)`. During initialisation JACCL exchanges RDMA connection metadata between ranks over a byte-level all-gather; the default is "a simple TCP star all-gather". The factory is called once per rank with `(rank, size)` and must return a callable `f(src: bytes, n_bytes: int) -> bytes` whose result has length `size * n_bytes` with all ranks' inputs concatenated in rank order. In `jaccl.cpp`, `Config::set_all_gather_factory` and `Config::set_all_gather` store the user function, and `Config::get_side_channel` prefers the factory, then the plain function, and only then builds a `TCPAllGather` from the coordinator address. `Config::is_valid` now accepts a config when the coordinator string is non-empty OR a factory OR an all-gather function is set, so a run with no coordinator is valid. The strict-mode error text still names a coordinator ("a coordinator ip/port (JACCL_COORDINATOR/MLX_JACCL_COORDINATOR)") and does not mention the factory. The Python binding was moved into `mlx/distributed/distributed.cpp` after review so the group registers with the backends map; the first version called `jaccl::init` directly from the binding and the group was not registered, which reviewer nastya236 flagged would break `mx.distributed.all_sum` without a group and `clear_backends()`. After the JACCL refactor (PR 3412, merged 2026-04-15) it scans the GID table for an IPv4-mapped GID (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`) instead of using the fixed index 1. Issue 3467, opened 2026-04-29, reports that with no such GID the variable was left uninitialized and the RTR step failed with errno 22. A Thunderbolt RDMA port publishes only one GID, a link-local `fe80::` address at index 0, until its network interface has an IPv4 address. Once the interface has one, an IPv4-mapped GID appears at index 1 (for example `::ffff:169.254.10.1`) and unmodified MLX works. The GID table length on these ports is 1024 entries (`gid_tbl_len: 1024`). Current main initializes `gid = {}`, tracks `found_gid`, and throws `[jaccl] No IPv4-mapped GID for this device. Thunderbolt RDMA ports only publish one once the interface has an IPv4 address; assign a link-local address to it, for example: ifconfig <interface> inet 169.254.0.1 netmask 255.255.0.0 alias`. `queue_pair_rtr` still hard-codes `grh.sgid_index = 1`, while `info()` accepts an IPv4-mapped GID at any index. The destination GID is used (`is_global = 1`) only when its interface-id half is non-zero. 2026-04-29: issue 3467 opened ("PR follows"); PR 3468, which closes it, zero-initialized `gid`, added a `try_gid()` helper and a fallback to the first non-zero GID preferring index 1. A wrong partial sum, not a connection error, is the symptom. It was merged on 2026-05-11 as commit 1322... mlx PR 3451, "[jaccl] Fix race on local_staging in MeshImpl::all_reduce", by kernelpool, fixes a data race that PR 3412 (the JACCL refactor) introduced in the fully connected "mesh" all_reduce. A wrong partial sum, not a connection error, is the symptom. It was merged on 2026-05-11 as commit 1322065 after approval by angeloskath. `MeshImpl::all_reduce` is a pipelined fully connected reduction with a fixed reduction order: it copies rank 0's data to the output and then reduces each later rank into the output in place. Its own data goes to a staging buffer so it can be reduced into the output at the right step. `PIPELINE` is 2, so it double-buffers. The bug: the SEND-completion handler refilled `local_staging(buff)` as soon as all peers had acknowledged the previous send, whether or not the own-rank reduction step had consumed that chunk. Whether it did depended on RDMA timing, so the sum was wrong only sometimes, and only for messages that span more than one pipeline chunk. The fix: SEND completion refills only `send_buffer` (free once the data is on the wire) and posts the next send. `local_staging(b)` is refilled inside the reduce loop right after the own-rank reduction has read it, and that refill also bumps `recv_end[rank_]`, which gates the next step. The diff is 15 additions and 8 deletions in `mesh_impl.h` only. The ring backend does not use this code path. The library does carry release paths: `Connection` has a destructor and the verbs table includes `dealloc_pd`, `destroy_qp` and `destroy_cq`. The reported leak is therefore not a missing call in JACCL's own code path as read here; it matches the reports that the kernel side does not return PDs after teardown. A larger mesh or more wires per pair burns the pool faster per init, so a 5-node mesh should hit the limit in fewer restarts than a 2-node pair. The reported counts do not fit this simple model (about 60 sessions at 2 nodes against 2 to 3 broadcasts at 5 nodes), so other consumers of the pool probably exist (orphans, probes). Ring init allocates a PD, a completion queue and a queue pair per connection, `2 * n_conns` PDs per rank Mesh init allocates a PD per connection to every peer, so a rank uses `(size - 1) * n_wires` PDs JACCL registers each send and receive buffer to the PD of the connection it serves JACCL's verbs table includes `dealloc_pd`, `destroy_qp` and `destroy_cq` and `Connection` has a destructor mlx-lm issue 955 recommends one N-node broadcast over N-1 sequential 2-node transfers to limit init cycles, and periodic reboots for heavy use mlx-lm issue 955 says RDMA device names change after every reboot, so `mlx.distributed_config --auto-setup` must be rerun and the hostfile redistributed after a PD-exhaustion reboot

items.summary: In the JACCL ring backend, `all_gather` sent the same half of every rank's region in both ring directions, so the other half of each peer's data was never transferred and the output held stale or zero bytes there. `all_sum` was not affected.
items.text: JACCL ring all_gather direction-1 slice bug (mlx PR 4443) In the JACCL ring backend, `all_gather` sent the same half of every rank's region in both ring directions, so the other half of each peer's data was never transferred and the output held stale or zero bytes there. `all_sum` was not affected. In the JACCL ring backend, `all_gather` sent the same half of every rank's region in both ring directions, so the other half of each peer's data was never transferred and the output held stale or zero bytes there. `all_sum` was not affected. The cause is the PR 3900 refactor: `all_gather_wire` gave both directions identical `wire_offset` and `wire_end`, so both covered the lower-half slice of each peer region. `all_reduce_wire` computes a per-direction term `lr * n_wires * size_per_wire`, which is why `all_sum` worked. The fix adds `n_wires` to `all_gather_wire`'s signature and computes `wire_offset[lr] = lr * n_wires * n_bytes_per_wire + lw * n_bytes_per_wire`, clamped to `min(n_bytes, (lr + 1) * n_wires * n_bytes_per_wire)`. The diff touches `mlx/distributed/jaccl/lib/jaccl/ring_impl.h` (20 added, 9 removed lines) and adds `test_all_gather_rank_data` to `python/tests/mlx_distributed_tests.py`. The new test gathers `arange(size) % 100003 + rank` for sizes 7, 1024, 1000003 and 4*1024*1024, so each rank's region is distinct and odd sizes exercise tail clamping; the old all-ones test could not detect a missing or misplaced region. Opened 2026-08-31 by Drifter4242, who disclosed that the AI model "Fable" found and fixed the bug and wrote the code; the author says he did not fully understand it. zcbenz labelled it low priority and, after the test was added, "await verification". Reproduction in the PR: `MLX_JACCL_RING=1`, 2 ranks, `all_gather` corrupts at every size while `all_sum` passes. On two M3 Ultras over Thunderbolt, wheel `0.32.3.dev20260901+37c26e575` (PR base) failed both `test_all_gather` and `test_all_gather_rank_data` on both ranks, and the fix build `+9b6b10c76` passed both. items.concept: JACCL RTR sgid_index hard-coded to 1
items.summary: In JACCL's `Connection::queue_pair_rtr`, the source GID index sent to the verbs driver is the literal `1`, independent of which GID table entry `Connection::info()` selected for the peer.
items.text: JACCL RTR sgid_index hard-coded to 1 In JACCL's `Connection::queue_pair_rtr`, the source GID index sent to the verbs driver is the literal `1`, independent of which GID table entry `Connection::info()` selected for the peer. In JACCL's `Connection::queue_pair_rtr`, the source GID index sent to the verbs driver is the literal `1`, independent of which GID table entry `Connection::info()` selected for the peer. `info()` loops over `gid_tbl_len` entries and keeps the first whose first 8 bytes and bytes 8-9 are zero and bytes 10-11 are `0xffff` (an IPv4-mapped GID), then `break`s; if none is found it throws the "No IPv4-mapped GID" error. The chosen GID is advertised to the peer as the destination GID. The local GID that the RTR transition names as source is looked up by `sgid_index = 1` inside the driver. The two choices agree only when the first IPv4-mapped entry is at index 1. ds4 does not have this coupling: its RTR passes `r->gid_index`, the index it scanned or the operator gave with `--rdma-gid-index`. On an explicit index ds4 calls `query_gid` on just that index and does not check that the entry is IPv4-mapped. Exo issue 1390 (Feb 2026, before the April JACCL refactor) already reports `Changing queue pair to RTR failed with errno 22` on two nodes whose `en2` to `en7` had no IPv4 address, and an exo maintainer replies that those interfaces "need to have reachable IP addresses, but after macOS 26.2 they do not self-assign by default". No entry in the cached MLX release notes for v0.30.4 through v0.32.3 mentions a change to RTR GID selection or to PR 4191's "usable GID" report. If the first IPv4-mapped entry is at index N other than 1, JACCL advertises the GID at N and routes from GID 1. A table whose entry 1 is zero or stale is the case the issue 3467 thread links to errno 96. No fetched issue or pull request proposes making `sgid_index` follow the scanned index. Two targeted searches found nothing. Is the hard-coded 1 a bug? On every table reported in the sources the IPv4-mapped entry is at index 1 (index 0 is `fe80::`), so the literal works there. ds4's author chose the scanned index anyway. No source shows a failing table that has the mapped entry at another index and a verified cause. Whether the Apple driver honours an `sgid_index` other than 1, which would make the hard-coded value harmless or harmful in a real table. Whether JACCL will follow ds4 and pass the chosen index. Policy API: `LoadConfiguration.default` auto-detects, falls back to environment variables, and caps residency at 70% by default; `config.jangPress = .enabled(coldFraction: 0.70)` pins the cold fraction, `.disabled` restores pre-JangPress behavior, `maxResidentBytes = .unlimited` removes the cap, and `runtime.status()` reports `enabled` and `coldFraction`. The wrapper script exposes `pct` (recommended 100 on a 128 GB Mac, "maximum routed-expert mass evicted", 50-70 on 256 GB+), `--jang-press-force-mode soft|force` (default soft; `force` only when first inference needs more aggressive reclaim, with slowdown), `--enable-jangpress-router-advice`, and `VMLX_JANGPRESS_ROUTE_TELEMETRY`. `JANGPRESS_PRESTACK` (default on) regenerates a prestack overlay of about 150 GB per Kimi variant on first load into `JANGPRESS_PRESTACK_CACHE_DIR` (default under `~/Library/Caches`); later loads of the same bundle are fast. The overlay connects the on-disk JANGTQ tile layout to the shape Metal expects without making routed weights resident. `VMLX_MEMORY_BUDGET_OVERRIDE` (default 256 GB in the script) bypasses the load gate's "model requires about 234 GB peak" check; calling `vmlxctl serve` directly without it fails with `insufficient memory: model requires ≈234 GB peak`. Low-RAM serve flags (`KIMI_LOW_RAM=1`) disable prefix, memory and disk KV caches and idle behavior, set `kv-cache-quantization=none` and default thinking off. Reported published bundles keep a subset of the routed experts: Kimi-K2.6-Small-JANGTQ keeps 211 of 384 (153 GB), Med 250 of 384 (167 GB), Large 288 of 384 (about 190 GB). These are pruned/re-quantized derivatives, not the full 384-expert model. A JANG bundle's routed experts are packed as JANGTQ tiles aligned for direct mmap, so no `MLX.stacked` materialization happens at load. 2026-05-04: JangPress guide "validation status" date. 2026-05-09: "Tighten JANGTQ runtime and JangPress bring-up" commit in jang-runtime. jang 2.5.18 release notes mention JangPress, DSV4 hybrid SWA+CSA+HSA runtime and Swift/Python examples. items.concept: JangPress RSS accounting after expert deactivation on macOS
items.summary: `TASK_VM_INFO.resident_size` is read from the `phys_mem` ledger, and `external` and `internal` are separate ledgers read next to it. The `phys_mem` ledger is the pmap-resident total, so it includes clean file-backed pages that a process has faulted in.
items.text: JangPress RSS accounting after expert deactivation on macOS `TASK_VM_INFO.resident_size` is read from the `phys_mem` ledger, and `external` and `internal` are separate ledgers read next to it. The `phys_mem` ledger is the pmap-resident total, so it includes clean file-backed pages that a process has faulted in. `TASK_VM_INFO.resident_size` is read from the `phys_mem` ledger, and `external` and `internal` are separate ledgers read next to it. The `phys_mem` ledger is the pmap-resident total, so it includes clean file-backed pages that a process has faulted in. `phys_footprint` is documented in the kernel as the sum of (internal - alternate_accounting), (internal_compressed - alternate_accounting_compressed), iokit_mapped, purgeable_nonvolatile, purgeable_nonvolatile_compressed and page_table. It has no term for `external` (file-backed) pages. Consequence for a mmap safetensors bundle: clean expert pages that stay mapped appear in `resident_size` (RSS) and never in `phys_footprint`. A tool that reports footprint shows a small idle number for a mapped bundle even if no page was ever dropped. Consequence for `MADV_DONTNEED`: the call leaves pmap entries in place (existing dossier), so `resident_size` should not fall at the call; it falls only when the pageout scan steals the deactivated pages. `phys_footprint` is unaffected either way. `iokit_mapped` counts the whole size of every IOKit mapping in the task "regardless of clean/dirty or internal/external state", and `vm_map_iokit_mapped_region` credits both `iokit_mapped` and `phys_footprint` with the full byte count at map time. In the page-query code, non-purgeable IOKit internal memory is reported as present and dirty for its entire virtual range ("phys_footprint includes the entire virtual mapping"). No dated history for JangPress accounting claims was found beyond the 2026-05-04 guide date already in jangpress-cold-expert-eviction-for-moe-larger-th.md. If a runtime wraps mmap pages as no-copy Metal buffers and those buffers are counted as IOKit mappings, `phys_footprint` would be charged the full mapped size at map time. That would explain a footprint near 130 GB at first prefill, but no source states how vMLX's no-copy buffers are accounted. The Kimi runtime README reports "~130 GB process footprint" before token 1 and "about 1 GB" idle RSS for the same bundle. The two numbers can both be correct only if they come from different ledgers or from different moments; the README does not name its tool. Activit

For Node.js language/runtime APIs and event-loop internals, defer to the sibling references javascript-nodejs.md and nodejs-concurrency-internals.md - this file assumes that foundation and focuses on what differs. There are now four practically-relevant server-side JS/TS execution targets: The unifying thread is WinterTC (formerly WinterCG): the standard defining the Minimum Common Web Platform API - the subset of browser/Web APIs every server runtime implements identically, so code written to that surface is portable across all of them. Understand WinterTC first; it is the shared branch every runtime below inherits from. History. WinterCG (Web-interoperable Runtimes Community Group, a W3C CG founded by Cloudflare, Vercel, Deno, Shopify and others) incubated a "minimum common API." In January 2025 WinterCG was wound down and the work moved to Ecma TC55 ("WinterTC" - Technical Committee on Web-interoperable Server Runtimes). The spec is now ECMA-429 ("Minimum common web API"), adopted by the Ecma General Assembly in December 2025, with yearly snapshots. The engine types every value. A filter or test missing from the receiver type's table throws instead of coercing, so a template that passes a list to a string filter works only where Python is lenient. `Undefined` is a distinct type. `message['tool_calls'] is not none` is true for a missing key, because the test is a strict type check and `Undefined` is not `None`. Python Jinja2 accepts an undefined value as an empty iterable, so `undefined | length` works there. The C++ engine threw "filter 'length' for type Undefined" until a fix was promised on 2026-01-27. 2026-01-17, issue 18899: a request with a tool whose schema had `"default": false` made the gpt-oss template fail with "Unknown (built-in) filter 'tojson' for type Boolean" on build 7761. On master read 2026-10-04 `tojson` is registered for int, float, string, bool, array, object and none, so this class is fixed. 2026-01-27, issue 19130: the Apriel 1.6 Thinker GGUF template failed on `length` of undefined. A user reported it had worked before a llama.cpp change; maintainer CISC said it never worked with the new engine and that the template should use `{%- if message['tool_calls'] -%}`. 2026-04-03, issue 21347: Gemma 4 GGUF (Unsloth) returned 500 "Unknown (built-in) filter 'upper' for type Array" because `value['type'] | upper` received a list; a user's edited template file worked around it. 2026-06-24, PR 24971 proposed honouring `case_sensitive` in `sort` and `dictsort`; it was closed on 2026-06-25 without merging. The FIXME "sorting is currently always case sensitive" is still in `value.cpp` on master. 2026-08-12, issue 26974: render time grew quadratically with tool count; PR 27034 fixed it on 2026-08-14. Silent divergence: `sort(case_sensitive=false)` and `dictsort(case_sensitive=false)` are accepted and ignored, so the rendered order differs from Python with no error. items.concept: Job Description Writing
items.summary: A job description is a marketing document, a legal document, and a filter — at the same time. It must attract candidates the company wants, deter candidates who would be a poor fit, comply with US pay
items.text: Job Description Writing A job description is a marketing document, a legal document, and a filter — at the same time. It must attract candidates the company wants, deter candidates who would be a poor fit, comply with US pay A job description is a marketing document, a legal document, and a filter - at the same time. It must attract candidates the company wants, deter candidates who would be a poor fit, comply with US pay-transparency law in 15+ states, and avoid language that systematically suppresses applications from underrepresented groups. What you'll do - Responsibilities. Day-to-day work. Outcomes the role owns. What we look for - Requirements split into must-haves (3-5 dealbreakers) and nice-to-haves. What we offer - Compensation range, benefits, growth path, working model. Responsibilities describe what the person does. Verbs in the present tense: "Design and ship," "Mentor," "Own." Requirements describe what the person must already have. Adjectives and nouns: "5 years of," "Experience with," "Familiarity with." Cap must-haves at 3-5. A must-have is a dealbreaker - if the candidate doesn't have it, you won't hire them. The evidence: Women apply for jobs only when they meet ~56% of listed requirements vs men at ~52%. Long requirement lists deter applications from underrepresented groups more than from majority groups (Bohnet 2016). Heuristic: If your must-haves list has more than 5 items, ask which two you'd drop. Then drop them. Textio's research found that gender-coded language measurably skews who applies. Masculine-coded words to avoid: aggressive, ambitious, analytical, assertive, challenge, competitive, confident, decisive, determined, dominant, driven, fearless, forceful, independent, ninja, outspoken, principled, rockstar, self-reliant, superior. Action: Run the JD through a tool like Textio, Gender Decoder, or Datapeople. Aim for balance or feminine-leaning if the role is historically male-coded. States requiring salary range disclosure (verify before posting): California (15+ employees) - required Colorado (all employers with 1+ CO employee) - required Illinois (15+ employees, effective Jan 2025) - required Massachusetts (25+ employees, effective Oct 2025) - required New York - required statewide Washington (15+ employees) - required + benefits description Practical rule: If you post a JD that may be viewed from any of these jurisdictions, include a good-faith salary range. Age bias signals: "digital native," "energetic," "fast-paced youn

items.summary: The MongoDB Connector for Apache Kafka is a Kafka Connect plugin that bridges MongoDB and Kafka in both directions:
items.text: kafka-sink-connector The MongoDB Connector for Apache Kafka is a Kafka Connect plugin that bridges MongoDB and Kafka in both directions: The MongoDB Connector for Apache Kafka is a Kafka Connect plugin that bridges MongoDB and Kafka in both directions: Source connector: MongoDB change streams → Kafka topics (CDC pipeline) Sink connector: Kafka topics → MongoDB collections (event consumer) Supports Confluent Platform, Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK, and self-managed Kafka. This publishes change events to topic mongo.mydb.orders (format: <prefix>.<db>.<collection>). The connector automatically persists the resume token in a Kafka Connect offsets topic. On restart, it resumes from the saved token. If the token expires (oplog window exceeded during connector downtime): Configure DLQ to route failed messages instead of stopping the connector: DLQ messages include headers with error context. Process DLQ messages with a separate consumer for alerting or manual replay. ChangeStreamHistoryLost (error code 286): The oplog has been truncated past the resume token. Resolution: Set startup.mode=timestamp to start from a recent time Or re-snapshot with startup.mode=copy_existing Increase oplog size to prevent future occurrences InvalidResumeToken: Resume token is corrupted or from an incompatible MongoDB version. Resolution: clear stored offset and restart connector. DuplicateKey (11000): Configure ReplaceOneDefaultStrategy instead of InsertOneDefaultStrategy to make sink idempotent. DocumentValidationFailure (121): Kafka messages don't match MongoDB $jsonSchema validator. Check message schema vs collection validator. Worker parallelism: Set tasks.max equal to the number of Kafka partitions for the topic. For near-real-time with low latency: Use poll.await.time.ms: 100 (shorter poll interval) Monitor consumer lag on the Kafka topic Keep poll.max.batch.size small (100-500) for lower latency at cost of throughput Single-partition topics with multiple sink tasks: Multiple sink tasks on a single partition = contention; match tasks.max to partition count Not configuring DLQ: Connector stops on first unprocessable message; always configure DLQ in production InsertOneDefaultStrategy for idempotent pipelines: Insert fails on duplicate; use ReplaceOneDefaultStrategy or BulkWriteStrategy for idempotent sinks Monitoring consumer lag but not resume token age: Consumer lag tells you about Kafka backlog; resume token age tells you about oplog risk (if token becomes invalid = full resync

items.concept: Keyset pagination with compound sort keys
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Keyset pagination with compound sort keys. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Keyset pagination with compound sort keys Source-anchored research for Keyset pagination with compound sort keys. Run status: COMPLETED. Although _id is a useful unique tie-breaker, an ObjectId is not a strict clock: MongoDB notes that ObjectIds have one-second timestamp resolution and client clocks can differ. For chronological feeds, sort on an explicit timestamp followed by _id. (medium confidence) Keyset paging is less affected than offset paging by inserts or deletes before the current boundary because it anchors to values, but it is not snapshot-consistent. Concurrent changes or updates to mutable sort fields can make items appear twice or be missed. Prefer immutable sort fields and a unique tie-breaker when walking a changing collection. (medium confidence) Use a compound index whose sort-key fields appear in the same order, with directions matching the index pattern or its full inverse. Equality-prefix fields can precede those keys only when the query constrains each prefix field by equality. Inspect explain as well: a multi-key $or boundary can prevent one index from efficiently serving both the range filter and requested sort in some query plans. (high confidence) A compound lexicographic $or can still yield a poor plan. In one MongoDB case study, a find() predicate using a > cursorA OR (a == cursorA AND b > cursorB) with sort({a: 1, b: 1}) did not efficiently combine index filtering with ordered retrieval; the author used a staged aggregation to position near the cursor before applying the full boundary. This case report does not establish a general MongoDB limitation. (low confidence) Treat the sort tuple as the cursor position. For sort {createdAt: -1, _id: -1}, the next-page boundary is createdAt < lastCreatedAt OR (createdAt == lastCreatedAt AND _id < lastId). For more keys, compare the first differing key after matching preceding keys for equality, using the comparison direction that matches that key's sort direction. (high confidence) Sort fields that can tie need a unique final key to define a repeatable page boundary, often _id. MongoDB documents that tied sort keys can be returned in any relative order; MongoDB examples and implementations add _id after a timestamp or other paginated field. The unique tuple defines a deterministic order for a fixed dataset, but it does not create a snapshot across requests. (high confidence) An indexed keyset range boundary avoids walking the prefix that skip() must pass, so it typically scales better f

items.text: KLD-based quant evaluation methodology llama.cpp workflow (`llama-perplexity`, formerly `perplexity`): run the reference once with `--kl-divergence-base <file>` (saves all logits), then run each quant with `--kl-divergence-base <file> --kl-divergence`. The quant run ignores `-f`; tokens come from the saved file, which guarantees ident... llama.cpp workflow (`llama-perplexity`, formerly `perplexity`): run the reference once with `--kl-divergence-base <file>` (saves all logits), then run each quant with `--kl-divergence-base <file> --kl-divergence`. The quant run ignores `-f`; tokens come from the saved file, which guarantees identical tokens. The file is huge (README: 11 GiB LLaMA 2, 37 GiB LLaMA 3 on Wikitext-2) because it stores all n_vocab logits; logits are stored as scaled 16-bit integers, so an FP16 model scored against its own base shows a nonzero floor (4e-6 in PR #5076; 2.5e-5 for BF16 vs FP16 on LLaMA 3 8B). llama-perplexity statistics from `--kl-divergence`: mean KLD with uncertainty (Gaussian assumption), max KLD, 99.9% / 99.0% / 90% / median KLD, ln(PPL(Q)/PPL(base)) and its ratio, PPL correlation, mean Δp and percentiles of Δp for the correct token, RMS Δp, and Same top p with binomial uncertainty. llama.cpp scores only the second half of each context window (n_ctx/2 onward), so each scored token has at least n_ctx/2 of context. PR #5076 reviewer ikawrakow measured that including early positions (a Python script did) shifted mean KLD by about 7 standard deviations. The KLD in llama.cpp is the mean of per-token KLs, not the KL of averaged distributions (ikawrakow, PR #5076). mlx-kld (sammcj, fork of TipKnuckle/mlx-kld; MLX-native): two stages. Stage 1 caches the reference as sparse top-K log-probs (K=256 default, ~420-1000x smaller than dense) plus one tail-mass scalar. Stage 2 feeds each quant the reference's cached token IDs verbatim (never re-tokenised). Sparse K=256 underestimates KLD by about 4% (K=64: -6.6%, K=1024: -2.3%), rank-preserving. Forward passes chunked with a shared KV cache (`--chunk-tokens 2048`), numerically equivalent. Self-comparison must give KL 0 (his cached reference once silently re-tokenised under differing chat-template settings). mlx-kld modes: `--short` (about 50 bundled prompts, chat template applied, first 8 tokens skipped) and `--long` (WikiText-2 test, 32 chunks x 2048 tokens = 65,536 tokens, second half scored, llama.cpp convention). Reports mean, median, std, P95, P99, max, prefill tok/s, effective bpw, per-t

items.concept: Knowledge Graphs and Semantic Analytics
items.summary: A knowledge graph (KG) represents entities (nodes) and the typed, meaning-bearing relationships between them (edges), with attributes (properties) on both, plus a schema/ontology that says what the ty
items.text: Knowledge Graphs and Semantic Analytics A knowledge graph (KG) represents entities (nodes) and the typed, meaning-bearing relationships between them (edges), with attributes (properties) on both, plus a schema/ontology that says what the ty A knowledge graph (KG) represents entities (nodes) and the typed, meaning-bearing relationships between them (edges), with attributes (properties) on both, plus a schema/ontology that says what the types mean. The point is not just to store connections (that is da-27's graph-algorithms angle) but to encode semantics - shared, machine-interpretable meaning - so that data from many sources can be integrated, queried by meaning, validated against a model, and reasoned over to infer new facts. Reach for a KG when the connections and their meaning carry the signal and must be queried, integrated, or reasoned about: multi-hop questions, heterogeneous data integration under one vocabulary, provenance/lineage, regulatory traceability, and grounding LLMs. A KG beats relational/dimensional modeling when traversal depth is variable and deep. If the question is answerable with a GROUP BY or a couple of JOINs over a stable schema, you do not need a KG - use a warehouse/dimensional model (da-29). This is the semantic/ontology node of the data-analytics curriculum (da-1 onward). da-27-network-graph-analytics owns graph algorithms (centrality, community detection, link prediction, GNNs). This skill owns meaning: ontologies, RDF/OWL/SHACL, semantic queries, reasoning, KG construction, GraphRAG. ai-datastores ("Knowledge Graphs for AI") owns the vector-DB / agent-memory / KG-as-storage angle. This skill owns the analytics/semantic-integration angle. da-18-semantic-layer-headless-bi owns the metrics layer (dbt SL, Cube, MetricFlow). A KG semantic layer is about entities and their meaning. da-30-data-governance-catalogs owns governance/catalog policy generally; this skill covers modeling the catalog itself as a knowledge graph. Two graph data models: Labeled Property Graph (LPG; Neo4j/TigerGraph/Memgraph; Cypher/GQL) vs RDF triple store (subject-predicate-object with global IRIs; GraphDB/Jena/Stardog/Virtuoso; SPARQL). Plain RDF can't attach properties to one relationship instance - RDF-star fixes this. Choose RDF for interoperability/reasoning/standards, LPG for speed/traversal/AI; hybrid (RDF of record + LPG projection) is common.
