items.concept: Ollama Anthropic adapter tool_use block fidelity
items.summary: In `FromMessagesRequest` a `tool_use` block without `id` or `name` returns an error ("tool_use block missing required 'id' field" or 'name'), and its `input` becomes the Ollama tool call's `Arguments`.
items.text: Ollama Anthropic adapter tool_use block fidelity In `FromMessagesRequest` a `tool_use` block without `id` or `name` returns an error ("tool_use block missing required 'id' field" or 'name'), and its `input` becomes the Ollama tool call's `Arguments`. In `FromMessagesRequest` a `tool_use` block without `id` or `name` returns an error ("tool_use block missing required 'id' field" or 'name'), and its `input` becomes the Ollama tool call's `Arguments`. A `tool_result` block becomes an Ollama message with role `tool` and `ToolCallID` set to `tool_use_id`; in a user turn the tool messages are placed before the user text message. Content block types other than text, image, tool_use, tool_result, thinking, server_tool_use and web_search_tool_result fall to a default case that only counts them as unknown, so they are dropped without an error. A message with several `thinking` blocks keeps only the last one (each assignment overwrites the string). A `system` array has its text blocks concatenated with no separator and non-text blocks (including `cache_control` metadata) are ignored. The `MessagesRequest` type parses `tool_choice` (with `disable_parallel_tool_use`) but no conversion code reads it. An invalid tool `input_schema` fails the request with `invalid input_schema for tool "<name>"`; a tool whose `type` starts with `web_search` is mapped to a function named `web_search` with one required `query` string. `max_tokens` becomes `num_predict`, and `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k` and `stop_sequences` map to the matching Ollama options. In streaming, a tool call is emitted whole: `content_block_start` with an empty input, one `input_json_delta` holding the complete marshalled arguments as `partial_json`, then `content_block_stop`; no incremental argument JSON. Streaming de-duplicates tool calls by `tc.ID`, so a repeated chunk with the same ID emits nothing and a tool call with an empty ID would collide with any other empty-ID call. Thinking is streamed as a `thinking` block with `thinking_delta` events; the delta type defines `signature_delta` but the stream converter never emits one, so streamed thinking blocks have no signature. Thinking text that arrives after the thinking block was closed (after text or a tool call started) is not emitted, so interleaved thinking after the first content is lost. `stop_reason` is `tool_use` whenever the response has any tool call, even when the done reason is `length`; otherwise `stop` maps to `end_turn`, `length` to `max_tokens`

items.summary: Ollama is a local LLM runtime whose core platform is a native REST API (/api/generate, /api/chat with NDJSON streaming, errors and usage fields), a Modelfile build format (FROM, PARAMETER, TEMPLATE, SYSTEM, ADAPTER), a Docker-v2-style registry with content-addressed blobs and manifests, GGUF/safetensors import and quantization tags, LoRA adapters, OpenAI and Anthropic compatible endpoints, and a think capability. Compiled from 44 source files (cached /dr page bodies, /dr claim units and the docs.ollama.com mirror) across 20 hosts.

Compiled from 44 source files (cached /dr page bodies, /dr claim units and the docs.ollama.com mirror) across 20 hosts. Ollama is an application based on llama.cpp to interact with LLMs directly through your computer. You can use any GGUF quants created by the community ([bartowski](https://huggingface.co/bartowski), [MaziyarPanahi](https://huggingface.co/MaziyarPanahi) and [many more](https://huggingface.co/models?pipeline_tag=text-generation&library=gguf&sort=trending)) on Hugging Face directly with Ollama, without creating a new `Modelfile`. At the time of writing there are 45K public GGUF checkpoints on the Hub, you can run any of them with a single `ollama run` command. We also provide customisations like Documented PARAMETER defaults on the Modelfile reference: num_ctx 2048, temperature 0.8, seed 0, top_k 40, top_p 0.9, min_p 0.0, repeat_last_n 64 (0 disabled, -1 = num_ctx), num_predict -1 (infinite). stop has no default and is repeated once per pattern. Only FROM is required in a Modelfile; PARAMETER, TEMPLATE, SYSTEM, ADAPTER, LICENSE, MESSAGE and REQUIRES are optional. Instructions are case-insensitive and may appear in any order. Hermes specifically is a textbook case of the /v1 problem. Hermes computes a context window for each request and sends num_ctx, but it talks to a local Ollama over the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so Ollama ignores it and every model loads at the server default. A native /api/chat adapter is in progress upstream (hermes-agent PR #4505), and there's a community stopgap package that reroutes Hermes to the native endpoint until it lands. Until then, OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH is the fix for Hermes users, full stop. Starting from an existing model's definition is the recommended authoring path: `ollama show --modelfile <model>` prints its Modelfile including TEMPLATE and parameters. items.concept: Ollama count_tokens 404 stall with Claude Code
items.summary: The reporter's logs show four 404s in about two seconds (one `count_tokens?beta=true` and three `/v1/messages?beta=true`), not only on `count_tokens`.
items.text: Ollama count_tokens 404 stall with Claude Code The reporter's logs show four 404s in about two seconds (one `count_tokens?beta=true` and three `/v1/messages?beta=true`), not only on `count_tokens`. The reporter's logs show four 404s in about two seconds (one `count_tokens?beta=true` and three `/v1/messages?beta=true`), not only on `count_tokens`. After the 404s the log shows `/v1/messages` returning 500 after 1m22s, then 10.5 s, 20.7 s and 41.7 s, after which the server was unresponsive and needed `docker restart ollama`. The reporter ran Ollama 0.15.2 in Docker behind Traefik with HTTP/1.1 forced and a 1 ms flush interval, and says `curl` against `/v1/messages` with `stream: true` returned correct SSE every time right after a restart. The reporter reproduced with both `llama3.2:1b` and `qwen3-coder:30b`, and says Claude Code triggers the problem "consistently every time it connects". A second user saw similar behaviour on Ollama 0.15.2 started with `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve` on macOS under Homebrew. A collaborator replied that Ollama does not support Claude telemetry and suggested `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1`, `DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1` and `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1` to stop the 404s. The reporter set all three variables on both the Ollama container and the Claude Code machine (with `ollama launch claude --model qwen3-coder:30b`) and still saw no reply to "hi". Inferred: since the 404 is documented as harmless, the practical test is to run Claude Code against Ollama with a reverse proxy that answers `count_tokens` with a 200 and a rough `input_tokens`, and see whether the hang persists. Inferred: an Ollama host that hangs after unsupported-route 404s is better diagnosed by checking the runner log for a model-load failure than by blaming `count_tokens`. This CONTRADICTS the causal framing in ollama-anthropic-adapter-tool-use-block-fidelity.md ("count_tokens 404 ... stalls"): Claude Code's protocol page lists `/v1/messages/count_tokens` as optional and says a gateway lacking it gets a character-based estimate, so `/context` shows approximate counts, with no error.

Ollama docs: "Tasks which require large context like web search, agents, and coding tools should be set to at least 64000 tokens." Ollama docs: cloud models are set to their maximum context length by default. Ollama docs example: `ollama ps` columns are NAME, ID, SIZE, PROCESSOR, CONTEXT, UNTIL, e.g. gemma4:latest 9.6 GB, 100% GPU, context 131072. Ollama docs advise using the model's maximum context for best performance while keeping PROCESSOR at 100% GPU (no CPU offload). Per-token KV cost differs by model: a maintainer measured 32k context at 6.2 GB for phi4:14b and 12 GB for gemma3:12b (gemma3 also needs memory for its image projector). A maintainer showed OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=3 turned a 128000 request into --ctx-size 384000, needing 181.6 GiB KV and leaving only 12 of 63 layers on GPU. Changing num_ctx causes a model reload, which is why the first request after a change is slow. If a model is sharded across several devices the VRAM needed rises because each device runs a copy of the compute graph.

(from www.centron.de) When Ollama runs as the macOS application, set environment variables with `launchctl setenv` (e.g. `launchctl setenv OLLAMA_HOST "0.0.0.0:11434"`) and restart the Ollama app. The menu-bar app is launched by launchd, not the shell, so exports in ~/.zshrc are not seen. On Windows, change the model directory by setting OLLAMA_MODELS as a user-account environment variable (Settings or Control Panel, 'Edit environment variables for your account'), then quit the tray app and relaunch it from the Start menu or open a new terminal. Same mechanism applies to OLLAMA_HOST. The light version is a reverse proxy. In nginx, limit_conn caps simultaneous connections and limit_req caps the arrival rate per client, so the overflow is refused at the proxy and never reaches Ollama. The heavy version is a job queue with a database in front of a worker that calls Ollama, which is what you want once requests must outlive a process restart. Sizing that for real traffic is its own exercise: planning a self hosted LLM for concurrent users goes through the arithmetic, and running Ollama on a VPS covers the base install these variables assume. Ollama environment variables are settings the Ollama server reads at startup to control networking, model storage, memory behavior, and inference performance. Ollama v0.32.5 reads 26 OLLAMA_ variables plus the GPU selection and proxy variables it inherits from the environment. The server reads them once when it launches, so changing one only takes effect after you restart Ollama. Revert OLLAMA_HOST to 127.0.0.1:11434 in the drop-in when the proxy runs on the same host. items.summary: Draft limit is blockSize-1. A round proposes n = min(maxTokens, blockSize-1) tokens after the unvalidated current token.
items.text: Ollama DFlash block-diffusion draft model in mlxrunner Draft limit is blockSize-1. A round proposes n = min(maxTokens, blockSize-1) tokens after the unvalidated current token. Draft limit is blockSize-1. A round proposes n = min(maxTokens, blockSize-1) tokens after the unvalidated current token. The input is the anchor token plus n mask tokens, not the full trained block. The source says this is exact for causal layers and measured as free for bidirectional ones. Row i predicts the token at its own position, so the anchor row is dropped, and rows 1..n are sampled from one batched distribution. The draft KV holds only context rows from target hidden features, each derived from the feature at its own slot. The block is written then rewound, and accepted tokens return later as context. Pending feature rows buffer up to 256 tokens, then flush in one context-only forward. Sits beside the MTP drafter behind one `drafter` interface; the MTP path is the older one in this tree. A committed run that starts past the buffered frontier panics ("leaves a context gap"), since it would leave a hole in draft context. Every write path must rewind the previous block first, or new rows land after it and cache contents no longer match positions. Penalties see only committed history, not other rows of the block. Because context entries need no look-ahead, the cache trie keys need no pairing, unlike MTP's token-pair keys. Which DFlash checkpoints Ollama ships for MLX and their measured speedup; no fetched source gives it. `dflashDrafter.draftLimit()` returns blockSize-1. `dflashPendingFlushTokens` is 256. The drafter sends only the anchor and the rows being sampled; the source calls this exact for causal layers and "measured as free" for bidirectional ones. The draft sees the block's mask tokens (`maskToken` from `BlockParams()`), with row 0 unused because row i predicts its own position. Proposals are sampled from one batched distribution via `Sampler.Distribution` and `SampleDistribution`. `commitBlock` rewinds the block out of the draft caches and every write path must call it first. The draft cache keeps only context rows, and a context entry at slot S derives only from the target features at S. Media items are ignored in `committed` because the target hidden at a slot already carries image content. `propose` returns nil when no context has been committed yet. `newSpeculation` chooses `newDFlashDrafter` when the draft implements `model.BlockDraft`.

Embedding models are often used in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) flows, both as part of indexing data as well as later retrieving it. For more detailed instructions, please see our RAG tutorials. Below, see how to index and retrieve data using the embeddings object we initialized above. In this example, we will index and retrieve a sample document in the InMemoryVectorStore. In this section, you load an embedding model locally and generate vector embeddings by using data from the sample_airbnb database, which contains a collection called listingsAndReviews. Setting OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 forces it on and OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=0 disables it. (from docs.ollama.com) Cache size scales with num_ctx and is not changed by weight quantization. For llama3.1:8b at f16 the cache is about 128 KiB per token: 4 GiB at 32,768 tokens, 8 GiB at 65,536; q8_0 at 32,768 tokens is about 2.13 GiB. Sliding-window or shared-KV models (Gemma family) break this formula, so sum the 'llama_kv_cache: size' log lines instead. Capping the context is one of two fixes. The other keeps the long context and shrinks the cache instead. On the RTX 4090, Qwen3.8 27B at a 128K context spilled with the default f16 cache and dropped to 16.4 tok/s. With OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q4_0 and flash attention active, the identical context stayed 100 percent on the GPU. The KV cache type selector in the calculator reproduces both outcomes. The KV cache type is the lever that acts on the right-hand bars. Weight quantization does nothing to them. This is the single most out-of-date piece of Ollama advice in circulation, and this page carried it too until this update. The change landed in commit fdb1094 on 2025-10-01, which swapped the variable from a plain boolean to a three-state one and deleted the branch that required you to opt in. If the result no longer fits in VRAM, Ollama pushes layers onto the CPU and every request slows down, including a single one with no competition. If the system is running an older driver (ROCm 6.x or earlier), GPU initialization will hang during device discovery and eventually time out, causing Ollama to fall back to CPU. * If you are using a container, is the container runtime working? Try `docker run --gpus all ubuntu nvidia-smi` - if this doesn't work, Ollama won't be able to see your NVIDIA GPU. * Is the uvm driver loaded? `sudo nvidia-modprobe -u` * Try reloading the nvidia\_uvm driver - `sudo rmmod nvidia_uvm` then `sudo modprobe nvidia_uvm` * Try rebooting * Make sure you're running the latest nvidia drivers Vulkan itself is a cross-platform graphics API that works across a wide range of GPU manufacturers, including Intel and older AMD cards outside the ROCm compatibility list. Additional GPU support on Windows and Linux is provided via [Vulkan](https://www.vulkan.org/). Vulkan is enabled by default when the backend is installed. On Windows most GPU vendors drivers come bundled with Vulkan support and require no additional setup steps. Most Linux distributions require installing additional components, and you may have multiple options for Vulkan drivers between Mesa and GPU Vendor specific packages Vulkan is the documented path for GPUs that ROCm does not cover. Per the current docs it is enabled by default when the backend is installed. OLLAMA_VULKAN=0 or GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1 disables all Vulkan GPUs. GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES takes numeric IDs to select specific Vulkan GPUs. On a mixed iGPU/dGPU system where the Vulkan iGPU is unstable, keep Vulkan on and set GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES to the discrete GPU index (for example 1 when Vulkan1 is the discrete GPU). ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES selects AMD ROCm GPUs. List devices with `rocminfo`, and use the Uuid when available. An invalid ID such as -1 forces CPU. Launching ollama with the OLLAMA_VULKAN=1 environment variable set will now enable Vulkan API support as an alternative to the likes of AMD ROCm and NVIDIA CUDA acceleration. Each card carries its own runtime overhead, which the calculator counts per GPU. NVLink is not required; a pair of cards on ordinary PCIe slots works, adding a small inter-GPU latency. The catch is that VRAM scales but speed does not. Fix: cap OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH or num_ctx. No, not on a single 24 GB card in a usable way. A 70B at Q4_K_M needs 42.5 GB before context, and a 24 GB card is short by almost half. The real options for a 70B are a single 48 GB card such as the RTX 6000 Ada, two 24 GB cards splitting the model, or a unified-memory machine with 64 GB or more. By fully supporting the core MCP primitives (tools, prompts, and resources), it provides a controlled terminal space where you steer, and the agent executes. With a rich, user-friendly interface, it lets you safely manage your setup in real time with no coding required. Whether you're building, testing, or exploring, this client streamlines your workflow with features like fuzzy autocomplete, advanced MCPHost is a CLI tool that allows you to interact with various AI models through a unified interface. Ollama MCP Bridge - A Python API layer that sits in front of Ollama, automatically adding tools from multiple MCP servers to every chat request. To include servers from Claude Desktop, pass --claude-desktop explicitly. The Ollama context window defaults to 4096 tokens across standard models, silently truncating conversation history when inputs exceed runtime memory limits. While tuning the num_ctx parameter allows moderate expansion, inflating the context window on local GPUs rapidly triggers out-of-memory crashes. Connecting your assistant to an intelligent workspace via the Model Context Protocol allows semantic search across large document corpuses without exhausting local video memory. items.text: Ollama mlxrunner speculative depth controller (committed tokens per second) `newSpeculation` builds the subsystem only when the checkpoint has a draft head; a block-draft model gets the DFlash drafter, anything else the MTP drafter. `newSpeculation` builds the subsystem only when the checkpoint has a draft head; a block-draft model gets the DFlash drafter, anything else the MTP drafter. The drafter's `draftLimit` is passed to the controller, so a depth the drafter never produces is never scheduled. Depth 0 runs through an inner pipelined plain decoder (parked), which keeps the draft cache level. Replaced a heuristic schedule that grew toward a fixed cap (existing dossier). A drafted round that resumes from parking drains the inner decoder's in-flight sample as the current token and attributes no cost to that round. A stall can inflate a cost sample severalfold, so samples are clamped (see sibling dossier). No source gives measured tokens per second gained by the controller against a fixed depth on a Mac. `newSpeculation` returns nil when the model has no draft head, and then requests decode plainly. The speculation picks the DFlash drafter when the draft model implements `model.BlockDraft`, otherwise the MTP drafter. The controller's `drafterLimit` is set from the drafter's `draftLimit()`, which is blockSize-1 for DFlash and 0 (unbounded) for MTP. A parked request runs an inner pipelined decoder and counts each plain token as a depth-0 round. Resuming drafting from a parked stretch emits the inner decoder's sampled-but-unforwarded token as the current token and records no cost for that round. Each request opens with `limit = depth.scheduled` so a new request starts at the proven depth. Round wall time runs from one round start to the next and spans the next emit's sync.

BF16 is a common numerical format used during inference of many large models. It means that the model parameters are represented with 16 bits of precision. Using BF16 for all models helps us to make an apples-to-apples comparison of models in a common inference setup. This allows us to compare the inherent capabilities of the models themselves, removing variables like different hardware or optimization techniques like quantization, which we'll discuss next. <Note> Currently this is a global option - meaning all models will run with the specified quantization type. </Note> All variants struggle on Normal incidents — this is a training data imbalance issue, not a quantization artifact Ollama manifests reuse the Docker image manifest v2 schema 2 envelope (schemaVersion 2, mediaType, a config object and a layers array whose entries carry mediaType, size and sha256 digest); Ollama substitutes its own layer media types (model, template, license, params) for image layers. The models directory holds blobs/ with content-addressed files named by digest with ':' replaced by '-' (sha256-<64 hex>), and manifests/ with per-tag JSON, e.g. manifests/registry.ollama.ai/library/gemma3/270m. Blobs are shared by digest, so tags with the same weights layer share one file. Default model directory: ~/.ollama/models on macOS, /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models on Linux with the standard installer, C:\Users\%username%\.ollama\models on Windows. Setting OLLAMA_MODELS overrides it; on Linux the ollama service user needs read/write access to the new directory. items.summary: Decision order in `mmprojOffloadDisabled()`: first `requiresMMProjGPUOffload()` (gemma3n with a GPU in use) forces offload on; then `forceNoMMProjOffload` (set by the OOM retry) forces it off with reason `startup-oom-retry`; then `shouldDisableMMProjOffload`.
items.text: Ollama multimodal projector offload disable policy Decision order in `mmprojOffloadDisabled()`: first `requiresMMProjGPUOffload()` (gemma3n with a GPU in use) forces offload on; then `forceNoMMProjOffload` (set by the OOM retry) forces it off with reason `startup-oom-retry`; then `shouldDisableMMProjOffload`. Decision order in `mmprojOffloadDisabled()`: first `requiresMMProjGPUOffload()` (gemma3n with a GPU in use) forces offload on; then `forceNoMMProjOffload` (set by the OOM retry) forces it off with reason `startup-oom-retry`; then `shouldDisableMMProjOffload`. `shouldDisableMMProjOffload` applies three tests in order. `NumGPU == 0` gives `cpu-only`. `NumGPU > 0`, model layers known and `NumGPU` below the layer count gives `partial-text-offload`; the layer count is the GGUF block count plus one. Otherwise, for each GPU in the list, memory is its free memory (its total memory if free is zero or total is smaller than free); if any GPU has a nonzero value below projector bytes plus 1 GiB, the result is `limited-vram`. Projector bytes (`mmprojMemory`) are the summed size of tensors whose names start with `v.`, `mm.` or `a.` in the model file when the projector is inline, or the whole tensor size of a separate projector file. A file with zero such bytes makes the launch fail with "no projector tensors found". When offload stays on and `mmprojMemory` is nonzero, Ollama also raises llama.cpp's fit target: it sets `LLAMA_ARG_FIT_TARGET` to the projector bytes plus 1 GiB, rounded up to MiB. It adds that to a target already set in the launch config and leaves an inherited user environment value alone. This makes `--fit` leave room for the projector. Startup OOM retry: if `llama-server` fails to start with an out-of-memory error, a projector exists, the model is not gemma3n-on-GPU, offload was still on and no retry has happened, Ollama stops the process, clears its load accounting and starts again once with `--no-mmproj-offload`. The code comment says `--fit` can pick a text-layer placement that fits before mtmd/CLIP allocates the projector. The code comment calls the size estimate "a stopgap until fit accounts for mmproj memory directly". Per the issue 16496 reporter, Ollama 0.24.0 offloaded the projector whenever VRAM allowed. Ollama 0.30 (released by 2026-06-03, after the 2026-05-29 switch to llama-server) introduced a blanket floor, `limitedMMProjOffloadMemory = 10<<30`, so any GPU with less than 10 GiB disabled projector offload. 2026-06-03 to 06-05: issue 16

It parses a call only after it sees the closing tag, and it streams no partial tool content. While looking for the open tag it withholds a possible partial tag and any trailing whitespace (including Unicode spaces such as non-breaking and ideographic space) so a tag split across chunks is not leaked as content. `transformToXML` rewrites `<tag=abc>` into `<tag name="abc">` with the value XML-escaped, then escapes `&`, `<` and `>` in the character data between the `function` and `parameter` tags, leaving newlines and tabs intact. Go `xml.Unmarshal` then reads `<function name>` with `<parameter name>` children. A tag the regex does not recognise stays unescaped, and an unclosed or mismatched element fails with the XML syntax error; the parser logs "qwen tool call parsing failed" and returns the error. Each value is looked up against the matched tool's schema. With a declared type, the order is null, boolean, integer, number, array, object, string; with `anyOf`, all member types are pooled; with no schema entry, the value stays a string. The OpenAI layer launched 2024-02-08 as 'initial experimental support' for chat completions only; embeddings, function calling, vision and logprobs were listed as future work and have since been added (except logprobs). Most likely your framework calls Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint at /v1, which ignores num_ctx in the request body because it isn't on the allowlist of OpenAI parameters Ollama maps. Only the native /api/generate and /api/chat endpoints accept it. Set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH on the server or bake num_ctx into a Modelfile, then confirm with the CONTEXT column in ollama ps. Chat completions does not support tool_choice, logit_bias, user or n per Ollama docs. A llama-stack project fix (PR #2047, Apr 2025) worked around Ollama still calling tools when tool_choice="none" by stripping tools from the request. Most agent frameworks talk to Ollama over the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, because that's the thing every SDK already speaks. So you set num_ctx in your framework config, the framework passes it into an OpenAI-shaped request, and Ollama drops it on the floor. Your window stays at 4096 and nothing anywhere reports a problem. Server-wide, OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH. The default for every request that doesn't carry its own. This is the one to use for agents, because it survives the OpenAI-compatible endpoint problem above. Use the API key in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. This also applies to the hosted Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint; `x-api-key` alone is not supported. items.text: Ollama qwen3_5 MTP loader and SelfDraft path MLX loader: the Qwen3.5 loader keeps the `mtp.*` tensors instead of freeing them and implements `Draft` to propose one token per step. The head is enabled only by the tensors being present. A model whose head ships inline with the target weights is its own draft through `SelfDraft`, which returns... MLX loader: the Qwen3.5 loader keeps the `mtp.*` tensors instead of freeing them and implements `Draft` to propose one token per step. The head is enabled only by the tensors being present. A model whose head ships inline with the target weights is its own draft through `SelfDraft`, which returns the head or nil when the checkpoint shipped none. Interfaces (`mlxrunner/model/model.go`): `Model.Forward` returns both the hidden state to unembed and the "draft-conditioning" state (plain models return the final hidden for both); `DraftModel` has `LoadWeights`, `NewCaches`, `Forward(b, targetCaches, draftCaches)` and `Unembed`; `BlockDraft` adds block length and mask token for block-diffusion drafters; drafts register by architecture name and unsupported ones fail with `unsupported draft architecture`. MTP drafting: a persistent `mtpDrafter` is built at model load and opens a session per request. The draft KV pairs slot S with the look-ahead token at S+1 fused with the target hidden at S, so a pair completes only when the next token arrives. Pending pairs flush in batches of up to 256 tokens. Prefix cache: the cache trie is keyed by token pairs (look-ahead 1) so a prefix match also verifies the paired token, and a restored prefix arrives with draft caches already written. Depth control: a controller picks the draft depth that maximizes committed tokens per wall-clock second from live per-position acceptance and per-width forward cost, with depth 0 (plain decode) as the floor; it probes one past its choice every 4 rounds, backing off to every 512, and keeps its state across requests. Verification: one target forward per decode step over the current token plus drafts, and one host sync per round; sampling honors any temperature, penalty and top-k/p/min-p, with logprobs the only gated feature. GGUF launcher: MTP turns on automatically when no draft model path is set and the GGUF has `nextn_predict_layers > 0` or (legacy) architecture `qwen35`/`qwen35moe` with `mtp.`-prefixed tensors. Flags: `--spec-type draft-mtp`, `--spec-draft-n-max <DraftNumPredict>` only when above zero, `--spec-draft-backend-sampling` for MTP only. 0.32.

A stock `qwen3.8:27b` logs `selected=renderer_parser renderer=qwen3.8 parser=qwen3.5`, so Qwen3.8 reuses the Qwen3.5 parser. The xhigh sentence is "Reasoning effort is set to xhigh. Please think carefully through the task, validate key assumptions, consider plausible alternatives, and prioritize correctness, consistency, and clarity in the final answer." The low sentence is "Reasoning effort is set to low. Keep your thinking brief and focused, moving directly to the conclusion without unnecessary elaboration." `qwen38ReasoningInstructions` returns the xhigh sentence when `think` is nil, the low sentence for `"low"`, nothing for `"medium"` or `false`, the xhigh sentence for `"xhigh"` and for any other valid string, and the error "invalid thinking value %v" for an invalid value. Cache size scales with num_ctx and is not changed by weight quantization. Ollama bundles ROCm 7 linux libraries which require a compatible ROCm 7 kernel driver. If the system is running an older driver (ROCm 6.x or earlier), GPU initialization will hang during device discovery and eventually time out, causing Ollama to fall back to CPU. Capping the context is one of two fixes. The other keeps the long context and shrinks the cache instead. On the RTX 4090, Qwen3.8 27B at a 128K context spilled with the default f16 cache and dropped to 16.4 tok/s. items.text: oMLX boundary snapshot store serialization and async cache-store worker locking Engine thread, boundary capture: `Scheduler._on_prefill_boundary_snapshot` calls `BoundarySnapshotSSDStore.save()` on the engine (owner) thread. `save()` extracts per-layer state, compacts pooling and DeepSeek-V4.1 deltas, then `_serialize_extracted()` runs `mx.eval(*arrays.values())` and copies ... Engine thread, boundary capture: `Scheduler._on_prefill_boundary_snapshot` calls `BoundarySnapshotSSDStore.save()` on the engine (owner) thread. `save()` extracts per-layer state, compacts pooling and DeepSeek-V4.1 deltas, then `_serialize_extracted()` runs `mx.eval(*arrays.values())` and copies each array to raw bytes with `_extract_tensor_bytes`. The MLX container is deleted right after, so only raw bytes are retained. Pending buffer: raw bytes sit in `_pending_writes` (key `(request_id, token_count)`) for zero-I/O read-back, bounded by `pending_max_bytes` (default 512 MiB; the scheduler passes `gdn_ssd_pending_max_bytes`). A single checkpoint may exceed the cap when the buffer is empty so wide recurrent states make progress. Backpressure: if the cap would be exceeded, `save()` waits on a condition variable for up to 2.0 s; on timeout, or when the 128-entry write queue is full, it writes the snapshot inline on the engine thread and returns only when it is on disk. Time spent waiting accumulates in `backpressure_ms`. Writer: a daemon thread `boundary-snapshot-writer` drains the queue and writes safetensors without MLX (`_write_safetensors_no_mx`). A lock `_writer_busy` is held while it processes one item. Locks in the store: `_pending_lock` (with `_pending_cond`), `_registry_lock`, `_cancelled_lock`, `_gdn_dequant_lock` and `_writer_busy`. None of them is the MLX buffer lock. `cleanup_request` takes `_writer_busy` with a 2.0 s timeout (5.0 s for `cleanup_all`); on timeout it falls back to a counter rescue and may leave an orphan file until the next constructor cleanup. Registry publication happens while the pending lock is held, so `cleanup_request` cannot remove the pending marker and then race the registration. Async store worker: the scheduler creates a `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1, thread_name_prefix="omlx-store-cache")`, so stores run one at a time and never race on the paged SSD index. Detection key: the function reads `<model_name>/config.json` and looks only at `quantization_config.quant_method`; it does not read the `quantization` dict that mlx-lm itself writes. A missing file or an unreadable JSON file returns None (the parse error is logged at debug level). The comparison is case-insensitive. Because the path is joined as `Path(model_name) / "config.json"`, only local model directories can trigger a custom loader; a bare hub repo id has no such file at that path and falls through to mlx-lm. Branch 1, `compressed-tensors`: it imports `patches.qwen38_modelopt_mixed` and, if `is_supported_config(config)` is true, requires `is_vlm`, raising ValueError ("refusing the text-only fallback loader") otherwise, and returns that module's `load(model_name)`. An unsupported compressed-tensors config falls through to the end and returns None, so every other compressed-tensors checkpoint stays with mlx-lm. Branch 2, `paroquant`: it lazily imports `paroquant.inference.backends.mlx.load.load`, turns an ImportError into one that says to install `paroquant[mlx]` separately, calls `paro_load(model_name, force_text=not is_vlm)`, and raises ValueError if a VLM load came back text-only. Any other `quant_method` value (AWQ, GPTQ, FP8 and so on) returns None with the comment that mlx-lm may already support it, so the dispatcher never rejects a format; it only claims the ones it lists. Call-site contract: the batched LLM engine runs the dispatcher inside `_load_model_sync` on the global MLX executor thread (so loading never overlaps other Metal work), and when it returns a pair the engine keeps `getattr(processor, "tokenizer", processor)` as the tokenizer. The call passes only the model name and `is_vlm=False`, so the custom path receives neither the `lazy=` flag used for MoE expert offload nor the MTP sidecar kwargs that the stock `lm_load_compat` path gets. Issue 2334 is open as of 2026-10-05 with no maintainer reply in the cached copy, and `omlx/utils/fatal.py` on main still sets `FATAL_TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_S = 60.0` as a constant and `FATAL_EXIT_CODE = 70`. `fatal_exit` logs `%s; exiting process so the supervisor can restart with a clean state`, dumps all thread tracebacks with `faulthandler`, and calls `os._exit(exit_code)`; `exit_if_gpu_submissions_ignored` also calls it when an error contains `kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorSubmissionsIgnored`. In issue 2334 the unload of a GLM-5.2 mxfp4 engine (about 420 GB wired, oMLX 0.5.2, mlx 0.32.0, macOS 26.5.2, `--memory-guard-gb 470`) logged `Unloading model: ... (immediate abort)` and `Engine stopped`, then 60 s later the CRITICAL teardown timeout line, with the server idle for about 90 s beforehand. The faulthandler dump in issue 2334 showed the API thread inside `engine_core.close` (line 1037) called from `engine/batched.py` `stop` and `engine_pool.py` `_unload_engine`, while a pool worker was in `scheduler._cleanup_finished`, so the teardown was waiting on a slow but live cleanup. The reporter's 40 GB Qwen3.6-35B engine unloaded through the same path in about 26 s on the same day, so the 60 s budget fits 40 GB and not 420 GB. After the watchdog exit, launchd restarted oMLX, the new process began reloading the pinned model, and wired memory climbed to the iogpu ceiling (about 486 GB) for about a minute with the GUI frozen, then settled at 381 GB wired with zero oMLX processes for more than 30 minutes. The reporter proposed scaling the teardown timeout per GB or making it configurable, releasing Metal buffers before `os._exit`, and running cleanup with a deadline once an unload is pending. A 2026-07-23 comment on issue 2334 recorded a post-idle scheduler wedge on 0.5.3 where `/health` and `/api/status` stayed healthy for about 14 hours, a `sample` showed the inference thread parked in `mlx::core::eval_impl` on a condition variable, and request threads waited on a Python lock held by it. That comment suggests `/health` should reflect scheduler liveness, not only the HTTP loop and model residency, and says the reporter now probes a real tiny completion. On a 10,813-token cold turn the store log read `storing 10240/10813 tokens (9 intermediate snapshots)` and left 8.6 GB in the hot cache across 10 entries; a warm turn stored 2 snapshots and added 1.7 GB of SSD in 2 files. Issue 2647's author proposes a configurable snapshot stride (store every 2nd or 4th boundary) and lists deduplicating or delta-encoding rotating state, or KV-quantizing the sidecar, as alternatives. Issue 2647's author says PR 2620's incremental KV segments for distributed ranks would shrink only the roughly 160 MB sliceable share, not the roughly 820 MB rotating sidecar. items.concept: oMLX /health liveness versus scheduler wedge
items.summary: `/health` is unauthenticated in its signature (no `verify_api_key` dependency), while `/api/status` depends on `verify_api_key`.
items.text: oMLX /health liveness versus scheduler wedge `/health` is unauthenticated in its signature (no `verify_api_key` dependency), while `/api/status` depends on `verify_api_key`. `/health` is unauthenticated in its signature (no `verify_api_key` dependency), while `/api/status` depends on `verify_api_key`. `/health` returns status code 503 and `"status": "loading"` only when `pinned_preload_complete` is false; otherwise 200 and `"status": "healthy"`. `/health` body fields are `status`, `default_model`, `engine_pool` (`model_count`, `loaded_count`, `final_ceiling`, `current_model_memory`) and `mcp`; no field reads scheduler, step or request state. If `enforcer.get_final_ceiling()` raises, `/health` logs a warning and reports ceiling 0 instead of failing. `/api/status` computes `active_requests` as the sum of `len(core._output_collectors)` over loaded engines and `waiting_requests` as the sum of `len(scheduler.waiting)`; it always returns `"status": "ok"`. A probe that detects a wedge must therefore either watch `waiting_requests > 0` with `active_requests == 0` over time, or send a real tiny completion; `/health` cannot detect it on this code. The server comment says binding the port before the pinned preload lets "port watchdogs see liveness instead of a closed port" and cites issue 2184. A pinned preload that outlasts a port watchdog's timeout would otherwise get the process hard-killed mid-load (server.py comment near line 616).

items.summary: The intermittent CI log line `Rejecting split-GDN placeholder block 3 because its recurrent checkpoint was not committed` came from `BoundarySnapshotSSDStore.take_staged_file` removing the request directory with `file_path.parent.rmdir()` after promoting an earlier boundary.
items.text: oMLX hybrid GDN boundary snapshot capture regression The intermittent CI log line `Rejecting split-GDN placeholder block 3 because its recurrent checkpoint was not committed` came from `BoundarySnapshotSSDStore.take_staged_file` removing the request directory with `file_path.parent.rmdir()` after promoting an earlier boundary. The intermittent CI log line `Rejecting split-GDN placeholder block 3 because its recurrent checkpoint was not committed` came from `BoundarySnapshotSSDStore.take_staged_file` removing the request directory with `file_path.parent.rmdir()` after promoting an earlier boundary. In the race the writer thread had run `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` but not yet written the temp file, the `rmdir` succeeded on the empty directory, and `_write_safetensors_no_mx` failed with ENOENT. The failed write was logged at debug level only; the pending marker was released with no file behind it, `take_staged_file` returned None, `commit_gdn_checkpoint` returned False, and the split-GDN store stopped one block short. PR 3563 fixed it by no longer removing the request directory in `take_staged_file`, leaving removal to `cleanup_request`; the maintainer reproduced the old behavior, confirmed targeted boundary and split-GDN tests pass, and merged on 2026-09-11. MLX creates one Metal command queue per stream (`mlx/backend/metal/device.cpp:309-324`), so two busy oMLX engines submit to two command queues of one process. PR 1304 added `_ensure_wired_limit()` so the process-global `mx.set_wired_limit()` runs once instead of racing across concurrent BatchGenerator inits. The `_engine_loop` docstring at `engine_core.py:491-497` still says the executor guarantees MLX GPU operations are never concurrent, which has held only within one engine since PR 1304. Whether 5 grace polls cover a slow prefill chunk, since the chunk-boundary drain waits for the end of the current chunk. `Scheduler` keeps `_pending_reclaim_request` for idle reclaim and `_pending_pressure_clear` for hard-pressure reclaim; the second "drains at the next step boundary even under load". `request_pressure_reclaim` only sets `_pending_pressure_clear = True`, and its docstring says the actual `_sync_and_clear_cache` runs on the inference thread at the next `step()` boundary. `_consume_pressure_clear` returns False when the flag is unset, otherwise resets it and returns True, and it is deliberately not idle-gated. `has_requests()` includes `_pending_pressure_clear`, so an idle engine loop keeps calling `step()` until the clear fires. The external prefill loop calls `_consume_pressure_clear()` after each chunk and then `Scheduler._clear_cache(self)`, because a single `step()` can last minutes. A comment at that site says the abort escalation was measured firing 0.1 GB over the watermark with 3.7 GB pooled. `Scheduler._clear_cache` calls `_sync_and_clear_cache(self._stream)` and records the pooled bytes for the prefill transient tracker when flat-overhead tracking is on. `_process_pending_reclaim` returns without consuming the idle request while any request is running, prefilling or waiting, and cites issue 2179. The enforcer's grace gate requires level not ok, not emergency, `OMLX_DISABLE_PRESSURE_RECLAIM != "1"` and fewer than `_PRESSURE_RECLAIM_GRACE_POLLS_MAX` (5) polls, and returns early after a successful request. At hard level the enforcer calls `_request_scheduler_cache_reclaim(freed_hot)` after the hot-cache shrink unless the env var is "1", and then recomputes the pressure level from current usage. `_request_scheduler_cache_reclaim` calls `request_pressure_reclaim` on each pooled engine's scheduler, tolerates exceptions per scheduler, and returns the count of accepted requests.

Detection of the preserve default (model_discovery.py `detect_preserve_thinking`): read `chat_template.jinja` from the model directory, else the `chat_template` string in `tokenizer_config.json`; if the text contains the substring `preserve_thinking`, the model's default is true. This is a plain substring test, so a template that mentions the name only in a comment also qualifies. The default is stored in the model entry as `preserve_thinking_default`. Consequence: for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8 templates oMLX turns preserved thinking on by itself, which is what the held dossiers listed as an open question. The same code sets the output-caching flag (see reasoning-token-cache-invalidation-across-turns.md). API reasoning effort enters through `merge_reasoning_effort_chat_template_kwargs` with `setdefault`, so an explicit kwarg in settings or request wins over the API field. If it raises `TypeError`, oMLX removes every key the user supplied, `tools`, and `enable_thinking`, and renders again; a template with strict signature therefore silently loses the user's kwargs on the retry. Fix for 2064 (commit 28fe5cb, in v0.4.5.dev1): a second index, `_incompatible_index`, holds blocks that fail the signature check. `_tracked_ssd_size()` = compatible index size + incompatible index size; the startup scan enforces the cap against that total; a write that needs space triggers `_enforce_size_limit_for_new_block`; when a block hash is rewritten it is removed from the incompatible index. Log line gained `incompatible_files=N`. Maintainer policy (issue 2662, 2026-08-15): incompatible blocks are counted against `max_size` and LRU-evicted at startup if the directory is over the limit and on every save that needs space. They are deliberately not deleted on scan because that "would wipe valid cache for other models sharing the directory". So a cache full of dead blocks at 54.94 of 55 GB was within budget; nothing is reclaimed until a new write needs room. Consequence (inference from the two statements above): isolation today is by signature plus global LRU, not by namespace. A model that writes often evicts a quieter model's valid blocks, because LRU is global across models. `auto` cap (commit 0faa19c, 2026-09-22, issue 3829): limit = (free disk + existing SSD cache incl. items.summary: Pressure levels are ok below the soft mark, soft between soft and hard, and hard at or above the hard mark, both marks being fractions of the recomputed hard-limit ceiling; the ceiling moves every tick with system availability.
items.text: oMLX ProcessMemoryEnforcer pressure levels and adjust_store_cache_cap Pressure levels are ok below the soft mark, soft between soft and hard, and hard at or above the hard mark, both marks being fractions of the recomputed hard-limit ceiling; the ceiling moves every tick with system availability. Pressure levels are ok below the soft mark, soft between soft and hard, and hard at or above the hard mark, both marks being fractions of the recomputed hard-limit ceiling; the ceiling moves every tick with system availability. At soft pressure the enforcer evicts idle non-pinned LRU models only while more than one is loaded, pauses new admissions, and leaves in-flight requests alone. At hard pressure it unloads even the last idle non-pinned model, aborting its requests first, since an idle model holds no KV worth keeping. At hard pressure with a sole busy non-pinned victim it aborts that model's requests and keeps the model loaded unless emergency pressure holds, in which case it marks a pending unload. At hard pressure with nothing evictable it first flags in-progress model loads to abort, and only if none exist does it abort active requests (emergency only) or call `request_idle_reclaim` on each scheduler. Emergency pressure is not the hard watermark: it requires usage at or above the real ceiling and either 2 GiB over it or 2 consecutive polls over it (`_EMERGENCY_OVER_CEILING_MARGIN_BYTES`, `_EMERGENCY_OVER_CEILING_POLLS`). Before pausing admission or evicting, a tick at or above soft calls `clear_image_decode_cache` and re-measures usage. The reclaim request is skipped unless the MLX buffer pool exceeds `_POOL_RECLAIM_FLOOR` (2 GiB) or a hot-cache shrink just freed references. items.summary: Work on the global executor and a decode on an engine thread run on different threads and streams, so they can overlap on the GPU. The global executor's "serialized" claim holds only among global-executor users.

The global executor's "serialized" claim holds only among global-executor users. Work on the global executor and a decode on an engine thread run on different threads and streams, so they can overlap on the GPU. The global executor's "serialized" claim holds only among global-executor users. The keep-warm tick runs on the global thread and touches the default stream, not any engine's stream. `get_mlx_executor()` creates a lazy single-worker `ThreadPoolExecutor` with thread name prefix `mlx-global`, and its docstring cites issue #85 for serializing MLX GPU work onto one thread. `EngineCore` creates `mx.new_thread_local_stream(mx.default_device())` and a single-worker executor named `mlx-engine-<first 8 chars of engine id>` and gives the stream to its `Scheduler`. The engine loop runs `_step_burst` on `_mlx_executor` and routes `add_request` and `fail_all_requests` through the same executor. `AsyncEngineCore._mlx_executor` is documented as exposing the engine's executor "for VLM vision encoding". Decode-burst defaults are `OMLX_DECODE_BURST_MAX_STEPS=64`, `OMLX_DECODE_BURST_BUDGET_SINGLE_S=0.1` and `OMLX_DECODE_BURST_BUDGET_S=0.03`. A burst stops early when a request produces its first chunk, no work remains, a prefill eviction needs the async callback, or the deadline passes. The burst comment reports about 80 tok/s in an in-process sync loop versus about 74 tok/s through per-token async hand-off, and about 1 ms per token of GIL contention. Engine `close()` submits `scheduler.shutdown` and `scheduler.deep_reset` to the engine executor and calls `fatal_exit` if either times out. `_final_engine_thread_reclaim(stream)` runs `gc.collect()`, `_sync_and_clear_cache(stream)`, `gc.collect()` and `clear_thread_streams()` on the engine worker thread. A comment in `close()` says the final reclaim must run on the engine's own thread and stream because clearing on the global executor cannot reliably return thread- and stream-local Metal memory. `shutdown_mlx_executor` submits `_final_global_mlx_thread_reclaim`, calls `fatal_exit` on timeout and then `executor.shutdown(wait=False)`. `EnginePool` runs `_touch_gpu` on `get_mlx_executor()` from a keep-warm loop that fires only when a loaded model was recently used and has no active request.

items.text: oMLX store-cache admission gate and 60 s admission stall error `_StoreCacheGate` is guarded by a lock and exposes `note_submitted`, `note_done`, `set_cap`, `cap`, `in_flight` and `has_capacity`; `has_capacity` is `in_flight < cap` and the cap is at least 1. `_StoreCacheGate` is guarded by a lock and exposes `note_submitted`, `note_done`, `set_cap`, `cap`, `in_flight` and `has_capacity`; `has_capacity` is `in_flight < cap` and the cap is at least 1. The store-cache executor is a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with `max_workers=1` and thread name prefix `omlx-store-cache`, so stores are serialized and never race on the paged SSD index. `ProcessMemoryEnforcer` adjusts the gate cap on every poll through `adjust_store_cache_cap`: one step up toward `max_num_seqs` at ok pressure, one step down to a floor of 1 at soft or hard pressure. `note_submitted()` is called before `executor.submit`, `note_done()` is called if the submit raises, and otherwise `note_done()` runs in `_drain_pending_async_removes` after the request cache references are released, not when the write finishes. `_schedule_waiting` defers admission when the gate has no capacity or when `len(_pending_async_removes) >= gate.cap`, and logs `Admission deferred: store-cache pipeline full (in_flight=%d pending_cleanups=%d cap=%d)` at debug level. If the gate is full and process memory is already at or above the limit (or admission is paused), the scheduler uses `_memory_admission_stall_output("store_cache_backpressure")`, whose error code is `memory_admission_stalled`, instead of the store-cache timer. `_MEMORY_ADMISSION_STALL_TIMEOUT_S` and `_STORE_CACHE_ADMISSION_STALL_TIMEOUT_S` are both 60.0 seconds. The stalled request's output has `finish_reason="error"`, `error_code="store_cache_admission_stalled"` and `error_metadata` with `request_id`, `reason`, `stalled_seconds`, `store_cache_in_flight`, `pending_store_cleanups` and `store_cache_cap`. In June 2026 the maintainer listed what made partial-tail reuse expensive (from PR 1149 review): cache layout checks, hybrid-cache safety, rollback on splice failure, eviction and memory accounting, and cache-clear behavior. PR 3835 captures one extra prefill snapshot in front of the chat template's generation prompt (the region the next turn renders differently, such as Qwen's empty think block) and stores it as a short tail terminal block; raw prompts fall back to the prefill end. PR 3835 hashes tail blocks in their own domain, indexes them by chain parent in `PagedCacheManager._tail_index`, verifies them on every lookup, and rebuilds them from SSD metadata (`parent_hash`, `tail_terminal`) after a restart. In PR 3835 a request that reused a tail re-lays its own store from the last full block so the grid never drifts, rotating models drop superseded tails through the existing tip lineage, and templates that strip the generation prompt from history (Qwen, GLM, DeepSeek, gpt-oss) stop snapshot selection at that marker. PR 3835 measured a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 13.4K-token prompt at block 4096: next-turn prefill fell from 1,174 tokens (cached 12,288) to 37 (cached 13,425) and TTFT from 0.83 s to 0.42 s. PR 3835's validation: tail restore was bit-identical to a cold forward of the same chunk shape (Qwen3.5-0.8B, 8.2K tokens, block 2,048, max logit diff 0.000), and 100K-164K-token ten-turn needle conversations with Lightning MTP on Qwen3.8-27B, Flash-Next and DeepSeek-V4.1 reused the previous prompt minus the generation prompt every turn. PR 3835 also caps a fitted prefill chunk at the requested slice in the memory guard so a shrunken chunk under context priority cannot run past a boundary or tail position, and fixes `pooling_delta` deriving the delta start from block_size for an unaligned snapshot. The 0.7.0rc1 release notes headline the change as 'Less Waiting Between Messages - Partial Block Caching' with the 1,174-to-37 token and 0.83 s-to-0.42 s figures. items.summary: One-pagers are the highest-impact document format in business: a single page that earns a meeting, secures a budget, aligns a partner, or briefs an exec in under three minutes.
items.text: One-Pager Writing One-pagers are the highest-impact document format in business: a single page that earns a meeting, secures a budget, aligns a partner, or briefs an exec in under three minutes. One-pagers are the highest-impact document format in business: a single page that earns a meeting, secures a budget, aligns a partner, or briefs an exec in under three minutes. A one-pager fits on one page. The moment you flow to page 2, the document is now a half-finished two-pager. Everything else in this skill exists to enforce this rule. Cut by 30-50% from your first draft. Always. Drop full sentences for fragments where fragments work. Move evidence to an appendix link, not a footer. If three things won't fit, you have three things - not one. The reader scans before they read. What lives above the fold: Headline - the one-line value prop, written in the reader's language. Subhead or value-prop sentence - what changes for the reader if they say yes. The "if you only read one line" sentence - bolded, set off visually. A visual anchor - chart, screenshot, diagram, photo, or large pull-quote. Every one-pager has one sentence the reader must take away. Find it. Bold it. Place it above the fold. Repeat it in different words at the end. The Amazon 1-pager / PR-style opener: Heading: the product or initiative name. Subheading: who it's for, in their language. Summary paragraph (3-4 sentences): what it does, who benefits, why now. Problem paragraph: the customer's status quo. Solution paragraph: how this changes the status quo. Quote (optional): an executive or customer making the value claim concrete. Call to action: what the reader does next. Two non-negotiables: written as full sentences; written as if the product already launched. Use paragraphs when: The reader needs to see how ideas connect; describing a customer's strategic status quo; Amazon 1-pager opener. Use bullets when: Listing 3-7 parallel items; scannable facts; the reader is an exec who triages. Heuristic: paragraphs for the upper half (the narrative), bullets for the lower half (the facts and the ask). A single page gives you roughly 550-650 words of usable real estate: Headline + value prop: 20-30 words Above-the-fold callout: 15-25 words Body - problem / context: 80-120 words Body - solution / approach: 100-150 words Body - outcomes / proof: 80-120 words The ask: 30-50 words Account brief - for an internal audience to brief before a customer meeting. items.text: Online Archive partition-field selection Source-anchored research for Online Archive partition-field selection. Run status: COMPLETED. Partition fields are an archive-query cost lever. Atlas organizes archived data by the configured fields, can target matching partitions, and charges for each partition queried. Queries that omit the configured fields can require a full scan of archived documents, increasing scan time and query cost. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Atlas does not allow partition fields or partition structure to be modified through the UI or API after archive creation. Changing the layout requires migrating or rehydrating the archived data, deleting the archive, and creating a new one, so review actual archive queries before selecting fields. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Use explain to inspect which data partitions Atlas used for a query before deciding whether a proposed field order prunes the expected archive data. (low confidence) Use consistently typed partition values from Atlas's supported types: date, double, int, long, objectId, string, or boolean. Atlas warns that polymorphic values may prevent documents with mismatched values from archiving. The current Pulumi provider documentation also says partition values longer than 700 characters are not archived. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-13) Current configuration limits allow up to two non-date query fields, or up to three partition fields when one is the Date Match field; the date field must be included for Date Match archives. Treat the limit as a ceiling and choose only fields that match real archive-query patterns. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) MongoDB's current guide scopes its warning about high-cardinality string partition fields creating many partitions to archives created before June 2023 and says that warning does not apply to archives created after that date. items.summary: The op-ed is the shortest serious argument form in public writing. In ~750 words you must make a single argument that a previously-uninterested reader believes by the end. Every deviation from convent
items.text: Op-ed writing The op-ed is the shortest serious argument form in public writing. In ~750 words you must make a single argument that a previously-uninterested reader believes by the end. Every deviation from convent The op-ed is the shortest serious argument form in public writing. In ~750 words you must make a single argument that a previously-uninterested reader believes by the end. Every deviation from convention is a friction point that costs pickup. One argument. A piece that tries to make two arguments makes neither. Standard target: 750 words. New York Times caps at 800. Washington Post caps at 800. Most regional dailies sit at 600–700. The thesis is one sentence. It is a claim someone could disagree with. Tests for a strong op-ed thesis: Disagreeable. "Schools should teach reading" is not a thesis. Singular. "We need to fix housing, healthcare, and education" is three theses. Provable in 750 words. Front-loaded. The thesis appears in the first paragraph. Op-eds are not evergreen. Every published op-ed has a reason it ran this week. Acceptable pegs: A news event - a bill introduced, a court ruling, an election result A counter to recent coverage The op-ed "why now" is why this argument matters this week, not "why I'm releasing this product this week." An administrator creates it with the `setQuerySettings` command, and the server then rejects new `find`, `distinct`, and `aggregate` operations that have that query shape. MongoDB states the purpose as preventing an operation from causing excessive cluster workload. (high confidence) A filter has no client, user or application selector. The oplog is a capped collection, but it can grow past its configured size to avoid deleting the majority commit point. Treat oplogSizeMB and the replSetResizeOplog size as targets, not hard caps. (high confidence) With a minimum retention period (storage.oplogMinRetentionHours, --oplogMinRetentionHours, or minRetentionHours in replSetResizeOplog), mongod removes an entry only when the oplog has reached its maximum size and the entry is older than the configured hours on the host wall clock. A value of 0 means size-only truncation. To honor the window the oplog can grow without constraint, which may reduce or exhaust disk under high write volume and a long window. Clock drift between cluster components can skew retention. (high confidence) A mongod with `oplogMinRetentionHours` removes an oplog entry only when the oplog has reached its maximum size and the entry is older than the configured hours. Because of this, the oplog can grow without constraint to keep entries for the configured hours, and MongoDB warns this may reduce or exhaust disk space under high write volume with a large retention period. Separately, the oplog can exceed its configured size to avoid deleting the majority commit point. Alibaba Cloud's docs describe the same effect: high write rates can make the oplog grow well beyond `oplogSizeMB`. (high confidence) On an Atlas Core cluster, Atlas delays an auto-scaling event until the oplog window covers the estimated scaling time. Layers: CLI (`infer`, `train`, `bench`), model layer (configs, BPE/SentencePiece tokenizers, BLOBFILE weight loading), compiler plus kernel layer (graph IR, five passes, MIL codegen, weight-dict builders, program cache with store/lookup/evict), core runtime (`orion_compile_mil` to `OrionProgram`, `orion_eval` with IOSurface I/O, delta reload). Program cache: composite key (model name, layer index, sequence length, weight version); a hit skips the per-program compile cost. Delta compilation: `_ANEModel` exposes `unloadWithQoS:` and `loadWithQoS:`; unloading lets the backing BLOBFILEs on disk be rewritten and a reload (qos 21) picks up new weights without calling `ANECCompile()`. The program keeps its `hexStringIdentifier` (a composite of three SHA-256 hashes) because MIL text and weight-dict keys are unchanged, so the old and new program share a temp directory whose ownership must be transferred before release. LoRA adapter-as-input: the base weight W is baked in as a BLOBFILE and adapter matrices A and B are IOSurface inputs, so hot-swapping adapters needs no recompilation; two frontends exist (single linear and full attention with 8 adapter matrices for Q, K, V, O). Cache tiers: L1 is an in-memory paged block pool (64-token blocks by default, SHA-256 chain hashing); L2 is SQLite plus safetensors keyed by prompt hash and survives process restarts; a third SSM-companion tier holds Mamba or similar state per layer and is disk-paged for hybrids when L2 is on. The cache key combines `modelKey`, a `cacheScopeSalt` (reasoning mode plus media) and, if set, the MoE top-k override, so requests at different reasoning modes never alias. TurboQuant KV compression stores the cache at 3 key bits and 3 value bits in the documented example, claims 4.7 to 5.0 times smaller cache using a randomized Hadamard rotation, a Lloyd-Max codebook and (keys only) QJL residual correction, and skips non-KV layers (Mamba, rotating sliding-window caches, ZayaCCA). Speculative decoding has three strategies selected by `GenerateParameters.draftStrategy`: classic autoregressive drafter, DFlash and DDTree. At temperature 0 the output is byte-identical to plain greedy decode; drafters load from `z-lab/<model>-DFlash` snapshots. `VMLX_MOE_TOPK_OVERRIDE=<n>` lowers the routed-expert top-k at load time for supported MoE families, never raises it, leaves top-1 families (ZAYA) alone, and is folded into the cache key; a legacy `VMLINUX_` prefix is accepted. items.concept: ParoQuant pairwise-rotation quantization for MLX
items.summary: Transform: T = S then a product of K=8 independent rotations R(P_t, Theta_t). Each rotation is a set of non-overlapping channel pairs (a channel appears in at most one pair per rotation), so all pairs run in parallel with no ordering dependency.
items.text: ParoQuant pairwise-rotation quantization for MLX Transform: T = S then a product of K=8 independent rotations R(P_t, Theta_t). Each rotation is a set of non-overlapping channel pairs (a channel appears in at most one pair per rotation), so all pairs run in parallel with no ordering dependency. Transform: T = S then a product of K=8 independent rotations R(P_t, Theta_t). Each rotation is a set of non-overlapping channel pairs (a channel appears in at most one pair per rotation), so all pairs run in parallel with no ordering dependency. Why pairs: a full n x n rotation is a product of up to n(n-1)/2 Givens rotations, but optimizing only the top 10% of pairs (largest magnitude difference) matches a full rotation on a k_proj weight of LLaMA-3-8B; channel-wise scaling alone plateaus at higher error. Scaling and rotations are complementary. Optimization: layer-wise, minimizing the output error of each decoder layer against the original input, fed by the already-quantized earlier layers; stage 1 trains rotations and scales, stage 2 is an EfficientQAT-style fine-tune of weights and quantization parameters. 10 epochs per stage, AdamW. Kernel: a single fused CUDA kernel, parallel across tokens, channel groups and pairs; a 128-channel group fits in shared memory and rotation parameters fit in registers. The paper reports under 10% overhead versus AWQ. On MLX the rotation is applied in the loader's own path before mlx affine quantized matmul. Apple Silicon loader: the official MLX backend quantizes lm_head and embed_tokens at load time with mlx nn.quantize (affine, group size and bits read from config, default 128 and 4) using an is-I/O-layer predicate. Cold start is slow as a result. 2025-11-13: arXiv 2511.10645v1. 2026-03-10: feature request to add ParoQuant to mlx-lm (issue 977); z-lab offered native support; the issue is still open with no assignee in the cached copy. 2026-03: oMLX PR 209 adds a custom-quantization loader dispatcher for paroquant; maintainer merged it in May 2026 after a bench on Qwen3.6-27B-PARO, with a follow-up to route all load call sites through the dispatcher. 2026-05: z-lab releases larger PARO checkpoints (gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-27B, later Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B); paroquant 0.1.15 adds Gemma 4 and MoE optimization; 0.1.16 on 2026-07-01. mlx-swift-lm gained ParoQuant support (PR 164) and a follow-up extending it to MoE and speeding the path (PR 471). Parse-then-render byte round-trip tests for reasoning turns Ollama's Qwen3-Coder parser trims trailing whitespace before a `<tool_call>` tag and leading whitespace after `</tool_call>`, and strips one leading and one trailing newline from every parameter value. Ollama's Qwen3-Coder parser trims trailing whitespace before a `<tool_call>` tag and leading whitespace after `</tool_call>`, and strips one leading and one trailing newline from every parameter value. The Ollama renderer then writes a tool call as `
<tool_call>
<function=NAME>` plus, per argument, `
<parameter=NAME>
` VALUE `
</parameter>`, so the removed newlines come back only if the model used exactly that layout. Values are coerced by schema type on parse: `null` in any case becomes nil, boolean accepts `true` and `false` in any case, a number with no decimal part becomes an integer, and an invalid boolean becomes false. The renderer prints booleans and numbers with `%v`, strings raw, and maps and slices as compact JSON. The Ollama Qwen3.5 renderer runs `strings.TrimSpace` on the stored thinking and on message content before writing `<think>
` REASONING `
</think>

` CONTENT. The Ollama Qwen3.5 parser eats whitespace after `</think>` and trims leading whitespace in the thinking, so generated whitespace in both places is dropped on parse. llama.cpp's PEG parser tests stream the input one character at a time through `parser.parse(prefix, is_partial)`, with a UTF-8 safe truncation, and compare the accumulated message with the expectation. `test_template_generation_prompt` in llama.cpp checks the generation prompt string a template adds for plain, content-continuation and reasoning-continuation cases. Ollama's parser carries a comment that it follows a "reference implementation" for newline trimming and type coercion, which is the Qwen Python parser; its renderer notes a TODO to match Python `json.dumps` spacing for nested JSON. Number: the model writes `1.0` for an integer-or-number parameter; parse returns int 1; render prints `1`. Boolean: the model writes `True`; parse returns true; render prints `true`. Null: `NULL` parses to nil and the renderer prints `null`. Whitespace: a model that puts two newlines before a tool call, or no blank line, comes back with the template's own spacing. Reasoning: leading or trailing whitespace in generated thinking is trimmed on parse and again by `TrimSpace` on render, so the re-rendered think block can be shorter than the generated one. items.concept: Peacock terms and undue emphasis
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Peacock terms and undue emphasis. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Peacock terms and undue emphasis Source-anchored research for Peacock terms and undue emphasis. Run status: COMPLETED. The Words to watch Bob Dylan example replaces 'defining figure ... brilliant songwriter' with a Time 100 inclusion, a quoted description, and a fact (hundreds of covers by the mid-1970s): the fix is attributed, checkable evidence, not a milder adjective. (low confidence) Wikipedia's Words to watch defines puffery as unattributed promotional words (legendary, best, great, acclaimed, iconic, visionary, outstanding, leading, celebrated, award-winning, landmark, cutting-edge, innovative, revolutionary) and prescribes replacing them with facts and attribution. (high confidence) Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing lists undue emphasis on significance: LLM text overuses 'stands/serves as', 'is a testament/reminder', 'crucial/pivotal/vital role', 'underscores importance'. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) The same guide lists promotional LLM adjectives: 'boasts a', vibrant, rich, profound, showcasing, nestled, natural beauty, groundbreaking. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Wikipedia editors attribute the pattern to LLMs regressing to the statistical mean: specific facts get replaced by generic importance claims, so text becomes both less specific and more exaggerated. (low confidence) Hype language (hyperbolic or subjective wording used to glamorize or exaggerate) is a recognised phenomenon in human scientific writing; an NLP paper on NIH grant applications shows annotators can reliably label candidate hype adjectives with written guidelines, but the task needs domain knowledge and temporal awareness of facts. (low confidence) Promotional wording alone does not prove AI authorship: Wikipedia notes not all promotional writing is AI-generated, humans write press releases and travel guides this way, and newer models are subtler than GPT-4-era ones; the signal is consistent overuse across unrelated topics. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Fixing only the marker words can hide deeper problems: the guide calls the phrases signs of a problem, not the problem itself, and warns that superficial swaps make detection harder without fixing the unsupported claims. (low confidence) Automated AI-text detectors are unreliable as a substitute for phrase lists: a multi-tool evaluation found neither accurate nor reliable results, with false positives on human text and false negatives on AI text. (medium confidence)

items.text: per-expert coverage and per-expert KLD attribution for MoE quants llama-imatrix's `--show-statistics` does not report per-expert numbers: compute_statistics averages each expert's sums by that expert's count, silently skips any expert with count 0 (debug log only), and concatenates the remaining experts' channels into one vector, giving one row per tensor. The ... llama-imatrix's `--show-statistics` does not report per-expert numbers: compute_statistics averages each expert's sums by that expert's count, silently skips any expert with count 0 (debug log only), and concatenates the remaining experts' channels into one vector, giving one row per tensor. The N column is therefore the channel count times the number of experts that received tokens, so N divided by the row size is a coverage count recoverable from that table. Per-expert counts live only in the GGUF imatrix (`<tensor>.counts`); no stock llama.cpp command prints them as a histogram. Quantization granularity is the whole merged tensor: llama-quantize assigns one ggml type per tensor, and the 3D `ffn_*_exps` tensor holds every expert, so all experts of a layer share one type and one block layout. Expert-wise mixed precision (the router-norm ranking line, the DynaExq hotness line) cannot be written as a GGUF recipe; the only per-expert levers in llama-quantize are the imatrix slices. llama-perplexity's `--kl-divergence` computes KLD per token over the vocabulary and reports mean, percentile and Same-top-p statistics; it carries no expert index, so attributing loss to an expert would need a second pass that logs the routed expert ids for the same tokens (imatrix's MUL_MAT_ID hook already reads those ids) and a join by token position. Published substitutes for attribution are proxies: expert activation frequency, router-gate probability mass (EMA hotness), weight outlier ratio, and block-output cosine similarity. QuantMoE-Bench scores them by downstream accuracy under GPTQ, not by KLD. Calibration imbalance is the cause the literature points to: on the first MoE layer of DeepSeek-MoE-16B the sample distribution across experts is strongly skewed for both C4 and WikiText-2 (128 x 4096 tokens each), and EAQuant's fix is to resample until under-used experts reach their expected activation counts. 2024-06: QuantMoE-Bench (arXiv 2406.08155) benchmarks MoE structure-aware bit allocation with GPTQ on Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-base. 2025-06: EAQuant (arXiv 2506.13329) adds expert-level calibration balan

items.text: Per-model memory measurement with footprint and IOAccelerator footprint de-duplicates mlock-wired memory shared between kernel_task and user processes, so per-process sums can differ from system wired memory. footprint de-duplicates mlock-wired memory shared between kernel_task and user processes, so per-process sums can differ from system wired memory. Clean file-backed memory (an mmapped GGUF) is not Dirty, so it does not add to footprint even when it holds all the weights; it appears as Clean mapped file. llama.cpp PR 26082 found per-process counters (including footprint) drop after a model is freed while system wired memory stays high, so a Metal leak is visible only system-wide (see llama-cpp-pr-25309 dossier). footprint must run as root for other users' processes. Whether MLX weights loaded through make_buffer over mmapped safetensors show as Dirty IOAccelerator or Clean mapped file. footprint displays all addressable memory but emphasizes memory the kernel counts as dirty for accounting. A process's footprint is equal to the total of all Dirty memory associated with that process. Dirty is memory written to that is neither file-backed nor marked reclaimable; it includes Swapped memory and zero-filled memory. (Wired) is Dirty memory that must stay at a fixed physical location; the man page gives GPU graphics textures placed by the driver as the example. File-backed memory, even if dirty, can be evicted and re-read from disk, and the man page warns a large clean working set can thrash when physical memory is short. Memory from mmap(2) appears as "mapped file" with the path; tagged categories appear as names like "IOKit (graphics)". footprint de-duplicates wired memory between kernel_task and user processes, including memory locked via mlock(2). vmObjectDirty reads dirty memory from kernel VM objects instead of the pmap; it is expensive, cannot run in real time, may not match top or Activity Monitor, and was the default before macOS 10.15. sample secs samples repeatedly (fractional seconds allowed, best effort) and --sample-duration limits it; JSON output gains a samples array. swapped and --wired add the swapped/compressed and wired columns; --json path saves a JSON copy; -p accepts a name or pid. vmmap's DIRTY column excludes the compressed or swapped memory that footprint folds into Dirty. footprint --sample 1 -p <pid> with --json gives a time series of a model server's Dirty and (Wired) totals across prefill and unload, which is a repeatable per-mod

items.text: Per-query fusion weighting Depth-first rabbithole dossier for Per-query fusion weighting; source-anchored research pack. [low] In Atlas Hybrid Fusion, the `weight` parameter is an optional Double that multiplies the `score` expression by a number after normalization. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/score.md [high] This is not Weaviate. In Elastic's linear retriever, each retriever's `weight` multiplies its scores, must be >= 0 and defaults to 1.0. In Azure AI Search, the vector weighting multiplier defaults to 1.0 (no weighting) and is applied to the initial score before RRF scoring. Sources: https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/retrievers/linear-retriever, https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-ranking [medium] In Atlas Hybrid Fusion, the `scoreDetails` option defaults to `false` and, when enabled, breaks down scoring factors to analyze why a document matched a query and received its score.
