items.text: Per-token collective count times per-call latency model Per-token synchronisation time on a tensor-parallel Mac cluster is modelled as `T_sync = G x t_gate`, where `G` is the number of cross-machine exchanges per decoded token and `t_gate` is the time one exchange adds to the critical path. Per-token synchronisation time on a tensor-parallel Mac cluster is modelled as `T_sync = G x t_gate`, where `G` is the number of cross-machine exchanges per decoded token and `t_gate` is the time one exchange adds to the critical path. `G` depends on the engine. ds4 resident TP uses 2 gates per layer (`DS4_TP_GATES_PER_LAYER = 2`); ds4 GLM with streaming uses one per sparse layer (existing dossiers); an mlx-lm TP run uses about two all-sums per layer. `t_gate` is not one number. For ds4 it is the number of 16384-byte messages in a gate times the per-message cost, plus the wait for the peer's partial result: `chunks_per_gate = ceil(vec_bytes / 16384)` with `vec_bytes = n_embd x 4`, so a model with `n_embd <= 4096` sends one message per gate and larger ones send more. ds4 keeps 16 gates of receives posted ahead during decode (`DS4_TP_RDMA_RECV_WINDOW = 16`), so the receive side is not on the critical path for each gate; the send and the peer's compute are. A measured per-round cost exists for JACCL with and without fast synch. Exo PR 2377's standalone loop on 2 Mac Studio M3 Ultra over Thunderbolt 5 does 8 rounds per step of a bf16 matmul followed by `all_sum` of 16x5120 values, and the step takes 3.2 ms with fast synch off and 1.56 ms on, with exo's pinned MLX and with upstream MLX main alike. Dividing by 8 gives about 0.40 ms per round off and 0.195 ms per round on, so fast synch saves about 0.2 ms per round. Each round includes the matmul, so 0.195 ms is an upper bound on the collective's own cost with fast synch on, and the 0.2 ms saving assumes the matmul time does not change. At 160 KiB per `all_sum` (16x5120 bf16, assuming bf16 payload) the loop is larger than a batch-1 decode partial (about 10 KiB at `n_embd = 5120` in bf16), so it likely overstates small-message cost. The existing dossiers could not confirm the figure of 0.26 ms saved per `all_sum` by fast synch. The PR 2377 loop is the first fetched measurement of the same quantity and gives 0.2 ms, the same order. With fast synch off, a 100-collective token costs about 100 x 0.4 = 40 ms of matmul-plus-collective in that loop; with it on, about 19.5 ms. items.concept: Performance, Motivation & Resilience Psychology
items.summary: The evidence-based psychology of sustaining performance over the long haul —
items.text: Performance, Motivation & Resilience Psychology The evidence-based psychology of sustaining performance over the long haul — The evidence-based psychology of sustaining performance over the long haul - your own and your team's - without burning out. Ten constructs, organized into three layers: What drives effort - mindset, grit, achievement goals, regulatory focus. What sustains it in the moment - flow, self-efficacy, self-regulation. What protects against collapse - stress appraisal & coping, burnout, recovery & resilience. The throughline: high performance is not a trait you have or lack; it is a state you engineer - through how you frame ability, structure goals, manage attention and arousal, appraise stress, and recover. Each section gives a self-management note (sustaining your own performance) and a team / coaching note (leading and developing others). This field has a serious replication problem, and this skill is honest about it: two of its most famous constructs (growth-mindset interventions, ego depletion) have weak or failed-to-replicate evidence, and a third (grit) is largely redundant with an older trait. Use the strong constructs confidently; treat the contested ones as heuristics, not laws. Where the science is thin, the section says so. Core idea. People hold an implicit "lay theory" about whether ability is fixed (an entity theory - you have a fixed amount of intelligence/talent) or malleable (an incremental theory - ability grows with effort and strategy). A fixed mindset makes effort feel like evidence of low ability and makes failure identity-threatening, so people avoid challenge and disengage. A growth mindset reframes effort and failure as the mechanism of getting better, so people seek challenge and persist (Dweck - Mindset Works). Be honest about the effect size. This is the single most over-sold construct in popular performance psychology. The Sisk et al. (2018) two meta-analyses are the key correction: Across 273 studies / ~365,000 people, mindset accounted for only ~1% of the variance in academic achievement (a weak correlation). Across 43 intervention studies / ~57,000 people, growth-mindset interventions produced a standardized mean difference of d ≈ 0.08 - very small (Sisk et al. 2018, Psychological Science; PubMed). Moderator finding: low-SES and academically at-risk people benefited more, which is the strongest remaining case for targeted intervention. items.text: Performance Review Writing Performance reviews are not new information — they are synthesis. The cardinal rule is "no surprises": anything that appears in a written review should already have been said in a one-on-one. Performance reviews are not new information - they are synthesis. The cardinal rule is "no surprises": anything that appears in a written review should already have been said in a one-on-one. If a written performance review contains feedback the employee is hearing for the first time, the manager has failed earlier in the year. Situation - When and where the behavior occurred. Behavior - What the person actually did. Observable, factual, non-interpretive. Impact - What followed from the behavior. Example (negative): > Situation: In the design review for the refund system on March 12. Behavior: You interrupted the junior engineer three times. Impact: She stopped contributing to the discussion, and we lost her input on the rollback design. Example (positive): > Situation: During the Q2 incident on April 8. Behavior: You took on the comms role within five minutes. Impact: The CSMs were able to respond to customers without paging engineers. Weak: "Sarah is a great team player and is always willing to help." Strong: "Sarah led the cross-team migration of the billing service in Q2, partnering with three teams and coordinating four deployment windows; the migration shipped two weeks ahead of plan with zero customer-visible incidents. Next step: I'd like to see Sarah take on a bigger system design role in Q4." Weakness phrasing (avoid): "Tom is too quiet in meetings." Growth-area phrasing (use): "In larger forums (5+ people), Tom contributes less than I think he could. He has the strongest understanding of the search service on the team, but in the Q3 architecture reviews his ideas often landed in the followup chat rather than in the meeting itself. Growth focus for next cycle: Tom and I have agreed he'll lead two of the next four architecture reviews." Two axes: how much you care personally about the person, and how directly you challenge them. Radical Candor: Care + Challenge. The target. Ruinous Empathy: Care without challenge. Soft, vague, no real feedback. The most common manager failure mode. Obnoxious Aggression: Challenge without care. The failure mode in writing is almost always Ruinous Empathy - burying real feedback in praise sandwich. Lead with strengths, not weaknesses. Use concrete examples or cut the point. Negative feedback goes in p

items.text: Personal Banking > Framing. This is general educational information, not financial advice. > Framing. This is general educational information, not financial advice. > Rates, fee schedules, and regulations change, and details vary by institution > and state. Verify current figures against the primary sources at the end before > relying on anything here. Content is current as of 2026. Spoke of the consumer-finance family (the personal-money side of the broader consumer-credit-and-debt hub). This skill covers where you keep money: deposit accounts, the insurance behind them, the fees that erode them, and how to pick and safely use a bank or credit union. It covers scam prevention and what the reimbursement rules are (Section 8), but not borrowing, investing, or the step-by-step recovery after fraud or identity theft. See the cross-references at the end. HYSA vs MMA. Both are deposit accounts (insured, variable rate). MMAs add limited transactional access (checks/debit). Neither is a money market fund, which is an investment (not deposit-insured). That last point is a common and costly confusion. CDs trade liquidity for a locked rate. A CD ladder (staggered maturities) balances rate and access. Watch for auto-renewal at maturity; there's a short grace period (often ~7-10 days) to withdraw penalty-free. "Withdrawal limits." Federal Regulation D's 6-per-month limit on savings transfers was suspended in 2020 and remains optional, but many banks still enforce a limit by their own policy. Check the account's terms. A higher APY beats a low one mechanically: on $10,000, the gap between 0.40% and 4.0% is roughly $360/year. For an emergency fund, an HYSA is usually the default home. Truth in Savings (TISA), implemented by Regulation DD (12 CFR 1030), exists so you can comparison-shop deposit accounts on uniform terms. (For credit unions the parallel rule is NCUA's Truth in Savings, 12 CFR 707, same substance.) APY (annual percentage yield) is the standardized number for comparing accounts. It bakes in the interest rate and compounding frequency over a 365-day period, so two accounts are directly comparable. Always compare APY, not the nominal "interest rate." An ad that states a return must state it as an "annual percentage yield" using that term. That's a Reg DD requirement, not marketing courtesy. Banks must disclose fees, the rate, the APY, and other terms before you open and on request. A change that lowers the APY or otherwise hurts you requires ≥30 days' advance

In this installation the consumer-finance family is registered as consumer-credit-and-debt - route there for sibling topics. Neighboring spokes are cross-referenced at the end. A US individual return (Form 1040) flows top to bottom: Gross income - wages (W-2 box 1), self-employment, interest, dividends, capital gains, retirement distributions, etc. − Above-the-line adjustments (Schedule 1) → Adjusted Gross Income (AGI). AGI is the pivotal number; most phase-outs key off AGI or modified AGI (MAGI). − Standard deduction OR itemized deductions (Schedule A) → taxable income. Apply the tax brackets to taxable income → tax before credits. − Tax credits (some refundable, some not) → tax after credits. − Payments (withholding from W-2/1099, estimated payments) → refund or balance due. > TCJA note: Most of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act individual structure was > set to sunset after TY2025. OBBBA made the TCJA rate brackets and the > larger standard deduction PERMANENT and added new (some temporary) deductions. > The "2025→2026 sunset cliff" people feared did not happen - but several > OBBBA add-ons (senior deduction, tips/overtime deductions) are temporary > (≈TY2025–2028), so a different uncertainty now applies. It explains how the system is structured and governed, how Educational domain reference for a North Carolina cause venture working on organ, eye, and tissue donation awareness and donor registration. It explains how the system is structured and governed, how people register, the major policy debates, the myths and equity barriers a campaign must navigate, and the NC-specific law and registry mechanics. It is a knowledge foundation, not medical or legal advice - see the Disclaimer, and always re-verify live numbers and law before publishing. Quick framing for a venture: in the US you cannot "make" anyone a donor and you do not run the recovery or matching - that is the OPO and OPTN's job. A donation-awareness nonprofit's real levers are education, myth-correction, trust-building, and driving registry sign-ups (especially in under-registered communities). Keep that scope in mind throughout. A note on vocabulary: the field's preferred phrase is "organ, eye, and tissue donation" (eyes/corneas are tracked separately from other tissue). Say "deceased donor," not "cadaveric"; say "recover/recovery," not "harvest." "Donor" registration normally means deceased donation; living donation is arranged separately. The US system is a public-private structure created by the National Organ Transplant Act (NOTA) of 1984, which banned the sale of organs and established the national network. HRSA (Health Resources & Services Administration) - the HHS agency that oversees the OPTN via federal contract and runs the public-facing education site organdonor.gov (organdonor.gov; HRSA). HRSA sets the rules of the road; it does not itself match organs. OPTN (Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network) - the national transplant system mandated by NOTA. The OPTN sets allocation policy, operates the matching technology, and collects the data. Membership includes transplant hospitals, OPOs, and labs (optn.transplant.hrsa.gov). UNOS (United Network for Organ Sharing) - a private nonprofit that held the sole OPTN contract from 1986 until 2023-2024. UNOS built and ran the matching system (UNet) and supported OPTN policy work. As of 2024-2025 UNOS is one contractor among others (see Modernization below) (UNOS.org). SRTR (Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients) - the analytics arm

items.summary: The evidence-based science of stable individual differences, meaning who a
items.text: Personality and Individual Differences The evidence-based science of stable individual differences, meaning who a The evidence-based science of stable individual differences, meaning who a person reliably is across time and situations, applied to one practical job: tailoring how you communicate with and manage different stakeholders, grounded in evidence and avoiding the MBTI trap. The single most important thing this skill enforces: use the dimensional trait model (Big Five / HEXACO), not type systems (MBTI, DISC, Enneagram, True Colors). The Big Five is the consensus, replicated, predictive model of personality structure in academic psychology. Type systems are popular, fun, and psychometrically weak. This distinction is the whole game. Get it wrong and every downstream inference is built on sand. > Hard ethical frame (read first). Traits are probabilistic, not > deterministic; descriptive, not diagnostic. You observe behavior, you do > not "diagnose" or label a person. Never use trait inferences for hiring, > promotion, or selection decisions about a real individual - that is both > scientifically unjustified and, in many jurisdictions, illegal. The legitimate > use here is adapting your own communication to observed behavior, holding > every inference loosely. See Ethics & Limits at the end - it is not optional. Five broad, continuous dimensions describe the bulk of stable personality variance. The acronym is OCEAN (Wikipedia: Big Five): Each dimension is a continuum, normally distributed. Most people are in the middle on any given trait; extreme scorers are rare. There are no "types", which matters enormously for the MBTI critique below. Facets matter. Each of the five domains splits into six narrower facets (30 total in the NEO-PI-R; Costa & McCrae 1992, 240 items) (Big Five history). Two people can share an Extraversion score but differ sharply on facets: one high on Assertiveness/low on Warmth (a driving, task-focused executive), another high on Warmth/low on Assertiveness (a relational, non-pushy collaborator). When a domain score doesn't fit what you observe, drop to the facet level. The Big Five was discovered, not invented, via the lexical hypothesis: the idea that the most important individual differences become encoded as single words in natural language (Wikipedia). items.text: Persuasion & Influence Psychology (Attitude-Change Theory) The mechanism layer of attitude change. This skill answers why a persuasion attempt succeeds, fails, or backfires — the cognitive and motivational machinery underneath the tactics. It does not teach y The mechanism layer of attitude change. This skill answers why a persuasion attempt succeeds, fails, or backfires - the cognitive and motivational machinery underneath the tactics. It does not teach you which line to say (that is negotiation-and-persuasion) or how to word an exec memo (executive-comms). It tells you what is happening in the other person's head so you can diagnose a stalled rollout, predict whether a change will stick, and choose an approach that fits how that audience actually processes your message. Reach for it when the question is diagnostic or mechanistic, not tactical: "I keep making the case and the champion just won't move - why?" "We mandated the migration and adoption went down. What happened?" "The exec agreed in the room but reversed in writing two days later." "Will this attitude change survive contact with their internal skeptics?" "Should I lead with deep technical arguments or with a credible reference customer?" "How do I get a buy-in decision to stick instead of unravelling?" Almost every model here is an answer to one of two questions: How hard is this person thinking about my actual argument? (the dual-process axis: ELM and HSM) What motivates the change - and what makes it durable or fragile? (consistency, freedom, attribution, norms, source, resistance) Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM - Petty & Cacioppo, 1986). Attitude change runs through one of two routes depending on elaboration (how much the person thinks about the issue-relevant arguments): Central route - high elaboration; scrutinizes argument quality; requires both motivation (personal relevance) and ability (no distraction, knowledge, time). Attitudes formed this way are strong: persistent, resistant to counter-persuasion, predictive of behavior. Peripheral route - low elaboration; leans on cues (source attractiveness/credibility, number of arguments, mood, consensus). Resulting attitudes are weak: decay, flip under attack, weakly predict behavior. Sources: https://www.practical-mongodb-aggregations.com/guides/sharding.html [high] To optimize MongoDB aggregation pipelines, filter documents with a $match stage as early as possible so that later stages process fewer documents. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md, https://studio3t.com/knowledge-base/articles/mongodb-aggregation-framework/ [high] Use an index to satisfy the sort operation so that MongoDB does not sort documents in memory, and move the $sort stage to near the start of the pipeline if it does not depend on preceding $unwind, $group, or $project stages. items.concept: Pitch Deck Writing
items.summary: A pitch deck is a slide-based artifact that compresses a fundraising, sales, or partnership case into a tight narrative arc — usually 10 to 14 slides — designed to be skimmed in minutes and remembered
items.text: Pitch Deck Writing A pitch deck is a slide-based artifact that compresses a fundraising, sales, or partnership case into a tight narrative arc — usually 10 to 14 slides — designed to be skimmed in minutes and remembered A pitch deck is a slide-based artifact that compresses a fundraising, sales, or partnership case into a tight narrative arc - usually 10 to 14 slides - designed to be skimmed in minutes and remembered in seconds. Guy Kawasaki's rule for investor/pitch contexts: 10 slides - the human mind cannot absorb more than ten concepts in a single sitting in a pitch context 20 minutes - even if you have a full hour, present in 20 minutes; leave the rest for discussion 30-point minimum font - if you cannot fit your message in 30pt type, you have too many words 10–12 slides in this order: Title / Company purpose - one-line description Problem - the customer pain, with evidence Solution - your product as the answer Why now - timing argument; why this couldn't have been built 5 years ago Market size - TAM/SAM/SOM, bottom-up preferred Competition - who else is in the space, how you differ Product - screenshots, demo, key features Business model - how you make money Team - why this team can win Traction - what you've already proven Financials - current state and projections Ask - how much you're raising, what you'll do with it Slide 4 ("Why now") is the slide most founders skip and the slide most VCs care about. Strip away the template specifics and every effective pitch deck follows five beats: Problem - establish the pain. The reader nods. Solution - show your answer. The reader believes the answer is plausible. Traction - prove it's working. The reader believes the answer is real. Team - prove you can execute. The reader believes you specifically can win. Ask - close. The reader knows what you want and what they get. Strong decks have an appendix - 5 to 20 extra slides beyond the main 10–12 - NOT shown in the live pitch but sent with the deck. Pitch decks are NOT mystery novels. Slide 1 should already answer "what does this company do" at headline level. End the deck with one slide that names the single thing you want the audience to walk away remembering. Not a recap - one sentence, one number, one image. Every slide has a title. The title is a thesis, not a category. Category title (weak): "Market Size" Thesis title (strong): "$47B TAM growing 22% annually; we serve the underserved bottom 60%" The mystery opening - first 3 slides don't say what the comp

items.summary: Source-anchored research for Planner plan scoring and EOF bonus. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Planner plan scoring and EOF bonus Source-anchored research for Planner plan scoring and EOF bonus. Run status: COMPLETED. In current MongoDB plan_ranker_util.h, pickBestPlan() sets eofBonus to 1 and adds that point when the candidate root statistics report common.isEOF. The code comment says multiple candidates that hit EOF during the same round-robin calls also receive the bonus. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) A trial sample can mis-rank plans when index order and predicate values are correlated: MongoDB issue SERVER-20616 describes a range scan that looks productive on the early sample, and a University of Sydney study found MongoDB 7.0.1 could prefer index scans over faster collection scans, with more than twice the optimal runtime in some tested cases. (medium confidence) The EOF formula describes the classic multi-planner path, not every eligible query choice: the current manual says multi-planning with a cost-based ranker backup is the default plan-selection mechanism for eligible queries starting in MongoDB 8.3, and the backup may evaluate plans when the initial trial is unsuccessful. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) A University of Sydney study evaluated FPTP on MongoDB 7.0.1 using simple two-range query families. It found cases where the optimizer chose index scans even though collection scans ran faster, and argued that advanced-per-work scoring can undercount index access plus document-fetch cost. The study does not isolate EOF bonus as the cause of every misranking. (medium confidence) EOF is a distinct classic trial stop condition from reaching the result-batch limit or maximum work limit; it means the candidate returned all of its results during the trial. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) The productivity score is not elapsed time: an idealo report on MongoDB 4.0 describes a candidate with a slower estimated execution time (23 ms versus 6 ms) winning because it produced more advanced results during the trial. (medium confidence) A Nov 2025 example by Franck Pachot reports candidate scores of 2.012, 1.010, and 1.007; the first candidate’s one-point lead mostly comes from reaching EOF during the trial. This illustrates how trial completion can dominate small productivity differences, but it is one query example rather than a general performance result. (medium confidence) In the current classic ranker, a candidate's basic score starts at 1 and adds root productivity (advanced divided by works) plus smal

items.concept: Platform Consolidation TCO (Atlas Search/Vector Search vs Separate Search or Vector DB)
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Platform Consolidation TCO (Atlas Search/Vector Search vs Separate Search or Vector DB). Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Platform Consolidation TCO (Atlas Search/Vector Search vs Separate Search or Vector DB) Source-anchored research for Platform Consolidation TCO (Atlas Search/Vector Search vs Separate Search or Vector DB). Run status: COMPLETED. Customer evidence for removing a bolt-on Elasticsearch and sync layer is qualitative and published by MongoDB. THL: about two years of sync, stability and outage problems, then Atlas Search replaced Elasticsearch iteratively, 'a couple of months' to migrate everything, Elasticsearch cluster and dedicated sync resources turned off, no cost figures given. Orbweaver: search move took about two weeks including testing, no separate ETL tool, latency down over 70%, previously 'kept scaling Elasticsearch ... extremely expensive', cost reduction stated without a number. (medium confidence) The search index is eventually consistent with the database. MongoDB's sizing guide sets a goal of under one second from collection to index and lists lag causes: cluster load, change-stream read pressure, Search Node indexing capacity, very heavy ingestion (over 10k inserts/updates per second may need sharding) and many indexes. Initial indexing and ongoing sync 'can impose considerable read pressure on the cluster'. Pinecone's page notes that neither it nor MongoDB publishes a guaranteed time for a write to become searchable. Consolidation moves sync load onto the cluster's read path; it does not remove it. (medium confidence) Forrester and Pinecone both scope the consolidation case. Forrester (via BigDATAwire, 2024-08-22) recommends native vector databases for exceptional performance and low-latency access to very large vector volumes and says most vector databases 'haven't yet demonstrated high-end scalability and performance, particularly when handling billions of vectors'; it recommends multimodel databases when vector and non-vector data, hybrid search or existing infrastructure matter. Pinecone's compare page says a separate store wins when retrieval grows at a different rate than the database beside it, and to 'stay on Atlas' if a document and its embedding must be written in one transaction or single-query hybrid search matters. (medium confidence) A separate search or vector system adds costs that list prices omit: application-side dual writes with a retry or reconciliation job (Pinecone: write the document, then upsert the vector; 'Count it when you compare the two'), a second consistency model, and another system to operate and page on. items.concept: Policy and Governance Writing
items.summary: Policies prescribe. They do not propose, persuade, or describe — they bind. A reader of a policy needs three things in the first 60 seconds: who is bound by it, what they must do, and what happens if
items.text: Policy and Governance Writing Policies prescribe. They do not propose, persuade, or describe — they bind. A reader of a policy needs three things in the first 60 seconds: who is bound by it, what they must do, and what happens if Policies prescribe. They do not propose, persuade, or describe - they bind. A reader of a policy needs three things in the first 60 seconds: who is bound by it, what they must do, and what happens if they don't. RFC 8174 clarification: The normative meaning attaches only when the keyword is in ALL CAPITALS. Lowercase "must", "should", and "may" carry their normal English meaning and have no normative weight. Required incantation: > The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here. Policy - what must be true, and why. Mandatory. Strategic. Changes rarely. Standard - which specific implementation satisfies the policy (TLS 1.3, AES-256). Mandatory. Tactical. Procedure - how to perform a specific task. Mandatory for the role performing the task. Operational. Guideline - suggested approach when no mandatory standard applies. Advisory. The hierarchy test: if you can answer "yes" to "would this need to change when we upgrade the firewall?", it is not a policy. It is a standard or procedure. Title and identifier - unique policy ID, version number, effective date Purpose - one-paragraph statement of why the policy exists Scope - who, what, where the policy applies; explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists Definitions - every term of art, listed alphabetically Policy statements - the normative rules, using BCP 14 keywords in ALL CAPS Roles and responsibilities - named role titles (not individuals) mapped to obligations Exceptions - how to request and approve a documented deviation Enforcement - consequences of violation Related documents - pointers to standards, procedures, and laws Review schedule - review cadence, owner, next review date, change-history table A defensible scope section answers: People - which employees, contractors, vendors, partners, customers? Assets - which systems, data classifications, networks, locations, devices? Activities - which operations, transactions, or behaviors? State each as an inclusion list AND an exclusion list. items.summary: Source-anchored research for Positive substitution style guides. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Positive substitution style guides Source-anchored research for Positive substitution style guides. Run status: COMPLETED. Anthropic's own guidance is not purely positive: for removing preambles it recommends 'Respond directly without preamble. Do not start with phrases like Here is..., Based on..., etc.', and adds post-processing as a fallback. Positive substitution is a preference, not a rule the vendor applies to itself. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Anthropic's prompting best-practices doc lists 'Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do' as a way to steer output formatting, with the example: replace 'Do not use markdown in your response' with 'Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs.' (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) The stated rationale is that a negative instruction 'removes one option and leaves the rest open', so the model chooses an unintended alternative; a positive style description gives the model a voice to hold instead of a list to steer around. This is asserted reasoning, not measured in the sources. (low confidence) In a small August 2026 code-review experiment (three synthetic samples), a positive inclusion-criteria phrasing flagged 0/3 false problems versus 2/3 for both no instruction and a prohibition; on the production prompt, positive and negative phrasing detected the same bugs. The authors conclude positive framing helps judgment calls and generative tasks, while simple behavioral guardrails tolerate negative phrasing. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-31) Anthropic's docs also advise matching the prompt's own style to the desired output (for example, removing markdown from the prompt reduces markdown in the output), which is a positive-by-example lever alongside stated instructions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) The same experiment's authors state that a prohibition weakens across a long, open-ended generation, which they use to argue for positive phrasing in stylistic output. This is the closest source found to the lexical-tic use case; it is a blog claim, not a controlled result. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-31)

items.concept: Post-training effects on LLM vocabulary
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Post-training effects on LLM vocabulary. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Post-training effects on LLM vocabulary Source-anchored research for Post-training effects on LLM vocabulary. Run status: COMPLETED. The popular explanation that 'delve' is overused because OpenAI's outsourced RLHF annotators in Nigeria favor Nigerian formal English was proposed by Alex Hern and is framed as a plausible theory; circumstantial support is PubMed 'delve' usage rising 10-100x, with no direct causal evidence. (medium confidence) Current lexical-shift studies cannot test ChatGPT directly because it lacks a public base variant, and they use mid-size open models on English scientific text, limiting generalization to frontier chat assistants. (low confidence) Top overused lemmas in instruction-tuned models versus human abstracts include suggest, highlight, enhance, furthermore, additionally, crucial, potential, strategy; many are ordinary scientific vocabulary, so models amplify already-typical wording rather than inventing novel words. (low confidence) Base models also diverge from human word usage (misalignment scores 0.0329-0.0345 vs human baseline 0.0304), so not all lexical drift is post-training; content-word alignment trends are weakened or reversed after instruction tuning. (low confidence) A 2026 study of 42,000 PubMed abstract continuations across six open model families (Falcon, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, OLMo, Yi; 4B-8B) defines curation-free metrics (Lexical Alignment Score, Triangulated Preference Shift) to isolate overuse relative to human text and shifts attributable to preference-learning stages. (medium confidence) Instruction tuning does not uniformly change lexical diversity: in Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B on three multiple-choice benchmarks, cross-rationale similarity diversity (1-SelfBLEU) consistently fell while surface Unique-2 diversity moved in both directions, so 'post-training narrows vocabulary' is model- and metric-dependent. (medium confidence) Markdown-heavy training data leaves stylistic fingerprints such as em-dash frequency; post-training can modify but does not fully erase these markers. (low confidence)

items.concept: Postmortem Writing
items.summary: A postmortem is a learning artifact disguised as an incident report. It must satisfy three audiences simultaneously: the engineers who need to understand what failed, the leadership who need to evalua
items.text: Postmortem Writing A postmortem is a learning artifact disguised as an incident report. It must satisfy three audiences simultaneously: the engineers who need to understand what failed, the leadership who need to evalua A postmortem is a learning artifact disguised as an incident report. It must satisfy three audiences simultaneously: the engineers who need to understand what failed, the leadership who need to evaluate organizational risk, and the people who lived through the incident. Three substitutions do most of the work: Names → roles. "Alice deployed the bad change" → "The release engineer deployed change #4821." Judgments → actions. "Bob failed to notice the alert" → "The on-call engineer did not see the alert because it was routed to a paused channel." Causal verbs → enabling conditions. "X caused Y" → "X created conditions under which Y became possible." The single most damaging phrase: "should have." Replace it with "the system did not surface the information that would have enabled X." UTC timestamps, always. Source for each event: which dashboard, which log line, which Slack message. Actor + action + observable result, in that order. Decision points called out explicitly, with the information the decider had at the time. Real incidents have a root cause plus contributing factors. Structure the analysis as: Triggering event (the proximate change). Root cause (the latent defect the trigger exposed). Contributing factors, categorized: Technical (missing monitoring, single points of failure) Process (insufficient testing, communication gaps) Environmental (time pressure, on-call fatigue) Apply iteratively: "Why did the API return 503s? Because the database connection pool was exhausted." Continue until you reach an organizational or design-level factor. Allow branching. A single chain of whys is rare. Multiple parallel chains converging on multiple contributing factors is common. A defensible action item has: Owner: a single named person (not a team). Due date: a real calendar date. Severity / priority: P0/P1/P2 calibrated to actual risk reduction. Traceability: which contributing factor it addresses. Definition of done: how the writer will know the action is complete. What worked: the alert fired correctly, the rollback procedure was executable. What we got lucky on: things that worked but only by accident. What we want to preserve: practices that should be formalized. Linguistic markers of hindsight bias to delete in revision: "Clearly..." (it wa

items.concept: PRD Writing
items.summary: A Product Requirements Document (PRD) is a PM-owned artifact that defines what a product team will build and why, before engineering proposes how. PRDs sit upstream of RFCs, design docs, and implement
items.text: PRD Writing A Product Requirements Document (PRD) is a PM-owned artifact that defines what a product team will build and why, before engineering proposes how. PRDs sit upstream of RFCs, design docs, and implement A Product Requirements Document (PRD) is a PM-owned artifact that defines what a product team will build and why, before engineering proposes how. PRDs sit upstream of RFCs, design docs, and implementation specs. A PRD captures validated decisions. It does not perform validation. Validation happens through customer interviews, prototypes, user testing, and data analysis - the PRD records the conclusions. A modern PRD opens with the problem, not the solution. Sections proceed in this order: Problem - what user/business pain are we solving, with evidence Users - who is affected, segment size, current workarounds Goals - desired outcomes and what success looks like Proposed solution - at a high level (often a prototype link) Success metrics - measurable definition of done Open questions / risks - what's unresolved Non-goals - what we are explicitly NOT doing Rollout / milestones - MVP → v1 → roadmap Marty Cagan's classic PRD structure: Purpose, Features, Release Criteria, Rough Timing. MVP - minimum viable: smallest scope that lets us learn whether the proposed solution works. v1 (GA) - broadly shippable: meets release criteria, addresses the core user need. Roadmap (vNext) - follow-on work that the PRD acknowledges but does not commit to. Anti-pattern: Writing one undifferentiated feature list and labeling it "the PRD." Always tag each feature with its scope. Basecamp's Shape Up framework replaces the PRD with a pitch: problem, appetite (2 or 6 weeks of fixed budget), solution sketch (fat marker, not Figma), rabbit holes (risks to bound), and no-gos (explicit exclusions). Key inversion: In Shape Up, scope is the variable; time is fixed. Engineers and reviewers consistently raise questions like "what about X?" A Non-Goals section answers these preemptively: > Non-goals (v1): > - Mobile app support - desktop only > - Bulk import - single-record only > - Real-time sync - daily batch acceptable Leading indicators - observable within 1–4 weeks (adoption %, feature engagement, task completion rate) Lagging indicators - observable in 1–2 quarters (retention, revenue, NPS, churn) Always include at least one leading indicator that the team can act on during the first month post-launch. PRD (this skill) - PM-owned. WHAT to build, for WHOM, WHY now. RFC / Desi

The pack holds 91 source-anchored units from 4 sources (3 hosts: MongoDB docs and pricing page, a third-party pricing guide, a right-sizing guide) across 10 facets, mostly worked examples and facts, with one conflict over whether the hourly rate applies per node or per cluster. Memory refers to the total physical RAM available on each data bearing node of your Atlas cluster. For example, an M30 Atlas Core cluster standard replica set is configured with 8 GB RAM on each of the 3 data bearing nodes. Choosing the correct Atlas cluster tier and configuration is an important step in setting up a successful production MongoDB deployment. You can always modify a cluster at a later time, but getting started with the right configuration is possible with a few calculations based on your data set size and network requirements. MongoDB's pricing page directs users to an 'Atlas Core' Pricing Calculator for estimating monthly cost, and lists the drivers: cluster tier and type, cloud provider and region, data storage (data plus indexes), data transfer (mainly egress and cross-region), backup (snapshots and oplogs), and add-ons such as Stream Processing and dedicated Search Nodes. MongoDB Atlas pricing runs from $0 on the free tier to more than $33 per hour on the largest dedicated cluster, billed by the hour. The cluster rate is only part of the story. Most teams get surprised by the backups, data transfer, and add-on services on the same invoice, not the tier they picked. Backup services: Costs are based on the region and the monthly storage consumed by snapshots and oplogs for continuous backups. Note that backup services are not available for the Free tier. (Cluster $/hr x 730 hrs x nodes) + (storage GB x $/GB) + (backup GB x $/GB) + (egress GB x $/GB) + multi-region multiplier An Atlas Infinite cluster has the same amount of RAM at each cluster tier as an Atlas Core cluster, but a different number of nodes and a separate storage layer. items.summary: oMLX entry point: `prepare_system_messages_for_template` (omlx/api/utils.py). It runs for requests that have a non-leading system message and are not partial (continue-final-message) requests.
items.text:
Prefix-cache-safe handling of non-leading system turns oMLX entry point: `prepare_system_messages_for_template` (omlx/api/utils.py). It runs for requests that have a non-leading system message and are not partial (continue-final-message) requests. oMLX entry point: `prepare_system_messages_for_template` (omlx/api/utils.py). It runs for requests that have a non-leading system message and are not partial (continue-final-message) requests. Step 1, relocation hook: a tokenizer attribute `_omlx_relocate_mid_system_messages`, or `relocate_mid_system_messages` on its template object, may rewrite the messages first (model-specific, for templates with a native reminder role). Step 2, placement check: `_mid_system_placement_kinds` accepts a non-leading system run only if the previous message is `user` or `tool` and the next is nothing (tail) or `assistant` (between). Any other shape returns "unsupported". `developer` counts as system. Step 3, capability probe: `chat_template_preserves_mid_system` renders a synthetic conversation (user, optional assistant tool call and tool result, system with a marker, optional assistant) through the real template and requires the system marker to appear after the preceding-role marker (and before the assistant marker for the "between" case). A render exception means false. An explicit `_omlx_supports_mid_system_messages` or `supports_mid_system_messages` attribute set to false short-circuits it. Results are memoised in a process-wide dict. Probe cache key: tokenizer object id, hash of the template string, whether tools are present, the frozen chat-template kwargs, preceding role, placement and partial flag. So a change in `enable_thinking` or `preserve_thinking` re-probes. Step 4, if the probe passes: consecutive system messages are merged in place with "

" and the prefix is untouched. Step 5, if it fails: server setting `preserve_mid_system_cache` (default true) selects `user_note_safe`; false selects `strict`. `user_note_safe` (`_downgrade_mid_system_to_user_notes`): wraps the system text as `[System note]
...
[/System note]` and appends it to the preceding user message if that message is a plain-text user turn and the system run is last or followed by an assistant; otherwise prepends it to the next user message; refuses (returns None) when the previous message is a tool message, when an assistant tool call sits on the boundary, or when the user content is multimodal. `strict` fallback, also used when `user_note_safe` return

items.text:
Prefix-stability regression testing of chat templates `scripts/test_v22.py::run_prefix_test`: for k from 1 to n, renders `messages[:k]` with `add_generation_prompt=False` and requires each render to start with the previous one. On failure it prints the first differing character index and 80 characters either side of it for both strings. `scripts/test_v22.py::run_prefix_test`: for k from 1 to n, renders `messages[:k]` with `add_generation_prompt=False` and requires each render to start with the previous one. On failure it prints the first differing character index and 80 characters either side of it for both strings. Boundary rule shared by both scripts: a k that would split a run of consecutive `system` messages or consecutive `tool` messages is skipped, because a server never generates between them. Test cases 92 and 93 run one scripted agentic session (system, user, assistant with think text plus tool call, tool, assistant, tool, assistant, user) with default settings and with tools plus `reasoning_effort="xhigh"`. Test 94 checks that the minified one-line template renders byte-identically to the multi-line file. `scripts/fuzz_template.py`: a seeded generator (default 500 cases) of structurally valid conversations, asserting nine invariants: render succeeds, jinja/oneline parity, `<|im_start|>`/`<|im_end|>` balance, content appears verbatim, XML parameter fidelity, JSON validity, error-warning precision, prefix stability, and the empty-think prefill when thinking is off. It exits non-zero and prints a JSON repro per failure. The fuzz prefix check has two parts: each history render must start with the previous one, and the render with `add_generation_prompt=True` at turn k-1 must be a prefix of the history render at turn k whenever message k-1 is an assistant. It exempts one case: a non-thinking prompt (ends `<think>

</think>

`) followed by history that has real reasoning, because the generator injects reasoning there. Generation-prompt check is the closest template-level model of what the server cached: the cached tokens are the prompt plus the generated text, so the generation-prompt render is what must prefix the next request. Server-side check, llama.cpp: `n_past` is the token-level common prefix of the stored slot tokens and the new prompt tokens. With env `LLAMA_SERVER_SLOTS_DEBUG` set and `LLAMA_SERVER_SLOTS_N_DIFF` giving a window size, the server logs four warning lines at the mismatch: old text, new text, old token ids, new token ids, sepa

items.concept: Prescriptive Analytics and Optimization
items.summary: Prescriptive analytics is the fourth and highest rung of Gartner's analytics maturity ladder (descriptive → diagnostic → predictive → prescriptive). It answers "what should be done?" rather than "what
items.text: Prescriptive Analytics and Optimization Prescriptive analytics is the fourth and highest rung of Gartner's analytics maturity ladder (descriptive → diagnostic → predictive → prescriptive). It answers "what should be done?" rather than "what Prescriptive analytics is the fourth and highest rung of Gartner's analytics maturity ladder (descriptive → diagnostic → predictive → prescriptive). It answers "what should be done?" rather than "what happened?" or "what will happen?" by recommending (or automating) a specific action. Gartner defines it as advanced analytics that examines data to answer "what should be done?" using techniques such as optimization, simulation, complex event processing, graph analysis, heuristics, recommendation engines, and machine learning (Gartner, Data & Analytics). The mental model: predictive feeds prescriptive. A demand forecast (da-15) or a propensity model (da-7) produces parameters; prescriptive analytics wraps those parameters in a decision model - an objective to optimize, decision variables you control, and constraints you must respect - and returns the action that best trades off the objective against the constraints. This skill is the optimization + decision-science layer of the curriculum; da-6/da-7 supply the predictions it consumes. A useful framing is the decision = objective + decision variables + constraints + uncertainty quadruple. Choosing a method is mostly about which of those four is hard: linear and continuous → LP; discrete choices → MILP/CP; nonlinear-but-convex → convex/QP; uncertainty dominates → stochastic/robust; many competing objectives → multi-objective; analytical model intractable → simulation. Descriptive/diagnostic give hindsight; predictive/prescriptive give foresight, and human involvement decreases as you move toward prescriptive (which can drive automated action). Prescriptive consumes a prediction and adds a decision rule or optimization on top (EAG, 4 types of analytics; Qlik; Gartner glossary). Continuous variables, linear objective and constraints. Solved at a polytope vertex by simplex or interior-point. Canonical teaching cases: blending (min-cost mix meeting specs) and product-mix (max profit s.t. resource limits). LP is the substrate everything else extends (SciPy linprog; PuLP; Real Python LP). Some/all variables integer or binary (yes/no: open a facility, assign a job, select an item). NP-hard; solved by branch-and-bound / branch-and-cut with LP relaxations. Binary variables unlock ass

items.concept: Press Release Writing
items.summary: A press release is a short, journalist-facing news document with a single goal: make it so easy to publish your news that a busy reporter (or a wire-service automated feed) can run it nearly verbatim.
items.text: Press Release Writing A press release is a short, journalist-facing news document with a single goal: make it so easy to publish your news that a busy reporter (or a wire-service automated feed) can run it nearly verbatim. A press release is a short, journalist-facing news document with a single goal: make it so easy to publish your news that a busy reporter (or a wire-service automated feed) can run it nearly verbatim. The defining traits of a press release: Third person, past or present tense, never "we" Inverted-pyramid structure AP Style dateline at the top of the body Stable boilerplate at the bottom (the "About" paragraph) Quote attribution that is publication-ready End mark: ### centered on its own line 400–600 words is the sweet spot Under ~100 characters. No marketing puffery: avoid "industry-leading," "revolutionary," "best-in-class." State the news, not the spin. FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE - the default EMBARGOED UNTIL: [Day, Month Day, Year, HH:MM TIME ZONE] MEDIA ADVISORY - for an upcoming event/availability Always include the time zone for embargoes. City name in ALL CAPS AP state abbreviation (not USPS!) Date written out: Nov. 12, 2026 (AP uses abbreviated months for Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.) Em dash (—) before the lede The first sentence must contain Who, What, When, Where, Why. Bad lede: > Acme Corp, a leading provider of analytics solutions, is excited to announce today an important new milestone in its ongoing growth journey. Good lede: > Acme Corp today announced it has acquired Beta Analytics, a Boston-based real-time data platform, for $400 million in cash and stock. Paragraph 2: amplification - the size, the scope, the differentiator. Paragraph 3: the executive quote. Paragraph 4–5: supporting detail. Paragraph 6: optional second quote. Paragraph 7: practical info - availability, pricing, link. Boilerplate: stable "About" paragraph(s). Media contact block. Standard pattern: > "We chose Beta because their real-time architecture is the strongest in the market," said Jane Doe, CEO of Acme Corp. Attribution after the first sentence of the quote. said is the AP-standard verb. Avoid stated, commented, noted, exclaimed. Full name + title + company on first reference. 60–120 words. Updated when a hard fact changes. The release ends with ### centered on its own line (or the older -30-). items.concept: Pricing and Revenue Analytics
items.summary: Pricing and revenue analytics is the analytical discipline of estimating how price
items.text: Pricing and Revenue Analytics Pricing and revenue analytics is the analytical discipline of estimating how price Pricing and revenue analytics is the analytical discipline of estimating how price moves demand, revenue, and margin, and converting those estimates into pricing decisions. It sits at the intersection of microeconomics (demand theory, elasticity), econometrics (causal estimation under price endogeneity), survey/choice methodology (stated- and revealed-preference WTP), and operations research (constrained price optimization). The defining question is always "what happens to quantity, revenue, and margin if we change the price?" - distinct from forecasting a time series, from attributing marketing spend, or from generic optimization. Scope boundary (what this skill is NOT): da-15-forecasting - predicting demand/revenue forward in time with no price decision lever. This skill uses demand models where price is the causal driver. da-22-marketing-mix-modeling - decomposing sales into media/promo/base with adstock and saturation for budget allocation. Promotion analytics here is the price-discount slice (lift, cannibalization, pantry-loading), not media ROI. da-33-prescriptive-analytics - the LP/MILP/convex solver machinery and decision science generally. This skill applies that machinery to the pricing objective (profit/revenue subject to elasticity and business constraints) and frames it. da-12-ab-testing-causal-inference - experiment design and causal theory in general. Here we cover only the price-specific experiment and its pitfalls. Own-price elasticity e = (%dQ)/(%dP); demand is elastic (|e|>1), unit-elastic (|e|=1), or inelastic (|e|<1). Revenue is maximized at |e|=1; profit-maximizing price sits where |e|>1 (you never price in the inelastic region with positive marginal cost). Cross-price elasticity e_AB = (%dQ_A)/(%dP_B): positive = substitutes, negative = complements. The full own/cross elasticity matrix drives portfolio and cannibalization analysis. Functional forms. Linear demand Q = a - bP gives elasticity that varies along the curve. Log-log / constant-elasticity ln Q = a + b ln P makes b the (constant) elasticity directly - the workhorse spec. Semi-log ln Q = a + bP gives a constant semi-elasticity. Add ln P_competitor, promo flags, seasonality, and ln income as controls. Arc vs point elasticity: arc (midpoint) elasticity for two discrete price points; point elasticity = derivative-based, read off a fitted curve. The Lerner / inverse-el

items.concept: Prism ML ternary Hadamard-rotated weights kernel on Metal
items.summary: Ternary Bonsai 2 27B weights are rotated blockwise by an orthogonal Hadamard transform (block 1024, fixed plus/minus 1 signs) before ternary assignment, and the runtime applies the matching transform to activations
items.text: Prism ML ternary Hadamard-rotated weights kernel on Metal Ternary Bonsai 2 27B weights are rotated blockwise by an orthogonal Hadamard transform (block 1024, fixed plus/minus 1 signs) before ternary assignment, and the runtime applies the matching transform to activations Ternary Bonsai 2 27B weights are rotated blockwise by an orthogonal Hadamard transform (block 1024, fixed plus/minus 1 signs) before ternary assignment, and the runtime applies the matching transform to activations The rotation is folded into the stored weights offline and costs no extra bits or weight traffic The packed model declares its rotation as metadata so a runtime must apply the matching transform or refuse to load Ordinary MLX loaders skip the activation transform and the inverse embedding lookup and return wrong output rather than an error The weight format is ternary g128 with one FP16 scale per 128 weights, about 1.71 bits per weight, 1.72 for the whole language model MLX stores the ternary levels as 2-bit codes with scale s and bias -s, which costs 2.25 bits per weight against 2.13 for PQ2_0 The MLX pack is 8.60 GB: 7.67 GB language model plus a 0.92 GB unquantized FP16 vision tower that needs no rotation 26.2M parameters (0.0976 percent of the language model) stay in higher precision Two GGUF packings exist: PTQ1_0 at 5.95 GB and PQ2_0 at 7.21 GB, and neither is uniformly faster across GPUs The model card's M5 Pro Metal row (llama.cpp fork, PQ2_0) is 28.1 tok/s TG128 and 387 tok/s PP512 with decode streaming about 204 GB/s of weights and drawing 27.5 W on the GPU rail Earlier pre-rotation Apple numbers: M5 Max 47.0 TG128 and 765 PP512, M4 Pro 18.0 TG128 and 125 PP512, all at 7.2 GB Stock llama.cpp cannot run the Bonsai 2 GGUF packs; the PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp fork is required Prism ML states 1.76 effective bits, 5.9 GB, 98.2 percent aggregate retention (83.9 against 85.4 for Qwen3.8 27B) and 46.8 tok/s on M5 Max The announcement is dated 2026-09-17 and says the first Ternary Bonsai 27B retained about 95 percent

items.text: Product Analytics The analytical discipline of measuring what users do inside a product, why, and whether it creates value — then feeding that back into product decisions. Distinct from generic web analytics (page-leve The analytical discipline of measuring what users do inside a product, why, and whether it creates value - then feeding that back into product decisions. Distinct from generic web analytics (page-level) and from instrumentation (the plumbing). Product analytics is event-centric, user-centric, and decision-oriented. This skill covers the analysis layer. Leave to adjacent skills: Cohort/retention curves, N-day/unbounded retention, retention math → da-34-cohort-retention-analytics SDK wiring, autocapture vs manual, identity stitching plumbing → da-3-2-7-web-app-analytics-instrumentation Experiment statistics, p-values, CUPED, sequential testing theory → da-12-ab-testing-causal-inference A product-analytics practice answers four recurring questions: (1) Are users reaching value (activation)? (2) Do they keep coming back and going deeper (engagement/adoption)? (3) Where do they drop off (funnels/paths)? (4) Is the whole thing growing toward a single meaningful outcome (North Star)? The analytical quality of every answer is capped by the quality of the event taxonomy underneath it - so taxonomy and governance come first, not last. A taxonomy is the hierarchical naming + classification scheme for events and properties so a platform can produce comparable insights. Design it deliberately before instrumenting. Object-Action naming: pick objects (Song), define actions (Played, Paused), agree a tense (past tense recommended), produce Song Played. Alternatively verb_noun snake_case (checkout_completed). Pick one and enforce it. (Amplitude event taxonomy, 2024; Avo naming conventions, 2025; Heap naming conventions, 2024) Parameterize, don't proliferate: one Add to Cart event with a campaign property - never Add to Cart Summer Sale as a separate event. (Amplitude data planning playbook, 2025) Tracking plan = the central contract: every event, its properties, data types, owner, trigger, and examples. The spreadsheet is the legacy form; dedicated tools (Avo) version-control it. (Amplitude tracking practices, 2024) Goldilocks granularity: too few events = blind spots; too many = noise and maintenance debt. Track events that map to decisions. items.concept: Profile writing
items.summary: A journalistic profile is not a biography, a hagiography, a resume in prose, or a Q&A. It is a narrative reported piece that uses reporting, scene, anecdote, and selected detail to reveal something tr
items.text: Profile writing A journalistic profile is not a biography, a hagiography, a resume in prose, or a Q&A. It is a narrative reported piece that uses reporting, scene, anecdote, and selected detail to reveal something tr A journalistic profile is not a biography, a hagiography, a resume in prose, or a Q&A. It is a narrative reported piece that uses reporting, scene, anecdote, and selected detail to reveal something true about a person. Three pieces of writing define the modern profile tradition: Gay Talese's "Frank Sinatra Has a Cold" (Esquire, 1966) for scene-based reporting; Janet Malcolm's "The Journalist and the Murderer" (The New Yorker, 1989) for the ethics of the form; and Walt Harrington's work in Intimate Journalism - the discipline of "deep, not wide." The biographer's question: what happened? The profile writer's question: what is this person actually like, and how do I show it? Lead (lede). A scene, anecdote, or paradox that introduces the subject in a specific moment. 1–3 paragraphs. Nut graph (nutgraf). The "why this story now" paragraph. 1 paragraph. Context / background. What the reader needs to know about the world the subject operates in. 2–4 paragraphs. Biography and present moment. Selected biographical material, interleaved with scenes from current reporting. Kicker. The closing scene or quote. Often a callback to the lede. In-scene lede. Open inside a moment. The subject is doing something. Anecdotal lede. Open with a story - a discrete past event that illustrates something about the subject. Paradoxical lede. Open with the contradiction at the heart of the subject. What never works: opening with the subject's birth, their resume, or their official title. The "nut graph" tells the reader what the piece is about and why they should keep reading. It answers: Who is this person? (One-sentence positioning.) Why now? (What just happened that makes them newsworthy.) What does this piece argue or reveal? The nut comes early enough that the reader doesn't bail, late enough that the lede has done its work. Walt Harrington's craft rule: render the important moments as scenes; summarize everything in between. Pick 3–5 scenes that do narrative work. Render those in close, sensory, present-tense detail. Everything else is summary prose. Scene → summary → scene → summary → scene → kicker. Quote sparingly. Direct quotes should do work no paraphrase could do - voice, idiosyncrasy, surprise, contradiction. Never start a paragraph with a long quote. Action

In v2.1.37 the hash suffix changed between calls in one session (.981 vs .fbe). Claude Code tool block: with a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, MCP tool search is disabled by default, so all MCP tool definitions load upfront (one report counts 259 tool definitions with plugins). Adding or removing a definition mid-session changes the prefix. OpenCode and similar harness env block: `<env>` with working directory, platform and date, then a `<files>` section that changes after the agent writes a file, capping the common prefix there. Date or time template at the top of a custom system prompt (Home Assistant case: qwen3:4b reply 5 s to under 2 s after moving or removing it). Live slot KV; the host-memory prompt cache (`--cache-ram`, default 8192 MiB, `--cache-idle-slots` default on, saves idle slots to it when a new task arrives); and manual disk files via `--slot-save-path` plus `POST /slots/{id}?action=save|restore`. The first two die ... llama.cpp offers three tiers. Live slot KV; the host-memory prompt cache (`--cache-ram`, default 8192 MiB, `--cache-idle-slots` default on, saves idle slots to it when a new task arrives); and manual disk files via `--slot-save-path` plus `POST /slots/{id}?action=save|restore`. The first two die with the process; sleep mode unloads "the model and its associated memory (including the KV cache)". The disk path restores KV and token list but, on SWA and hybrid/recurrent models, not the context checkpoints those models need to reuse any prefix. PR 26004 appends a tagged checkpoint payload (magic `SCKP`, version, count, per-checkpoint pos fields and blobs) after the llama state payload so one file carries both; old servers stop reading at the end of their payload and old files restore as before. llama-swap kills the upstream process on swap, so a persistence layer has to live outside it: a wrapper that restores after the health check and saves on SIGTERM, or lifecycle hooks (`afterHealthy` runs after the health check and before the model accepts requests; `beforeStop` runs before the kill; both proposed in PR 595). The wrapper must make `/health` return 503 until restore finishes, otherwise llama-swap routes the first request before the cache is back. oMLX keys cold-tier blocks by a layer-cache signature (layer count and cache-type mix), not just by prefix hash. Loading a model with a different signature makes the previous model's blocks incompatible: they are skipped, reported in one startup log line, and not evicted. Two of the three docsets contributed (the OpenAI export is empty). Automatic caching — Automatic caching is the simplest way to enable prompt caching. Instead of placing `cache_control` on individual content blocks, add a single `cache_control` field at the top level of your request body. Prompt caching — Prompt caching doesn't reduce the number of tokens in context, but it reduces what you pay for them on subsequent requests. If your tool definitions are stable, cache them once and reuse the cached prefix across thousands of requests. Cache miss reason types — `cache_miss_reason` is a discriminated union on `type`. The response reports the earliest divergence only, so fix it first; later ones may be hidden behind it. Caching — Some endpoints/models provide implicit caching of prompts. This keeps repeated prompt data in an in-memory cache in the provider's datacenter, so that the repeated part of the prompt does not need to be re-processed. Cache storage and sharing — Prompt caching uses [workspace](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workspaces)-level isolation. Caches are isolated per workspace, ensuring data separation between workspaces within the same organization. Advisor prompt caching — There are two independent caching layers. How it works — Set `max_tokens: 0` in your request. The API reads your prompt into the model and writes the cache at any `cache_control` breakpoint, then returns immediately without generating any output. How automatic caching works in multi-turn conversations — With automatic caching, the cache point moves forward automatically as conversations grow. Each new request caches everything up to the last cacheable block, and previous content is read from cache. items.text: Prompt processing versus decode on Apple GPUs and Neural Accelerators Per-chip llama.cpp numbers (Llama-2 7B, llama-bench -p 512 -n 128 -ngl 99, one shared table) let you separate the two regimes: pp tracks GPU core count and generation, tg tracks bandwidth and weight bytes. See Claims for the full M1-M5 Q4_0 matrix. Per-chip llama.cpp numbers (Llama-2 7B, llama-bench -p 512 -n 128 -ngl 99, one shared table) let you separate the two regimes: pp tracks GPU core count and generation, tg tracks bandwidth and weight bytes. See Claims for the full M1-M5 Q4_0 matrix. M1-M4 GPUs have no dedicated matrix units. Matmul runs on the shared FP32 ALU pipeline (simdgroup_matrix improves utilisation only). The M5 GPU adds a per-core Neural Accelerator reached through Metal 4 TensorOps / Metal Performance Primitives. That is why pp jumps about 3.3-3.8x between M4 and M5 at equal core count while tg moves only with bandwidth. Effective prefill compute, derived as pp512 x 13.5 GFLOP per token (6.74 B params x 2): M4 Max 40-core about 12 TFLOPS, M5 Max 40-core about 43 TFLOPS, M5 Ultra 80-core about 67 TFLOPS. A third-party pre-launch spec estimate gives 18.4 TFLOPS FP32 (M4 Max) and about 70 TFLOPS FP16 (M5 Max) peak, so M5 Max reaches roughly 60% of that estimate in llama.cpp. Per-GPU-core pp512 (Q4_0): M1 base 8-core 14.7; M1 Max 32-core 16.6; M2 Ultra 76-core 16.3; M3 Max 40-core 19.0; M3 Ultra 80-core 18.4; M4 base 22.1; M4 Max 40-core 22.1; M5 base 72.3; M5 Pro 20-core 81.0; M5 Max 40-core 80.5; M5 Ultra 80-core 61.8. A generation of pre-M5 chips changes per-core pp by under 35%; the M5 step is about 3.6x. The M5 Ultra loses about 23% per core versus M5 Max (two-die scaling shortfall). Quant independence is visible inside every row: Q4_0, Q8_0 and F16 pp512 differ by under 8% on M1-M5 (M5 Max 3347/3220/3190), while tg moves about 3x. Prefill does not get faster by quantizing harder; decode does. Batch tuning: `-b` is the logical batch (README default 2048), `-ub` the physical micro-batch (README default 512). Prompt tokens are fed to the GPU in ub-sized slices, so ub is the knob that sets matmul tile size; raising only `-b` does nothing while `-ub` stays at 512. MLX's equivalent is `--prefill-step-size` (default 2048). Cache reuse removes prefill instead of speeding it. llama-server defaults: `--cache-prompt` on (only the unseen suffix of an identical prefix is evaluated), `--cache-reuse` 0 (KV shifting off), `--cache-ram` 8192 MiB, `--ctx-checkpoints` 32 per slot spac

items.text: Prompt-token counting parity across runtimes llama-server OpenAI-style responses carry a `usage` object with `prompt_tokens` and `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, and a separate `timings` object with `cache_n` (prompt tokens reused from cache) and `prompt_n` (prompt tokens being processed). llama-server OpenAI-style responses carry a `usage` object with `prompt_tokens` and `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, and a separate `timings` object with `cache_n` (prompt tokens reused from cache) and `prompt_n` (prompt tokens being processed). In llama-server, `prompt_n` is the processed count only: the README's example has cache_n 236 and prompt_n 1, with prompt_per_second 32.3 for one token in 30.958 ms. The README states total context equals prompt_n + cache_n + predicted_n. The llama-server native `/completion` response uses different names: `tokens_evaluated` is "number of tokens evaluated in total from the prompt" and `tokens_cached` is the reused part, so `tokens_evaluated` includes cached tokens while `timings.prompt_n` excludes them. mlx_lm.server sets `usage.prompt_tokens` to the full prompt length, `len(ctx.prompt)`, and `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` to the cache-hit count, so its prompt_tokens includes cached tokens. mlx_lm.server emits a streamed usage chunk only when the request sets `stream_options.include_usage`; without it a streaming client sees no token counts. Ollama's native API defines `prompt_eval_count` as the number of tokens in the prompt, `prompt_eval_cached_count` as prompt tokens read from the cache, and `prompt_eval_duration` as time evaluating uncached prompt tokens. Rate formula that follows: the prefill rate is (total prompt tokens - cached tokens) divided by prefill time. For Ollama, `prompt_eval_count / prompt_eval_duration` overstates the rate whenever the cache hits, because the numerator includes cached tokens and the denominator does not. For mlx-lm, `prompt_tokens` has the same property. For llama-server, `timings.prompt_per_second` is already per processed token. The three servers therefore disagree on what a bare "prompt tokens" number means: processed-only (llama-server `timings.prompt_n`), total (llama-server `usage.prompt_tokens` and `tokens_evaluated`, mlx-lm `prompt_tokens`, Ollama `prompt_eval_count`). A parity check must read the cached count from each server too. llama-server `/tokenize` does not add BOS by default (`add_special` false) and parses special tokens by default (`parse_special` true

items.text: Proposal and Grant Writing Grant proposals are a constrained writing genre. Reviewers read against a rubric, in a hurry, under fatigue. A proposal that "reads well" but ignores the funder's stated criteria scores low. A proposa Grant proposals are a constrained writing genre. Reviewers read against a rubric, in a hurry, under fatigue. A proposal that "reads well" but ignores the funder's stated criteria scores low. A proposal that follows the rubric mechanically but tells a coherent change story scores high. Three reviewer-tested moves: Open in the funder's frame. Quote the funding opportunity's priority area in the first two sentences. Quantify the problem at the right scope. National statistics are weak without local data; local data is weak without national context. End on the gap. Close with the specific knowledge, service, or capacity gap your project will fill. "We need money" is a felt need. Demonstrated need is evidence - a quantified disparity, an unmet target, a documented service desert. Pull from peer-reviewed literature, government data (Census, BLS, CDC, HRSA), and community needs assessments. Avoid undated statistics; reviewers flag anything older than 5 years. A theory of change is the narrative map of how change happens: if we do X (activities), given Y (assumptions), then Z (outcomes), because of M (mechanism). Reviewers check whether the aims, methods, and evaluation plan trace back to the theory of change. Critical distinction: outputs are not outcomes. "Conducted 100 workshops" is an output. "Participants reduced X behavior by Y%" is an outcome. Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Weak: "Improve youth literacy." SMART: "By June 2027, increase the proportion of 4th-grade students at our three partner schools reading at grade level from 42% to 60%, as measured by the state ELA assessment." One page. Four paragraphs: Hook + significance. Open with the broad problem. Narrow to the specific gap. Central hypothesis + rationale. State your hypothesis. Explain why it is plausible. Establish that you are the right team. Specific Aims. 2-4 aims. Each aim is independent. Use confident verbs: "We will determine," not "We hope to." Payoff. State the expected outcomes and their impact on the field. Each cost category (personnel, fringe, travel, equipment, supplies, contractual, indirect) gets a paragraph answering: what, why, how calculated, why this rate. Reviewer red flags: round numbers without basis, salaries above the federa

Distinct from fundraising-and-donor-psychology (which covers what to DO given they might give) and from psychology-of-charitable-giving being about the underlying motives. Core motives: Andreoni's warm-glow / impure-altruism model (people give partly for the utility of giving itself, not only for the outcome). The identifiable victim effect and singularity: Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic's work - one identifiable child gets more donation than statistics on many. Compassion fade / psychic numbing / pseudoinefficacy - help drops as the number of victims rises, because "helping any one of them feels like a drop in the bucket." The martyrdom effect (Olivola and Shafir - willingness to give rises when the pledge requires personal suffering). items.text: Psychology of Human-AI Interaction (Trust & Appropriate Reliance) > Standalone skill authored via the /dr deep-research workflow. Full SKILL.md > Standalone skill authored via the /dr deep-research workflow. Full SKILL.md > with TRIGGER/SKIP frontmatter and three references/ files is installed at > ~/.claude/skills/human-ai-interaction-psychology/. How humans decide whether to follow, override, or ignore an AI system, and how to design and coach for the right amount of reliance. This is human-factors and decision psychology applied to trust in machines, not interpersonal trust. The central problem is not "more trust" or "less trust" but calibrated trust: reliance that tracks the system's actual reliability in the specific task at hand. A TAM, customer, or team is over-relying (rubber-stamping AI output) or under-relying (ignoring a tool that outperforms them). An AI feature hits adoption resistance rooted in distrust, or dangerous over-adoption where users stop checking. You are designing an AI-assisted workflow (copilot, recommender, triage assistant, autoremediation gate) and must decide what to surface (confidence, explanations, friction) to get appropriate reliance. A confidently wrong AI answer was believed and you need the vocabulary to diagnose why. You are coaching a customer on a human-in-the-loop override policy. Trust is an attitude; reliance is a behavior; appropriate reliance is the goal. They are routinely conflated and must be kept separate. Optimizing for "trust" (a survey number) is the wrong target - optimize for reliance that matches reliability: follow the AI when it is right, override it when it is wrong. Most failures in AI-assisted decisions are miscalibration, not a global trust deficit. Trust = "the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual's goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability." Reliance = the observable behavior that follows. Calibration = correspondence between trust and the system's true capability. Over-trust → over-reliance / misuse. Defers when it shouldn't. Under-trust → under-reliance / disuse. Rejects help that would have worked. The trust-calibration curve plots trust against true reliability; the diagonal is perfect calibration. Resolution = fine-grained trust that discriminates which cases the system handles well from those it doesn't (good calibration on average can still have poor resolution).
