items.summary: Answer four questions before touching a slide tool:
items.text: Public Speaking and Presentations Answer four questions before touching a slide tool: Answer four questions before touching a slide tool: Who is in the room? Job function, seniority, and domain expertise. What do they already believe? Start from their current position. What one action do you want them to take? Name the action. What is the one thing they must remember? Write that sentence before slide 1. Presentation slides (Reynolds / "Presentation Zen" model) exist to support a live speaker. The speaker carries the argument; the slide carries visual reinforcement. One idea per slide. Minimal text. Large images or diagrams. Slide-docs (Tufte-influenced) are standalone documents formatted as slide-shaped pages. They contain complete sentences, dense supporting data, footnotes. They can be emailed and read without a presenter. The core failure mode: the slidument - bullet-heavy slides that are too dense to look good on screen and too sparse to be useful to a reader. 10 slides - humans can't absorb more than ten concepts in a single sitting 20 minutes - even if you have a full hour, present in 20 minutes 30-point minimum font - if you cannot fit your message in 30pt type, you have too many words The central insight: every great speech moves back and forth between "what is" and "what could be." The contrast pattern: Establish the current reality (what is) Describe the future possibility (what could be) Repeat this oscillation; each cycle raises the stakes End with the "new bliss" - the world after the audience acts The STAR moment (Something They'll Always Remember): one designed moment of high contrast, surprise, or visceral demonstration. Act 1 - Setup (10–15% of total time): Establish stakes; define the problem; signal what the audience will be able to do differently by the end. Act 2 - Exploration (70–75%): Develop the argument. Front-load complex material; place a re-energizing moment two-thirds of the way through. Act 3 - Resolution (10–15%): Do not introduce new material. Synthesize, do not summarize. Every slide title is a complete, standalone sentence stating the takeaway, not a topic label. Bad title: "Market Analysis" Good title: "The North American market is growing 12% YoY and outpacing EMEA in every segment." A reader who reads only slide titles should follow the full argument. Startling fact or statistic: drop a number the audience does not expect Story: open with a specific scene - one person, one moment, sensory detail Contrarian claim: state

items.text: Python in the Browser & WebAssembly (Pyodide, PyScript, WASI/CPython) "Python in the browser" means compiling a Python interpreter to WebAssembly (WASM) so it runs inside the browser's WASM VM (or a server-side WASM runtime) instead of a native OS process. There is no n "Python in the browser" means compiling a Python interpreter to WebAssembly (WASM) so it runs inside the browser's WASM VM (or a server-side WASM runtime) instead of a native OS process. There is no native Python in a browser; everything routes through one of two WASM targets of CPython: wasm32-emscripten - CPython compiled with Emscripten, which emulates a POSIX-ish environment (a virtual filesystem, a JS-backed libc) on top of the browser/JS host. This is the target Pyodide ships, and is the one that runs in a browser tab or in Node.js. CPython tier-3 since 3.14 (restored Oct 2024). wasm32-wasi - CPython compiled against the WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) ABI, a capability-based syscall layer. Runs in standalone WASM runtimes (wasmtime, Wasmer, WasmEdge) for server-side/edge/sandboxed/plugin use, not the browser DOM. CPython tier 2 since 3.13.0 (the first final release to ship it). A third lever is the interpreter choice: full Pyodide (CPython) - large but complete, with NumPy/SciPy/pandas - versus MicroPython - tiny (~300 KB) and near-instant but a reduced language/stdlib. PyScript lets you pick per-page. The defining reality of all WASM Python: single-threaded, sandboxed, no OS. No real threads, no raw sockets, no blocking stdin, and a multi-megabyte cold-start download for full CPython. Design around these from the start. Both targets cross-compile CPython. Emscripten produces a .wasm + a JS loader (pyodide.js) plus a packaged stdlib; WASI produces a python.wasm you feed to a runtime. WASM is single-threaded by default; pthreads need SharedArrayBuffer + cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers) and are still not generally usable for CPython's threading model. The PEP 11 platform tiers govern support: WASI is tier 2 (3.13+, PEP 816 pins WASI + WASI-SDK versions per release), Emscripten is tier 3 (3.14+, PEP 776 defines it). Everything else (Pyodide FFI, packaging) layers on top of this. Pyodide is a port of CPython to Emscripten/WASM providing three things: (a) the CPython interpreter compiled with Emscripten + a few patches; (b) a JS⟺Python foreign function interface (FFI); (c) a catalog of third-party packages (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, etc.) precompiled to WASM. Not a standalone skill. > Sibling topics in this family are reference files under the hubs (programming-languages, software-engineering-patterns) - not standalone skills. > Cross-refs: references/python-patterns.md (PEP 695 type-hint syntax, generics - this file covers the checkers), references/pydantic-v2.md (runtime validation + the pydantic.mypy plugin), references/typescript-expert.md (the TS analog of gradual static typing). Python type checkers are external static-analysis tools, not part of the interpreter. The CPython runtime ignores annotations (beyond storing them in __annotations__); a separate tool reads the same annotations a human reads and proves type consistency before the code runs. As of mid-2026 the landscape is a two-generation split: established Python-implemented checkers (mypy, Pyright) and new Rust-implemented checkers (Astral ty, Meta Pyrefly) that are 10-80x faster. Pyrefly reached stable 1.0.0 (May 2026); ty is still beta (0.x). PEP 483 + PEP 484 (2015) define gradual typing: hints are optional, coexist with dynamic typing, added incrementally. Goal is NOT runtime enforcement - annotations exist for external tools. Any is consistent with every type (assignable to/from anything) - the seam between static and dynamic. Unannotated code is effectively Any. The gradual guarantee: removing an annotation should never add new errors (adding annotations only narrows errors). ty and Pyright honor it strictly; mypy and Pyrefly infer aggressively and can violate it. PEP 561: inline-typed packages ship a py.typed marker; stub-only packages are types-<pkg> (types-requests) or <pkg>-stubs; stub files are .pyi; resolution order stubs → inline → typeshed (the community stub repo). typing-spec conformance suite is the shared benchmark. Pyrefly 1.0.0 reports >90% (above ty and mypy); Pyright tracks the spec closely. Declared types (you annotated) vs inferred types (deduced) - checkers agree on declared, disagree on inference (§3). CLI: mypy <path>, pyright <path>, ty check <path>, pyrefly check <path>. For my_list = []; my_list.append(1): mypy, Pyrefly infer list[int] from usage → later append("foo") is an error. items.summary: Python application security splits into two layers that share one toolchain:
items.text: Python Supply-Chain & Application Security Python application security splits into two layers that share one toolchain: Python application security splits into two layers that share one toolchain: Application security (SAST) - find vulnerabilities in your own code (bandit). Supply-chain security - defend the dependencies and the path your artifacts travel: know what you ship (SBOM), know if it is vulnerable (pip-audit), prove where it came from (sigstore/PEP 740 attestations), and guarantee you install exactly what you locked (hash pinning). The canonical layered ("defense in depth") posture for a 2026 Python project: pin + hash dependencies → audit them in CI (pip-audit) → SAST-scan your code (bandit) → generate an SBOM → publish with Trusted Publishing + attestations. Each layer closes a gap the others cannot; none is sufficient alone (hash pinning, for example, will faithfully pin a package that was already malicious on day one). The four foundational PyPA/PyCQA tools - pip-audit, bandit, pip hash mode, and the PEP 740 attestation chain - are free, open source, and require no account or API key for the scanning paths. What it is: the official PyPA tool that audits Python environments, requirements files, and dependency trees for packages with known vulnerabilities (SCA - software composition analysis). Maintained by the Python Packaging Authority. Vulnerability sources: queries the PyPA Advisory Database and the OSV database. Select via --vulnerability-service {osv,pypi} (osv is default); --osv-url points at a custom OSV mirror. Input modes: audit the live environment (pip-audit), a requirements file (pip-audit -r requirements.txt), or a PEP 751 lockfile (pylock.toml, supported in recent releases). For fully pinned input, skip resolution with --no-deps (pinned, no hashes) or --require-hashes (pinned + hashed). Auto-fix: --fix upgrades vulnerable pins in place to the first non-vulnerable version; --dry-run previews. Output / SBOM: -f {columns,json,cyclonedx-json,cyclonedx-xml,markdown} - it can itself emit a CycloneDX SBOM with vulnerabilities linked to affected components via the affects field. Why: a machine-readable inventory of every component (incl. transitive) so downstream consumers and scanners can answer "am I affected by CVE-X?" Increasingly required by regulation (US EO 14028, EU Cyber Resilience Act). CycloneDX - security-first; built for vulnerability identification and outdated-dependency analysis. items.text: Q4_K_M dequantization cost vs MLX affine g64 on dense decode Q4_K Metal mat-vec: per 256-weight super-block a simdgroup loads 4 groups of activations (32 weights each) pre-summed for the minimum correction; per row it unpacks the 12 scale bytes with three masks (0x3f3f, 0x0f0f, 0xc0c0) into 8 scale and min values, accumulates nibble products without shifti... Q4_K Metal mat-vec: per 256-weight super-block a simdgroup loads 4 groups of activations (32 weights each) pre-summed for the minimum correction; per row it unpacks the 12 scale bytes with three masks (0x3f3f, 0x0f0f, 0xc0c0) into 8 scale and min values, accumulates nibble products without shifting (corrected by 1/256 and 1/16 factors), then returns dh[0]*(sum scale-weighted accumulators) - dh[1]*(sum sumy*min). MLX affine qdot: activations are pre-scaled by 1/16, 1/256, 1/4096 so masked nibbles can be multiplied directly; per group of 64 weights the result is scale * accum + sum(x) * bias with one 16-bit scale and one 16-bit bias read from memory; no packed-scale decode. Each threadgroup has 2 simdgroups of 4 output rows (8 rows). Q4_0 and IQ4_NL for context: Q4_0 is arithmetic-only with one fp16 scale per 32 weights; IQ4_NL adds a threadgroup-memory table. Mixed file effect: Q4_K_M sends half of attn_v and ffn_down to Q6_K, a second kernel with its own unpack, so Q4_K_M decode is a blend of two kernels; MLX uniform 4-bit uses one kernel for every linear layer. 2023-2024: K-quants (ikawrakow) become the llama.cpp default file types. 2025-2026: MLX gains mixed recipes (mixed_4_6) and third-party mixed quants that copy Q4_K_M's rule, which brings MLX's one-kernel advantage partly back to two kernels. Group size confound: Q4_K sub-blocks are 32 weights, MLX default is 64; at equal 4.5 bpw Q4_K spends its metadata bits on finer groups with 6-bit scales and mins, MLX on coarser groups with 16-bit scale and bias. File-size confound: Q4_K_M is about 4.85-4.89 bpw average, so it moves about 8% more bytes per token than uniform MLX 4-bit g64 (4.5 bpw) before any arithmetic difference. Chip confound: ALU limits matter more on high-bandwidth Ultra/Max parts where decode approaches a bandwidth ceiling; 2024 data show a table-lookup kernel losing 17.5% of Q4_0 decode on an M2 Max at equal bytes. Rattner-style inference (existing dossier): Q8_0 decode only 7% slower than Q4_K_M at 76% more bytes, so Q4_K_M unpacking costs a lot. items.concept: Q6_K Metal mat-vec cost inside Q4_K_M files
items.summary: Bytes: a Q6_K block is 128 B of low nibbles (ql), 64 B of high 2-bit pairs (qh), 16 B of scales and 2 B of d, 210 B per 256 weights or 6.5625 bpw, against 144 B and 4.5 bpw for Q4_K, so a Q6_K tensor moves 1.458 times the bytes of the same tensor in Q4_K.
items.text: Q6_K Metal mat-vec cost inside Q4_K_M files Bytes: a Q6_K block is 128 B of low nibbles (ql), 64 B of high 2-bit pairs (qh), 16 B of scales and 2 B of d, 210 B per 256 weights or 6.5625 bpw, against 144 B and 4.5 bpw for Q4_K, so a Q6_K tensor moves 1.458 times the bytes of the same tensor in Q4_K. Bytes: a Q6_K block is 128 B of low nibbles (ql), 64 B of high 2-bit pairs (qh), 16 B of scales and 2 B of d, 210 B per 256 weights or 6.5625 bpw, against 144 B and 4.5 bpw for Q4_K, so a Q6_K tensor moves 1.458 times the bytes of the same tensor in Q4_K. Reconstruction work: the Q6_K kernel builds each weight from a low nibble and two high bits (mask-shift-or per weight), subtracts 32 as an integer, multiplies by the float activation, and applies one int8 sub-block scale per 16 weights and the fp16 d once per super-block. It has no per-row minimum term and does not pre-sum activations, unlike Q4_K. Memory access style: the Q6_K kernel reads ql, qh and scales through single-byte pointers (uint8_t, int8_t) while the Q4_K kernel reads packed data and scales through uint16_t pointers. Launch shape: both kernels use two output rows per simdgroup and two simdgroups per threadgroup (N_R0 2, N_SG 2), so a Q6_K threadgroup produces the same 4 rows as a Q4_K one but over 1.46 times the bytes; Q5_K is the odd one at N_R0 1. Lane mapping: two lanes (tiisg % 2) split a super-block between them and stride by 2 over blocks; each lane keeps 16 activations in registers and, for each of the nr0 rows, rebuilds 16 weights per block. MoE path: expert matmuls use kernel_mul_mv_id_q6_K_f32, a thin wrapper that calls the same kernel_mul_mv_q6_K_f32_impl with N_R0_Q6_K, so a Q6_K routed expert costs per selected expert what a dense Q6_K matrix of that shape costs. Share of a MoE Q4_K_M file that is Q6_K: for MoE models (n_expert > 1) the "more bits" test is by layer, and it is true for the first eighth, the last eighth and every third layer between, about half the layers. It applies to every ffn_down-category tensor, so in those layers the merged `ffn_down_exps` and the shared `ffn_down_shexp` are Q6_K, together with attn_v-like tensors and output.weight. Order of magnitude for that share: if the down projection holds about one third of expert parameters, about half the layers at Q6_K add roughly (6.5625 - 4.5) x 1/3 x 1/2, about 0.34 bits per expert weight, or about 7% more expert bytes than an all-Q4_K file before dilution by non-expert tensors. items.concept: Quantile Estimation (DDSketch)
items.summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for Quantile Estimation (DDSketch); source-anchored research pack.
items.text: Quantile Estimation (DDSketch) Depth-first rabbithole dossier for Quantile Estimation (DDSketch); source-anchored research pack. [low] The bucket index for DDSketch is calculated as ceil(ln(value) / ln(gamma)), where gamma is defined as (1 + alpha) / (1 - alpha) and alpha represents the desired relative accuracy. Sources: https://infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency [low] DDSketch is capable of handling endpoints that process over 10M points per second, providing accurate latency quantiles for these high-throughput scenarios. Sources: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1908.10693 [low] The MongoDB $percentile accumulator requires quantile elements in p to be numeric values in the range 0.0 to 1.0 inclusive, and because its t-digest approximation uses pseudorandomness, computed percentile values on the same dataset might differ on each run. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/percentile.md [high] DDSketch is the first fully-mergeable, relative-error quantile sketching algorithm with formal guarantees, providing O(1) constant-memory quantile estimation with relative-error guarantees of plus or minus one percent. Sources: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1908.10693, https://infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency [high] DDSketch has a critical-path overhead of approximately thirty-five nanoseconds per request, making it suitable for real-time per-host latency tracking, and can accurately maintain upper half order statistics of over a million samples with a sketch size of 273 with probability greater than 0.99991. Sources: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1908.10693, https://infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency [low] Adding a hundred million values to an empty DDSketch takes less than 5 seconds on a 3.1GHz MacBook Pro, while merging two DDSketches containing up to fifty million values each takes around 10 microseconds or less. Sources: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1908.10693 [low] A tumbling window fix uses two DDSketches rotating at a fixed interval, such as thirty seconds, to manage data aging. items.concept: Query Efficiency as a Cost Lever
items.summary: Inefficient queries (collection scans, high scanned-to-returned ratios) burn CPU, disk I/O and WiredTiger cache, which can push a team toward a larger Atlas cluster tier; Atlas surfaces the signal through Query Targeting alerts (default 1000:1, ideal near 1), the Query Profiler and Performance Advisor index suggestions ranked by Impact, covered queries skip document reads, and every unused or redundant index adds write cost, storage and cache pressure. Drawn from 7 sources (MongoDB Atlas and manual pages, a community forum thread, Netdata and OneUptime guides, a third-party blog), covering definitions, mechanisms, parameters, how-to, measures and problems; no source states a measured tier reduction from tuning, and the evidence on the write penalty of many indexes is thin and disputed.

Drawn from 7 sources (MongoDB Atlas and manual pages, a community forum thread, Netdata and OneUptime guides, a third-party blog), covering definitions, mechanisms, parameters, how-to, measures and problems; no source states a measured tier reduction from tuning, and the evidence on the write penalty of many indexes is thin and disputed. A covered query is answered entirely from an index with no document reads. It requires all queried and returned fields in the index, _id excluded in the projection unless indexed, no null comparisons, and no array-field coverage on multikey indexes. On sharded collections the index must contain the shard key. MongoDB attributes the speed to index keys being smaller than documents and typically in RAM. Overlapping indexes are redundant: Performance Advisor de-duplicates suggestions so only { a: 1, b: 1 } is suggested when { a: 1 } is its prefix. The Query Profiler contains several metrics you can use to pinpoint specific inefficient queries. You can visualize up to the past 24 hours of query operations. The Query Profiler can show the Examined : Returned Ratio (index keys examined to documents returned) of logged queries, which might help you identify the queries that triggered a Query Targeting: Scanned / Returned alert. The chart shows the number of index keys examined to fulfill a query relative to the actual number of returned documents. The query targeting alert typically occurs when there is no index to support a query or queries or when an existing index only partially supports a query or queries. $indexStats counters reset on mongod restart and internal operations can inflate them. Wait a full workload cycle (24h+ of normal load) before treating zero usage as removable, run it per shard primary on sharded clusters (not on mongos), and exclude _id and unique indexes. items.text: Query planner, explain plans and covered queries How a database decides to use an index: explain plans, index scans versus collection/table scans, covered queries, selectivity and cardinality, the ESR guideline for compound-index key order, hints and in-memory sorts. Child pack of Indexing. Selectivity is a query property that describes the ratio of documents matching the query versus the total number of documents in a collection. The selectivity of an index describes how many documents a unique index key matches. A query or index has high selectivity when proportionally few documents match a query or a given index key. Index prefixes are the beginning subsets of indexed fields. Compound indexes support queries on all fields included in the index prefix. The order of the indexed fields impacts the effectiveness of a compound index. Compound indexes contain references to documents according to the order of the fields in the index. To create efficient compound indexes, follow the [ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) guideline.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline/#std-label-esr-indexing-guideline) The [`dropIndexes`](https://www.mongodb.com#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.dropIndexes) operation only kills queries that are using the index being dropped. This may include queries considering the index as part of [query planning.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-plans/#std-label-query-plans-query-optimization) An index covers a query when the index contains all of the fields scanned by the query. A covered query scans the index and not the collection, which improves query performance. The best way to filter in Convex is to use indexes. Indexes build a special internal structure in your database to speed up lookups. Each index that the Performance Advisor suggests contains the following metrics. items.text:
Qwen 3.8 chat-template fixes and reasoning-level mapping Effort handling (template lines 46-57): inside `enable_thinking is undefined or true`, effort resolves to `reasoning_effort|default('xhigh')`. Accepted values are `xhigh`, `medium`, `low`. Any other value calls `raise_exception('Unexpected reasoning effort ... Supported types are xhigh (default),... Effort handling (template lines 46-57): inside `enable_thinking is undefined or true`, effort resolves to `reasoning_effort|default('xhigh')`. Accepted values are `xhigh`, `medium`, `low`. Any other value calls `raise_exception('Unexpected reasoning effort ... Supported types are xhigh (default), medium, and low.')`. `xhigh` and `low` set a one-sentence instruction; `medium` sets none. Where the instruction goes: it is placed at the very start of the system turn, before the `# Tools` block and before the user's system text. With no tools and no system message, a non-empty instruction still creates a system turn. Because the default is `xhigh`, every thinking request with no kwarg carries an extra system turn that the Qwen3.6 template never produced. Validation only runs when thinking is enabled. With `enable_thinking=false` an unsupported effort value is never checked and the instruction is empty. Cache consequence (inferred from the line order above): changing effort between requests changes bytes at offset 0 of the prompt, so the whole prefix is re-prefilled. `medium` leaves the prompt byte-identical to a template with no effort support. Preserve default (line 117): the condition `preserve_thinking is undefined or preserve_thinking is true or loop.index0 > ns.last_query_index` keeps every historical `<think>` block unless a caller passes `preserve_thinking=false`. In Qwen3.6 the condition required `preserve_thinking is defined and is true`. Dropped extraction: Qwen3.6 had a branch that, when `reasoning_content` was missing and the content held `</think>`, split reasoning out of the content. Qwen3.8 removes it. A client that sends reasoning inline in `content` therefore gets an empty `<think>

</think>

` block rendered ahead of the inline text. Empty system: Qwen3.8 emits a system turn for the user's system text only if the text is non-empty after trim; Qwen3.6 emitted `<|im_start|>system
<|im_end|>` for an empty one. Empty arguments: `tool_call.arguments != ''` is now required before iterating `arguments|items`, which stops the crash on an empty-string argument. llama-server mapping (server-common

Fixed re-wrap on render: a historical assistant turn is written as `<|im_start|>assistant
<think>
` + trimmed reasoning + `
</think>

` + trimmed content. The generation prompt is `<|im_start|>assistant
<think>
`. A model that emitted extra blank lines or trailing spaces around the think block is therefore rewritten to the canonical form on the next request. Tool-call wrapper: `

<tool_call>
<function=NAME>
` when the turn has text, bare `<tool_call>
<function=NAME>
` when it has none, `
<tool_call>
...` for later calls in the same turn; each parameter is `<parameter=KEY>
` + value + `

</tool_call>`. Value serialisation: a string argument is written verbatim; any other value is written as `args_value | tojson | safe`. Number formatting, nested-object key order and JSON spacing in the re-render come from the template runtime's `tojson`, not from the model's raw text. Tool results: consecutive `tool` messages are merged into one `user` turn of `<tool_response>` blocks; the body is trimmed. Maintainer position (QwenLM/Qwen3.8 #131, 2026-04-14): the normalisation difference "lacks a perfect solution" because token-level generation and message-level templating are separate; the suggested experiment is to remove the normalisation in the chat template. Third-party claims: froggeric states it applies "strict single newline normalization at autoregressive boundaries" and rewrites `content | replace(...)` as `content.split(...) | join('')` because the C++ minja engine silently drops the whole text if the replaced string sits at index 0. Neither claim is shown with a measured token diff. 2026-04-09/10: #131 reporter lists two template fixes (guard empty historical think; optionally drop historical think entirely) and a reproduction on oMLX plus OpenCode and Pi, and says llama.cpp-style backends show the same drift.

items.text: Qwen3.6 preserve_thinking chat-template flag and prompt-cache reuse Default template behaviour: reasoning is dropped from history except in the current tool-use turn. Between request N and N+1 the rendered prompt for turn N's assistant message therefore loses its `<think>...</think>` text. The tokens the server cached (prompt plus generated reasoning) no longer m... Default template behaviour: reasoning is dropped from history except in the current tool-use turn. Between request N and N+1 the rendered prompt for turn N's assistant message therefore loses its `<think>...</think>` text. The tokens the server cached (prompt plus generated reasoning) no longer match the next prompt, so the shared prefix ends where the first dropped think block began. Qwen's own explanation of the cache problem (maintainer reply on QwenLM/Qwen3.8 #131): stripping past thinking changes the prefix; a planned option to preserve thinking, even empty blocks in non-thinking mode, fixes cause 1; cause 2 is whitespace normalisation differences of thinking and tool-call blocks between model output and template re-render, which has no perfect fix because token-level generation and message-level templating are separate. On hybrid models (Qwen3.5/3.6 delta-net layers) a mismatch is far costlier than on pure attention, because the recurrent state cannot be trimmed back to the divergence point; llama.cpp must restore a checkpoint at or before it or reprocess from zero. That is why the flag matters more here than for dense Qwen3. Second, template-level cache bug: the stock template emits an empty `<think>\n\n</think>` wrapper on past assistant turns that had no reasoning (tool-call-only turns). Qwen3.8 #131 proposes guarding with `and reasoning_content`. LM Studio's froggeric MLX card calls this "empty preserve_thinking spam" and ships a rewritten template that emits think blocks only when reasoning is non-empty. Client side contract: the server must receive reasoning back. llama-server returns it as `reasoning_content`; the client must echo it on the assistant message. If the client drops it, preserve_thinking has nothing to render. pi's `qwen-chat-template` thinkingFormat set only `enable_thinking`; the reported fix was to also send `preserve_thinking: true`. llama.cpp naming split: the server-side generic flag `--reasoning-preserve` / `--no-reasoning-preserve` (env `LLAMA_ARG_REASONING_PRESERVE`) sets the template kwarg `preserve_reasoning`, not `preserve_thinking`. arg.cpp (master) inject

(medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Current behaviour, verified in the code at v0.25.0 (2026-09-25, the latest release on 2026-10-14): RamaLama has no implicit default transport. Resolution order for a model name is: an explicit prefix (ollama://, huggingface://, hf://, hf.co/, modelscope://, ms://, oci://, docker://, rlcr://, http(s)://, file:); then a name containing a slash goes to Hugging Face when no transport is configured; then a transport set by RAMALAMA_TRANSPORT, --transport or the transport key in ramalama.conf; otherwise a KeyError reads "'<model>' is not a known shortname and no transport was specified. Use a shortname from shortnames.conf, or specify a transport explicitly". The Ollama transport still works when you ask for it: ollama://, --transport ollama, or RAMALAMA_TRANSPORT=ollama. The dataclass default transport = "ollama" in config.py does not act as an implicit default: New() passes a configured transport to TransportFactory only when config.is_set("transport") is true, meaning the value was set explicitly in a config file, the environment or the command line, and TransportFactory's own transport parameter defaults to None. [low] In Weaviate, keyword search is based on the BM25F scoring algorithm and is called BM25 search. Sources: https://weaviate.io/blog/hybrid-search-fusion-algorithms [low] Pipeline names must not start with a `$`, contain the ASCII null character `\0`, or contain a `.`. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/scoreFusion.md [low] If an input pipeline does not inherently return a score, such as when using `$geoNear` which returns distance, it must include an explicit `$score` stage. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/scoreFusion.md [low] In a hybrid query, `top` determines the number of results in the response, with the top 50 highest ranked matches returned by default. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-ranking [low] For `$rankFusion`, the ticket says the `StageConstraints` on DocumentSourceRankFusion are likely unreachable code because constraints() is only called after desugaring. It does not state this as a general rule for all pipeline processing. Sources: https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-101701 [low] When you upgrade from MongoDB 8.0, you might have to pause executing `$rankFusion` queries. The statement that no further action is required for Free (M0) and Flex clusters belongs to the Automated Embedding auto-scaling prerequisites, not to the upgrade note. (verified as of 2026-10-15) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/hybrid-search/hybrid-search-overview.md [low] Using `$nativeVectorSearch` in a `$scoreFusion` input pipeline is rejected with error code 12108713, and these rejections occur at parse/LP time without referencing shard names. Since commit 1394f16 a budgeted (shutdown) save first measures a 16 MiB fsynced write, halves the result to cover serialization overhead, and bounds the first prediction to 150-600 MB/s; later entries use the throughput observed on real writes. A hybrid entry's recurrent-state checkpoints are written to an `entry_K_ckpt.safetensors` sidecar; on load the sidecar is re-attached only if every array matches its layer's state slot in shape and dtype, every position lies inside the entry, and every recurrent layer is covered. items.text: Read Concern Levels MongoDB replication provides redundancy and high availability through replica sets -- groups of mongod processes that maintain the same data set. A replica set contains one primary member that receive MongoDB replication provides redundancy and high availability through replica sets -- groups of mongod processes that maintain the same data set. A replica set contains one primary member that receives all writes and one or more secondary members that replicate the primary's data asynchronously via the oplog (operations log). Replica sets are the foundation of MongoDB's data durability, fault tolerance, and read scaling strategy. Key guarantees of a properly configured replica set: Automatic failover: if the primary becomes unavailable, an election promotes a secondary to primary within ~12 seconds (median, with default settings). Data redundancy: every data-bearing member holds a complete copy of the data set. Read scaling: applications can distribute reads across secondaries using read preferences. Tunable consistency: write concern and read concern let applications choose their durability and consistency guarantees per operation. Primary: The only member that accepts write operations. Records all writes to its oplog. At most one primary per replica set at any time. Secondary: Maintains an identical copy of the primary's data set by asynchronously applying operations from the primary's oplog. Can serve read operations when read preference allows it. Can be elected primary during failover. Arbiter: Participates in elections but holds no data. Provides a tiebreaking vote in even-member-count topologies. Must not run on the same system as primary or secondary members. Has exactly 1 election vote and a default priority of 0. Hidden Members: Must have priority: 0, so they cannot become primary. Excluded from default client read routing. Use for dedicated tasks: reporting queries, backups, analytics workloads. Only reachable by direct connection. Delayed Members: Maintain a time-delayed copy of the data (configured via secondaryDelaySecs). Must be hidden and should be non-voting. Serve as a defense against accidental data destruction -- the delayed copy preserves the state from N seconds ago. Three-member replica set (P-S-S): One primary, two secondaries. Minimum recommended production topology. Tolerates one member failure while maintaining majority for elections and w: "majority" writes. Primary-Secondary-Arbiter (P-S-A): Costs less but carr

Run status: COMPLETED. The manual's Computed Pattern refresh job is one aggregation: `$group` the `screenings` collection by `movie_id` summing `num_viewers` and `revenue`, then `$merge` into `movies` with `on: '_id'` and `whenMatched: 'merge'`. The `merge` action adds the new total fields to the existing movie document and keeps its other fields. The job only reads `screenings` and only writes `movies`, so it can run at any time. (high confidence) An on-demand materialized view is a precomputed aggregation result stored on and read from disk, typically written by a `$merge` or `$out` stage. A standard view is computed at read time and not stored. MongoDB says the read-performance benefit grows with pipeline complexity and data size, and gives no benchmark numbers. (high confidence) A MongoDB on-demand materialized view is a pre-computed aggregation pipeline result that is stored on and read from disk, usually written by a `$merge` or `$out` stage. A standard view is computed each time it is read and is not stored, so an on-demand view reads faster than a standard view. (high confidence) Treat the derived store as disposable and non-authoritative. Azure says a materialized view can be entirely rebuilt from its source stores and is maintained by a dedicated component, 'so it's a specialized cache'. Facebook's memcache 'is not the authoritative source of the data and is therefore allowed to evict cached data'. (medium confidence) MongoDB's on-demand view example refreshes only part of the data. The `updateMovieStats(startYear)` function runs `$match` on `year >= startYear`, `$group` by year, then `$merge` with `whenMatched: 'replace'` and `whenNotMatched` defaulting to insert, so only groups from that year forward are rewritten and earlier groups are untouched. (high confidence) Precompute only when the same expensive result is read repeatedly, reads far outnumber writes and some staleness is acceptable. The Azure Architecture Center says the Materialized View pattern may not suit data that is simple to query, data that changes very quickly, or workloads where consistency is a high priority. MongoDB's manual frames the Computed Pattern the same way: repeated calculations and a high read-to-write ratio. (high confidence) `$out` is the full-rebuild option with an atomic swap.

items.concept: Real-Time OLAP and Analytical Databases
items.summary: Real-time OLAP databases are the query and storage engines that answer
items.text: Real-Time OLAP and Analytical Databases Real-time OLAP databases are the query and storage engines that answer Real-time OLAP databases are the query and storage engines that answer analytical questions (aggregations, group-bys, filters, top-N, time-series rollups) over large, continuously updating datasets with sub-second latency and high concurrency. They sit between stream processing (which transforms events in flight - da-14) and the BI/semantic layer (da-18), serving as the low-latency serving layer for dashboards, monitoring, and user/customer-facing analytics. What makes an engine "real-time OLAP" rather than a cloud data warehouse: Fresh data: rows are queryable seconds (often sub-second) after they land, via streaming ingestion - not after a nightly batch load. High concurrency / QPS: built to serve thousands of concurrent queries (a per-user dashboard feature), not a handful of internal analysts. ClickHouse reports 1,000+ concurrent queries per node; Snowflake defaults to ~8 queries per warehouse, Redshift caps ~50 concurrent across queues (ClickHouse, 2025). Tight latency SLAs: tens of milliseconds, achieved with columnar storage, vectorized execution, and pre-aggregation/indexing. This skill covers the engines and the query layer. It is the OLAP-database node of the data-analytics curriculum (da-1 onward); it does not cover stream processing (da-14), pipeline orchestration (da-13), or the metrics layer (da-18). Data is stored by column, not by row. Analytical queries touch few columns but many rows, so columnar layout reads only the needed columns, drastically cutting I/O, and stores like-typed values together so they compress far better (delta, dictionary, RLE, LZ4/ZSTD). This is the foundational OLAP advantage over row stores (SQLFlash, 2025; Airbyte, 2024). Compression both saves storage and increases effective scan throughput. Instead of processing one row at a time through a tuple-at-a-time interpreter, the engine processes batches (vectors) of column values in tight loops, exploiting CPU SIMD instructions, cache locality, and amortized virtual-function/branch overhead. This yields multi-x to order-of-magnitude speedups and is paired with columnar storage in every modern engine (SQLFlash, 2025; Cockroach Labs). Even hybrid OLTP/OLAP systems (Google Spanner's columnar engine, OceanBase 4.3) adopt columnar + vectorized execution for analytics, up to ~200x faster on live data (InfoQ, 2025). items.summary: Really Simple Licensing (RSL) is an open XML standard (launched 2025-09-10, RSL 1.0 Recommendation 2025-12-10, governed by the RSL Technical Steering Committee and the RSL Collective) for expressing machine-readable licensing, payment, and legal terms for digital content, discovered chiefly through a new robots.txt License: directive and composing with — not replacing — robots.txt, llms.txt, ai.txt, IETF AIPREF, Cloudflare Content Signals, W3C TDMRep, and C2PA/CAWG. Drawn from 4 sources covering the specification itself, deployment/tooling/anti-patterns, the standards landscape, and measured adoption/legal weight, this pack shows RSL as a well-engineered declaration layer with thin real-world uptake: direct measurement found roughly 3 independent publisher deployments (of which most are non-conformant with the spec's own rules), no AI company has agreed to honor it, and its legal force stands on notice/evidentiary value and an EU DSM Art. 4(3) reservation rather than technical enforcement.

items.text: Reasoning field naming across servers vLLM RFC #27755 (opened 2025-10-29 by hmellor) proposed removing `reasoning_content` completely after PR #27752 had already switched output to `reasoning` with backwards compatibility vLLM RFC #27755 (opened 2025-10-29 by hmellor) proposed removing `reasoning_content` completely after PR #27752 had already switched output to `reasoning` with backwards compatibility vLLM PR #33402 'Remove reasoning_content' was merged on 2026-01-30 (commit c5113f6) after months of deprecation with no objection on the RFC The stated reason for the vLLM rename was OpenAI's guidance for gpt-oss: return CoT in a `reasoning` field on Chat Completions even though the official API has no such field OpenAI's raw-CoT guide tells Chat Completions implementers to follow OpenRouter: `reasoning` on the message, `reasoning` on stream deltas, and omit it when the request sets `reasoning: {exclude: true}` The same guide says previous reasoning should be accepted back on later requests as `reasoning` and handled per the Harmony replay rules OpenRouter accepts `reasoning_content` as an input alias that behaves identically to `reasoning` OpenRouter also defines `message.reasoning_details` (array, also in `delta.reasoning_details`) for encrypted or summarised reasoning types; it must be passed back unmodified, while models that return plain strings can use `reasoning` A vLLM RFC participant (Riatre, 2025-10-31) pointed out that the OpenRouter convention OpenAI cites uses `reasoning_details` for replay, so a `reasoning`-only rename may need a second migration; the RFC left input-side replay out of scope (bbrowning, 2025-10-30) llama.cpp discussion #15362 (aldehir, 2025-08-16) asked for a configurable reasoning field because several clients, including OpenAI's own gpt-oss test, expect `reasoning` while llama-server emits `reasoning_content` In #15362 ggerganov suggested sending both `reasoning` and `reasoning_content` until the community converged; mostlygeek objected that two keys would confuse the API and proposed a flag such as `--reasoning-format openai` instead Ollama's native API uses `message.thinking` (chat) and `thinking` (generate), and `think` accepts true, false, null or a model-defined level string taken from `/api/show` `thinking.values`; numbers are not supported Inferred: a client written for the 2025 llama.cpp and vLLM convention (`reasoning_content`) now needs to read three keys (`reasoning_content`, `reasoning`, `thinking`) and write back

items.concept: Reasoning Models and Test-Time Compute
items.summary: The frontier (2024–2026) shift from "scale the model and prompt it well" to "train the model to reason, then spend extra compute at inference to reason harder." Two coupled ideas drive it:
items.text: Reasoning Models and Test-Time Compute The frontier (2024–2026) shift from "scale the model and prompt it well" to "train the model to reason, then spend extra compute at inference to reason harder." Two coupled ideas drive it: The frontier (2024–2026) shift from "scale the model and prompt it well" to "train the model to reason, then spend extra compute at inference to reason harder." Two coupled ideas drive it: Test-time / inference-time compute (TTC): a model can be made more accurate on a hard problem by spending more compute when answering - sampling many solutions, searching over reasoning steps, or generating a long internal chain of thought - instead of (or in addition to) growing the model. Snell et al. (2024) showed this can be more parameter-efficient than scaling pretraining on a fixed compute budget for many problems. Reasoning models (o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini "thinking", Claude extended thinking): models post-trained with reinforcement learning to produce long chains of thought before answering. The RL teaches the model to use its inference budget well, so the two ideas reinforce each other: the model both generates a long CoT and benefits from being allowed to. This reference = the model's reasoning: long-CoT, reasoning-specific RL (GRPO, RLVR), process vs outcome reward models, test-time-compute scaling (best-of-N, self-consistency, search), inference-time scaling laws, the o-series/R1 landscape, budget forcing, reasoning distillation, reasoning benchmarks, and the cost/latency/accuracy trade-off. Classic preference alignment - RLHF with PPO, the DPO-variant family (DPO/IPO/KTO/ORPO/SimPO/CPO), RLAIF, Constitutional AI - is a different objective (match human preference via a learned reward model). It lives in references/llm-alignment-post-training.md. The line: **reasoning-RL optimizes verifiable correctness; alignment-RL optimizes human preference.** GRPO/RLVR-for-reasoning are here; the same algorithms used for preference tuning are there. Agent loops / tool use (a model calling tools in a multi-step loop) → references/agent-ecosystem.md, references/autonomous-loops.md, references/agent-harness-construction.md. This reference is about the model's own reasoning, not the orchestration around it. (Reasoning models can call tools mid-thought - "agentic reasoning" - but the orchestration belongs to those references.) Serving throughput (vLLM batching, speculative decoding, KV-cache) → references/llm-inference-serving.md. Speculative decoding

items.text: Reasoning-parser versus tool-parser interaction vLLM: reasoning extraction runs first and the tool parser reads only `content`; a call left in `reasoning` is lost. vLLM PR #39055 (merge state not confirmed; non-streaming only) makes `qwen3_reasoning_parser` promote complete XML tool-call blocks from `reasoning` into `content` so `qwen3_coder` ... vLLM: reasoning extraction runs first and the tool parser reads only `content`; a call left in `reasoning` is lost. vLLM PR #39055 (merge state not confirmed; non-streaming only) makes `qwen3_reasoning_parser` promote complete XML tool-call blocks from `reasoning` into `content` so `qwen3_coder` can parse them. llama.cpp: a lazy grammar trigger is separate from the reasoning parser. pwilkin (2026-03-21): the trigger sees `<tool_call>` inside thinking, the grammar forces end-of-generation after the call, and the model cannot go on to close the think block and redo the call. markqvist: tool-call parsing runs after, and separately from, reasoning parsing. llama.cpp fix direction: the reasoning-budget sampler (PR #20297, opened 2026-03-09) tracks IDLE, COUNTING, FORCING, WAITING_UTF8 and DONE states; a lazy tool grammar stays dormant while the sampler is in COUNTING (inside `<think>`), so a literal `<tool_call>` in thinking does not arm it. llama.cpp parser reference debate: aldehir (2026-03-22) says llama.cpp and vLLM emit a tool call found in reasoning as a real call, while sglang's reasoning parser consumes those tokens so the tool parser never sees them, and he takes sglang as the reference behaviour. mlx_lm.server (main branch): one text state machine with states normal, reasoning and tool. `make_text_state_machine` adds transitions think_start to reasoning, think_end to normal, and tool_call_start to tool from both normal and reasoning, so a call opened inside thinking is collected as a tool call. The response carries `message.reasoning` and `message.tool_calls`; `finish_reason` becomes `tool_calls` after a call. mlx_lm.server picks the initial state from the rendered prompt: if the last think-start token comes after the last think-end token, generation starts in `reasoning` (covers templates that pre-open `<think>`). Rapid-MLX: its docs say the parser strips thinking content before extracting tool calls, including implicit-think prompts that contain only `</think>`; a call written inside thinking is therefore discarded, not recovered. vllm-mlx: reasoning parser is text-based and stateless over accumulated outpu

items.text:
Reasoning-token cache invalidation across turns oMLX tracks the condition per request. `needs_think_prefix` is true when the prompt ends with an open think tag (found within the last three or so prompt tokens; a think-open followed by a think-close, the disabled-thinking pattern, returns false). `preserve_reasoning` on the request says the nex... oMLX tracks the condition per request. `needs_think_prefix` is true when the prompt ends with an open think tag (found within the last three or so prompt tokens; a think-open followed by a think-close, the disabled-thinking pattern, returns false). `preserve_reasoning` on the request says the next turn keeps the reasoning. Rule (scheduler `_output_tokens_cacheable`): output tokens are storable if the request did not need a think prefix, or if `preserve_reasoning` is true. Otherwise only the prompt tokens are stored. Effect on storage: the stored token count is `num_tokens` (prompt plus output) when output is cacheable, else the prompt length. The fallback store after a parser-side stop (for example a tool-call end marker) uses the same rule and rounds down to a whole block. Logs label the store "prompt + output" or "prompt only". Where `preserve_reasoning` comes from (api/utils.py `cache_reasoning_output`): the model setting `cache_reasoning_output` if set; else false when `preserve_thinking` in the merged kwargs is false; else true when the model is a "native reasoning" family or `preserve_thinking` is true. oMLX auto-sets `preserve_thinking=true` for any model whose template text contains that name (see omlx-per-model-chat-template-kwargs-and-cache-ke.md), so Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8 are cached with their reasoning by default. History rebuild: for templates that read `message.reasoning_content` (Qwen 3.6+, the "native" case), oMLX keeps content clean and passes reasoning separately, and when the client sent `<think>...</think>` inline it extracts it into `reasoning_content`. For non-native templates it inlines the reasoning back as `<think>
{reasoning}
</think>

{text}`. Void assistant messages (no content, no tool calls, no reasoning) are dropped before rendering. Qwen3.8 template side: with `preserve_thinking` undefined the template keeps every historical think block, so a thinking-mode turn replayed with its `reasoning_content` is byte-stable. If the client drops `reasoning_content`, each such turn renders `<think>

</think>

` in place of the real reasoning, a mismatch at the first reasoning token and a c

items.concept: Recommender Systems and Learning-to-Rank Analytics
items.summary: A recommender system predicts, for each user, which items from a (often huge) catalog they are most likely to engage with, then orders a small slate to show. As a data-analysis discipline it sits at t
items.text: Recommender Systems and Learning-to-Rank Analytics A recommender system predicts, for each user, which items from a (often huge) catalog they are most likely to engage with, then orders a small slate to show. As a data-analysis discipline it sits at t A recommender system predicts, for each user, which items from a (often huge) catalog they are most likely to engage with, then orders a small slate to show. As a data-analysis discipline it sits at the intersection of three problems: (1) modeling preference from sparse interaction data, (2) ranking candidates under a relevance objective, and (3) evaluating both offline and online while fighting the bias the system itself creates. Scope boundaries (read first): vs da-7 (machine learning): da-7 covers generic supervised/unsupervised model training, regularization, and hyperparameter tuning. da-38 covers the recommendation- and ranking-specific objectives (BPR/WRMF losses, NDCG-aware LambdaMART), the retrieve-then-rank funnel, and recsys evaluation. Use da-7 for "train a classifier"; use da-38 for "rank items for a user." vs da-27 (network/graph analytics): da-27 owns graph structure metrics (centrality, community detection, link prediction as graph analysis, GNNs as graph models). da-38 references GNN-for-recsys and bipartite user-item graphs only at the recommendation level; graph-structure questions belong to da-27. vs da-12 (A/B testing & causal inference): da-12 owns general experiment design and causal estimators. da-38 owns the recsys-specific online-eval wrinkles: interleaving, feedback-loop confounding, and off-policy/counterfactual evaluation (IPS, doubly-robust) of a ranking policy. vs rag-architecture / vector search: semantic retrieval with no personalization or ranking-quality objective is RAG; ranked personalization is da-38. Explicit vs implicit feedback. Explicit = ratings/likes (sparse, signed). Implicit = clicks, views, dwell, purchases (abundant but positive-only and ambiguous - a non-click is not a dislike). Implicit dominates production and forces positive-unlabeled modeling: model confidence that an interaction is a preference, not a rating value. Popularity bias & the feedback loop. A deployed recommender only logs feedback on items it showed, chosen because they scored high - so the next training set over-represents popular/previously-recommended items (exposure bias). Unchecked, a self-reinforcing loop narrows the catalog and creates filter bubbles. Breaking it needs exploration and/or

items.concept: Reference self-flip floor from cache_prompt and batch-size nondeterminism
items.summary: A llama.cpp user running 8 server slots with temperature 0, a fixed seed and cache_prompt false got 5 to 8 distinct completions from the same prompt on an H100, reproduced on an M1 MacBook Pro and an A100, and always one completion with one slot but still small logit variations.
items.text: Reference self-flip floor from cache_prompt and batch-size nondeterminism A llama.cpp user running 8 server slots with temperature 0, a fixed seed and cache_prompt false got 5 to 8 distinct completions from the same prompt on an H100, reproduced on an M1 MacBook Pro and an A100, and always one completion with one slot but still small logit variations. A llama.cpp user running 8 server slots with temperature 0, a fixed seed and cache_prompt false got 5 to 8 distinct completions from the same prompt on an H100, reproduced on an M1 MacBook Pro and an A100, and always one completion with one slot but still small logit variations. A llama.cpp maintainer's answer: bit-identical floating point output needs the exact same operations in the same order, and multiple slots are faster precisely because they do not run that way; multi-slot output stayed not fully deterministic on master, and a per-slot RNG fix (PR 6835) was needed because slots first shared one RNG state. The issue was closed by the stale bot after 14 days with no root-cause fix. vLLM documents "batch invariance" as an opt-in beta (VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1) that makes output independent of batch size and request order, supported on NVIDIA GPUs of compute capability 8.0 or higher and Intel XPUs with Triton; Apple GPUs are not listed. No llama.cpp or MLX switch with the vLLM guarantee was found, so on a Mac the floor has to be measured, not configured away. KLD analogue: llama-perplexity derives n_seq from n_batch / n_ctx and runs sequences together, so the reference pass and each candidate pass use batch shapes set by -b and -c; the candidate pass must reuse the reference's -c, and equal -b is the only way to keep batch composition equal. A direct floor measurement: run the reference file's own model through the --kl-divergence pass with a different -b and read mean KLD and Same-top p; any nonzero KLD or Same-top p under 100% is the batch-shape floor. 2024-05: issue 7052 reports the multi-slot effect. 2025-2026: vLLM adds batch invariance (docs read 2026-10-04). Single-slot variation in logits does not necessarily change argmax, but a near-tie position can flip, so the floor concentrates on low-margin positions, the same positions a quant flips. The issue's hardware was CUDA plus one M1 report; Metal reduction order differs, so the size of the floor on Apple GPUs is unknown. items.concept: Release Blog and Launch Narrative
items.summary: A launch is a one-shot narrative event — distinct from a landing page (steady-state conversion), an exec memo (internal alignment), or a changelog (continuous release log).
items.text: Release Blog and Launch Narrative A launch is a one-shot narrative event — distinct from a landing page (steady-state conversion), an exec memo (internal alignment), or a changelog (continuous release log). A launch is a one-shot narrative event - distinct from a landing page (steady-state conversion), an exec memo (internal alignment), or a changelog (continuous release log). Heuristic: If you can't name the archetype in 10 seconds, the launch isn't ready. Open with a one-paragraph claim about a shift in the world. Never open with the product. Andy Raskin's whole thesis: "the old game is over; a new game is starting." What does the reader lose by staying with the old way? Quantify if possible. Now - and only now - name the product and the one-line description. Apple's pattern: "Today, Apple introduced [X], a [category] that [primary benefit]." Customer logos, quotes, measurable outcomes, demo link. One outside voice is worth ten internal claims. Clear CTA - one primary CTA, one secondary at most. What's not in v1 - the honest-disclosure section. A working "why now" paragraph: Names a shift that has already occurred. Establishes the cost of operating as if the shift hadn't happened. Creates urgency that is "you're already behind if you ignore this." Template: > Until recently, [old default] was the only way to [task]. But [shift A] and [shift B] have changed what's possible. Teams that adapt are [outcome]. Teams that don't are [cost]. Today we're announcing [product] to help you [verb] in this new world. Anti-pattern: "AI is everywhere." This is a backdrop, not a why-now. It has no specific shift, no cost, no urgency. Sequencing rules: The blog post is the canonical source. Every other piece links to it. Analyst and press briefings are under embargo. Release notes accompany the announcement. When the blog post says "today we're launching X," the docs and the changelog must already reflect X. Template: > v1 deliberately ships without [X], [Y], and [Z]. We chose this scope to get [primary benefit] in your hands sooner. [X] is on the roadmap for [quarter]. If [X] or [Y] is a hard requirement for you today, [alternative path]. What this section does: Lets engineers in evaluation mode answer "can I use this yet?" without booking a call. Pre-empts the inevitable Hacker News commenter who finds the missing feature. The "we're excited to announce" opener. Cut. Open with the shift. The "this changes everything" overclaim. The "product-first" structure. Specs, then

items.text: Replanning loops and replanReason Source-anchored research for Replanning loops and replanReason. Run status: COMPLETED. Two other replanReason forms exist. 'cached plan returned: <status>' means the cached plan failed during its trial, for example with QueryExceededMemoryLimitNoDiskUseAllowed on a blocking sort. In that case the server replans but neither deactivates the cache entry nor caches the replanned winner. The SBE path also uses 'Foreign collection <ns> is not eligible for hash join anymore'. That form replans without running a trial and allows the new winner to be cached. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) The manual says planningTimeMicros (new in 6.2) is not a clean measure of replanning cost. Before 7.0.22, 8.0.5 and 8.1.0 it can include non-planning work such as a sharding metadata refresh. It can also include cached-plan trial-run time even when the query does not replan. The manual says not to rely on the field alone. SERVER-92476 fixed the non-planning part; SERVER-106502 (Backlog) covers the trial-run part. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-19) If a query shape has an Active plan cache entry, the server runs a bounded trial of the cached plan before it uses the plan. If the trial costs more than internalQueryCacheEvictionRatio times the cost recorded when the plan was cached, the server deactivates the cache entry and plans the query again from scratch. MongoDB calls this second planning pass replanning. (high confidence) The Database Profiler Output reference defines two fields. replanned is a boolean that means the query system evicted a cached plan and re-evaluated all candidate plans. replanReason is a string that gives the specific reason a cached plan was evicted. Both appear only when replanned is true. In the server code, replanned is emitted only when replanReason is set. (high confidence) Plan cache entries are Active or Inactive. A new entry starts Inactive, and the planner does not use it. A later planning run for the same shape promotes the entry to Active when that run's works are less than or equal to the stored works. If the new run's works are higher, the entry stays Inactive and its stored works grow by at least 1, by internalQueryCacheWorksGrowthCoefficient (default 2.0, so they double). SERVER-32452 introduced this design in 4.1.1, which shipped in 4.2. items.concept: Replica Set Node Topology Cost
items.summary: An Atlas replica set's cost scales with the number and tier of its data-bearing nodes: electable nodes must total 3, 5 or 7, read-only and analytics nodes add capacity without voting, and each data-bearing node is billed at the cluster tier's hourly rate plus its storage. Analytics nodes can use a different tier priced prorated per node, while arbiters are documented only for self-managed sets and the sources disagree on whether the three-node minimum is justified for test environments. Drawn from 9 source pages (MongoDB Atlas docs, manual and blog, forum threads, IBM Community and oneuptime blogs) across definitions, parameters, mechanism, problems and how-to.

In addition to consumption charges displayed in MongoDB Atlas Cluster Configuration UI, data transfer, backup and support charges are added on top of hourly price. Analytics node tiers provide greater control and flexibility by allowing you to customize the exact infrastructure you need for your analytics workloads. On Atlas Infinite clusters, data-bearing servers don't apply. Atlas stores and manages your data in a storage layer that is separate from the compute layer. The electable, read-only, and analytics nodes are compute nodes that access data in the storage layer. To learn more, see MongoDB Atlas Infinite: Architecture. items.text: Replica Set Transactions Source-anchored research for Replica Set Transactions. Run status: COMPLETED. MongoDB Jira issue SERVER-88746 documents a snapshot-isolation violation in replica-set transactions on version 7.0.0 when writes raced with a collection drop or rename; the issue lists 7.0.10 as the fix version. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-05-06) With transaction commit write concern w:1, MongoDB acknowledges after the primary applies the commit, so a failover can roll the transaction back before replication; when the former primary rejoins, it reverts writes that were not replicated to secondaries. Sources: https://grpc.io/docs/guides/request-hedging/ [low] The goal of speculative executions is to improve overall latency at high percentiles, though they can lead to stream id exhaustion due to many cancelled requests. Sources: https://docs.datastax.com/en/developer/java-driver/3.3/manual/speculative_execution [low] A pattern for request hedging involves deferring the secondary request until the first has been outstanding for more than the 95th-percentile expected latency, limiting additional load to approximately 5% while shortening tail latency. items.text: Responses API client-executed tool_search support in local servers OpenAI's tool-search guide defines two modes: hosted, where OpenAI searches the deferred tools declared in the request and returns the loaded subset in the same response, and client-executed, where the model emits a `tool_search_call`, the application does the lookup and returns a `tool_search_ou... OpenAI's tool-search guide defines two modes: hosted, where OpenAI searches the deferred tools declared in the request and returns the loaded subset in the same response, and client-executed, where the model emits a `tool_search_call`, the application does the lookup and returns a `tool_search_output`. Client mode is configured by adding a `tool_search` tool with `execution: "client"` and a parameters schema for the arguments the application expects. The client returns `{"type": "tool_search_output", "execution": "client", "call_id": <the call's id>, "status": "completed", "tools": [...]}` in the next request's `input`, after the earlier output items. In hosted mode the `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output` items carry `execution: "server"` and `call_id: null`. `tool_search_output.tools` lists the tools the model can call on later turns; tools not in the array are not loaded, and the client need not load the same tool again on later turns. Client mode also permits returning tools that were absent from the original `tools` list; OpenAI calls this an advanced workflow and says to validate the returned schemas carefully. An `additional_tools` input item makes its tools available only from the point where the item appears, so a client that replays items by hand must keep the item's position. Loaded tools are placed at the end of the model's context window in both modes so the cached prefix survives. A LiteLLM Responses-to-chat translation layer rejected Codex's `type: "tool_search"` entry with `400: Field required ... tools[13].function`, which shows a chat-translating router cannot carry the item type unchanged. OpenAI's guide limits `tool_search` in the Responses API to `gpt-5.4` and later, so a local model gets it only if a server or proxy emulates the item types.

items.concept: Resumable index builds
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Resumable index builds. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Resumable index builds Source-anchored research for Resumable index builds. Run status: COMPLETED. 'Resumable' means three different things across engines. MongoDB resumes by itself after a clean shutdown or rollback, and its manual documents no command to pause or resume a build. SQL Server lets a DBA pause, resume and abort a resumable operation. PostgreSQL has no resume: a failed concurrent build must be dropped and retried. (medium confidence) Index builds can take from moments to days. Before resumable builds, a restart discarded the finished scan and sort work and started the build again. Resume keeps that work when a node restarts mid-build, which saves CPU, I/O, cache pressure and elapsed time on large collections. (medium confidence) Since 5.0, a rollback during an index build saves the build state with the same mechanism as clean shutdown. If work remains after the rollback, mongod recovers the build and continues from the checkpoint. If the rollback reverts the build itself, the user must re-create the index. (high confidence) A member restarted as a standalone does not resume the build. SERVER-37637 (Fixed 4.3.4) made standalone nodes ignore in-progress builds so they do not deviate from the replica set, and says the builds are recovered and finished when the node rejoins in replica set mode. The manual says the build stays paused until someone drops it. (medium confidence) MongoDB tests detect a resume by log line only. SERVER-128117 (Backlog, unresolved) proposes an OpenTelemetry metric named index_builds.resume.started with a phase attribute, because the bounded log buffer has dropped the resume line in test failures (BF-43501, BF-40886). (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-25) On a MongoDB primary or secondary, a clean shutdown with force: true or a SIGTERM during an index build saves the build's progress to disk when the commit quorum is the default votingMembers. After restart, mongod recovers the build automatically and continues from the saved checkpoint. (high confidence) Since MongoDB 5.0, a node that rolls back during an index build saves the build's progress to disk. If work remains when the rollback ends, mongod recovers the build and continues from the saved checkpoint. The server README says the rollback algorithm (recover to a timestamp) supports resuming a build interrupted at any phase. Two-column layouts and tables scramble field order. Custom or decorative headings ("My Journey," "What I Bring") confuse the parser. Text boxes, graphics, embedded images are often dropped entirely. Non-standard fonts can render as glyph junk. PDF vs DOCX - both work if text-selectable. Image-only PDFs fail the parse. For each target role: (a) reorder bullets so the top 3 in each job align with the target JD's stated priorities, (b) swap in keywords from the JD into the skills section, (c) rewrite the summary in the language the JD uses. Keep a skills section but limit it to: (a) hard tools and technologies, (b) certifications, (c) languages. Do not list soft skills ("communication," "leadership") - they are not parseable signals. The resume is third-person implicit and clipped ("Led a 5-engineer team that shipped..."). LinkedIn is first-person and conversational ("I lead a team that builds..."). CV (curriculum vitae): used for postdocs, faculty, some government-lab and research-institute roles. Several pages. Comprehensive: publications, presentations, grants, teaching, service. Resume: industry standard. One page (early career) to two pages (senior, ≥10 years). Brief, achievement-focused. Going from academia to industry: do not submit your CV. Translate to a 2-page resume. Caregiving / family leave - name it in one line on the resume. Education / certification - list as its own entry: "Independent study in [topic], earned [credential]." Health,

items.concept: Reverse ETL and Operational Analytics
items.summary: Activating warehouse-modeled data into the tools where work happens. Reverse ETL
items.text: Reverse ETL and Operational Analytics Activating warehouse-modeled data into the tools where work happens. Reverse ETL Activating warehouse-modeled data into the tools where work happens. Reverse ETL (rETL) is the inverse of ingestion ETL: it reads curated tables from the data warehouse/lakehouse and writes them into operational SaaS systems (CRM, marketing automation, ad platforms, support, finance), closing the loop between analytics and action. This is the "last mile" of the modern data stack. This skill is the GAP-filler in the da-* curriculum adjacent to da-13 (pipelines) and da-18 (semantic layer). Use when designing, reviewing, or troubleshooting a system that pushes warehouse data into business tools, building a composable/warehouse-native CDP, syncing audiences/traits to destinations, or reasoning about identity resolution, sync idempotency, destination rate limits, or activation governance. For loading data into the warehouse, see da-13. For metric definitions, see da-18. ETL/ELT: source systems → warehouse (ingestion). Reverse ETL: warehouse → operational tools (activation). Reverse ETL "makes the warehouse actionable" by pushing modeled data back out (Fivetran). The warehouse becomes the single source of truth / source of computation; rETL distributes curated entities (customer 360, scores, segments) - it does not recompute them (phData, 2025). Standard pattern is unidirectional (warehouse → tool). It is not a two-way operational sync; bidirectional sync between SaaS apps is a different problem (Stacksync, 2025). Data activation = delivering insights to the systems and people that act on them, so analytics drives frontline workflows (marketing personalization, sales enablement, success automation, finance ops) (RudderStack). Operational analytics is the discipline: the value is "moving decisions, not just data" - bridging analytics with daily workflows (Medium/Moronta, Sep 2025; Workato). Packaged CDP (e.g., Segment, mParticle, Tealium): preassembled - collects, stores, models, and activates data inside its own system. Faster to deploy, less engineering, but copies your data and risks lock-in (Hightouch; CDP Institute). Composable CDP: unbundled, warehouse-native - leverages your existing Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks as the foundation and adds identity resolution, segmentation, and activation on top, reading (not copying) the data (Hightouch). Reverse ETL is the de-facto activation layer of composable CDP architectures. Hybrid CDP (fast-growin

items.text: Rewriting llama-server overflow errors to Claude Code's recognised wording llama-server sends errors through `res->error()`, which sets the HTTP status to the object's `code` and the body to `{"error": <object>}`. llama-server sends errors through `res->error()`, which sets the HTTP status to the object's `code` and the body to `{"error": <object>}`. For `ERROR_TYPE_EXCEED_CONTEXT_SIZE` the error object is `{"code": 400, "message": ..., "type": "exceed_context_size_error"}` plus two extra integer fields, `n_prompt_tokens` and `n_ctx`. `n_ctx` in that body is the slot's context (`send_error(slot, ...)` passes `slot.n_ctx`), so with `--parallel` slots sharing `-c` it is the per-request share, not the server total. A captured body reads `{"error":{"code":400,"message":"request (131088 tokens) exceeds the available context size (131072 tokens), try increasing it","type":"exceed_context_size_error","n_prompt_tokens":131088,"n_ctx":131072}}`, about 240 characters. llama-server has two prompt-size wordings, both typed `exceed_context_size_error`: "input (%d tokens) is larger than the max context size (%d tokens). skipping" (a prompt that cannot be split and exceeds `n_ctx`) and "request (%d tokens) exceeds the available context size (%d tokens), try increasing it" (splittable prompt at or above `n_ctx`). A third, different failure reads "Context size has been exceeded." and comes from a failed decode when the batch size is 1; it is reported mid-stream and means the KV pool ran out, not that the prompt was too long. One user hit the KV-pool failure with `-c 262144` and automatic `--parallel` (four slots sharing one unified pool) when a main stream of about 200 messages ran alongside judge calls, and llama.cpp then failed every in-flight slot. Rewriting the KV-pool message to "prompt is too long" would send Claude Code compacting a prompt that was not the problem. When the first result of a streaming request is an error, llama-server returns it as an ordinary non-streamed HTTP error, matching OpenAI behaviour, so a proxy sees a plain JSON 400 for prompt overflow even on a streaming request. A mid-stream error on the Anthropic route is sent as `event: error` with the flat error object as data, while the OpenAI route wraps it as `{"error": ...}`; neither is Anthropic's `{"type":"error","error":{...}}` shape. llama-server's Anthropic route has a `/v1/messages/count_tokens` handler as well as `/v1/messages`. items.concept: Rhythm uniformity and burstiness
items.summary: Source-anchored research for Rhythm uniformity and burstiness. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Rhythm uniformity and burstiness Source-anchored research for Rhythm uniformity and burstiness. Run status: COMPLETED. Burstiness is defined as how much writing patterns and perplexities vary over a whole document; the claim is that humans vary naturally while LLMs choose next words by the same rule and so show low burstiness. (medium confidence) Across six LLMs from three families, human news text shows more scattered sentence-length distributions, more varied vocabulary and dependency types than LLM text; differences between humans and LLMs exceed differences between LLMs. (low confidence) GPTZero stopped relying on perplexity and burstiness as primary detection signals in autumn 2023, moving to a deep-learning classifier; the stats remain one of seven indicators. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) Perplexity/burstiness are relative to a specific scoring model, so results shift with each model release; closed models expose no token probabilities, forcing open-model proxies. (low confidence) Text heavily present in training data (e.g. the Declaration of Independence) scores as low perplexity and is misflagged as AI; non-native English writing also scores low perplexity/burstiness (2023 Stanford TOEFL study), so the metric produces false positives. (low confidence)

items.text: Right-sizing Atlas tier from cache and CPU metrics Source-anchored research for Right-sizing Atlas tier from cache and CPU metrics. Run status: COMPLETED. Atlas treats M10 and M20 CPU thresholds differently because cloud providers can cap CPU after burst periods; their scale-down thresholds use provider-specific baseline CPU. A generic CPU p95 cutoff such as the one in the OneUptime guide should not be applied unchanged across tier families. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-19) Atlas Core reactive scale-down uses multiple signals across both 10-minute and 4-hour windows: operational nodes must average below 45% normalized System CPU, below 90% of maximum WiredTiger cache use, and below 60% projected memory utilization on the next lower tier. MongoDB's manual cost guidance separately calls for reviewing CPU, cache, memory, and IOPS together. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-19) For manual right-sizing, Atlas recommends monitoring CPU, WiredTiger cache, memory, and IOPS over a rolling 30-day period of normal use; sustained use below 45% of allocated resources is a general signal to consider scaling down. A OneUptime guide recommends a two-week baseline, so that shorter window should be treated as practitioner advice rather than Atlas policy. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) Cache hit rate is not a safe standalone tier gate. MongoDB says the working set does not have to fit entirely in RAM because WiredTiger evicts pages and the OS filesystem cache can hold compressed data. Guy Harrison also notes that a high cache hit ratio can coexist with an inefficient workload that repeatedly reads the same blocks. Atlas scale-down checks use cache occupancy and projected memory rather than a cache hit-rate threshold. (medium confidence) Assess WiredTiger cache pressure with multiple signals instead of cache occupancy alone. Atlas exposes cache and dirty-fill metrics alongside disk IOPS and latency; Percona's WiredTiger monitoring guidance says sustained high read-into-cache indicates the working set is not fitting in cache, and sustained dirty-page eviction can delay operations. Near-maximum cache use or rising disk reads therefore warrants checking query latency and I/O before downsizing, even when CPU is low. (high confidence) A candidate tier must also fit workload limits beyond CPU and cache: Atlas says connection capacity depends on tier, network bandwidth varies by instance, and disk IOPS should be compared with the provisioned max
