This is deliberately not the RL algorithm (PPO/GRPO/DPO — those live in the The systems stack that post-training reinforcement learning runs on - RLHF, RLVR, reasoning-RL, and agentic-RL all share it. This is deliberately not the RL algorithm (PPO/GRPO/DPO - those live in the alignment, reasoning, and agentic-RL references) and not generic supervised distributed training (FSDP/ZeRO for pretraining - that lives in distributed-training). It is the third thing those two references keep pointing at: how do you actually run an RL post-training job - generate samples, score them, update weights, and not leave half your GPUs idle. The one-sentence framing: a supervised step is one engine doing forward+backward; an RL step is three engines - a generator, a scorer, and a trainer - passed through an experience buffer, and the whole discipline exists because the generator dominates wall-clock (60–90%+ of step time) and the naive synchronous schedule leaves the trainer's GPUs idle while the generator works. Every design decision below - colocate vs disaggregated placement, the per-step weight resync, async/off-policy systems, the train/inference logprob mismatch - follows from attacking that bottleneck. This reference = the RL systems layer: the actor–rollout–learner architecture and experience buffer; GPU placement (colocate/hybrid vs disaggregated); the rollout/generation bottleneck and the inference-engine-in-the-loop; the train→infer weight resync (NCCL/IPC/resharding); async/off-policy systems and staleness; the framework landscape (veRL, OpenRLHF, NeMo-RL/-Aligner, TRL, slime, AReaL, ROLL, SkyRL, TorchForge); reward-model serving + verifier/code-sandbox infra; scaling the trainer (FSDP/Megatron) alongside the rollout engine (TP); the RL utilization "bubble" and overlap fixes; and RL-systems failure modes (logprob mismatch, weight-sync desync, reward over-optimization). **The RL algorithm itself - what PPO's clipped objective is, how GRPO drops the value model, what a KL penalty does, the DPO loss - is out of scope. items.concept: robots.txt and the Content-Signal AI-preference extension
items.summary: robots.txt is the Robots Exclusion Protocol (RFC 9309, Sept 2022, Proposed Standard): a crawl-access file of User-agent groups with Allow/Disallow rules, MUST-level wildcards (*, $), octet-based longest-match precedence with an allow-wins SHOULD tie-break, a 500 KiB parsing floor, and explicit non-goals (it is not access authorization). Riding inside it is a newer, unstandardized AI-preference layer — Cloudflare's Content-Signal (search/ai-input/ai-train, plus a testing content-use field) and its IETF successor draft (Content-Usage, AIPREF) — which states what a crawler may do with content after fetching it, has no announced enforcing consumer, and is evidenced (Perplexity dispute, Consent in Crisis study, Google's 'no effects whatsoever') to be a stated preference rather than a technical control. Drawn from two /dr-authored references (RFC 9309 spec analysis and the Content-Signal/AIPREF layer), 34 sourced footnotes.
items.text: robots.txt and the Content-Signal AI-preference extension robots.txt is the Robots Exclusion Protocol (RFC 9309, Sept 2022, Proposed Standard): a crawl-access file of User-agent groups with Allow/Disallow rules, MUST-level wildcards (*, $), octet-based longest-match precedence with an allow-wins SHOULD tie-break, a 500 KiB parsing floor, and explicit non-goals (it is not access authorization). Riding inside it is a newer, unstandardized AI-preference layer — Cloudflare's Content-Signal (search/ai-input/ai-train, plus a testing content-use field) and its IETF successor draft (Content-Usage, AIPREF) — which states what a crawler may do with content after fetching it, has no announced enforcing consumer, and is evidenced (Perplexity dispute, Consent in Crisis study, Google's 'no effects whatsoever') to be a stated preference rather than a technical control. Drawn from two /dr-authored references (RFC 9309 spec analysis and the Content-Signal/AIPREF layer), 34 sourced footnotes. RFC 9309 answers exactly one question — *may you fetch this URL*. It says nothing about what a crawler may then **do** with what it fetched. This reference covers the layer that has grown inside robots.txt to answer that second question: Cloudflare's `Content-Signal:` extension, the evidence on whether anyone obeys it, and the IETF work standardising a successor. For the protocol itself, see `references/robots-txt.md`. For whether any of this constitutes a legally effective opt-out under EU law, see the `eu-ai-act-tdm-opt-out` skill — this reference deliberately stops at the technical and evid The framing sentence in §1 is the one every downstream decision falls out of, and it stands alone as its own paragraph: **"These rules are not a form of access authorization."**[^rfc-1] robots.txt is a cooperative signal to well-behaved automation — not a security boundary, not an ACL, not enforceable by the protocol. - **`Sitemap` is named in RFC 9309 — explicitly as a record that is *not part of the protocol*.** "Sitemap isn't in RFC 9309" is half right: the token appears, the semantics are disclaimed, and the only mandate is that it must not break group parsing. - **`Crawl-delay` does not appear in RFC 9309 at all.**[^rfc-1] Nor does `Host`. - **`Allow` *is* normative** — §2.2.2 is literally titled *"The 'Allow' and 'Disallow' Lines"*. Sources that group `Allow` with the non-standard extensions are describing the pre-RFC era. - **An empty `Disallow:` value has no defined meaning in RFC 9309.**

[low] Live Migration and Mongosync are not supported on minor versions and will not work if the cluster uses Latest Version With Auto Upgrades. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-versions.md [medium] A major version upgrade in MongoDB Atlas requires at least one replica set election and uses a rolling update process to maintain cluster availability. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/tutorial/major-version-change.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-versions.md [low] To upgrade a sharded cluster, stop the balancer, upgrade the Config server replica set first, then upgrade the Shard replica sets in parallel using a rolling manner, and finally upgrade the last mongos, restarting the balancer afterwards. Sources: https://www.percona.com/blog/upgrade-process-of-percona-server-for-mongodb-replica-set-and-shard-cluster/ [low] An Atlas Core cluster on a minor version with Latest Version With Auto Upgrades can only switch to a major-version cadence when the next major version becomes available, such as remaining on the latest minor until MongoDB 9.0 is released if opting in during MongoDB 8.3. (verified as of 2026-10-15) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-versions.md [low] Atlas uses a rolling update strategy for maintenance and infrastructure operations, directing the primary node to step down to secondary state to trigger an election of a new primary. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/faq/deployment.md [low] For replica set upgrades, start by upgrading secondaries one by one, then log into the Primary node and stepDown it, repeating the process once a new primary is elected. Sources: https://www.percona.com/blog/upgrade-process-of-percona-server-for-mongodb-replica-set-and-shard-cluster/ [medium] Always take a full backup of the database before performing an upgrade, and when making downgrades, remove incompatible features or update incompatible configuration settings. Sources: https://www.percona.com/blog/upgrade-process-of-percona-server-for-mongodb-replica-set-and-shard-cluster/, https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/update-major.html [low] Atlas Infinite clusters always use Auto Upgrades with the Latest Version With Auto Upgrades option enabled, which cannot be disabled in the Atlas UI, and are updated about once a month without the option to select a spec

items.text: Routed-expert ownership split under ds4 streaming TP Under ds4 TP each rank computes only the routed experts whose global id falls in its half of the 256-expert range (rank 0 low half, rank 1 high half, rank 1 taking any odd remainder) and exchanges the partial FFN sums at one gate per sparse layer. Under ds4 TP each rank computes only the routed experts whose global id falls in its half of the 256-expert range (rank 0 low half, rank 1 high half, rank 1 taking any odd remainder) and exchanges the partial FFN sums at one gate per sparse layer. In a streaming TP run the split is the same by expert id, but it is enforced inside the kernels, not by mapping only half of the file. Resident (non-streaming) TP: `tp_shard` is true and `weights_model_map_sharded_spans` maps only this rank's contiguous expert range of each gate, up and down tensor, so the kernels see a blob that starts at the first owned expert. `tp_expert_base` rebases expert ids to that blob. Streaming TP: `tp_shard = role != DS4_TP_NONE && !e->ssd_streaming` is false, so no sharded map is built. The Metal routed-MoE binders set `streaming_tp = g_ssd_streaming_mode && g_tp_split_world == 2` and then reset `first_expert = 0` and `n_bind_expert = n_total_expert`. The binders' own comment gives the reason: streaming address tables are indexed by global expert id, so model offsets stay global and "the kernels enforce rank ownership before dereferencing the selected address". The ownership test lives in `metal/moe.metal`: with `tp_world <= 1` every expert is owned; otherwise `first = tp_rank * (n_total / tp_world)` and `last` is `n_total` for the last rank, else `first + n_total / tp_world`. Many kernels begin with `if (!owned) return` (or `continue` inside loops) and index weights with `expert - args.tp_expert_base`. The split is carried by `tp_rank`, `tp_world`, `tp_expert_base` and `tp_addend` fields added to the mul-mv-id kernel argument structs. The host function `ds4_gpu_tp_expert_range` implements the contiguous split: `low_experts = n_total / 2`; rank 1 starts at `low_experts` and owns the remainder. Consequence for streaming: each rank selects the same 6 routed experts per token (the router runs on both ranks, replicated), but only the experts that land in its half are fetched and computed; experts owned by the peer are skipped before any address is dereferenced. A rank therefore needs the SSD stream only for its own half of each layer's experts. The ownership split is mandatory on the decode p

Entry point: a request for a non-running model joins a first-in-first-out queue (requests for the same model share one entry). Only the model at the head of the queue may claim a slot, and only when the running count is below `models_max`. `is_running()` is true for LOADING, LOADED and SLEEPING. UNLOADED is set only when the child process exits. A model that has been told to stop still counts as running until its process has exited. Eviction: `tick()` and `unload_lru()` choose a victim that is idle (no in-flight request), ready or sleeping, not already stopping, not wanted by a queued request, and least recently used. The router sends the stop command and the monitor force-kills after `stop_timeout` (default 10 s, per-model preset key `stop-timeout`). A child still LOADING is killed at once. Load: `load()` calls `unload_lru()` first; that call blocks on a condition variable until the victim reaches UNLOADED. Then `load()` re-checks capacity under the lock and throws "model limit reached, try again later" if the cap is still hit. Only after that does it pick a free port and spawn the new child. Waiters re-check every 200 ms; if every model is busy, no victim exists and the request waits. Result: unload completes before the replacement process is spawned, so at most `models_max` children exist at once, plus the kernel's lag in returning the exited process's memory. Older reports (discussion 18939, early 2026) show a second model failing with an allocation error instead of evicting, and `--models-max` ignored when set only in the INI file; the queue scheduler (`server_lru_sched`) present on master on 2026-10-04 is newer. The PR that added it was not found. `--models-max 0` disables the cap and eviction. The cap counts models, not bytes: two large models that fit under the count can still exceed memory. A sleeping model (idle-sleep) keeps its slot, so `--sleep-idle-seconds` does not free a router slot. [asserted from `is_running()`] If the number of startup models exceeds `models_max`, the router refuses to start with "number of models to load on startup (N) exceeds models_max (M)". items.text: router top-k agreement under quantization as a diagnostic Why top-k is a cliff: the router picks experts with a hard top-k on scores, so a small perturbation of hidden state or router logits flips an expert only when it moves the k-th and (k+1)-th scores across each other. The change in computation is then a different expert, not a small numeric error. ... Why top-k is a cliff: the router picks experts with a hard top-k on scores, so a small perturbation of hidden state or router logits flips an expert only when it moves the k-th and (k+1)-th scores across each other. The change in computation is then a different expert, not a small numeric error. Margin between the k-th selected and nearest non-selected score is therefore what makes a token fragile. Two perturbation routes: the router's own weights (quantization error in the gate matrix) and the router's input (hidden states already perturbed by quantized attention, earlier experts and shared experts). With llama-quantize the router is copied at source precision, so GGUF disagreements come only from the second route; with an MLX 4-bit conversion the gate is 8-bit g64 on newer model classes (and 4-bit on Mixtral), so both routes act. Metric used by VSRAQ: Jaccard(T_fp, T_q) = |T_fp intersect T_q| / |T_fp union T_q| per token and MoE layer, over 616,759 tokens drawn from the stem, chat, math and code subsets of Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2, plotted layer by layer under W4A16. Other agreement forms in use: overlap of the selected set under teacher forcing; rank order among the selected experts; margin to the first non-selected expert; and the divergence between full-precision and quantized routing probability distributions (EAQuant uses KL on routing probabilities as a training loss). Teacher forcing is required: both models must read the same BF16-chosen token stream (as KLD runs do), otherwise free-running text diverges and agreement is undefined. Where to hook on a Mac: llama.cpp's imatrix collector already copies the routed `ids` of every MUL_MAT_ID (expert matmul) node to the host, so a two-model comparison tool can reuse that callback; MLX has no stock hook and needs a patched gate module that records its argpartition indices. 2025-06: EAQuant (arXiv 2506.13329) adds router-logit distribution alignment (logit reconstruction plus KL between full-precision and quantized routing probabilities) and keeps the router at W8A8. 2025: EAC-MoE (ACL 2025) calibrates routers and uses a top-n-k "TopK-MSE" loss

items.text: Runbook Craft A runbook is not a piece of documentation. It is a procedural script someone must execute correctly while tired, under pressure, with paging alerts firing in the background. Every step must be unambig A runbook is not a piece of documentation. It is a procedural script someone must execute correctly while tired, under pressure, with paging alerts firing in the background. Every step must be unambiguous to a person who did not write it and may never have run it before. A runbook is only correct if a person who has never run it before, on a freshly provisioned environment, with no tribal context, can complete it successfully. Schedule a quarterly drill where someone who did not author the runbook runs it end-to-end on a sandbox or staging clone. Every pause is a defect in the runbook, not in the runner. Each step performs exactly one action that produces exactly one verifiable result. The verb comes first. Bad: "Now we need to make sure that the broker is running and you may also want to check the lag, and if the lag is high then restart things." Run kafka-broker-api status --broker mdb-prod-1. Expected output: STATUS: HEALTHY. Run kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group mdb-tam-consumer. Record the LAG column. If LAG > 50000, go to step 7 (broker restart). Otherwise continue to step 4. Section banners at the top of each major phase: === PHASE 2 of 5: failover the primary ===. State-check steps at the boundary of each phase. Numbered top-level steps that never restart: use 1-25 across the whole runbook. A complete prerequisites block contains: Access: which SSO group, which IAM role, which secrets vault entry. Tools and versions: mongosh >= 2.0, aws-cli >= 2.13, jq. Inputs: cluster ID, account ID, ticket number. Approvals: who must sign off in writing before step 1. Communication: which Slack channel to post in. A rollback section answers four questions: What signals trigger a rollback? Quantitative thresholds. ("Error rate > 2% sustained for 5 minutes." Not "if things look bad.") What is the rollback command? Exact, copy-pasteable. What is the rollback verification? What is the data-loss / state-loss implication? Bad: "If memory looks high, restart the service." Good: "If mem_used_pct > 85 for 3 consecutive samples, restart the service (step 12)." items.summary: Anemll's docs credit rustane as the inspiration for cached-read fanout, describe the idea in prose and publish no rustane figures.
items.text: rustane warm-page-cache pread fanout (ncdrone/rustane) Anemll's docs credit rustane as the inspiration for cached-read fanout, describe the idea in prose and publish no rustane figures. Anemll's docs credit rustane as the inspiration for cached-read fanout, describe the idea in prose and publish no rustane figures. ncdrone/rustane describes itself as a Rust training and inference engine for the Apple Neural Engine and Metal GPU, validated for training from 48M to 5B parameters on an M4 Max 128 GB using reverse-engineered private ANE APIs. The rustane README sections are Benchmarking, Checkpoint Inference (a generate CLI with Metal KV-cache decode) and HTTP Serving (OpenAI-style completion routes); none concerns expert streaming or page-cache reads. The rustane results directory holds ANE and GPU TFLOPS, IOSurface staging, dual-load, f16 conversion, training probe and Rust-versus-Objective-C comparison notes, and no pread or page-cache note. The rustane bench directory holds three Python scripts (dual_load.py, gpu_metal_matmul.py, gpu_tflops.py). rustane's CREDITS file lists Anemll for ANE inference tricks and does not mention Flash-MoE or page-cache reads. Anemll says its cache I/O split experiment "is not a code import from rustane" and is built on Flash-MoE's existing async routed-expert pread path. Anemll's cachebench note says its scaling curve is "close to the pattern reported in rustane", naming only the shape, one worker near raw-storage speed then a sharp multi-worker climb. The Anemll cachebench with split greater than 1 schedules the same total bytes as split 1 (for 128 experts and split 4, 512 tasks instead of 128), so the gain comes from more concurrent cached reads, not extra data. ncdrone/rustane master shows its last commit on 2026-04-03 and 181 stars at the 2026-10-04 fetch. Nothing in rustane's public default branch supports or refutes the warm-cache pread scaling curve; the Anemll cachebench is the only measured evidence for that curve.

items.concept: Sales and Marketing Copy
items.summary: Reference for conversion-focused writing: landing pages, emails, ads, CTAs, and positioning copy. Sources: Schwartz Breakthrough Advertising (1966), Ogilvy Confessions of an Advertising Man, Sugarman
items.text: Sales and Marketing Copy Reference for conversion-focused writing: landing pages, emails, ads, CTAs, and positioning copy. Sources: Schwartz Breakthrough Advertising (1966), Ogilvy Confessions of an Advertising Man, Sugarman Reference for conversion-focused writing: landing pages, emails, ads, CTAs, and positioning copy. Sources: Schwartz Breakthrough Advertising (1966), Ogilvy Confessions of an Advertising Man, Sugarman The Adweek Copywriting Handbook, Cialdini Influence, Halbert/Carlton copy classics. When invoked, follow this sequence before producing any copy: Identify the awareness stage (Section 2) of the target audience. If unclear, ask: "Who is the primary reader - do they already know they have this problem, or are they discovering it for the first time?" Identify the conversion goal - one goal per piece (landing page demo request, email reply, ad click). If multiple goals are stated, flag the conflict and recommend choosing one. Choose the framework - AIDA for structured persuasion flows; PAS for pain-first framing; headline formulas for ad/email entry points. Produce copy or a skeleton - for pages, produce a full section-by-section skeleton with placeholder copy and notes on what each section must accomplish. For emails, produce a complete draft. For subject lines or CTAs, produce 3–5 options with rationale. When the request is ambiguous, ask one targeted question before producing copy. Do not ask more than one question per turn. The foundational direct-response sequence. Each stage earns permission to proceed to the next. Practical note: AIDA is a reader state sequence, not a section-by-section template. A long-form sales page may cycle through the sequence multiple times before the final CTA. Pain-first frame. Effective when the audience already feels the problem but has not connected it to your solution. Problem - Name the problem precisely. Specificity signals that you understand the reader's world. ("Your email open rates dropped 40% after iOS 15.") Agitate - Deepen the pain. Enumerate the downstream costs: lost revenue, wasted time, damaged relationships, compounding risk. Do not manufacture fear; surface consequences the reader already suspects but has not named. Solve - Present your product/service as the clear, logical resolution. The transition from agitation to solution should feel like relief. Schwartz warning: Agitation without a credible solve creates distrust, not conversion. Match the intensity of the pain to the scale of the pro

The single most useful structural finding in this synthesis is not stated in any one input report: **the federal statutory definition of a salvage automobile and the insurer's operating total-loss rule are the same inequality, algebraically rearranged.** Four sources that appear to describe different tests describe one test with different terms added to the left-hand side. The two agencies are not strictly in conflict — one governs first-party claim settlement, the other governs ad valorem property assessment — but they take opposite positions on whether the brand alone is a valid basis for a number. Only New York was checked among claims regulators; whether other states' regulators take the New York position is unknown. **Unresolved.** **Concept:** Salvage and Clean-Title Vehicle Valuation **Parent domain:** Used Car Auctions and Buying **Report type:** mechanism / internal structure **Date:** 2026-09-19 **C21. Salvage auction prices are driven by inputs largely unrelated to the individual vehicle's condition.** Copart's 10-K disclosure identifies market demand for rebuildable vehicles, used-car pricing, end-market demand for recycled and refurbished parts, sale mix, U.S. dollar exchange rates against foreign currencies, and commodity prices — particularly per-ton crushed-body prices — as the drivers of auction selling price. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/900075/000090007519000022/cprt07312019-10k.htm)) Scrap price and FX are therefore part of salvage valuation in a way th 10. The same rule constrains the adjustment layer that sits on top of the comparables: "Any additions or deductions from the actual cash value must be explained to the claimant and must be itemized showing specific dollar amounts." Permitted deductions include prior unrepaired damage (capped at the actual value decrease) and salvage value when the claimant retains the vehicle. — https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-391 **S23. Run status: COMPLETED. A network denial appears as `Sandbox: <App>(<pid>) deny(1) network-outbound <path>` plus a `Violation:` line, Process, Identifier, and a thread backtrace. The `Violation:` line names the operation and the backtrace locates the offending code. Apple's own example is a denied connect to `/private/var/run/mDNSResponder`. (high confidence) Some sandbox denials never reach the violation log; they show only in the app's stderr (Xcode Debug pane) as lines such as `connect() failed path:/var/run/mDNSResponder ... Operation not permitted`, `Sandbox is preventing this process from reading networkd settings file`, or `Sandbox does not allow access to com.apple.dnssd.service`. A harness should capture both stderr and the unified log. (medium confidence) The system creates the sandbox container, `~/Library/Containers/<bundle-id>/`, when a sandboxed app first launches. Inside it the app has unrestricted read/write; it does not have unrestricted access to the home folder. `NSSearchPathForDirectoriesInDomains`-style lookups return container paths for a sandboxed app. (medium confidence) To see sandbox denials, open Console, paste `type:error`, `subsystem:com.apple.sandbox.reporting` and `category:violation` into the search field (one at a time), save the search, click Start Streaming, then reproduce the problem. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02) Preflight checks such as `access()` never produce a sandbox violation report, so code that preflights can fail silently with no deny line. Run status: COMPLETED. vLLM Production Stack is a Kubernetes-native reference deployment that adds KV-cache-aware, load-aware and prefix-aware routing, KV cache sharing/offload, KEDA autoscaling and observability, which have no counterpart in a plain nginx-in-front-of-Ollama setup. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Switch trigger: Red Hat concludes Ollama suits local dev, prototyping and single-user apps while vLLM suits production and high-concurrency workloads. Because Ollama queues beyond its parallel slots (TTFT rises sharply) while vLLM batches, adding Ollama replicas buys slots linearly per GPU but not batching efficiency. (medium confidence) Rule for sizing a replica: its concurrency ceiling is its OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL, because a tuned Ollama throughput plateaus there (McDermott) and an untuned one at a few requests (the Applied Sciences paper, bottleneck near 10 users at NUM_PARALLEL=4). To serve N concurrent clients, either raise NUM_PARALLEL on each replica (memory grows by NUM_PARALLEL x context length) or add replicas. Past the point where VRAM limits the parallel slots, the benchmarks favour vLLM's continuous batching. (low confidence) LiteLLM routing strategies are `simple-shuffle` (default and recommended for production), `least-busy` (fewest active requests; suited to high concurrency), `usage-based-routing` (lowest TPM/RPM usage; documented as "bad for perf" because of Redis tracking), `latency-based-routing` and `cost-based-routing`. Set `rpm`/`tpm` on a deployment to cap it, and `order` to prioritise deployments. When running several LiteLLM proxy instances, set redis_host/redis_port so load-balancing state is shared. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Do not extrapolate one benchmark: each is one model on one box with a particular Ollama build and NUM_PARALLEL. Red Hat (a vendor of vLLM-based products) used one A100 and Llama 3.1 8B; the Applied Sciences paper used one H100 and Qwen3-4B; McDermott used two A6000s and Qwen3-14B. Treat the direction as established and the multiples (3x to 29x) as workload specific. Reproduce on your own model, context length and concurrency before migrating. (high confidence) Ollama's documented concurrency has two levels inside one server: several models loaded at once if memory allows, and parallel request

items.concept: Scheduled and Predictive Scaling for Atlas Cost
items.summary: Atlas has no documented native time-of-day tier schedule, so time-pattern cost control comes from two mechanisms: predictive auto-scaling, which scales eligible clusters up ahead of forecast cyclical spikes and never scales down, and customer-run pause and resume schedules for non-production dedicated clusters, where a paused cluster is charged for storage only and auto-resumes after 30 days. Reactive scale-down stays conservative (a 24-hour cooldown and 4-hour low-load window), so spiky batch workloads can sit on a larger tier for many hours. The pack holds 127 source-anchored units from 8 sources (5 hosts: MongoDB docs and engineering blog, a prototype write-up, a third-party pause guide, a customer feedback thread) across 11 facets, with 2 conflicts over scale-down rules and prototype versus shipped planner behavior.
items.text: Scheduled and Predictive Scaling for Atlas Cost Atlas has no documented native time-of-day tier schedule, so time-pattern cost control comes from two mechanisms: predictive auto-scaling, which scales eligible clusters up ahead of forecast cyclical spikes and never scales down, and customer-run pause and resume schedules for non-production dedicated clusters, where a paused cluster is charged for storage only and auto-resumes after 30 days. Reactive scale-down stays conservative (a 24-hour cooldown and 4-hour low-load window), so spiky batch workloads can sit on a larger tier for many hours. The pack holds 127 source-anchored units from 8 sources (5 hosts: MongoDB docs and engineering blog, a prototype write-up, a third-party pause guide, a customer feedback thread) across 11 facets, with 2 conflicts over scale-down rules and prototype versus shipped planner behavior. What it is: Predictive auto-scaling is an enhancement to Atlas auto-scaling. This predictive system uses demand forecasting to anticipate workload surges, meaning clusters' compute can scale up preemptively using past cyclical patterns, providing clusters with the necessary resources before a workload spike occurs. Note that this only occurs in scale-up events; scale-down is still triggered only by existing scaling logic. This enhancement adheres to the min and max cluster tiers configured by users. Pausing Atlas clusters during off-hours is the most straightforward cost-saving measure for non-production environments. Use the Atlas CLI for ad-hoc operations and GitHub Actions scheduled workflows to automate pause at end-of-day and resume at start-of-day. Always wait for the cluster to reach `IDLE` state before running application workloads after resuming. Predictive auto-scaling is an extension of auto-scaling. Forecaster: tries to predict each replica set's future workload Estimator: estimates CPU% for any workload, any instance size Planner: chooses the cheapest instance that satisfies forecasted demand By combining these components, we forecast each metric separately, creating a "Long-Term Forecaster" for each. Despite the name, the Long-Term Forecaster doesn't project far into the future; it's trained on several weeks of data to capture patterns, then predicts a few hours ahead. Reactive scale-down is conservative. Atlas scales down only if the cluster was not scaled, provisioned or unpaused in the past 24 hours and no node restarted in the past 12 hours. There are two important features related to storage that affect how space is used in MongoDB: BSON and dynamic schema. Shortening field names reduce expressiveness and does not provide considerable benefit for larger documents and where document overhead is not of significant concern. Shorter field names do not lessen the size of indexes because indexes have a predefined structure. In general, it is not necessary to use short field names. Shorter field names do not shrink indexes: index entries hold key values with a predefined structure, not field names. Allegro also found index size unchanged when switching _id from string to int32. MongoDB's own guidance: field names compress well under WiredTiger block compression, so the additional benefit of short field names is modest; do not abbreviate to single letters because it obscures data. I am sorry I just saw this in my box. Wiredtiger is still just storing the BSON structure which has the field name, its bit length, and then its content for each field. items.text: Scientific Phylogenetics (ETE Toolkit) ETE (Environment for Tree Exploration) is a Python toolkit for phylogenetic and hierarchical tree analysis. Core use cases: tree I/O and manipulation, evolutionary event detection, NCBI taxonomy integ ETE (Environment for Tree Exploration) is a Python toolkit for phylogenetic and hierarchical tree analysis. Core use cases: tree I/O and manipulation, evolutionary event detection, NCBI taxonomy integration, visualization, and clustering analysis. Use for: loading/pruning/rerooting/traversing Newick/NHX/PhyloXML trees; detecting evolutionary events (duplication, speciation) and identifying orthologs/paralogs; NCBI taxonomy queries, lineage retrieval, tree annotation; tree visualization (PDF/SVG/PNG) with custom NodeStyle/Faces/layout functions; Robinson-Foulds comparison; ClusterTree heatmaps. When not to use: generating sequence alignments, running inference tools (IQ-TREE, RAxML), or general bioinformatics not involving tree structures. NCBI Taxonomy first-run: NCBITaxa() downloads ~300 MB to ~/.etetoolkit/taxa.sqlite on first instantiation; subsequent calls are fast local lookups. Newick format codes (format= on read/write): 0 = flexible w/ branch lengths (default read); 1 = internal node names; 2 = bootstrap/support; 5 = internal names + branch lengths; 8 = all features; 9 = leaf names only; 100 = topology only. Resubmitting closes the Resolution Center line of communication, so the safe order is: reply with evidence (e.g. screen recording), wait for the reviewer to confirm or answer, then resubmit only if a code or metadata change is needed. Replies without resubmitting do get answers in practice, but replying alone does not necessarily trigger a fresh review cycle. (medium confidence) Apple's help text does not document file-size limits, accepted video formats, or whether a link versus an uploaded file is preferred for screen recordings; the pages checked state only that other file types are allowed. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02) Apple's Resolution Center reply lets Account Holder, Admin, or App Manager roles send up to 4,000 characters and attach files (screenshots, supporting documents) to a rejection reply; the thread stays open only until the developer resubmits to App Review. (high confidence) For features hard to reproduce in review (hardware, special environments, unusual behaviour), Apple expects a demo video or the hardware; a video can be attached via the Attachment field in App Review Information, with explanations or links in Review Notes. (high confidence) Apple's FAQ says screenshots may be attached to the Resolution Center reply to show how the app addresses the rejection, and that the Notes/attachments in App Review Information can explain where reviewers find specific features; this applies to a menu-bar app with no main window. (medium confidence) Appeals go to the App Review Board through App Store Connect: give specific reasons the app complies, submit one appeal per rejected submission, and answer any pending information request before appealing. Choosing between them involves evaluating cost, operational burden, feature availability, and your team's infrastructure expertise. If you’re running MongoDB yourself but need more than what the Community Edition offers, MongoDB Enterprise Advanced is the path MongoDB Inc. wants you to take. It’s a subscription-based model, typically priced per server or per core, and it gives you access to the full suite of enterprise features. MongoDB Community Edition is often the starting point for teams looking to avoid licensing costs. And on paper, it’s free to use. But once you start running it in production, the limitations and the hidden costs add up quickly. items.text: Semantic Layer and Headless BI A semantic layer is a centralized, version-controlled, code-defined layer that maps physical warehouse tables to business concepts — entities, dimensions, and metrics — so that "revenue," "active user A semantic layer is a centralized, version-controlled, code-defined layer that maps physical warehouse tables to business concepts - entities, dimensions, and metrics - so that "revenue," "active users," or "churn rate" are defined once and computed identically everywhere they are consumed. Headless BI is the architectural pattern that decouples this metrics layer from any single BI tool and exposes it through APIs so many "heads" (dashboards, spreadsheets, notebooks, embedded apps, and AI agents) query the same governed definitions (Cube - What is Headless BI?, 2023; Atlan - Headless BI 101, 2024). The problem it solves: without a central definition store, metric formulas scatter across tools, get recreated and silently diverge, and produce KPI disputes that "never fully disappear." Benn Stancil framed the metrics layer as "the missing piece of the modern data stack" - doing for metrics what dbt did for transformations: making them globally accessible to every downstream tool (Benn Stancil - The missing piece of the modern data stack, 2021; dbt Labs - semantic layer pitfalls, 2025). This topic exploded in relevance in 2024–2026 because AI agents and text-to-SQL need a governed, deterministic source of metric truth to avoid hallucinated joins and inconsistent numbers. The market is estimated at ~$1.73B in 2025 growing toward ~$4.93B by 2030 (5x - Semantic Layer Guide 2025, 2025). > Adjacent skill da-10-tools-and-languages covers SQL/dbt/BI tooling generically. items.summary: Deduplication is a foundational data-curation step in training large language models (LLMs) and creating high-quality text distillation pipelines. Redundant data causes models to memorize specific pas
items.text: Semantic vs Lexical Deduplication for Text Distillation Deduplication is a foundational data-curation step in training large language models (LLMs) and creating high-quality text distillation pipelines. Redundant data causes models to memorize specific pas Deduplication is a foundational data-curation step in training large language models (LLMs) and creating high-quality text distillation pipelines. Redundant data causes models to memorize specific passages, exacerbates overfitting, amplifies biases, and wastes significant computational resources. Deduplication strategies generally fall into two categories: Lexical Deduplication (surface-level string/character matching) and Semantic Deduplication (underlying meaning and intent). Modern text distillation and LLM training pipelines leverage a multi-stage, funnel approach. They typically start with ultra-fast lexical methods like Exact Hashing and MinHash to eliminate verbatim or near-verbatim copies at scale. This is followed by computationally heavier semantic methods utilizing embedding models and Cosine Similarity to remove paraphrased or contextually redundant information. Understanding the trade-offs between MinHash, SimHash, Exact Hash, and Cosine Similarity is critical for optimizing both training efficiency and downstream model generalization. Lexical methods scale exceptionally well but miss paraphrased redundancy. Exact Hash and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) algorithms like MinHash and SimHash operate in sub-quadratic or $O(1)$ lookup times. However, they fail entirely at detecting meaning-based duplicates (e.g., translated texts or rewrites). Semantic methods improve generalization but are bottlenecked by compute. Generating dense vector embeddings and computing pairwise Cosine Similarity (even with approximate nearest neighbor techniques like FAISS) is orders of magnitude more expensive than lexical hashing. MinHash outperforms SimHash for text-based near-duplicate detection. While SimHash is faster and highly efficient for detecting minor bit-level variations, MinHash using Jaccard Similarity on n-gram shingling is the industry standard for high-recall text deduplication in LLM datasets. Exact Hashing is too brittle for standalone use. Exact cryptographic hashes (MD5, SHA-256) are easily thwarted by trivial noise (e.g., trailing whitespace, invisible control characters). items.summary: llama-server, base reuse: `n_past` is the token-level common prefix of the slot's stored tokens and the new prompt. Everything after the first differing token is recomputed unless chunk reuse applies.
items.text: Server-side prefix cache behavior under rolling-window transcripts llama-server, base reuse: `n_past` is the token-level common prefix of the slot's stored tokens and the new prompt. Everything after the first differing token is recomputed unless chunk reuse applies. llama-server, base reuse: `n_past` is the token-level common prefix of the slot's stored tokens and the new prompt. Everything after the first differing token is recomputed unless chunk reuse applies. llama-server, chunk reuse (`n_cache_reuse` > 0): after the common prefix, two cursors scan the stored tokens (`head_c`) and the new prompt (`head_p`). When the next run of equal tokens is at least `n_cache_reuse` long, the server removes the KV cells between the cursors, shifts that run's positions by `head_p - head_c`, copies the token ids across and counts the run into `n_past`. Shorter matches advance `head_c` by one. This recovers the tail after a dropped middle block on pure-attention models only. Chunk reuse is gated: it needs `llama_memory_can_shift` and a prompt without multimodal tokens. Otherwise the server logs "cache reuse is not supported - ignoring n_cache_reuse = N". Slot choice: with `slot_prompt_similarity` non-zero, the idle slot with the highest ratio (common prefix length divided by the new prompt length) above the threshold wins; otherwise the least recently used idle slot is taken. `f_keep` is the share of the chosen slot's stored tokens that survive. If `f_keep` is below 0.5, or the slot came from LRU, the server saves the slot's old state to the host-memory prompt cache first and then tries to load the best stored match for the new prompt. Head-drop effect: when the window drops the oldest messages, the common prefix with the stored slot is only the system prompt; the similarity ratio collapses, an LRU or low-similarity pick follows, and the old long state is parked in the prompt cache where a later request that restores the longer history can still use it. oMLX: block hashes chain from the first block (each hash covers the parent hash and one block of tokens), so a head change makes every later block miss. The scheduler reports the "closest stored sequence" and how many leading tokens agree. There is no source showing an oMLX equivalent of llama.cpp's chunk shifting. items.text: Shard key selection for query isolation Source-anchored research for Shard key selection for query isolation. Run status: COMPLETED. High cardinality alone does not ensure even distribution: frequent shard-key values can bottleneck chunks, while monotonically increasing or decreasing values can concentrate new inserts on the MaxKey or MinKey range. Evaluate value frequency and insert patterns alongside cardinality when selecting a key. (high confidence) Scatter-gather is valid for some workloads: MongoDB documents that it can parallelize large aggregations. Repeated cross-shard requests for routine queries, however, add fan-out and do not scale linearly with shard count. A community discussion records a counterpoint that scatter-gather may help when each shard's working set fits in memory, then challenges whether that benefit survives the extra work as shards are added; evaluate the exception against the actual workload. (high confidence) MongoDB can target a query containing the full shard key or a prefix of a compound shard key to the shard or shards holding the matching data. Queries without shard-key fields are generally broadcast to all shards, so frequent request filters should align with the shard key when query isolation matters. (high confidence) An ordinary index on a non-shard-key field does not give mongos shard-level query isolation. A predicate that includes the shard key or a compound-key prefix can target the shard or subset that owns matching data; when mongos cannot determine the location from the predicate, it generally broadcasts to all shards. (high confidence) Choose a key against the dominant query and write workload rather than a convenient field. MongoDB describes the ideal key as one that distributes data evenly and facilitates common query patterns. Percona illustrates the tradeoff with a posts collection whose post_id key isolates single-post reads, even though append writes can concentrate on one shard. AWS gives similar query-frequency, usage-pattern, and cardinality guidance for Amazon DocumentDB Elastic Clusters; that is cross-system support for the selection heuristic, not evidence about MongoDB routing. (high confidence) Choose a shard key against both common query patterns and distribution needs. MongoDB recommends a key that distributes data evenly while facilitating common query patterns; Percona describes the practical balance as spreading insertions while serving each query from as few shards as possible, ideally one.

[1](1, 2) On Atlas Core clusters, data-bearing servers are the machines that run the nodes holding your application data. In a sharded cluster, each shard is a replica set whose members are the data-bearing servers. Sharded clusters may also use config servers, which are billed separately from the data-bearing servers. Sharding is a method for distributing data across multiple machines. MongoDB uses sharding to support deployments with very large data sets and high throughput operations. MongoDB partitions sharded data into chunks. Each chunk has an inclusive lower and exclusive upper range based on the shard key. Hashed Sharding computes a hash of the shard key field's value. Each chunk is then assigned a range based on the hashed shard key values. Ranged sharding divides data into ranges based on the shard key values, with each chunk assigned one of those ranges. config servers: Config servers store metadata and configuration settings for the cluster. Config servers must be deployed as a replica set (CSRS). Starting in MongoDB 8.0, you can deploy the config server as a config shard that also stores application data. shard: Each shard contains a subset of the sharded data. Each shard must be deployed as a replica set. Routing with mongos: The mongos acts as a query router, providing an interface between client applications and the sharded cluster. MongoDB uses the shard key to distribute the collection's documents across shards. The shard key consists of a field or multiple fields in the documents. MongoDB's explain output places chunkSkips within each shard's executionStages. Huawei Cloud's FAQ, updated 2025-07-24, interprets it as orphan documents skipped on the current shard and warns that its sample check scans all documents on all shard nodes. Treat chunkSkips as query- and shard-scoped evidence, not a cluster-wide orphan inventory; this scope follows from the per-shard explain structure. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-24) MongoDB's r6.0 query-planner code says it can omit INCLUDE_SHARD_FILTER when the query specifies the full shard key exactly, because that query can only target the owning shard. The current master regression test asserts that a full-shard-key equality plan omits SHARDING_FILTER and that partial-key or non-equality plans retain it. Therefore, absence can be a deliberate optimization and is not a cluster-wide check for orphan documents. (medium confidence) MongoDB defines SHARDING_FILTER as the explain-plan stage that filters orphan documents from shard results. (high confidence) MongoDB Jira SERVER-105047 records an aggregation plan after a shard-key rename and $or match that returned an orphan twice while explain showed no SHARDING_FILTER. Hype/promotional language is a studied problem independent of LLMs: biomedical NLP work formalizes automatic detection of promotional phrasing that overstates research significance. (low confidence) Research on word overuse finds focal words (delve, tapestry, testament, pivotal, underscore, showcasing, crucial, paramount, unwavering) spiked in scientific English and are overused by ChatGPT; human-feedback learning is implicated because participants prefer text containing such words. (medium confidence) Style-based AI detection is unreliable: OpenAI's retired classifier caught 26% of AI text and falsely flagged 9% of human text; a Stanford study found non-native writing is misclassified. Promotional phrasing alone should not be treated as proof. Ring all_reduce switches to one direction and one wire at 32768 bytes or less, mesh multi-wire starts at 512 KiB, and mesh switches algorithm at 32 KiB per wire when size is above 2, so a corruption test must cover sizes on both sides of each Ring sum_scatter changes wire count at 65536 bytes Ring all_gather splits every rank's region into `2 * n_wires` slices of `ceil(n_bytes / (2 * n_wires))` bytes, so tail clamping is exercised only when the size is not a multiple of `2 * n_wires` With constant input, an all_gather or all_sum that moves the wrong slice returns the same values, so constant data cannot detect it UC delivery never reports a lost message, so integrity tests need a timeout as well as an equality check Use `MLX_JACCL_RING=1` (or `--backend jaccl-ring`) to test the ring path separately from the mesh path Integer dtypes give exact expected sums, unlike bfloat16

A size-matched read needs no extra run. Equal-size pairs from that table (no imatrix unless stated): q5_0 and q5_K_S are both 5.21 GiB with KLD 0.022239 and 0.016595, so legacy q5_0 is 1.34 times worse at identical size. q4_0 is 4.34 GiB with KLD 0.071940 while q4_K_S is 4.37 GiB with 0.043136: q4_0 is 0.7% smaller and 67% worse (q4_K_S is 40% lower). Size ordering can invert quality ordering: q4_1 (4.78 GiB, KLD 0.071683) is 4.4% larger than q4_K_M (4.58 GiB, 0.031273) and 2.29 times worse; q5_1 (5.65 GiB, 0.018045) is 6.0% larger than q5_K_M (5.33 GiB, 0.010762) and 1.68 times worse. A smaller file can tie a larger one: q3_K_L with the WT 10m imatrix (4.03 GiB, 0.073077) is 7.1% smaller than q4_0 (4.34 GiB, 0.071940) and within 1.6% of its KLD. The importance matrix is a second axis at fixed size: q4_K_S at 4.37 GiB drops from 0.043136 (none) to 0.031951 (WT 10m), and q2_K at 2.96 GiB drops from 0.445132 (none) to 0.332223 (WT 10m), about 25%. Size-matching without matching imatrix status compares recipes, not formats. The size of the imatrix corpus barely matters there: q2_K with 1k to 10m Wikitext tokens spans KLD 0.3321 to 0.3371, and the README says it sees no consistent improvement from more tokens. Elasticity rule (derived): from q5_K_M to q4_K_M (5.33 to 4.58 GiB, -14%) KLD rises 2.9 times, and from q4_K_M to q3_K_M (4.58 to 3.74 GiB, -18%) it rises 3.3 times. The log-log slope is about -6 to -7, so on LLaMA 3 8B a 1% size gap corresponds to roughly 6 to 7% in KLD between 3- and 5-bit K-quants. Consequence: a 3% size gap can masquerade as a 20% KLD gap, which is the size of difference vendors report between their quants and others. Report KLD together with size difference in percent, and treat a KLD gap smaller than the elasticity times the size gap as explained by size. Baselines are large: the reference logits file for one 14B model on a 1.6 MiB corpus was about 55 GiB, and the guide suggests Q8_0 as the baseline if BF16 cannot be run. A Q8_0 baseline adds its own divergence floor (LLaMA 3 8B q8_0 mean KLD 0.001355), which is small beside 4-bit gaps but not beside 6-bit and 8-bit comparisons. R

items.summary: Frames are 4096 bytes and pipeline depth is 2, so an 8 KB message is two frames and a 32 KB message eight; latency steps with frame count, not with bytes.
items.text: Small-message JACCL all_sum latency microbenchmark protocol Frames are 4096 bytes and pipeline depth is 2, so an 8 KB message is two frames and a 32 KB message eight; latency steps with frame count, not with bytes. Frames are 4096 bytes and pipeline depth is 2, so an 8 KB message is two frames and a 32 KB message eight; latency steps with frame count, not with bytes. `all_sum` on an MLX array is lazy and goes through a distributed primitive on a stream. A timing loop must call `mx.eval` on the result inside the timed region, otherwise it measures graph construction. `barrier()` is itself an `all_sum` of one byte, so a barrier between iterations is a latency probe of the same path and can be used to align ranks. Sizes to sweep: 1 B (barrier), 4 KB (one frame), 8 KB, 16 KB, 32 KB, 32 KB plus 4 B, 64 KB, 512 KB minus 4 B, 512 KB. This crosses the mesh algorithm switch and the multi-wire switch and the ring 32768-byte switch. Warm up past the first call: the first call after init builds lazily allocated state in MLX and the first UC exchange follows the warm-up barrier; discard at least tens of calls. A 2-rank mesh all_reduce of 512 KiB or less runs one wire and one-phase A mesh above 2 ranks switches to reduce-scatter plus all-gather above 32 KiB per wire JACCL frames are 4096 bytes with pipeline depth 2 `MeshGroup::barrier` is a one-byte `all_sum` and can be used as a one-frame latency probe A latency sweep should straddle 32 KiB, 32768 B and 512 KiB, measure each of mesh and ring and each node count, call `mx.eval` inside the timed loop and verify values on the last iteration The MLX docs say JACCL gives communication latency an order of magnitude lower than the ring backend, with no number

Run status: COMPLETED. SMAppService requires that when a sandboxed app registers a daemon, that daemon is itself sandboxed. Apple DTS called this a deliberate change, enforced in macOS 14.4 and not listed in the release notes. An earlier restriction appeared in macOS 14.2. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2024-03-01) A Mac App Store app cannot bundle an unsandboxed privileged helper: Apple DTS states all code shipped via the MAS must be sandboxed, and SMJobBless was never usable from a sandboxed app. DTS advises shipping the privileged daemon as a separate product (installer package or separate app that uses SMAppService), downloaded outside the MAS. (high confidence) SMAppService.agent installs a per-user LaunchAgent only (current user, ~/Library/LaunchAgents); the API cannot install an agent for all users (Apple DTS). (medium confidence) A helper-app login item (SMAppService.loginItem(identifier:)) must be bundled at MyApp.app/Contents/Library/LoginItems/Helper.app. The older SMLoginItemSetEnabled is deprecated from macOS 13. Status 78 (EX_CONFIG) means launchd rejected the job plist; a stale Launch Services database from many dev builds is a common cause. (medium confidence) SMAppService.Status has four values: notRegistered, enabled, requiresApproval, notFound. A user can disable the item in System Settings > Login Items, which leaves it disallowed in the background-task database. The app should read status and prompt rather than assume success. (medium confidence) Under the same restriction, sandboxed daemons on macOS 14.4 may not set StandardInputPath, StandardOutputPath or StandardErrorPath in their launchd plist; registration fails if they do. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-03-01) App Review Guideline 2.4.5 forbids MAS apps from requesting escalation to root or using setuid (v), from auto-launching or running code at startup or login without consent (iii), and from downloading or installing additional code or standalone apps (iv). items.summary: Source-anchored research for Sort direction and compound index prefix rules. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Sort direction and compound index prefix rules Source-anchored research for Sort direction and compound index prefix rules. Run status: COMPLETED. MongoDB Jira issue SERVER-100910 records a reverse-scan planning defect for bounded sorts on compound time-series indexes and lists the fix version as 9.0.0-rc0. Check the deployed server version and explain() plan when applying general reverse-sort rules to this special index type. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) MongoDB can provide an index-backed sort on a compound index when sort keys appear in the same relative order as index keys. A leading subset of index keys can satisfy a sort, but reordering the sort fields does not match that index order. (high confidence) Compound indexes are ordered left to right. Their leading key or keys form the efficient search prefixes; a query that omits the first key cannot use later keys as an equivalent prefix. When a query matches a leading prefix and also filters a later indexed field, MongoDB can scan the prefix and filter that later field, but this can examine more keys than an index whose key pattern matches the query fields directly. (high confidence) MongoDB can use a compound index to provide a sort when requested sort keys follow their order in the index. A sort on a later, non-prefix subset requires equality predicates on every index key before the first sort key. Without those equalities, the index cannot efficiently provide that sort and the plan may need an in-memory SORT stage. (high confidence) For a multi-field sort, the sort key order must match the index key order, and the requested directions must either match the index directions or reverse every direction. For example, index {a: 1, b: -1} supports sorts {a: 1, b: -1} and {a: -1, b: 1}, but not {a: 1, b: 1} or {a: -1, b: -1}. (high confidence) A single-field index can satisfy ascending or descending sorts by scanning forward or backward, so its declared direction does not constrain the requested sort direction. Direction patterns matter for compound sorts with multiple keys. (high confidence) An index pattern that can provide a sort does not guarantee the planner will choose that index; competing indexes and the full query shape can change the winning plan. Check explain() to see whether the plan has an index-backed order or a SORT stage. items.concept: SORT_MERGE and $in sort expansion
items.summary: Source-anchored research for SORT_MERGE and $in sort expansion. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: SORT_MERGE and $in sort expansion Source-anchored research for SORT_MERGE and $in sort expansion. Run status: COMPLETED. SORT_MERGE is a non-blocking planner stage that merges the outputs of N child index scans, each already returning keys in the requested sort order. The planner builds it in two cases: a rooted $or whose clauses each use an index that provides the sort, and 'explode for sort', which rewrites one index scan with point-interval bounds (equality or $in) into one IXSCAN per point and merges them. (high confidence) 'Explode for sort' is the planner rewrite that produces SORT_MERGE for sorted $in queries. If the leading fields of an index scan have point bounds (equality or $in) and the next index fields supply the requested sort, the planner replaces the one multi-interval IXSCAN with one IXSCAN per point combination and joins them with a merge-sort stage. For find({a:{$in:[1,2]}}).sort({b:1}) on index {a:1,b:1}, the planner builds the scans a:[1,1] and a:[2,2], each with b:[MinKey,MaxKey]. Each scan returns documents in b order, so the merge keeps that order and no blocking SORT is needed. (high confidence) The maxScansToExplodeReached explain field arrived with SERVER-48625, 'Add query knobs to explain output and logs', committed on 2020-12-01. The r5.0.0 tag contains that commit (checked with a GitHub compare). The current manual and the server's explain README both list the field under queryPlanner. (medium confidence) The multiplanner scores each candidate as 1 + advanced/works + eofBonus + tieBreakers. The noSortBonus tie-breaker is at most 1e-4 and is withheld only from plans that contain SORT_DEFAULT or SORT_SIMPLE, so a SORT_MERGE plan keeps it. The bonus only breaks ties. A competing plan that is more productive in the trial period can still beat a SORT_MERGE plan. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Several $in lists multiply: two short $in lists on adjacent leading index fields can exceed 200 scans although each list is short, and SERVER-83712 notes that a query with several $in lists may lead to exponential growth. The docs' '201 elements' rule is exact only for a single $in on one leading field. (high confidence) A descending sort does not need a descending index: when the requested sort equals the exact reverse of the sort the index remainder provides, explodeForSort reverses every exploded scan (fixed for $in sorts in 2.6.1). A mixed-direction sort that matches neither the key pattern nor its reverse still ends in a b

items.summary: Source-anchored research for Source-domain collapse in LLM metaphor. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: Source-domain collapse in LLM metaphor Source-anchored research for Source-domain collapse in LLM metaphor. Run status: COMPLETED. Artificial Hivemind (NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks oral) documents mode collapse in open-ended generation on 26K real-world queries: intra-model repetition and, more strongly, inter-model homogeneity, where different models produce strikingly similar outputs. This is the general mechanism that would make the same vehicle domains recur across vendors. (medium confidence) Even when told to avoid metaphor, 6.27% of ChatGPT's text stayed metaphorical, and its metaphor identification differed significantly from a human linguist's: metaphor is used rhetorically without tracking conceptual boundaries, which is the condition under which mixed or ill-fitting source domains slip through. (low confidence) The same study found source-domain variety rose for abstract targets (Politics used 21 distinct source domains), so collapse is topic-dependent rather than uniform. (low confidence) A 2026 computational audit (Chang, Qu, Li, arXiv 2604.04732) reports 'representational collapse': LLMs flatten culturally distinct metaphorical framings, with some prompts (e.g. metaphors for Death under India and China personas) yielding compact clusters that reuse essentially one metaphor; a cultural persona sometimes narrows rather than widens the metaphor space. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) LLM-generated metaphor norms track word-co-occurrence properties (familiarity, metaphoricity) well but track aptness and concreteness, which need topic-vehicle reasoning, only weakly to moderately. That fits vehicle choice driven by frequency rather than fit. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23) In a 20-speech ChatGPT corpus (10 topics, MIPVU-coded), the model heavily favoured the Planting source domain across Education, Economy and Health (e.g. 'sowing seeds of growth', 'cultivating knowledge'): one vehicle domain reused across unrelated targets. (low confidence)

items.text: $source Operators Depth-first rabbithole dossier for $source Operators; source-anchored research pack. - **Concept:** `$source` Operators - **Parent domain:** MongoDB Atlas Stream Processing - **Report type:** mechanism (internal parts, invariants, limits) - **Researched:** 2026-09-19 36. MongoDB's ASP Product Team maintains a public example repository, `mongodb/ASP_example`, described as both a human-readable corpus and a RAG-optimised repository for code generation. Its canonical processor format is a JSON structure beginning with `{ "$source": { ... } }`. ([GitHub, mongodb/ASP_example](https://github.com/mongodb/ASP_example)) 1. `$source` specifies the connection a stream processor streams data from, and is the ingestion point of the pipeline. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-source/ 2. `$source` must be the first stage of any pipeline it appears in. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-source/ 3. A pipeline may contain at most one `$source` stage. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-source/ 4. Once `$source` has ingested a document, ordinary MongoDB aggregation stages may transform it downstream. — https://www.mongodb 11. `timeField` designates an authoritative event timestamp for each ingested message, and its value must be a `$toDate` or `$dateFromString` expression — not a bare field path. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-source/ 12. If `timeField` is omitted, ASP derives the timestamp from the source message's own timestamp; for Kafka this is the broker receipt time. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-source/ (default behavior) ; the Kafka-broker specialization is a secondary-source claim from https://medium.com/mongodb/mongodb-atlas-st 6. `timeField` sets the authoritative event timestamp and accepts only a `$toDate` or `$dateFromString` expression over a source field. When omitted, the source's own message timestamp is used. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-source/ 7. Watermarks are applied only when the pipeline contains `$tumblingWindow`, `$hoppingWindow`, or `$sessionWindow`; a watermark advances only when a document arrives with an event time later than any previously consumed document. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/architecture/ 8. items.concept: Spec Writing
items.summary: An engineering spec is a contract. It says WHAT a system, component, endpoint, or message must do — independent of HOW it is implemented.
items.text: Spec Writing An engineering spec is a contract. It says WHAT a system, component, endpoint, or message must do — independent of HOW it is implemented. An engineering spec is a contract. It says WHAT a system, component, endpoint, or message must do - independent of HOW it is implemented. Three forms dominate modern practice: API specs - machine-readable contracts for HTTP (OpenAPI 3.1) and event-driven (AsyncAPI 3.0) interfaces Behavior specs - executable narratives (Gherkin / Given-When-Then) Data specs - schema contracts (JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf) Joel Spolsky's 2000 series "Painless Functional Specifications" introduced the discipline: a functional spec describes how a product works from the user's perspective; a technical spec describes internal implementation. A spec that says "internally we'll use a Redis cache with 5-minute TTL" has leaked implementation. Litmus test: If you could swap out the implementation entirely and the spec still holds, the spec is at the right level. Contract-first development: agree on the contract before writing code. The OpenAPI / AsyncAPI document is the source of truth. Key top-level fields: openapi - version (3.1.0) info - name, version, description servers - base URLs per environment paths - endpoints, verbs, parameters, request/response shapes components - reusable schemas, parameters, responses, security schemes YAML is preferred over JSON for human authoring. Key concepts in v3.0: Channels are addressable destinations (Kafka topic, AMQP queue) - decoupled from operations Operations describe what an application does on a channel using action: send or action: receive Messages are defined once and referenced from channels and operations Use Gherkin for: business-logic behavior (pricing rules, eligibility checks, state transitions), workflows spanning multiple systems. Avoid Gherkin for: API shape (use OpenAPI), data format (use JSON Schema). A spec is a promise. Once published: Versioning - non-breaking changes bump minor; breaking changes bump major. That is why `mlx_lm.server --draft-model <Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-bf16>` fails with `ValueError: Model type qwen3_5_mtp not supported`. Exactness at temperature needs Leviathan-Chen rejection sampling (accept with probability min(1, p/q), resample from (p-q)+). Naive "sample both and compare" collapses acceptance: OptiQ measured 28% vs 67% greedy on Qwen3.5-4B at temp 1.0 until it implemented rejection sampling (then 57%). The draft and verify distributions must be truncated identically (same top-p/top-k support) or acceptance stays low: OptiQ's 9B acceptance went 32% to 63% and throughput 1.00x to 1.28x after truncating both sides. Why depth is capped on Metal: the K-token verify forward costs roughly K times a single-token forward on Metal, unlike CUDA where spare tensor-core throughput makes it nearly free. Root cause found in MLX: `mx.quantized_matmul` re-reads the weight matrix per row for M=2..8 and only amortizes from about M=16 (4-bit M=7 costs 5.28x M=1; bf16 is flat from M=2). Fixed shapes: ANE graphs are static, so verification is a separate program (CoreML-LLM `verify_qK`, K=3 or 8; Forge verify width T=8 with separate prefill width 64) or a function in a multifunction package; Orion decode already pads every token to a minimum sequence of 16, so a verify batch of up to 16 positions needs no extra dispatch. Commit rule: the target's argmax at each draft row decides acceptance; the longest matching prefix plus one correction or bonus token is committed. Forge commits only the accepted prefix to host-owned KV through `accept(k)`, so rejected drafts never touch the cache. Break-even arithmetic (CoreML-LLM): expected tokens per burst for a K=3 chain is 1 + p + p^2 + p^3; p=30% gives 1.42 and p=50% gives 1.88, which is the break-even on GPU verify; on ANE verify the stated bar is per-position acceptance of at least 70%. 2026-04-14/15 CoreML-LLM tries MTP Path A/C, EAGLE-3, PLD, cross-vocab and a union orchestrator on Gemma 4 E2B; PR #72 serial-decode check refutes batched-fp16 drift as the cause of the accept-rate gap and points at KV contamination; PR #62 earlier blamed bench methodology. 2026-04-17 DRAFTER_DEAD_FOR_E2B closes separate-architecture drafters on that model. Because accept runs per token, grammar and reasoning-budget state advance token by token inside one verify batch, including across the end of a think block. `grammar_should_apply()` returns false for a lazy grammar unless the reasoning-budget state is IDLE or DONE; so inside a think block a drafted token is never checked against the tool or JSON grammar. When the budget reaches DONE while the grammar was not accepting, `common_sampler_accept` replays the matched end sequence into the grammar so a trigger contained in the think-end tag still starts the lazy grammar. With `grammar_first` false, the sampler first draws from the normal chain, then tests the single drawn token against the grammar and, if invalid, resamples after applying the grammar mask; with `grammar_first` true it masks first. A draft token that the grammar rejects therefore ends acceptance at that position; verification keeps the earlier accepted tokens plus the resampled grammar-valid token. The probabilistic variant `common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n_rejection` accepts a draft token with probability min(1, p/q); when the grammar masks the target distribution it zeroes forbidden tokens and rescales the remaining mass (`p_norm = 1/p_sum`) so the residual distribution is not over-weighted. Before verifying, the server clones the slot sampler (`smpl_save`). If a partial acceptance needs a checkpoint restore, it copies the saved sampler back, restores the target and draft state, and re-verifies the accepted prefix in replay mode. For ngram-style drafters with synthetic acceptance probabilities, "synthetic draft tokens do not advance grammar or reasoning state"; only the final replayed token (from the target) calls accept with `is_generated = true`. items.text: Speech Writing A speech is built to be heard, not read. The writer's job is to construct sentences that survive the air between the speaker's mouth and the audience's ear — sentences that can be re-listened-to in re A speech is built to be heard, not read. The writer's job is to construct sentences that survive the air between the speaker's mouth and the audience's ear - sentences that can be re-listened-to in real time only by the listener's short-term memory. Every well-formed speech has the same five-beat skeleton: Hook - a sentence, image, statistic, or question that earns the next 30 seconds. Frame - what this talk is about and why the audience should care. One sentence. Three acts - the body. The rule of three is not aesthetic; it is cognitive. Three things stay with the audience, five don't. Turn - the moment where the talk pivots from explanation to implication. Call to action - what the audience should do, feel, or remember. Carmine Gallo's distillation of TED's curation rule: 18 minutes is the ceiling for a focused, memorable single-speaker talk. For longer slots, structure as multiple sub-talks with clear act breaks. Three is the smallest number that creates a pattern. Use it for: Top-level structure (three acts, three stories, three asks) Sentence-level lists ("government of the people, by the people, for the people") Repeated refrains (Jobs: "Stay hungry. Stay foolish." - repeated three times) Place applause lines at act transitions and the CTA. Never two in a row. Read every draft aloud. If you run out of breath, the sentence is too long. Stage directions are inline notes to the speaker about delivery. They live in the delivery script, not the published transcript. [pause] - short pause, one breath [long pause] - full silence, 2–4 seconds [lower voice] - drop volume to draw the audience in [slow] - drop pace to weight the line [wait for laughter] - explicitly note that the speaker should hold Place directions on their own line above the line they modify, in brackets. Amateur speeches over-explain. Professional speeches withhold, then resolve. Tell a story before naming its lesson; let the room reach the conclusion one beat ahead. Use specific detail, not abstraction. "A blue notebook on the kitchen table" beats "a personal object." Cut your second-best example. Two strong points land harder than three uneven ones. items.text: SSD bandwidth growth per Apple chip generation and 397B projection Apple's March 2026 MacBook Pro release says M5 Pro and M5 Max models deliver "up to 2x faster read/write performance compared to the previous generation", "reaching speeds of up to 14.5GB/s". Apple's March 2026 MacBook Pro release says M5 Pro and M5 Max models deliver "up to 2x faster read/write performance compared to the previous generation", "reaching speeds of up to 14.5GB/s". Apple's footnote: the 14.5 GB/s figure used a preproduction 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max, 128 GB, 8 TB SSD, FIO 3.41, 1024 KB request size, 10 GB test file, IO depth 8, tested January and February 2026. The comparison systems were an M4 Pro with 4 TB SSD and an M4 Max with 8 TB SSD. If "up to 2x" holds at the same test, the M4 Max 8 TB baseline is about 7.2 GB/s. This is derived from Apple's ratio, not stated by Apple. Third-party Blackmagic Disk Speed Test readings on an M4 Max Mac Studio: a 512 GB model reads about 5.0 to 5.2 GB/s (writes 3.9 to 5.7 GB/s); a 2 TB model reads 5.2 GB/s in one post (writes 6.3 to 8.4 GB/s, fluctuating), and another 2 TB owner reports 6.78 GB/s read and 6.94 GB/s write. A 5 GB test reads 5.2 GB/s and writes 4.3 GB/s. Forum posters in that thread say the 512 GB, 1 TB and 2 TB configurations are slower than the 4 TB and 8 TB ones, which matches fewer parallel NAND packages in smaller capacities. The thread shows no Apple confirmation. Per-token read volume for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B in the Anemll fork: 27.0 MB per layer at 4-bit and 21.8 MB per layer at Q3, 60 layers. That is 1.62 GB and 1.31 GB per token (derived by multiplication). Ceiling at zero cache hits: at Apple's 14.5 GB/s, 1.62 GB per token gives 8.9 tok/s (4-bit) and 1.31 GB gives 11.1 tok/s (Q3). At Flash-MoE's cold 4-thread `F_NOCACHE` rate of 5.5 GB/s (M3 Max), the ceilings are 3.4 and 4.2 tok/s. All four are derived, not measured. 2026-03: Apple states a 2x storage step from M4 Pro and M4 Max to M5 Pro and M5 Max. The Flash-MoE paper projected about 20% SSD gain per generation, so two generations after the M3 Max would be about 1.44x. Apple's own step for the latest generation alone is up to 2x. Capacity changes bandwidth: a 512 GB machine can read at about 5 GB/s while a large-capacity machine of the same chip reads faster. A streaming projection must name the SSD size. Blackmagic numbers are a different test from FIO at 1024 KB and IO depth 8, and vary run to run (one owner saw 8.4 GB/s write drop to 6.3 GB/s on repeat)

One NVMe "data unit" is 512,000 bytes: 303,071,863 units is printed as 155 TB, which is 303,071,863 x 512,000 B. Read counters do not age the drive the way write counters do; on the M1 reports large read totals (for example 161 TB) sit beside write totals of the same order, which is consistent with swap pages being written and then read back. A 1 TB Apple SSD ages by about 1% of Percentage Used per roughly 27-35 TB written (derived from the reported pairs below), implying a rated life near 2.7-3.1 PB written. Streaming experts from the weight file (Flash-MoE, ds4, SwiftLM) reads file-backed pages; evicting clean file-backed pages needs no write, so steady-state expert streaming should add essentially no wear, unlike OS swap of anonymous memory. Swap of an oversized eagerly loaded model is the write-heavy case: the cached Ollama default-load report of 4.3 million swapouts on a 16 GB Mac is the extreme example (already in moe-expert-offload-to-ssd-on-macos.md); each swapout is a write. Disk-persisted KV caches are the other writer. ds4's default budget is 4096 MiB, it stores a continued checkpoint every 10,240 tokens of a growing conversation, evicts by deleting files, and rewrites a 48-byte header on every hit; write volume therefore grows with total conversation length times checkpoint size, bounded by the budget only in resident bytes, not in lifetime writes. JangPress generates a "prestack" overlay of about 150 GB per Kimi variant on first load into `JANGPRESS_PRESTACK_CACHE_DIR`; that is a one-time 150 GB write per bundle. 2021-02-23: Hacker News item 26244093 (691 points) on a Linus Tech Tips thread reporting M1 Macs with very high SSD writes in the first weeks, attributed to aggressive swap. 2021-07-07: a Medium analysis ("may be overblown") of the 8 GB M1 MacBook Air SSD concern, concluding the user would replace the machine before the SSD failed; the text beyond that is behind a paywall. 2022-09-29: Ask HN 33024863 ("Has the Apple Silicon excessive disk read/write issue been fixed?") collects dozens of smartctl dumps; one reply says it has "mostly been fixed" and that individual apps may still trigger abusive writes.
