items.concept: Voice and Real-Time Agent Design
items.summary: > Scope note: This report covers the application / design layer of voice agents — architecture choices, real-time APIs, turn-taking, latency engineering, orchestration frameworks, components, UX, and
items.text: Voice and Real-Time Agent Design > Scope note: This report covers the application / design layer of voice agents — architecture choices, real-time APIs, turn-taking, latency engineering, orchestration frameworks, components, UX, and > Scope note: This report covers the application / design layer of voice agents - architecture choices, real-time APIs, turn-taking, latency engineering, orchestration frameworks, components, UX, and evaluation. Model-internal speech architecture (Whisper encoders, the Thinker–Talker decomposition, audio tokenization) is deliberately out of scope and is covered by the existing multimodal-llm-architecture reference. Cross-reference that reference for "how the model produces audio"; this report is "how you build and operate a voice product around such models." A voice agent is a real-time conversational system that listens, reasons, and speaks back inside a turn-taking loop tight enough to feel human. The dominant 2024–2026 design tension is cascaded pipelines (STT → LLM → TTS as discrete, swappable stages) versus speech-native / speech-to-speech (S2S) models (one model that ingests and emits audio directly, e.g., OpenAI's gpt-realtime and Google's Gemini Live API). Cascaded wins on control, debuggability, compliance, and provider choice; S2S wins on latency and emotional prosody but is hard to audit and gate (Coval, Speko, Hamming). As of mid-2026, most production voice agents still use cascaded architectures, with S2S adoption projected below 15% in H1 2026 and rising to roughly 25–30% by end of H2 2026 as evaluation tooling and compliance frameworks mature (Coval). The engineering north star is a voice-to-voice latency budget under 800 ms, and the field has converged on streaming everything, semantic turn detection, and first-class barge-in as the table-stakes pattern (Hamming, Smallest.ai). Cascaded = an orchestration layer coordinating specialized services: VAD → streaming STT → LLM → streaming TTS (Softcery). S2S = a single model that "processes the entire exchange in a single latent space with no intermediate representations" (Speko). Trade-off summary (confidence: High - multiple independent sources agree): When to use which: S2S for premium/empathetic experiences (mental-health, coaching, luxury, multilingual); cascaded for high-volume tier-1 support, regulated industries, and complex tool-driven workflows (Coval). A streaming cascade (Deepgram + GPT-4o-mini + Cartesia) can already hit sub-1-second latency, narrowing S2S

items.summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for VPC Peering; source-anchored research pack.
items.text: VPC Peering Depth-first rabbithole dossier for VPC Peering; source-anchored research pack. [high] VPCs are intransitive, allowing you to only expose those components of your application that need access to Atlas. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/network-security.md, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html [low] VPC peering connects customer VPCs to an Atlas VPC to route traffic privately, isolating data flow from the public Internet. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/network-security.md [low] For AWS deployments, Atlas also creates a VPC when you create a VPC peering connection to an AWS VPC, in the same region as the peered VPC. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/faq/networking.md [low] When a cross-account or inter-region VPC Peering Connection is created, a VPC Peering Connection resource is automatically created in the accepter's account. Sources: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/main/website/docs/r/vpc_peering_connection_accepter.html.markdown [low] A container is not created when you first create a project but when you first perform an action that needs a VPC, such as creating a cluster or a peering connection, if a container does not yet exist. Sources: https://github.com/mongodb/terraform-provider-mongodbatlas/issues/684 [low] Atlas creates a VPC when you deploy the first M10+ dedicated paid cluster to a given provider and region. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/faq/networking.md [low] To modify the CIDR block, the target project cannot have M10 or greater clusters with nodes in the target region, cloud backup snapshots stored in the target region, or other VPC peering connections. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/manage-vpc-peering.md [low] You cannot have more than one VPC peering connection between two VPCs at the same time. Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html [high] The Atlas VPC CIDR block must not overlap with the CIDR block of any VPC intended for peering, and you cannot create connections between VPCs with matching or overlapping IPv4 or IPv6 CIDR blocks. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/network-security.md, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/security-vpc-peering.md [high] Use only RFC 1918 private addresses for peering networks

items.text: Wall-power meter calibration of SoC-rail energy estimates The protocol in the one calibrated study: a metering smart plug (Shelly Plug US Gen4) on the Mac, a sustained-decode loop per model at three durations (120, 360 and 720 seconds), three passes each, and a 15-minute idle baseline between runs. The protocol in the one calibrated study: a metering smart plug (Shelly Plug US Gen4) on the Mac, a sustained-decode loop per model at three durations (120, 360 and 720 seconds), three passes each, and a 15-minute idle baseline between runs. The tool's built-in calibration fits the SoC counters to the wall figure with no hand tuning, and every published calibrated number carries the fit's error band (+/-2.6 to 4.5%). Two tiers exist in the same tool: a wall-calibrated tier (sustained loops, with bands) and an "estimated" tier (uncalibrated, used for the real-traffic ledger). The author trusts the estimated tier for ordering, not for the third decimal. The calibration is not constant across workloads. The author reports that the calibration "shifts slightly" for the largest, memory-bound models, so one fitted gain applied to every model would mis-state the biggest ones. Holding a large model resident adds standing power even between tokens. The measured overhead rose with model size and flattened near 21 W once the model was big enough. A per-request marginal estimate with an idle baseline taken with no model loaded would credit that overhead to the requests. Real traffic is more expensive per token than a saturated loop: running below saturation raised cost per token roughly 2 to 3 times over the best-case loop, and the real-traffic ledger prices per total token (prompt plus output) rather than per generated token. 2026-07: the TokenWatt calibration write-up on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (96 GB, macOS 26) followed an RTX 3090 cost study; this is the only calibrated Apple silicon energy-per-token dataset found. Comparing devices with uncalibrated powermetrics or IOReport numbers is unsupported by Apple's own man page ("should not be used for any comparison between devices"); only a wall fit gives a cross-device basis. The fit was made on one machine: a Mac Studio M3 Ultra. Nothing found validates the same gain on a MacBook, an M4 or M5 chip, or a non-Ultra Studio. Cost figures are marginal electricity only. The same article prices the machine at $5,299 (M3 Ultra, 96 GB, 1 TB), so the electricity cost of a few thousand requests ("a tenth of a cent") is dwarfed by amor

items.concept: Web Design
items.summary: Senior web graphic designer for interfaces, layouts, and visual systems.
items.text: Web Design Senior web graphic designer for interfaces, layouts, and visual systems. Senior web graphic designer for interfaces, layouts, and visual systems. Use when: designing pages, components, dashboards, landing pages, hero sections, color palettes, typography systems, UI layouts, or design systems. Skip when: backend-only code with no UI output; data visualization libraries; accessibility auditing of existing UI (use accessibility-ux-reviewer). Visual hierarchy: guide eye from most important to least important White space: breathing room improves readability and focus Consistent spacing: use a spacing scale (4px/8px base) Color: 60/30/10 rule (dominant/secondary/accent) Typography: max 2-3 font families, clear hierarchy (H1/H2/body/caption) Landing page: hero (large headline + CTA) + social proof + features + pricing + CTA Dashboard: sidebar nav + metric cards + charts + tables + status indicators Component: consistent padding, clear active/hover/disabled states, accessible colors Design system: tokens (colors, spacing, typography) → components → patterns → templates Structuring a new landing page, dashboard, or marketing site when there's no existing design system to follow. Reviewing an existing UI for basic visual-design problems (unclear hierarchy, inconsistent spacing, too many typefaces) before a deeper accessibility or UX pass. Establishing a starter design system (tokens → components → patterns → templates) for a product that's outgrown ad hoc, page-by-page styling. Choosing a color palette and typography system for a new interface that needs to look intentional rather than assembled from defaults. Build a landing page using the standard arc: hero (headline + CTA), social proof, features, pricing, closing CTA. Design a dashboard layout combining sidebar navigation, metric cards, charts, tables, and status indicators, applying a consistent spacing scale throughout. items.concept: Whitepaper Writing
items.summary: A whitepaper is a long-form, authoritative B2B document that educates a business reader on a problem and positions a solution.
items.text: Whitepaper Writing A whitepaper is a long-form, authoritative B2B document that educates a business reader on a problem and positions a solution. A whitepaper is a long-form, authoritative B2B document that educates a business reader on a problem and positions a solution. Lighter than academic: persuasion is allowed; citation density is moderate; the author has a point of view. Heavier than a blog post: data and methodology are visible; claims are sourced. Length: 8–20 pages typical; 8–12 is the sweet spot for engagement. Voice: third-person company-as-narrator. Gordon Graham identifies three structural types: Backgrounder: explains a technology, methodology, or product in depth. Numbered-list: "5 Reasons to Adopt X," "10 Pitfalls of Y." Problem/solution: describes an industry-wide problem, evaluates current solutions, presents a new approach. The arc is inverted from a sales pitch: a pitch starts with the product; a whitepaper ends with the product. States the problem, the proposed solution, the most compelling proof point, and the call to action. Written last, after the full paper is drafted. Vendor-neutral rules: Name the problem before naming the product. Discuss competing approaches honestly; their drawbacks should be real, not strawmen. Cite third-party sources for problem-scoping statistics. Use the sponsor "About" block as the only place where company puffery is acceptable. A whitepaper that reads as a thinly disguised sales pitch is rejected by 60% of B2B decision-makers. The right citation density is 2–6 cited claims per page. Source hierarchy (descending credibility): Peer-reviewed academic research and government data Major analyst firms (Gartner, Forrester, IDC, McKinsey) Standards bodies (NIST, ISO, IEEE, W3C) Industry surveys with disclosed methodology and sample size The sponsor's own anonymized data (acceptable for proof sections) The "verify the verifiable" rule: every claim of the form "X% of organizations report Y" must cite a source the reader can access. Embed a real (or anonymized) customer story in the proof section: Challenge → Approach → Result structure (mini case study) One direct customer quote, attributed Two-to-three quantified outcomes 8–12 pages: standard problem/solution 12–16 pages: technical or research-heavy 16–20 pages: research-grade with original primary data 20+ pages: split into a series Design budget: Branded title page, table of contents (clickable PDF), 2–4 charts/infographics minimum, pull quotes every 2–3 page

The contention measure that matters is WindowServer's share of GPU time while a long workload runs, not memory or heat; in the oMLX two-engine Hang class WindowServer held at most 2.8% of GPU time and the class is unrelated to this watchdog. A headless Apple silicon Mac still runs WindowServer against a virtual display; this is why "no monitor" is not the same as "display off". The display-sleep guidance in mlx 3267 (2026-04-27 comment) gives a concrete setting: System Settings, Lock Screen, "Turn display off when inactive: 1 minute". 2026-06-27: `pmset displaysleepnow` (display asleep, system awake) shown on the M5 Max to clear the watchdog panic that `caffeinate -s` plus the env var did not. On M1 and later Mac minis a virtual display is created automatically when no monitor is attached, at a default of 1920 by 1080 non-Retina; dummy HDMI plugs are an Intel-era habit. Whether that virtual display keeps the interactivity check armed is untested in any source found. A second Metal process at a higher scheduling class (`Nice=-5`, `ProcessType=Interactive`) was proposed as a contention cause on macOS 27 and then refuted by measurement (priority parity changed nothing). Scheduling class is not the mechanism for GPU-queue contention. None new. The existing split stands: the env var alone resolves the process kill for most reporters, but is insufficient on an M5 Max with a live display. Does a headless virtual display (no panel) avoid the interactivity kill and the M5 Max stall the way display sleep does? Does macOS 27 change the interactivity check? No source found. items.concept: WiredTiger Block and Prefix Compression as Storage Cost Lever
items.summary: WiredTiger compresses MongoDB collection data with block compression (snappy by default, zlib and zstd optional, zstd by default for time series collections) and compresses index keys with prefix compression (on by default), which cuts on-disk bytes and so the provisioned storage bill at the price of extra CPU; collection data stays uncompressed in the WiredTiger cache. Drawn from 6 sources (MongoDB manual and FAQ, WiredTiger documentation, a Percona benchmark, two third-party blogs), covering definitions, mechanisms, parameters, how-to, measures, problems and comparisons; the sources disagree on whether compact recompresses existing data and on typical compression ratios.
items.text: WiredTiger Block and Prefix Compression as Storage Cost Lever WiredTiger compresses MongoDB collection data with block compression (snappy by default, zlib and zstd optional, zstd by default for time series collections) and compresses index keys with prefix compression (on by default), which cuts on-disk bytes and so the provisioned storage bill at the price of extra CPU; collection data stays uncompressed in the WiredTiger cache. Drawn from 6 sources (MongoDB manual and FAQ, WiredTiger documentation, a Percona benchmark, two third-party blogs), covering definitions, mechanisms, parameters, how-to, measures, problems and comparisons; the sources disagree on whether compact recompresses existing data and on typical compression ratios. zlib and zstd are the alternative block compressors, set globally with storage.wiredTiger.collectionConfig.blockCompressor, or per collection/index at creation (e.g. configString block_compressor=zstd). Index prefix compression is disabled with storage.wiredTiger.indexConfig.prefixCompression. When it comes to optimizing MongoDB, compression is a key lever for reducing storage footprint, minimizing I/O bottlenecks, and even speeding up data transfer. The benefits are clear: significant cost savings and the ability to handle more data within the same infrastructure. But with options available, which method should you choose? When data is written to disk, MongoDB compresses it with a specified block compression method and then writes it to disk. When this data block is read, it decompresses it in memory and presents it to the incoming request. WiredTiger does not store information with file blocks to identify the compression engine used to compressed the block. Applications wanting to upgrade to some future compression engine (without requiring a file dump and re-load), should ensure each compressed block includes enough information to identify the compression engine used, so its compression code can correctly decompress old and new blocks. If any new collection is created in the default manner, it will always be the default snappy or compression method specified in the mongod config file. Data in the filesystem cache is the same as the on-disk format, including benefits of any compression for data files. The filesystem cache is used by the operating system to reduce disk I/O. zstd level defaults to 6 in WiredTiger and is tunable (MongoDB blockCompressorQuality 1-22 per blogs). items.summary: Source-anchored research for WiredTiger cache eviction and dirty ratio. Run status: COMPLETED.
items.text: WiredTiger cache eviction and dirty ratio Source-anchored research for WiredTiger cache eviction and dirty ratio. Run status: COMPLETED. The default WiredTiger cache is the larger of 50% of (RAM minus 1 GB) or 0.256 GB. WiredTiger reserves no separate part of the cache for reads and writes, so clean and dirty pages share one budget. Every threshold above is a fraction of this configured cache, not of RAM. (high confidence) Dirty ratio is dirty bytes divided by the configured maximum cache bytes, not by bytes currently in the cache. mongod's cache-pressure monitor computes cacheBytesDirty / cacheBytesMax and compares it with the dirty trigger, falling back to 0.20 when no explicit trigger is set. Netdata gives the same formula over serverStatus fields wiredTiger.cache['tracked dirty bytes in the cache'] and ['maximum bytes configured']. WiredTiger documents the thresholds as percentages of cache size. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Lowering eviction_dirty_target and eviction_dirty_trigger makes background eviction start earlier and caps the dirty data each checkpoint must flush, at the price of more eviction I/O and CPU (block compression) and earlier throttling of application threads. In 2016 WT-2735 stated that WiredTiger checkpoints work best when there is not too much dirty data in cache and proposed setting eviction_dirty_trigger automatically to bound checkpoint time; it was closed as a duplicate of WT-2666. (medium confidence) Every eviction target must stay lower than its trigger. The WiredTiger 3.0.0 tuning page example eviction_trigger=90,eviction_dirty_target=75 sets a dirty target far above the default dirty trigger of 20, which breaks that rule; the 12.0.0 page fixes the example by adding eviction_dirty_trigger=90. (high confidence) The WiredTiger 12.0.0 reference lists further eviction controls: eviction=(app_eviction_min_cache_fill_ratio) (0 to 50, default 0) delays application-thread eviction until a minimum cache fill; eviction=(cache_tolerance_for_app_eviction) (0 to 100, default 0, in steps of 10) loosens the dirty and updates triggers; eviction=(incremental_app_eviction) (default false) lets only some application threads evict; and eviction_checkpoint_target (default 1) evicts dirty content at the start of each checkpoint down to that level. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) In MongoDB's master branch, WiredTigerCachePressureMonitor reports cache pressure only when both checks pass: application cache-wait time e

items.text: WiredTiger Storage Engine Internals WiredTiger has been MongoDB's default storage engine since 3.2 (replacing MMAPv1). It is a B-tree backed, MVCC, copy-on-write engine with document-level concurrency, configurable in-memory cache, bloc WiredTiger has been MongoDB's default storage engine since 3.2 (replacing MMAPv1). It is a B-tree backed, MVCC, copy-on-write engine with document-level concurrency, configurable in-memory cache, block-level compression, and a write-ahead journal. Everything below the document model - durability, concurrency, compression, eviction, checkpoints - is WiredTiger. This skill is the deep internals reference. For surface-level performance triage, see mongodb-performance-troubleshooting. For diagnostic packaging, see atlas-diagnostics-expert. WiredTiger has a hybrid architecture optimized for multi-core CPUs and large memory: In-memory cache - uncompressed B-tree pages. Working set lives here. Default size: max(0.5 × (RAM − 1 GiB), 256 MiB). Block manager - translates pages to/from disk, owns checksums, compression, encryption, free-list. OS filesystem cache - holds compressed data blocks. Often roughly the same size as the WT cache (uncompressed) because of compression ratios. mongod exposes WiredTiger via a single WT_CONNECTION (per-process), holding one WT_CACHE struct and N WT_SESSION objects for application threads. The cache size formula (since 3.4): max(0.5 × (RAM − 1 GiB), 256 MiB), capped at 10 000 GiB. Override with one of (mutually exclusive): Or at the command line: --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 32 / --wiredTigerCacheSizePct 60. Containers and cgroups: WT's default sizing was historically based on host RAM. Always pin cacheSizeGB explicitly when running in a container with a memory limit, or you will OOM. Newer MongoDB versions detect cgroup limits in some configurations, but pinning is still safest. Sizing rule of thumb (dedicated host): target ~50% of RAM for the WT cache and leave the rest for the OS filesystem cache plus mongod overhead (connections, plan cache, TCMalloc fragmentation). On shared hosts or multi-mongod deployments, reduce proportionally per instance. <channel|>`. Issue 587 (opened 2026-04-09) gives the Gemma 4 thinking format as `<|channel>thought
...<channel|>` with `<|channel>` token ID 100 and `<channel|>` token ID 101, and says `enable_thinking=False` makes the template pre-close an empty channel `<|channel>thought
<channel|>`. Issue 587 argues that without a structural tag, grammar-constrained decoding and thinking are mutually exclusive for Gemma 4: constraints from the start break thinking tokens, and disabling thinking loses reasoning. PR 588 (merged 2026-04-13, commit 2f4a0c5) registered `gemma4` and describes the format as optional thinking, optional content, `<|tool_call>call:name{json}<tool_call|>` calls and optional `<turn|>`. PR 609 removed `force_empty_reasoning`, renamed model keys (`qwen` to `qwen_3`, `qwen_coder` to `qwen_3_coder`, `glm47` to `glm_4_7`, `gemma4` to `gemma_4`) and added a `qwen_3_5` key for Qwen3.5 and 3.6 XML tool calls with an empty reasoning part. Under PR 609 `reasoning=False` forces an empty reasoning block for kimi and qwen_3_5, omits the reasoning section for llama, qwen_3_coder, deepseek_r1, deepseek_v3_2, deepseek_v4, glm_4_7, gemma_4 and minimax, strips the `<think>` prefix for qwen_3, and omits the analysis channel for harmony. PR 609's review notes that renaming model keys is a breaking change and suggests aliases for backward compatibility. PR 923 says the `gemma_4` builtin "has been unregistered with a 'we will support it later' TODO since #609". PR 923 adds a `"gemma"` JSON-schema style that emits unquoted object keys and strings delimited by the single `<|"|>` token with no escape sequences at every nesting level, and re-enables `gemma_4` with auto, required and forced tool choice, the `<|channel>thought` reasoning prefix and `parallel_tool_calls`. PR 923 continues PR 684 (by iwanhae), which was closed unmerged after the converter was rewritten to build grammar trees directly (PR 745), and says engines fall back to unconstrained decoding for Gemma 4 tool calls because earlier converters cannot express `<|"|>`-delimited strings. items.concept: XNU vm_per_task_user_wire_limit and global wire sysctl defaults on Apple silicon
items.summary: The defaults are computed once at boot in kmem_init by kmem_set_user_wire_limits. The per-task limit is set equal to the global limit.
items.text: XNU vm_per_task_user_wire_limit and global wire sysctl defaults on Apple silicon The defaults are computed once at boot in kmem_init by kmem_set_user_wire_limits. The per-task limit is set equal to the global limit. The defaults are computed once at boot in kmem_init by kmem_set_user_wire_limits. The per-task limit is set equal to the global limit. The global limit is a percentage of physical RAM taken from a table indexed by floor(log2(RAM)) minus 32, clamped to the table's 10 entries. On macOS (no CONFIG_JETSAM, inferred) the table is 70, 73, 76, 79, 82, 85, 88, 91, 94, 97 percent; with CONFIG_JETSAM it is 80, 80, 80, 80, 82, 85, 88, 91, 94, 97. The unlockable remainder is capped: if RAM minus the limit exceeds 32 GiB (VM_NOT_USER_WIREABLE_MAX), the limit becomes RAM minus 32 GiB. With the boot-arg serverperfmode set and RAM of 32 GiB or more the limit is 95% of RAM. On macOS the RAM figure used is max_mem_actual (installed memory), not the post-carve-out usable amount. vm.global_no_user_wire_amount holds no state: reads return RAM minus the global limit and writes (rejected with EINVAL if larger than RAM) set the global limit to RAM minus the written value. This is why llama.cpp's hint tells users to lower it. The limit counts all wired memory system-wide (kernel, GPU, other processes), so the room actually left for mlock is the limit minus current vm_page_wire_count (existing dossier). A 512 GiB machine gets exactly RAM minus 32 GiB; machines above 256 GiB are limited by the 32 GiB cap and not the table. Raising vm.user_wire_limit alone does nothing if vm.global_user_wire_limit is lower, and the reverse holds, because the check ANDs both. The per-task default is not lower than the global default, so a single process can take the whole global budget on a stock Mac. Kernel callers that gate on wire budget (mach_vm_wire_level_monitor) use the same global limit. Community guidance reports the GPU default as roughly 2/3 of RAM up to 32 GB and 3/4 from 36 GB (apple-silicon-unified-memory-and-llm-sizing.md). The mlock default computed here is higher at every size (for example 76% versus 67% at 16 GB, 79% versus 75% at 36 GB). The two limits govern different operations and are not alternatives. Real `sysctl vm.global_user_wire_limit` readings on Apple-silicon Macs to confirm the computed table. items.concept: Zipfian hot-row cache tier for n-gram tables (DRAM over NVMe)
items.summary: ds4 opens its Engram table with F_NOCACHE and F_RDAHEAD 0 on Apple platforms and documents the table descriptor as "never an mmap or Metal model view".
items.text: Zipfian hot-row cache tier for n-gram tables (DRAM over NVMe) ds4 opens its Engram table with F_NOCACHE and F_RDAHEAD 0 on Apple platforms and documents the table descriptor as "never an mmap or Metal model view". ds4 opens its Engram table with F_NOCACHE and F_RDAHEAD 0 on Apple platforms and documents the table descriptor as "never an mmap or Metal model view". ds4's batch reader carries the comment "Fixed concurrency hides random-read latency without caching the table." `ds4_engram_read_batch` processes at most 2,048 tokens per round, builds row requests, sorts them by row id with qsort, and gives consecutive duplicates a memcpy of the previous row instead of a second read. ds4 uses 16 readers (`ENGRAM_READERS`) through `dispatch_apply_f` on the user-initiated global queue on Apple platforms, with a parallel threshold of 8 rows; on other platforms the threshold is 256 rows. ds4's header states temporary storage for a batch read is bounded to 384 KiB independent of table and prefix size. ds4's Qwen n-gram reader sorts requests by row id and reads at most 4,096 rows per round with up to 16 readers on Apple platforms. No cache, LRU, frequency or hot-row structure for Engram or n-gram rows appears in ds4's `ds4.c`, `ds4_engram.c` or `ds4_engram.h` at the 2026-10-04 snapshot. The paper says natural-language N-grams follow a Zipfian distribution and that this motivates a multi-level cache with hot embeddings in HBM or host DRAM and the long tail on NVMe. llama.cpp PR 27794 reads lazily marked tensors through the mmap with prefetch skipped and relies on the page cache, with no row-level cache. A downstream fork's measurement says the lazy-read win depends on the table not fitting in page cache, and that where it fits the benefit is far smaller. With ds4's 264-byte rows, a 1 GiB cache of stored rows holds about 4.07 million rows, about 0.53% of the roughly 768 million V4.1 rows. Decoded rows are 256 FP32 values (1,024 bytes) against 264 stored bytes, so caching stored bytes is about 3.9 times denser. A frequency cache would have to live above ds4's F_NOCACHE descriptor, since F_NOCACHE reads never enter the unified buffer cache. No source found measures the Zipf exponent, hit rate or row-reuse distance for any shipped Engram or n-gram table.
